payload.description:
Field incident shipping basicly-yzyd.1: running 'basicly loop advance' with cwd inside a loop worktree (not the base checkout) made the merge fail ('merge must run from the base checkout ... currently on harness/<name>') yet the ship-checkpoint approval and teardown still proceeded, leaving the child CLOSED but UNMERGED with its commit stranded on the harness branch. The engine should detect it is running from a linked worktree (or that 'main' is not the checked-out base) and refuse the merge/ship transition with a clear error, instead of approving-and-stranding. Also: worktree cleanup --force did not remove the orphaned .git/basicly-worktrees/<name>.json session record once the branch was already deleted, and that stale record counts toward the worktree concurrency cap. Recovery used: git rebase main harness/<name> + git merge --ff-only + git branch -d + rm the stale session json.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Provision a leaf worktree via the loop and cd into it (the linked worktree)
2. From inside the worktree, run 'basicly loop advance <id>' at the build or ship phase
3. Observe the merge fail on base-checkout assertion while ship approval/teardown still closes the bead, stranding the commit on harness/<name>

## Acceptance Criteria

* loop advance refuses the build and ship transitions when run from a linked worktree (git-dir != git-common-dir), returning a graceful blocked result that names the base checkout and mutates no tracker/worktree state
* worktree cleanup drops the session record when the branch is already gone, so no orphaned .json counts toward the concurrency cap
* regression tests cover the linked-worktree refusal and the already-deleted-branch cleanup
payload.title: loop advance from a linked worktree should refuse the merge/ship transition

payload.acceptance_criteria: Given a harness worktree whose hook source differs from the base checkout it was branched from when the landing verify runs the projection hooks check then the check does not report the change itself as drift and the landing proceeds, and given a consumer repo whose materialised hooks genuinely differ from the installed catalog then it still fails, and the failure message no longer advises a command that would revert the change when run in a worktree, with tests
payload.description:
## Context

Found 2026-07-31 while landing basicly-m0p1, which edits `.basicly/core/hooks/tool-usage.py`. The
build->verify landing failed with `projection-hooks`:

    Stale hook projection detected. Run `basicly hooks-build` to sync hooks.
      .basicly/core/hooks/tool-usage.py: differs from catalog

The projection was not stale. `hooks.check_hooks` compares `_catalog_hooks_dir()` - the hooks
directory of the **installed** basicly package - against `repo_root / core_hooks_dir`, and skips the
comparison entirely when the two resolve to the same path. In this repo basicly is installed editable
from the base checkout, so `_catalog_hooks_dir()` resolves to
`<base>/.basicly/core/hooks`. The loop's landing verify runs with `repo_root` set to the **lane's
worktree**. So the check compares the pre-merge BASE copy against the post-change WORKTREE copy and
reports a difference that is the change itself.

Measured: base copy md5 `97d34d0e...`, worktree copy md5 `389ad855...`, and calling
`check_hooks(<worktree>, Path(".basicly/core/hooks"))` from the base interpreter reproduces the single
mismatch exactly.

Consequence: **any change to a hook script is unlandable through the loop.** It is not "landed by its
own pre-merge version" (the documented `merge.py`/`loop.py`/`verify.py` trap) - it structurally cannot
pass, and it consumes the rework budget on each attempt (observed at 1/2 after one try).

**The dangerous part, and the reason this is P1 rather than an annoyance:** the failure message tells
the operator to run `basicly hooks-build`. In a worktree that copies the base's OLD script over the
new one, silently reverting the work while turning the gate green. An agent following the message
faithfully destroys the change and reports success.

Note the check is only meaningful for a CONSUMER repo, where `.basicly/core/` is materialised from the
wheel and can genuinely drift. In the dev repo `src` and `dst` are the same directory, so the content
comparison is skipped and the gate has no signal to give - which is why it passes from base and fails
only from a worktree.

## Steps to Reproduce

- Provision a worktree for any bead and edit any file under `.basicly/core/hooks/`.
- Commit it on the harness branch, then run `basicly loop run <id> --root <id>` from base.
- Observed: `projection-hooks` fails naming the edited script as differing from catalog, the merge is
  rolled back, and rework increments. Expected: the check compares like with like - or is skipped -
  when the repo under verification is a linked worktree of the checkout the package is installed from.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a harness worktree whose hook source differs from the base checkout it was branched from when
  the landing verify runs the projection-hooks check then the check does not report the change itself
  as drift and the landing proceeds, and given a consumer repo whose materialised hooks genuinely
  differ from the installed catalog then it still fails, and the failure message no longer advises a
  command that would revert the change when run in a worktree, with tests
payload.title: A hook script change cannot pass the landing verify from a worktree

payload.close_reason: Two defects, both shipped: the wait-meter tolerance now comes from a monotonic clock (177109f), and pytest workers are capped at 4 so br's machine-global write lock stops timing out (dea43cf). The br-backed integration files went from 10 errors in 3m47s under -n auto to 33 passed in 2m26s. Push landed: 52c1893..dea43cf.
payload.description:
tests/test_integration_wait.py asserted 'waited_s <= _WAITED_S + _SLACK_S' with _SLACK_S=5. The fixture pins policy._now to time.time()+600, so the recorded interval is 600 plus however long the two real br round-trips take. The upper bound therefore budgeted five seconds for two subprocess invocations.

On a loaded full-suite run (15m37s wall) they took nine, producing 'assert 609 <= (600 + 5)' and failing the pre-push gate for a defect that did not exist. Three test_integration_dor_scaffold setup errors in the same run were xdist contention, not real - that file passes 15/15 in 40s on its own.

Fixed by taking the overhead from time.monotonic() around the two calls and allowing it explicitly, per .claude/rules/platform-hermetic-tests.md ('wait for the condition, never for a duration'). The bound keeps its power: with ~1s elapsed the ceiling is ~606s, so a mis-zoned stamp hours off still fails.

Found while pinning br to 0.2.16 (basicly-o7z5); unrelated to that change.
payload.title: wait-meter tests budgeted 5s for two real br calls, so a loaded machine fails the push

payload.description:
## Context

Plan §4 Phase 4 step 1. Depends on 1a for its urgency.

Audit every baseline line against three questions:
- is this really a hook - can a git hook or a verify check enforce it instead of asking;
- can I write a glob for it - does it belong in the path-scoped tier rather than always-on;
- does it change behaviour versus the default at all.

Expect all three to fire. The third is the no-op test and the plan calls it the single most common defect in an always-on layer: a rule that restates what the model would do anyway costs context on every turn and delivers nothing.

Measured starting point 2026-07-26 at c175c1a: 7014/7209/7343 chars across AGENTS.md, .claude/CLAUDE.md and .github/copilot-instructions.md, about 1070 words each.

payload.description:
## Context

Found 2026-07-30 by applying oh-my-openagent's forbidden-token gate idea to our own projected output
(`reference-repos/_analysis/oh-my-openagent.md`).

`.github/copilot-instructions.md:9` and `AGENTS.md:9` both carry:

> Force-push, history rewrite, destructive resets, `rm -rf`, and `.env*` reads/writes - hard-denied
> in `.claude/settings.json` for Claude Code; this rule covers other agents, so treat a blocked
> command as the answer.

`CLAUDE.md` does **not** carry it, so per-target variation already exists and is deliberate: the
Claude file omits the sentence because for Claude the deny-list is the actual mechanism rather than
something to describe.

The inverse is the defect. Copilot and any `AGENTS.md` reader are told about a file they will never
read and a mechanism that does not apply to them, then told the rule covers them anyway. The
author clearly considered it - the "this rule covers other agents" clause is there on purpose - so
this is imprecise wording rather than an oversight, and it is mild.

**Stated at its real size:** this is not a secrets leak and nothing sensitive is disclosed;
`.claude/settings.json` is a committed file. The cost is a sentence of always-on baseline spent
telling an agent about another agent's enforcement, in a baseline already measured at cap
(`always-on-baseline-at-cap`). The fix is to state the rule in terms of the reader - a blocked
command is the answer - and let the Claude target alone carry the mechanism.

Worth generalising while in there: whether any other fragment names one target's mechanism inside
another target's output. A cheap catalog-lint rule could check that a fragment body rendered into
target X does not reference target Y's config path, which is the transferable half of the
forbidden-token idea.

## Acceptance Criteria

payload.description:
## Context

Retro finding from the 2026-07-30 session, approved by the owner and filed rather than self-applied
per the repo's retro rule. **Three distinct failures in one session share one root cause: reviewing an
external project without discipline.** All three reached committed files before being corrected.

1. **A README is a claim; the binary is the evidence.** I wrote into
   `docs/research/2026-07-26-sota-review.md` §2.11 that gastown ships a Bors-style merge queue that
   bisects to isolate a failing MR, and recommended building the same - from a fetched README summary.
   It is dead code: `AssembleBatch`/`ProcessBatch` have no call sites outside tests, the config field
   that enables them is never read, and the Go merge engine cannot be entered because its foreground
   mode hard-errors as deprecated while the real component is an agent working the queue sequentially.
   The corrected conclusion **inverted** the original.
2. **Read the licence before writing the adopt finding, not after.** In the same commit I wrote the
   warning that "deriving an implementation from a quoted snippet requires reading that project's
   LICENSE first" and then recommended porting ~400 lines from two repos whose licences had not been
   read. Both were restricted, and in **both cases the LICENSE file alone would have cleared them** -
   one hid a non-commercial Sustainable Use License with a per-subdirectory gap, the other put
   competition restrictions in `NOTICE.md`. That is three restricted repos in this reference set now.
3. **Correlation is not causation, and synthesis is where they get confused.** I wrote that every
   project adopting declarative phases traded away determinism, implying cause. Both failures were
   independent design errors in projects that also happened to be configurable. The decision to reject
   still held, on a different and better argument.

## The rules to record

- Before recommending adoption of a third-party feature, find its call sites; a symbol with no
  non-test caller does not ship, and neither does one behind a config flag nobody reads. Cite
  `file:line`, never a README line.
- Read every licence-bearing file including `NOTICE`, and check per-directory licences before assuming
  a monorepo is uniform - **before** writing adopt findings.
- A licence restricts copying expression, not learning a fact: measurements and concepts survive a
  restriction, implementations do not. That boundary is what keeps a competitive review usable.
- When a pattern appears across independent sources, state whether the mechanism is established or
  only the correlation.

## The open decision this bead must make, not assume

**Where these live is deliberately unsettled.** The obvious answer is a new on-demand skill
(`external-review` or similar), which costs nothing always-on - and the always-on baseline is at cap,
so that matters. But adding a 28th catalog skill is the wrong reflex right now: 27 existing skills have
never been invoked, and whether skills route at all is `basicly-m4zv.2`'s open question. Weigh at least
these before authoring anything:

- a new on-demand skill - zero always-on cost, but grows a catalog whose routing is unmeasured;
- a section in an existing skill - `catalog-authoring` is the closest fit and is already always-on for
  Copilot by a recorded decision;
- the **path-scoped rules tier**, which is built and almost unused, if a path predicate can express
  "editing a research or design document";
- prose in `docs/research/references.md` §2 only, accepting that a rule not in the catalog does not
  reach an agent that has not read that file.

Do not add always-on baseline text for this without measuring the delta - the tier exists precisely so
this class of conditional guidance costs nothing when it does not apply.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given the four external-review rules when their home has been chosen and justified against the always-on baseline cost then they are authored in that home, projected, and an agent reviewing a third-party repository is told to verify call sites and read licences before writing an adopt finding
payload.title: Record the external-review rules that three committed errors would have prevented

Known cost accepted: codex inlines scoped fragments so AGENTS.md grows (8484 of 12000 today); measure and record the delta per this bead's AC. A new skill was rejected because 27 skills have never routed and routing is unmeasured until basicly-m4zv.2.

payload.description:
## Context

Retro finding from the 2026-07-30 session, approved by the owner and filed rather than self-applied.
An environment trap, so it earns exactly one bullet: the trap plus its avoidance.

**The incident.** Removing seventeen deferred blocking edges from the release epic, I wrote:

```sh
DEFER="basicly-jr0l.35 basicly-jr0l.40 ..."
for d in $DEFER; do uv run br dep remove basicly-m3od "$d"; done
```

In bash that iterates seventeen times. **This repo's shell is zsh, which does not word-split an
unquoted parameter expansion**, so the loop ran once with all seventeen ids as a single argument. The
command failed, and the failure was quiet in the way that matters: the loop printed one line, the
summary said `removed 0`, and only a separate re-count of the edges revealed nothing had happened. Had
I trusted the exit status or the absence of an error, the release scope would silently still be blocked
by seventeen beads.

**The avoidance**: write the list inline in the `for` header, or use an array (`arr=(a b c)` then
`for d in "${arr[@]}"`), or pipe through `xargs -n1`. Never iterate an unquoted scalar and assume
splitting.

**Why this is worth a catalog bullet rather than a note.** `non-interactive-shell.fragment.yaml`
already owns exactly this class - it exists because some shells alias `cp`/`mv`/`rm` to interactive
mode - and the fragment's own framing is "prefer cross-platform implementations over shell-specific
behavior when a choice exists". Word-splitting is the same shape: a construct that is correct in one
shell and silently wrong in another, on a repo that targets Windows, Linux and macOS and whose own
hooks run under whatever shell the host provides.

It also compounds with an existing recorded trap - `uv run` inside a shell for-loop returning empty
output, which already made a per-item audit report "all clean" falsely
(`batch-queries-over-cli-loops`). Both failures are the same lesson from different directions: a
shell loop over a list is where a silent no-op hides, so prefer one batch invocation and verify the
count changed.

**Cost check before authoring.** This fragment is always-on and the baseline is at cap, so keep it to
one bullet and measure the delta rather than adding a paragraph.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given the non-interactive-shell guidance when it is read after this change then it warns that an unquoted parameter expansion does not word-split in every shell, names the array or inline-list avoidance, and the always-on baseline delta is measured and recorded
payload.title: Warn that an unquoted list does not word-split in every shell

payload.description:
Found shipping basicly-ajq. loop._build_children fan-in merges every child worktree via merge.merge_queue once all children are closed — but a child driven through its own loop (the flow the harness-loop skill documents: advance lands the worktree, ship tears it down and closes) leaves no worktree behind, so the parent's advance fails with "no worktree session named '<child>'" and the feature can never advance past build. Workaround used: record the parent verify gate directly (basicly verify --mode full --issue <id>), then approve ship and loop run.

Two coherent fixes; pick one and align the harness-loop skill with it:
(a) parent skips children whose branches are already merged (self-landing stays the documented child flow), or
(b) children stop self-landing (their loop ends at 'work committed'; the parent owns the merge queue) and the skill/docs change accordingly.

Chosen: (a) — in loop._build_children, filter merge-queue items to children with a live worktree session (worktree.list_sessions()); self-landed torn-down children count as already landed and are mentioned in the detail message.

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Create a feature issue with two child tasks (br create --parent).
2. Drive each child through its own full loop: advance provisions its worktree, build/verify pass, advance lands the worktree, ship tears it down and closes the child.
3. With all children closed and no child worktree sessions remaining, run `basicly loop advance <parent>` to trigger the build fan-in.
4. Observed: SystemExit "no worktree session named '<child>'" from merge.merge_queue; the feature can never advance past build. Expected: fan-in treats the self-landed children as already merged and advances build -> verify.

## Acceptance Criteria
- A feature whose children each landed and closed through their own loop advances build -> verify without manual gate recording
- merge_queue (or its caller) treats an already-merged, torn-down child as satisfied rather than an error
- A regression test covers the children-self-landed path
- The harness-loop skill's phase table matches the implemented flow
payload.title: loop: feature fan-in merge collides with child self-landing

payload.description:
## Context

Filed 2026-07-31 after basicly-kjc5.58 landed. **Re-scoped the same day by the owner, who was right and
the first framing was wrong**: this is NOT claude-only. GitHub Copilot custom agents carry a per-agent
`model` field too, so at least claude AND copilot must be supported. Re-verified against live
authoritative docs rather than recall.

basicly-kjc5.59 is the resolution seam but its scope is `runner.py`/`run_record.py`/`config.py` - the
HEADLESS runner dispatch path, where a model is set by `_apply_model` via a `--model` flag or a
`{model}` placeholder. A natively spawned subagent never goes through that path: the host reads a
per-agent file and takes the model from frontmatter. basicly-kjc5.58 removed that line for every
family, so a declared tier is currently decorative for every natively spawned agent.

Concrete regression from kjc5.58, deliberate and known: the shipped `test-runner` declared
`model: haiku`, now declares `tier: low`, and `.claude/agents/test-runner.md` carries no model line, so
an agent whose own prose says "cheap and fast on purpose" inherits the session model on every spawn.
Verified: `rg '^model' .claude/agents/` matches nothing.

kjc5.58 was still right - the defect was a NON-PORTABLE value in a family-agnostic source. The fix is
to emit the resolved per-surface spelling, which is what basicly-kjc5.61's map must provide.

## Verified facts (live docs, 2026-07-31)

- **Claude Code** reads `.claude/agents/<slug>.md`; `model` takes a hyphenated id (`claude-haiku-4-5`)
  or a short alias (`haiku`), or `inherit`.
- **GitHub Copilot** custom agents live at `.github/agents/<name>.agent.md` (org/enterprise: root
  `agents/`). Frontmatter: `description` (required), `name`, `target` (`vscode`|`github-copilot`),
  `tools`, `model`, `disable-model-invocation`, `user-invocable`, `mcp-servers`, `metadata`; body
  capped at 30000 chars, which `agents.MAX_BODY_CHARS` already matches.
- **Copilot's `model` value is a DISPLAY NAME**, not an id - `Claude Opus 4.5`, `Claude Sonnet 4` -
  and it accepts **a single string OR a prioritized array** tried in order
  (`model: ['Claude Opus 4.5', 'GPT-5.2']`). Our schema cannot express an ordered fallback list today.
- **VS Code reads BOTH** `.github/agents` and `.claude/agents` ("VS Code also detects `.md` files in the
  `.claude/agents` folder, following the Claude sub-agents format"). So basicly-ajq's rationale holds
  for VS Code but NOT for the Copilot cloud agent or Copilot CLI, which do not read `.claude/agents`.
- Copilot `tools` names differ from Claude's and are inconsistent across sources
  (`["read","search","edit"]` in the VS Code doc vs `codebase`/`terminal`/`edit`/`github` elsewhere), so
  a copilot projection needs a pinned tool-name mapping, not a copy.

## Prerequisite

The copilot half has no target file today: basicly still projects to `.claude/agents` only. Reopening
that is filed separately and must land first for the copilot half. The claude half is unblocked once
kjc5.61 lands.

## Open design decision for the owner

Per surface, either resolve the tier to that surface's own spelling and emit it, or emit nothing and
record that the tier was not honoured (the stance kjc5.59 already takes where a family has no slot).
Recommendation: resolve and emit wherever the surface has a model slot, because that is the only case
in which the tier vocabulary changes real behaviour instead of documenting an intention.

Scope: `src/basicly/agents.py`, `.claude/agents/`, `tests/test_agents.py`.
payload.title: Resolve a declared tier into each projected agent surface that has a model slot

payload.text: DYNAMIC INJECTION IS POSSIBLE ON CLAUDE CODE - PROVEN BY EXPERIMENT 2026-07-31. The owner asked whether the model could be left out of the projected file and injected before the host reads it, rather than baked in at build time. Answer: YES for claude code, via a PreToolUse hook on the Agent tool. Three probes, each isolated with 'claude --settings <file>' so no live config was modified: (1) returning updatedInput {model: haiku} alone FAILED - the call lost its required fields; (2) returning updatedInput {description: ...} alone also FAILED with 'required parameter prompt is missing'. So on the Agent tool updatedInput REPLACES tool_input rather than merging, which CONTRADICTS the documented behaviour 'Object with fields to merge into tool_input ... Fields not present in updatedInput are left unchanged'. Worth knowing: that doc statement is false for this tool. (3) The working pattern - copy the whole tool_input dict, add model, return the lot - SUCCEEDED. Proof it took effect: the probe agent's frontmatter declared model: opus, the hook injected haiku, and the subagent's own transcript under projects/<proj>/<session>/subagents/agent-*.jsonl carries 22 messages all with model claude-haiku-4-5-20251001, with ZERO occurrences of opus in any transcript of the run. The frontmatter was overridden. This is consistent with the documented resolution order, where the per-invocation model parameter (2) outranks the definition's frontmatter (3). Observed Agent tool_input keys: description, prompt, subagent_type, run_in_background - note model is ABSENT unless the caller sets it, which is why it must be added rather than rewritten. Robustness note: because the hook copies the input dict wholesale it forwards unknown and future fields verbatim, so a new required field upstream does not break it. CONSEQUENCE FOR THIS BEAD: there are now two viable mechanisms, not one. Static emission at agents-build time (this bead as originally scoped) OR a hook that resolves tier to model at spawn time from the committed map, leaving the projected file model-free. The hook variant is strictly more portable - a foreign harness needs only the map plus a ~15 line hook and no basicly code at all, which is the owner's stated plug-and-play goal - but it adds a process to the spawn path and is claude-code-specific as verified. The copilot equivalent is NOT yet verified: copilot custom agents and copilot CLI both document a hooks field (Preview) and that needs its own probe before any claim. Do not assume symmetry.

COPILOT CLI HOOK INJECTION DOES NOT WORK TODAY - tested 2026-07-31 at the owner's request. Copilot DOES document the capability: the hooks reference gives preToolUse an output schema of permissionDecision (allow|deny|ask), permissionDecisionReason, and modifiedArgs described as 'tool arguments to use instead of the originals' - i.e. argument substitution is specified. Documented CLI config locations: repo-level .github/hooks/NAME.json, user-level ~/.copilot/hooks/ (or COPILOT_HOME), plus policy.d and inline settings. BUT on the installed CLI the hook never fires. Three probes from a scratch repo containing .github/hooks/tierprobe.json with a preToolUse command hook that logged every payload and returned allow: (1) delegating to a custom agent - hook did not fire; (2) a plain shell tool with --allow-all-tools - did not fire; (3) the same shell tool WITHOUT --allow-all-tools, to rule out the permission pipeline being bypassed - did not fire. Zero payloads captured in any run, so this is not about which tool is intercepted; the repo-level hook config is simply not being loaded or run. Note 'hook' does not appear anywhere in copilot --help, and experimental was already true in settings. LIKELY EXPLANATION, not yet confirmed: the modifiedArgs capability is documented under the copilot-SDK hooks path (/copilot/how-tos/copilot-sdk/hooks/pre-tool-use), so it may be an SDK-only feature rather than a CLI one. Do not assume the CLI will grow it. VERSION DRIFT WORTH KNOWING: the binary reported 1.0.75 earlier in the same session and 1.0.77 by the end - it self-updates, so a pinned version in prose rots by itself and per-run adapter_version capture (which the runner already does) is the right design. WHAT DOES WORK ON COPILOT: static frontmatter. Verified twice - the /agent listing validated a declared model value, and a custom agent declaring NO model printed 'Tierprobe(claude-opus-5)' in the CLI transcript, i.e. it inherited the session model. Also note copilot prints the resolved model in its delegation line, which is a free observation channel for verifying any future mechanism. CONSEQUENCE: for a first version the mechanism is necessarily HYBRID - claude gets dynamic hook injection (proven working), copilot gets static frontmatter emission (proven working) plus session-level control via copilot --model for harness-launched sessions. That is not the uniform design the owner would prefer but it is what the two hosts actually support today.

CORRECTION - COPILOT HOOK INJECTION DOES WORK. The earlier comment on this bead concluded copilot CLI hooks never fire. That was WRONG, and the cause was the config LOCATION, not the capability. Repo-level .github/hooks/hooks.json is NOT loaded by copilot CLI 1.0.77 (retested with the canonical filename, with inline bash instead of a script path, and inside a real git repo - sessionStart did not fire either, so it was not about tool matching). User-level ~/.copilot/hooks/hooks.json IS loaded and fires. Also retracted: I claimed the CLI binary contains no hook identifiers based on a strings scan. That evidence was worthless - a control check showed strings I had directly observed the CLI emitting (allow-all-tools, premiumRequests, modelMetrics) also return zero matches, because the JS payload is a compressed bundle. The conclusion rests on behaviour only. PROVEN END TO END on copilot: the agent-spawn tool is named 'task' with args agent_type, description, mode, name, prompt - and NO model key, so model must be ADDED not rewritten, same as claude. A preToolUse hook matching toolName 'task' that returns modifiedArgs containing all original args PLUS model ran a custom agent declaring NO model on the injected model: the CLI delegation line printed Tierprobe(claude-haiku-4.5) where the session model was claude-opus-5. Copilot prints the resolved model in that line, which is a free verification channel. PER-HOST DIFFERENCES to encode: hook event PreToolUse vs preToolUse; tool name Agent vs task; rewrite field updatedInput vs modifiedArgs; payload tool_input as an OBJECT vs toolArgs as a JSON STRING that must be parsed first; model spelling claude-haiku-4-5 or the alias haiku vs the dotted claude-haiku-4.5; observation channel the subagent transcript vs the printed delegation line. Both REPLACE rather than merge, so both hooks must echo the full argument set back. IMPORTANT DESIGN CONSTRAINT for basicly-wbsz: because copilot only honours the hook at USER level, it applies to every repo on the machine. So the hook cannot assume a map is present - it must resolve against the current working directory and NO-OP silently, leaving the call untouched, whenever the cwd has no committed map. It also cannot be delivered by repo projection the way our other artifacts are; it needs a per-machine install step.

Committed 233419e. Unblocks basicly-ihs.

## Problem

The quality-gates commit-messages job feeds only the commit SUBJECT (git log %s) to beads-commit-msg.py, but the repo convention puts the beads issue id as a trailing BODY line (and dotted child ids like basicly-onb.6.2 cannot appear in the subject per the conventional-commits rules). So every commit with the id in the body fails CI with 'Missing/unknown beads issue id', even though the local commit-msg hooks (which see the full message) pass.

## Acceptance Criteria

- CI validates the full commit message (subject + body), matching the local commit-msg hooks
- A commit with the beads id in a trailing body line passes the CI commit-messages gate
- The previously-failing commit 5b5f3e9 passes under the fixed check

payload.description:
§9/§11.8: let a consumer choose a subset of the catalog at install time. Design settled 2026-07-16 (see comment): technology scoping — sources carry an optional `technologies:` list (absent = universal, always ships); install records the repo's selection in `basicly.toml` (default: all); projection commands filter unselected sources and the manifest sweep removes outputs a narrowed selection excludes; core sync stays full. Tag vocabulary is a controlled list enforced by catalog-lint. v2 (out of scope): per-block technology conditioning inside agent slots.

## Acceptance Criteria
- Catalog sources (skills, fragments, agents-fragments, hooks) accept an optional `technologies:` list; a source without it is universal and always projected
- catalog-lint rejects a `technologies:` value outside the controlled vocabulary (stack tags like python/go plus environment tools like zsh/tmux/starship/wezterm)
- `basicly install` accepts a technology-selection flag and records the selection in `basicly.toml`; omitting it selects everything (current behavior unchanged)
- `basicly build` / `skills-build` / `agents-build` / `hooks-build` skip sources whose `technologies:` has no overlap with the recorded selection; core sync still copies the full catalog
- Narrowing the selection then rebuilding sweeps the now-excluded projections via the manifest (no stale outputs left)
- A repo with no selection recorded in `basicly.toml` projects the full catalog (backward compatible)
- Regression tests cover: universal source always ships, tagged source filtered out, selection recorded/read from basicly.toml, sweep after narrowing, lint rejection of unknown tags
- docs/architecture.md documents the property, the selection, and the filtering point
payload.title: Catalog selection / flavors (install fragments+hooks but not skills)

payload.text: Design settled with the user (2026-07-16), superseding the kind-level framing: technology scoping. Sources (skills, fragments, agents, hooks) get an optional 'technologies: [go, java, python, ...]' property; absent means universal and always ships. Install flag records the repo's selection in basicly.toml (default: all); build/skills-build/agents-build/hooks-build filter unselected sources at projection time (core sync stays full for provenance-simple upgrades), and the manifest sweeps projections a narrowed selection excludes. Tag vocabulary is a controlled list enforced by catalog-lint; environment tools (zsh, tmux, starship, wezterm) use the same mechanism as stack tags. v2 (explicitly out of v1 scope): per-block technology conditioning inside agent slots. Agreed motivation: a non-Python consumer should not receive tool-uv et al.; see the verification discussion on 2026-07-16 (core fragments/agents are already stack-clean, the skills pack is the residual). Priority recommendation recorded: 2f4 -> a3d -> aff -> v0.1.3 + consumer refresh -> 7ca.

Vision: agent files become generated artifacts composed by the projector from an essential-blocks taxonomy (candidate blocks: security, planning, git, orchestration, conventions, documentation, hygiene, hardening, enforcement, verify, validate, authorize, authenticate, context, work tracking, work scoping, review, gates). Core blocks are owned by basicly devs; consumers extend or override specific blocks with custom building blocks via the .basicly-local overlay — the same core/overlay model fragments already use. Generated agent files carry the generated marker, are gated by protect-generated, and must never be edited manually.

Emission is single-source per the 2f4 policy: .claude/agents/ only — VS Code parses the Claude sub-agent format natively (user-shared research finding, 2026-07-16), and Claude Code reads only .claude/.

Prerequisite research: the 84v SOTA research covered instruction-file blocks, not subagent-file anatomy. A dedicated research pass (Anthropic sub-agents spec + VS Code custom-agent docs + curated corpus: awesome-claude-code, VoltAgent/awesome-claude-code-subagents, wshobson/agents) must establish the frontmatter contract, the recurring body anatomy, and a frequency-ranked block taxonomy before the schema is designed. Findings land as comments on this bead.

## Acceptance Criteria
- Research findings recorded on this bead: frontmatter contract, cross-tool field compatibility, body anatomy, ranked building-block taxonomy mapped to the candidate list
- New agents catalog kind: YAML sources in .basicly/core (schema + catalog-lint coverage + scaffold command consistent with skills-new/fragment-new)
- Projector composes and renders .claude/agents/*.md with the generated marker; protect-generated blocks manual edits

payload.text:
Research 1/2 — Subagent file specification (primary sources, 2026-07-16)

# Subagent Definition Files: Specification and Best-Practices Research

Research date: 2026-07-16. All quotes verbatim from the cited pages as fetched on this date.

---

## A. Frontmatter contract for `.claude/agents/*.md` per Anthropic

Source: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents (primary, official).

Subagent files are Markdown with YAML frontmatter; the body after the frontmatter is the subagent's system prompt. "The frontmatter defines the subagent's metadata and configuration. The body becomes the system prompt that guides the subagent's behavior. Subagents receive only this system prompt plus basic environment details like the working directory, not the full Claude Code system prompt."

### Fields ("Only `name` and `description` are required.")

| Field | Required | Type | Default | Constraints / semantics (per docs) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `name` | Yes | string | — | "Unique identifier using lowercase letters and hyphens. Hooks receive this value as `agent_type`. The filename doesn't have to match" |
| `description` | Yes | string | — | "When Claude should delegate to this subagent" — drives automatic delegation (see below) |
| `tools` | No | comma-separated string of tool names | inherit all | "Tools the subagent can use. Inherits all tools if omitted. If no entry in the list resolves to a tool, the subagent fails to launch with an error naming the entries. To preload Skills into context, use the `skills` field rather than listing `Skill` here." Accepts MCP server patterns `mcp__<server>` / `mcp__<server>__*`. `Agent` grants nested spawning; `Agent(type,…)` allowlist syntax applies only when the agent runs as the main thread via `claude --agent` (inside a subagent definition "any type list inside the parentheses is ignored") |
| `disallowedTools` | No | comma-separated string | — | "Tools to deny, removed from inherited or specified list." "If both are set, `disallowedTools` is applied first, then `tools` is resolved against the remaining pool. A tool listed in both is removed." Also accepts `mcp__<server>` and `mcp__*` |
| `model` | No | string | `inherit` | "`sonnet`, `opus`, `haiku`, `fable`, a full model ID (for example, `claude-opus-4-8`), or `inherit`. Defaults to `inherit`." Resolution order: `CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL` env var → per-invocation `model` parameter → frontmatter → main conversation's model; values are checked against the org `availableModels` allowlist |
| `permissionMode` | No | enum | `default` (inherited context) | `default`, `acceptEdits`, `auto`, `dontAsk`, `bypassPermissions`, `plan`, or `manual` (alias for `default`, v2.1.200+). Ignored for plugin subagents. A parent in `bypassPermissions`/`acceptEdits` "takes precedence and can't be overridden"; a parent in auto mode makes frontmatter `permissionMode` ignored |
| `maxTurns` | No | integer | — | "Maximum number of agentic turns before the subagent stops" |
| `skills` | No | YAML list | — | "Skills to preload into the subagent's context at startup. The full skill content is injected, not only the description." Cannot preload skills with `disable-model-invocation: true`; missing/disabled skills are skipped with a debug-log warning |
| `mcpServers` | No | YAML list (string refs or inline server defs) | — | Inline defs use the `.mcp.json` schema keyed by server name; types `stdio`, `http`, `sse`, `ws`. Inline servers connect at subagent start, disconnect at finish; string refs share the parent's connection. Ignored for plugin subagents |
| `hooks` | No | object (hook events) | — | "Lifecycle hooks scoped to this subagent." All hook events supported; frontmatter `Stop` hooks are "automatically converted to `SubagentStop`" when run as a subagent. Ignored for plugin subagents |
| `memory` | No | enum | off | `user` (`~/.claude/agent-memory/<name>/`), `project` (`.claude/agent-memory/<name>/`), or `local` (`.claude/agent-memory-local/<name>/`). Enables Read/Write/Edit automatically and injects the first 200 lines / 25KB of `MEMORY.md`

Research 2/2 — Community subagent corpus survey (2026-07-16)

# Community Claude Code Subagent Files: Anatomy, Building Blocks, and Quality Survey

**Corpus**: VoltAgent/awesome-claude-code-subagents — 154 agent files in 10 category dirs, median 287 lines, highly templated. wshobson/agents — 203 agent files under plugins/*/agents/, median 156 lines, bimodal (~30-line focused agents and ~150-350-line capability dumps). hesreallyhim/awesome-claude-code — current curated CSV has no dedicated subagents category; linked exemplars fetched from dshakes/compass (5 files). Stats computed over the 357 frontmattered files; 32 files read in depth across code review, security audit, pen-test, planning/architecture, orchestration/team-lead, documentation, tutorial, test, debugging, incident response, policy/governance, context management, C4 modeling, git workflow, prompt engineering, SRE.

---

## A. Recurring body anatomy

1. **Role/identity statement — ~95%** (339/357 open with "You are …"). Always first body line, seniority-inflected. Best files fuse identity with an epistemic stance, not a title: "**Default to doubt:** assume the change is broken until the checks prove otherwise. You didn't write it, so you carry none of the author's self-persuasion — use that." (compass code-reviewer)

2. **Purpose / mission expansion — ~33%** (`## Purpose` / `## Core Mission`), a 2-4 sentence elaboration; wshobson signature (59% of its files).

3. **Activation steps ("When invoked: 1…n") — 37% overall** (84% of Volt, 2% of wshobson). E.g. "1. Capture error message and stack trace / 2. Identify reproduction steps / 3. Isolate the failure location / 4. Implement minimal fix / 5. Verify solution works" (wshobson debugger).

4. **Domain capability inventory — ~85%+** carry topical bullet inventories. Good form: each bullet is an analysis move ("Error signature analysis: exception types, message patterns, frequency, first occurrence"). Bad form: aspirational encyclopedia ("Quantum-safe cryptography… Homomorphic encryption…" in a code security-auditor).

5. **Process / numbered steps — ~87%** — the most universal block after the role line. Best: "## Method (scientific, not shotgun) 1. **Reproduce.** … If you can't reproduce it, say so — don't guess-fix. … 4. **Prove it.** … Iterate until proven, not until it 'seems fixed.'" (compass debugger). Incident archetype adds timeboxing ("Immediate Actions (First 5 minutes)").

6. **Checklists — 42%** (85% of Volt, 9% of wshobson). Two species: verification checklists of checkable facts (good — "metadata.json is valid JSON") and fake-metric checklists (bad — see anti-patterns).

7. **Output format contract — ~22% overall but present in essentially ALL best-in-class files.** The clearest quality discriminator in the corpus. Styles: severity-grouped findings ("Group findings by severity: **Blocking** / **Should-fix** / **Nit**. For each: `path:line — what's wrong — concrete fix`. … If the diff is clean, say so in one line and stop. Don't pad." — compass), fenced literal sample outputs (compass test-runner's PASS/FAIL block), and per-finding schemas shared across parallel reviewers so results merge (wshobson team-reviewer: Location/Dimension/Evidence/Impact/Recommended Fix).

8. **Constraints / boundaries / never-do — ~10% explicit, universal in the best files.** "Never edit files. Never run anything that mutates state (no pushes, no migrations)." "NO architectural decisions — that is the architect's job." "Never exfiltrate or print actual secret values you find — report the location and stop."

9. **Tool discipline (mapping tools to steps) — ~10%, high-value where present.** "1. **Use Glob** to find all relevant files … 4. **Use Bash** only for directory existence checks" (conductor-validator); concrete first command beats tool names ("Get the diff first: `git diff HEAD`").

10. **Behavioral traits — 32%** (wshobson signature at 56%); mostly filler, occasionally operational ("Reports 'no findings' dimensions honestly rather than inflating results

Synthesis 3/3 — Design inputs for the agents catalog kind (2026-07-16)

Combines research 1/2 (primary-source spec) and 2/2 (357-file corpus survey) into decisions the schema design should start from.

## 1. Emission target and portable contract

- Emit to `.claude/agents/*.md` only (single-source, consistent with basicly-2f4). Claude Code treats the body as the full system prompt; VS Code has parsed the format natively since 1.109.
- Frontmatter to emit by default — the portable core only: `name` (kebab, required), `description` (required; drives delegation in both readers), `tools` (comma-separated string), plus `model` (Claude-only but harmless elsewhere). VS Code honors exactly name/description/tools/disallowedTools from the Claude format; everything else in Anthropic's 16-field contract (permissionMode, skills, memory, hooks, maxTurns, effort, isolation, mcpServers, background, color, initialPrompt) is Claude-only — the schema may expose a `claude:` extension map for them, emitted verbatim, defaulted empty.
- Enforce at lint time: body ≤ 30,000 chars (GitHub cloud-agent hard ceiling; cheap portability insurance), name lowercase+hyphens, description non-empty.

## 2. Description composition rule (schema-level, not free text)

Corpus best practice + official docs converge on a 4-part description: (a) what it does, (b) trigger conditions ("Use proactively when/after …" — 44% corpus adoption, officially endorsed; "MUST BE USED" is folklore, 0 corpus occurrences), (c) what it returns, (d) permission posture ("Read-only."). Schema: separate YAML fields (purpose, triggers, returns, posture) that the projector joins — guarantees no part is forgotten and keeps router-addressed text out of the body.

## 3. Body composition skeleton (the slot model)

Five ordered slots, validated independently by Anthropic's official examples and the corpus best-in-class:

1. **role** — identity + epistemic stance (encode the stance, not the résumé: "default to doubt", not "elite 25-year veteran")
2. **startup** — "When invoked:" numbered procedure, first step a concrete command (e.g. `git diff HEAD`)
3. **process** — domain method/checklist; checkable facts in priority order; never aspirational metrics
4. **output-contract** — deliverable shape, ideally with a literal fenced sample; severity taxonomy where applicable; include the "if clean, say so in one line and stop" clause
5. **constraints** — never-do list with alternatives, permission posture restated, escalation honesty ("if you can't reproduce it, say so — don't guess-fix")

Blocks are fragments filling slots; an agent source = archetype + slot fills + overrides. Core blocks basicly-owned; overlay adds agents and overrides individual slots/blocks (same precedence model as fragments).

## 4. Revised block taxonomy (candidate list, corrected by evidence)

- KEEP, strong corpus support: review, validate, verify, security (split into: security-conduct operating rules vs security-domain content), orchestration, context-priming, work-scoping, planning, documentation.
- KEEP, moderate: gates, enforcement, authorize, conventions.
- RECLASSIFY: authenticate → content fragment inside security-domain, not an operating block (zero corpus evidence as behavior). hygiene → single constraint lines (e.g. "remove temporary instrumentation"), fold into constraints slot. hardening → fold into security-domain.
- KEEP DESPITE weak corpus support: work-tracking and git — the corpus has no external-tracker integration at all (2%), but br/harness-loop integration is exactly basicly's differentiator; corpus absence here is a gap in the ecosystem, not evidence against. These blocks are where composed agents reference `br`, `basicly loop`, and the commit discipline.
- ADD (corpus-demanded, missing from the candidate list): role-identity, output-contract, severity-taxonomy, tool-discipline (incl. read-only posture), escalation-clarification, handoff/workflow-position (declared inputs/outputs/pipeline position), evidence-discipline (path:line citations; state what you did NOT see

payload.acceptance_criteria: Given a prompt naming a concrete model that the current host cannot run when an agent is spawned then it runs on the same tier model the host does support and the substitution is reported to the prompter naming both the requested and the actual model, and given a named model whose reverse lookup maps to more than one tier then the documented disambiguation rule is applied or the request is refused rather than a tier being guessed, with tests
payload.description:
## Context

Owner requirement 2026-07-31. A human prompter writes something like "spawn an agent that uses
gpt-5.6 sol and send it to analyze this document". The expectation: on copilot it succeeds literally,
because copilot serves that model; on claude it cannot, so it should fall back to the model of the SAME
TIER that the host can actually run. This is the reverse of basicly-kjc5.61's forward lookup and needs
its own mechanism plus catalog guidance, because the agent acting on the request is the thing that has
to do the resolving.

Verified constraint: **claude code cannot run a GPT model at all.** Its subagent `model` field accepts
`sonnet`, `opus`, `haiku`, `fable`, a full claude model id, or `inherit` - every value is Anthropic. So
a literal cross-vendor request is impossible there and substitution is the only non-failing option.
Copilot by contrast serves 6 vendors (measured: 29 models spanning OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Microsoft,
Moonshot AI, xAI), so it can honour most such requests literally.

## The sharp problem: reverse lookup is AMBIGUOUS

In the anchor set, `gpt-5.6-sol` occupies BOTH `high` and `maximum`, because OpenAI ships a three-class
ladder and the top class serves both tiers (docs/design/agent-roster-design.md R5). So resolving
"sol" backwards yields two tiers, and on claude they substitute differently: `high` gives
`claude-opus-5`, `maximum` gives `claude-fable-5` - which is double the input price and five times the
output price. A naive implementation picks whichever row it hits first and no one notices.

The same collapse applies to Moonshot (`kimi-k3`) and Google (`gemini-3.1-pro-preview`) in the derived
map, so this is the normal case, not an edge case.

## Two hard rules, both inherited from existing decisions

1. **Substitution must be VISIBLE.** If the prompter asked for `gpt-5.6-sol` and the agent spawns on
   `claude-opus-5`, that must be stated back to the prompter. basicly-kjc5.59 already establishes
   "record that the tier was not honoured rather than implying it was"; this is the same rule at the
   prompt surface. An invisible model swap is worse than a refusal because the prompter believes the
   request was honoured.
2. **An ambiguous reverse lookup is resolved by a documented rule or REFUSED, never guessed.** Options
   worth weighing: prefer the lowest tier that maps to the named model (cheapest, least surprising, and
   errs toward not overspending); or refuse and ask which tier was meant. Fail closed either way -
   "cannot tell" must never read as "safe to proceed". Whatever is chosen must be written down.

## Delivery shape

Per the owner, this needs distributing as guidance, not only as engine code: instructions and/or a skill
that teach an agent to (a) recognise a prompt naming a concrete model, (b) resolve it through the
committed map, (c) substitute tier-preserving where the host cannot honour it, and (d) say what it did.
It must work for custom agents and ad-hoc prompts, not just catalog-shipped agents - so it pairs with
basicly-wbsz's no-harness-required kit.

Mind the always-on budget: the baseline is at its soft cap, so this belongs in a skill or a path-scoped
fragment, not another `applies_to: [all]` fragment (see basicly-a3ab.1 and the headroom table in
docs/architecture/architecture.md section 7).

Depends on basicly-kjc5.61 for the map. Related: basicly-izda (ordered preference lists),
basicly-wbsz (portable kit), basicly-a3yi (emission), basicly-5xcj (tier-choice guidance, which this
should not duplicate).

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a prompt naming a concrete model that the current host cannot run when an agent is spawned then
  it runs on the same-tier model the host does support and the substitution is reported to the prompter
  naming both the requested and the actual model, and given a named model whose reverse lookup maps to
  more than one tier then the documented disambiguation rule is applied or the request is refused rather
  than a tier being guessed, with tests
payload.title: Resolve a prompter named model to the tier equivalent available on the current host

payload.text: DISAMBIGUATION RULE - owner question 2026-07-31, answered against the landed map's own numbers. The owner proposed (1) ask in an interactive prompt, (2) in non-interactive loop work prefer the HIGHER tier because an insufficient model does more harm. Verdict: (1) is right. (2) is directionally justified but WRONG for this case, and it has a constraint the proposal did not account for. WHY THE HIGHER-IS-SAFER INSTINCT HAS REAL SUPPORT: agent-roster-design R5 explicitly rejects 'cheapest sufficient model' and states the unit of cost is total tokens plus wall-clock plus human interventions PER LANDED CORRECT CHANGE, because a cheaper model's mistakes return as rework dispatches, extra review cycles, bounced merges and human attention. So under-powering is the expensive error by the repo's own decision. WHY IT IS STILL WRONG HERE: price parity contradicts it. From the committed map, gpt-5.6-sol is 5 in / 30 out; claude-opus-5 (high) is 5 in / 25 out - identical input; claude-fable-5 (maximum) is 10 in / 50 out - exactly 2x sol's input. So sol sits at opus's price point, and resolving sol to fable OVERSHOOTS by 2x input cost. The roster does not say sol is fable's peer; it says a three-class ladder has its top class do DOUBLE DUTY for high and maximum, which is a different claim. SECOND PROBLEM: the D3 grant token ceiling. Silently doubling per-dispatch cost can drive session spend to the grant budget, at which point spend_status reports halted and the lane goes human-only until re-granted. So 'prefer higher' trades a capability risk for a budget-exhaustion risk, and the latter stops the factory mid-run. RECOMMENDED RULE - a deterministic ladder, not a blind default. Forward direction (tier declared to model) has no ambiguity; this applies only to reverse lookup. Interactive: ASK, per the block-don't-guess needs-input protocol. Non-interactive, in this order: (a) PRICE PARITY against the named model, using the cost already in the map - deterministic, needs no new data, and yields sol to high to claude-opus-5; (b) if still tied, the bead's TASK_CLASS, which is already recorded on run records since basicly-jr0l.34 - design and decomposition resolve to maximum, implementation to high - so use information the harness already has rather than guessing; (c) only if still tied, prefer the higher tier as the documented last resort, justified by R5. Always report the substitution naming requested and actual, and record it on the run record per basicly-kjc5.59's record-rather-than-imply convention. GUARD: check the resolved model's forecast against the remaining grant budget BEFORE dispatch and refuse up front rather than halting mid-run - that is basicly-jr0l.22's job, so wire to it rather than duplicating. HONEST LIMIT: price is a vendor-published PROXY for capability, not a capability measurement. It is the right tiebreaker because it is deterministic and already committed (deterministic checks block, judged checks advise) - not because it is ground truth.

DECIDED BY OWNER 2026-07-31: price parity is the disambiguation mechanism for reverse lookup. Do not re-litigate. The rule to implement, in order: interactive -> ask the prompter; non-interactive -> (a) price parity against the named model using the cost already committed in .basicly/core/models/model-map.json, (b) task_class as the tiebreaker where price ties, (c) prefer the higher tier only as a documented last resort. Always report the substitution naming requested and actual, and check the resolved model's forecast against the remaining grant budget before dispatch rather than halting mid-run. Worked example that must hold as a test: a prompt naming gpt-5.6-sol on a claude host resolves to claude-opus-5 (high), NOT claude-fable-5 (maximum), because sol and opus-5 share a 5 dollar input price while fable-5 is 10.

payload.description:
Premise: basicly's core value is a deterministic software-factory loop that turns any user input (requirements, use cases, a vague idea) into production-grade, releasable software - built on top of coding agents (Claude/Codex/Copilot), agent-agnostic, and consumer-customizable without losing changes on update.

Three nested control loops:

1. Orchestrator loop (one per session, owns the tracker):
   - Intake -> decompose requirements into work packages - standalone, valuable, sized for parallelism (not too big, not too small).
   - Build and continuously maintain a dependency graph so lanes always schedule against fresh information.
   - Spawn parallel lanes, monitor them, synchronize between them.
   - Handle escalations: decide itself (autonomous mode) or hand the decision to the human (interactive mode).
   - When all lanes land: integrate -> verify -> validate -> ship (cut release autonomously, or ask human).
   - Verify/validate at this level are never skippable.

2. Lane loop (one per work package, isolated worktree):
   - Plan assigned package -> decompose into small tasks -> prioritize.
   - Per task: build -> verify -> validate -> finalize (verify/validate may be skipped when genuinely unnecessary).
   - When all tasks done: integrate the package -> verify -> validate -> signal the merge queue.

3. Merge queue (one per session):
   - Receives "ready" signals from lanes, decides merge order, merges back to base (usually main), resolves conflicts when they happen.

Cross-cutting requirements: agent-agnostic (same loop drives Claude, Codex, Copilot), engine-enforced determinism where it matters, and a customization layer where consumer overrides survive basicly install.

This epic is research-first: the opening child is a grounded gap analysis of the current basicly loop against this three-nested-loop target, ending in a proposed decomposition into implementable work packages. Implementation packages are filed and sequenced from that research. Coordinates with parallel loop-engine work in progress.
payload.title: Three-nested-loop software factory: deterministic input-to-release loop

payload.acceptance_criteria: Given the exact validation-error text br emits for a backwards clock step when the retry recogniser inspects it then it is classified as clock skew and the bounded retry runs and given a validation error that is not a clock step then it is not retried with a regression test whose fixture is the observed br output
payload.description:
## Context

Found 2026-07-31 while investigating an intermittent `pytest -q -n 4` failure. The bounded
clock-skew retry added by `basicly-jr0l.41` and re-examined by `basicly-jr0l.42` has never
fired, because the string it looks for is not the string `br` prints.

    br.py:136   _CLOCK_SKEW_MARKER = "updated_at: cannot be before created_at"

    br emits    Error: Validation errors: [ValidationError { field: "updated_at",
                message: "cannot be before created_at" }, ValidationError { field:
                "closed_at", message: "cannot be before created_at" }]

The marker spells the field and the message as one colon-joined phrase; `br` prints them as two
separate quoted fields of a Rust `ValidationError` struct, so the substring is absent and
`_is_clock_skew` returns False. `run_br` then raises on the first attempt and the retry loop,
the exponential backoff and the 5 second monotonic deadline are all dead code on the only
error they exist for.

Verified directly rather than inferred:

    >>> br._is_clock_skew(CompletedProcess(returncode=1, stderr=<the text above>))
    False
    >>> br._CLOCK_SKEW_MARKER in <the text above>
    False

This explains why the defect recurred after two closed fixes. `basicly-jr0l.42` concluded the
backoff was probably too short and lengthened it; the measurement it asked for would have shown
zero retries ever attempted. The marker most likely matched an older `br` spelling and stopped
matching silently, which is the recogniser-desync class `basicly-jr0l.51` hardened for gate
providers.

Measured on unmodified main at commit 766c70c, so this is not introduced by any in-flight work:
one failure in eight runs of `pytest -q -n 4` over `tests/test_integration_loop.py`
`tests/test_loop.py` `tests/test_decompose.py` `tests/test_run_record.py`, and one in twelve on
a second sweep. The failing assertion is always inside `test_integration_loop.py`, on a real
`br close`, and it charges a rework attempt to whatever lane is landing - the exact harm
`basicly-55yh` was filed about, standing immediately before the `basicly-u6jq.1` proof run.

The fix belongs in this repo, not upstream: `br`'s validation is its own business, and our
recogniser must match what it actually emits. Matching on the two field names independently -
rather than on one brittle phrase - is what stops the next spelling change from silently
disabling the retry again, and the regression test must use the real observed text as its
fixture. Note `closed_at` carries the same message, so the recogniser should cover it.

## Steps to Reproduce

- On main, run `pytest -q -n 4 tests/test_integration_loop.py tests/test_loop.py
  tests/test_decompose.py tests/test_run_record.py` repeatedly; roughly one run in ten fails.
- Observed 2026-07-31: `RuntimeError: br close fx-baj --reason shipped by the harness loop
  failed: Error: Validation errors: [ValidationError { field: "updated_at", message: "cannot be
  before created_at" }, ...]` raised from `br.run_br` at `br.py:189`, reached through
  `loop._on_ship`.
- Feed that exact text to `br._is_clock_skew`: it returns False. Expected: True, so the retry
  absorbs the skew as `basicly-jr0l.41` intended.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given the exact validation-error text br emits for a backwards clock step when the retry
  recogniser inspects it then it is classified as clock skew and the bounded retry runs, and
  given a validation error that is not a clock step then it is not retried, with a regression
  test whose fixture is the observed br output
payload.title: The clock-skew retry never fires because its recogniser does not match the error br emits

payload.description:
## Context

Found 2026-07-31 while landing basicly-kjc5.58 and deliberately left out of scope there, because
it is not part of that bead's acceptance criterion.

`kjc5.58` added a `tier` enum (low/medium/high/maximum, single-sourced as `schema.MODEL_TIERS`) to
`.basicly/core/schemas/agent.schema.json`. That enum is enforced by JSON Schema validation, which
`catalog_lint._validate_agent_schemas` runs over `.basicly/core/agents/*/agent.yaml` ONLY. The
`.basicly-local/agents` overlay is never schema-validated.

Verified behaviour at the kjc5.58 landing:

- core source with `tier: turbo` -> rejected, `'turbo' is not one of ['low','medium','high','maximum']`
- overlay source with `tier: turbo` -> ACCEPTED silently

This is the same core-vs-overlay asymmetry that put the deprecated-`model` rule in
`agents.lint_agent_sources` rather than in a `catalog_lint` local rule: `lint_agent_sources` walks
`default_agent_roots`, which is core PLUS overlay, so it is the only place a rule sees an overlay
source.

Harmless today because nothing resolves a tier to a model yet. It stops being harmless the moment
something does: an overlay typo would resolve to no model at all, and per the harness's own
fail-closed rule a "cannot tell" must never read as "safe to proceed". So this must land before
basicly-kjc5.61 (the generator that resolves a tier to a per-family model id) or basicly-kjc5.60.
No dependency edge is filed, to avoid perturbing the release ladder corrected by basicly-sy8c;
this note is the pointer.

Scope: `src/basicly/agents.py` (`lint_agent_sources`), `tests/test_agents.py`.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given an agent source in the `.basicly-local/agents` overlay that declares a tier outside
  `schema.MODEL_TIERS` when catalog lint runs then it fails naming the source the offending value
  and the allowed vocabulary, and given a valid overlay tier then lint passes, with tests

payload.acceptance_criteria: Given a checkout whose committed export holds more records than the local database when any mutating br command runs then it imports first or refuses and never flushes the smaller database over the larger artifact and given a flush that would publish fewer records than the file it overwrites then it reports the shrink and requires explicit intent and given a repository truncated this way then the documented repair restores every record and a test asserts the export never shrinks without intent
payload.description:
## Steps to Reproduce

Reproduced, not theorised, on a basicly checkout 2026-08-06. The committed
`.beads/issues.jsonl` held **612** records; the local database held **426**. A mutating
`br` command was run. `br` auto-flushed the older database over the newer file.

Observed:

- **187 records deleted, 47 of them open** - 100 bug, 66 task, 10 chore, 7 epic, 4 feature
- the export fell from **2,227,607 to 1,102,742 bytes**
- `br create` reported **success**; no gate fired; nothing in the tracker layer noticed

Expected - a write does not publish an older state over a newer committed artifact.

## Why this is a defect and not misuse

`br sync --status` on that same checkout reports, in its own words,
`Status: JSONL is newer (import recommended)`. **The tool had already evaluated the
condition and allowed the destructive write anyway.** Detecting a hazard and reporting it
from a different subcommand is not a guard.

## A refinement measured on a second checkout, 2026-08-06

On a healthy checkout the same status line appeared - `JSONL is newer (import
recommended)` at 612 records - and `br sync --import-only` was a **no-op**: 0 created,
0 updated, 612 skipped as up-to-date. So the status is computed from **timestamps**, and
says JSONL is newer when the content is byte-identical.

That matters for the fix. **A timestamp comparison is the wrong guard**: it fires on
healthy checkouts, so anyone who meets it routinely learns to ignore it, and it would not
distinguish this incident from a harmless clock ordering. The guard must be on **content** -
a flush that would publish fewer records than the artifact it overwrites.

## What caught it, and what did not

Not the tracker layer. The pre-push suite, via three positive controls:

- `tests/test_config.py::test_the_ledger_holds_the_metered_dispatches_that_named_no_model`
- `tests/test_decompose.py::test_the_spend_gate_measures_a_populated_ledger`
- `tests/test_runner.py::test_the_ledger_holds_occupancy_the_stale_declaration_called_impossible`

All three exist to prove a gate is not measuring an empty set. They are the only reason this
was found - worth remembering when their cost is next questioned.

## The repair, verified to restore every record

```sh
git show <good-ref>:.beads/issues.jsonl > .beads/issues.jsonl
br sync --import-only      # Created 187, Updated 27, Skipped 398
br sync --flush-only
uv run python -c "from pathlib import Path; import basicly.br as b; print(b.scrub_export(Path('.')))"
```

Verified after: zero records lost against the good ref, zero whose title or status changed,
zero path-leaking records, three tests green. **The export was recoverable only because it is
committed** - the database was the corrupt side, which is the whole argument of the
replacement's inversion.

## Where this belongs

`docs/design/work-tracker.md` section 2.1, the defects-already-billed-for register, as R9.
It is also **evidence for section 4's inversion**: with an append-only log authoritative and
every other file derived, there is no database-disagrees-with-export state that can be
resolved in the wrong direction. Decide deliberately whether it is a requirement to add or an
argument to cite - it is arguably both, since the replacement still needs the shrink guard for
its own derived snapshot.
payload.title: A stale database auto-flush silently deletes committed records

payload.description:
## Context

The landing page described basicly as a harness distribution shipping instructions, skills and gates, which is the framing docs/architecture/architecture.md section 0 now rejects: the loop and the work graph are what distinguish it from a guidance-only harness. payload.acceptance_criteria: Given a lane bounced by a landing rebase conflict when the next attempt runs then the lane is dispatched with the conflicting paths and both sides as its task rather than the same rebase being replayed and a second identical failure signature escalates immediately without consuming the rework cap
payload.description:
## Context

Observed three times on 2026-08-05/06. When a landing rebase conflicts, the lane is
bounced and the attempt is repeated — and the repeat replays the identical rebase
against the identical moved anchor, so it fails identically and the rework cap is spent
learning nothing:

```
routed: basicly-3ymj -> bounced  ... conflicts in: CHANGELOG.md (rework 1/2)
routed: basicly-3ymj -> decision ... conflicts in: CHANGELOG.md (rework 2/2)
```

The same sequence then repeated for `basicly-sco6` on the projection manifest and
`basicly-5gn2` on a design document.

Every one of those three conflicts was resolved by hand in about two minutes: they were
addition-versus-addition in prose, or a generated artifact needing a rebuild. An agent
handed the conflict as a task would have resolved all three.

## Verify before building

**This bead's premise is a claim about a code path this filer did not read.** Establish
first what a bounce actually does: whether it re-dispatches the lane's agent with the
conflict as the task, or re-runs the rebase mechanically. The observed behaviour — an
identical second failure with no intervening agent activity in the worktree — points at
the latter, but confirm it in `merge.py`/`supervise.py` before changing anything, and
close this as already-satisfied if the dispatch is there and something else is wrong.

## Fix shape, if the premise holds

A bounce dispatches the lane with a conflict-resolution brief: the conflicting paths,
the two sides, and the instruction to resolve and commit. Bounded — the lane already has
a rework cap — and paired with `basicly-m4zv.5` so a second *identical* failure
escalates immediately rather than consuming the cap.

Deliberately not proposed: auto-resolving prose conflicts. Consumer-facing release copy
merged by a strategy nobody reviewed is the outcome `basicly-o8p0` explicitly rejected.

## Steps to Reproduce

Observed three times on 2026-08-05/06 during the `basicly-u6jq.1` proof run, and
confirmed against the code on 2026-08-06 (see the verification comment).

1. Run a supervised pass with two lanes whose work touches one anchor in a file
   neither bead declares in its `## Scope`.
2. Let the first lane land. The second lane's landing rebase conflicts, so
   `merge._bounce_back` charges a rework attempt and `supervise._bounce_lane`
   routes it `bounced`.
3. Observe the next pass. The lane is re-dispatched — `"bounced"` is in
   `RETRIABLE_ROUTES` and is excluded from `carried_forward` — but its prompt is
   assembled by `build_bundle` from `loop.dispatch_prompt(issue_id)` plus any
   matching found-info records plus answered decisions, and the bounce published
   none of those. So the agent receives the prompt it already satisfied, for work
   already committed on its branch.
4. The agent changes nothing, the landing re-derives the identical conflict, and
   the second rework attempt escalates to a human having learned nothing:

```
routed: basicly-3ymj -> bounced  ... conflicts in: CHANGELOG.md (rework 1/2)
routed: basicly-3ymj -> decision ... conflicts in: CHANGELOG.md (rework 2/2)
```

Expected: the second dispatch tells the agent its branch no longer merges, which
paths conflict, and which lanes landed over it — the way `_preempt_lane` already
does for a collision the supervisor predicts.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/supervise.py`
- `tests/test_supervise.py`
payload.title: Re-dispatch a bounced lane to resolve its conflict instead of replaying the same rebase

payload.text:
verified 2026-08-06 against merge.py and supervise.py: the premise holds, but neither of the two hypotheses this bead offers is what happens.

A bounced lane IS re-dispatched to its agent. "bounced" is in RETRIABLE_ROUTES (supervise.py:2509) and is deliberately excluded from carried_forward (supervise.py:2552-2565) with the comment "which is exactly when a fresh dispatch *is* the right move". So the rebase is not replayed mechanically by a machine that never consults the agent.

What is missing is that the re-dispatch carries no conflict information. build_bundle (supervise.py:669) assembles a prompt from exactly three things: loop.dispatch_prompt(issue_id), which is a fixed string keyed only on the issue id (loop.py:756); matching found-info records; and answered decisions. _bounce_lane (supervise.py:3071) publishes none of the three. So the agent is handed the identical prompt it already satisfied, for work already committed on its branch, has nothing to do, and the landing re-derives the identical conflict.

The fix already exists in this codebase and is wired to the other half of the pair. _preempt_lane (supervise.py:3200) handles the PREDICTED collision - a lane a landing this pass broke - and publishes a kind=coupling found-info record for precisely this reason. Its docstring: "a re-dispatch that says nothing new would run the same agent, on the same tree, to the same collision. What makes it worth a run is the kind=coupling found-info record published here: that is D6 own propagation channel, and build_bundle folds it into this lane next prompt." The OBSERVED collision - the case that actually fired three times - was never given the same treatment.

So the fix shape narrows: reuse record_found_info rather than build a conflict-resolution dispatch in merge.py. No change to merge.py is needed, and D5 no-merge-time-resolution is untouched.

Placement is load-bearing. The record must be published in _attribute_pass_couplings (supervise.py:2673), not at the bounce, for the same D9 reason the coupling edge is written there: at the bounce the culprit lanes are not yet known, and naming whatever had landed by then would leak pass order into a durable record. _attribute_pass_couplings already completes the bounced lanes details with the attributed culprits, so both the conflicting paths and the culprits are in hand there.

payload.description:
From spike basicly-zv48 dimension 4. Runner selection is shutil.which (PATH presence) only; a binary whose headless flag (-p, exec) was dropped or renamed would still be auto-selected and then fail at dispatch. Probe the binary to confirm the assumed headless flag before auto-selecting, and surface it.

## Acceptance Criteria

- runner.probe_capability(spec, *, run=None) -> Capability{reachable, flag_ok, detail}: for a headless runner it runs the binary with --help and checks the static headless-flag tokens (command minus the binary and the {prompt}/{model} placeholders) appear in the output. flag_ok is False ONLY on positive evidence (the probe ran and a flag token is absent); a probe that cannot run assumes capable, so a flaky or slow probe never false-skips a working agent. A handoff runner is trivially capable.
- runner.is_capable(spec, *, which, run) -> bool: on PATH (is_available) and flag_ok.
- select_runner gains an optional capable predicate: auto skips a runner that is on PATH but probes as not capable, falling through to the next candidate and finally the manual handoff. Explicit selection is honored unchanged. With no predicate the current PATH-only behavior is preserved.
- The loop dispatch and the CLI runner resolution pass the real probe so auto confirms the headless flag before selecting.
- runner list surfaces each runner capability (PATH + probe result / detail).
- Regression tests: probe flag-present / flag-absent / unprobeable; headless-flag extraction; is_capable; select_runner skipping an incapable runner and preserving behavior without a predicate; runner list output.
- Architecture section 12.8 updated. pytest, ruff, and projection checks stay green.

## Scope

A --help flag-presence probe only: no --version parsing, no semantic per-flag validation, no basicly status integration (runner list is the surface). Builds on the runner seam (basicly-45ld model field, basicly-140a attribution).

Decision (2026-07-17): do NOT trim further. The c5to audit already collapsed the redundant verify guidance (6->4 bullets, every distinct rule kept) and the always-on fragments are now dense with no remaining duplication. Trimming ~150 more chars would cost real guidance for a round-number threshold. Instead, recalibrate the soft size-warning cap.

The 8000 cap is a non-blocking warning on 'basicly build' (not a gate, not checked by 'check'/CI), meant to catch always-on context growing enough to dilute attention. Codex already runs at 12000 with a documented rationale. Empirically these files are ~160 lines at ~50 chars/line; ~200 lines (~10000 chars) is the point where attention starts to dilute. A soft warning should fire before that point, not at it.

Fix: raise the claude and copilot targets' max_size_warning from 8000 to 9000 (with a rationale comment), leaving codex at 12000. 9000 clears the current files (CLAUDE.md 8012, copilot 8144) by ~850 chars / ~17 lines while still warning ~1000 chars before the ~10000 danger zone. The cap is warning-only, so no projected content or manifest changes.

- 'basicly build' no longer warns for .claude/CLAUDE.md or .github/copilot-instructions.md.

Design conclusion from the friction investigation (2026-07-17). Only .beads/issues.jsonl churns; config.yaml/metadata.json are static. br natively supports a git-ignored .beads/redirect file: a worktree redirected at base .beads shares ONE DB+JSONL (verified: redirect wins over checked-out tracked files, no local db created, worktree mutations write base jsonl). The beads-commit-msg hook accepts a fresh id from a redirected worktree (test). merge_worktree auto-commits tracker-only dirt with a conventional message and still refuses mixed dirt (test). Ship makes the closing tracker commit itself (test). verify --issue works from a redirected worktree and still refuses from a non-redirected one (test). Skills and architecture docs describe the new zero-touch discipline. Full gate suite passes.
