payload.acceptance_criteria: Given a root epic with open children and an unapproved decompose checkpoint when loop preflight runs then it refuses the verdict and names the approval command and distinguishes a checkpoint a live grant can auto-resolve from one it cannot serve
payload.description:
## Steps to Reproduce

```
uv run basicly loop preflight basicly-yc0x     # VERDICT: ready
uv run basicly loop supervise basicly-yc0x --autonomy L3
```

Observed 2026-08-04 - `preflight` printed **`VERDICT: ready`** with a clean base, a live L3 grant, a
funded forecast and five in-band lanes. `supervise` then dispatched **nothing**:

```
routed:   basicly-yc0x -> seed-blocked - no lane could be provisioned from 5 open
          child(ren) - decompose checkpoint awaiting human approval
blocked:  no ready lanes and nothing to land
```

Expected - a command whose stated job is "check everything a supervised run needs before it starts"
does not report ready for a run that cannot dispatch a single lane.

## Context

The epic's own `decompose` checkpoint is a human gate and **a covering grant cannot serve it** - an
L3 grant on the root does not approve the root's own decomposition. That is correct behaviour. The
defect is that `preflight` does not look at it, so its verdict is false precisely where an operator
most needs it: before spending the wall-clock of a fan-out that will refuse.

This is the promise `basicly-ze8z` exists to keep - if you need to remember a precondition,
`preflight` is wrong rather than the operator. It already checks the clean base, live worktrees,
stale bindings, the resolved runner, the grant, the budget, dispatchable-versus-seedable counts, the
per-lane cost and the pass bound. The checkpoint state is the one precondition it omits, and it is
the one that cost a refused pass this session.

Cheap to detect: `policy` already reconstructs checkpoint state for `loop status`, which reported
`checkpoints: (none)` on the epic at the same moment.

## Fix shape

- `preflight` reports the root's own unapproved checkpoints and **refuses the verdict** when one of
  them blocks provisioning, naming the exact approval command - the same shape it already uses for
  the missing-budget blocker.
- Distinguish a checkpoint a live grant *will* auto-resolve from one it cannot serve. Reporting every
  unapproved checkpoint as a blocker would make the verdict noise; the useful line is "this one needs
  a human because a covering grant cannot serve its own root".
- Regression test proven red first (`basicly-kjc5.49`): an epic with open children and an unapproved
  `decompose` checkpoint must not preflight as ready.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/cli.py`
- `tests/test_cli.py`
payload.title: Preflight reports ready for a pass the decompose checkpoint will refuse

payload.text:
A cheaper reproduction, measured 2026-08-05 at d31f6bd. The bead's case needs an unapproved decompose checkpoint; this one needs nothing but the epic's current state:

  uv run basicly loop preflight basicly-yc0x
  base:      clean
  grant:     L3, spent 53408271 under it, remaining 96591729
  lanes:     0 dispatchable now, 0 open child(ren)
  forecast:  ~82595185 tokens if all 5 lanes start (cap x per-lane)
  VERDICT:   ready

Every child of basicly-yc0x closed on 2026-08-04, so there is no lane to provision and no checkpoint involved at all - yet the verdict is 'ready'. This is the bead's own Expected line ('a command whose stated job is to check everything a supervised run needs does not report ready for a run that cannot dispatch a single lane') reached by a shorter path than the checkpoint.

Two consequences for the fix:

1. The refusal predicate is 'zero dispatchable lanes', of which the unapproved checkpoint is one cause and an all-closed child set is another. Fixing only the checkpoint case leaves this one green, so write the predicate on the dispatchable count and report the cause.
2. The forecast line is incoherent with the lane line in the same output - it prices 5 lanes while the line above says 0 open children, because it multiplies the concurrency cap by the per-lane figure without reference to what exists. A reader sizing a pass from that number sizes a pass that cannot run. Worth a regression assertion that the forecast never prices more lanes than there are dispatchable children.

Correction to the previous comment, same day, before any lane builds against it.

That comment proposed writing the refusal predicate on 'zero dispatchable lanes'. **That predicate is wrong and would refuse every legitimate pass.** The harness-loop runbook states it directly: 'lanes: 0 dispatchable now counts *adopted* lanes. Before any worktree exists it reads zero and that is not a blocker - the supervisor provisions from the ranked open children at pass start.' Verified here - with two open children both sized 'in band', preflight still prints '0 dispatchable now' and the pass is genuinely ready.

What the reproduction actually shows is narrower and still real: preflight printed VERDICT ready when basicly-yc0x had **0 open children**, so there was nothing to provision from. The distinguishing signal is the open-child set and the band table, not the dispatchable count:

- refuse when there are **no open children at all** (nothing to provision), and
- refuse when every open child is 'REFUSED - too large, split it' (children exist but none can dispatch).

Also verified: the epic's decompose checkpoint reports APPROVED here, so the checkpoint case in the bead body is a *third* distinct cause rather than the same one. Three causes, one verdict line - which is the argument for reporting the cause rather than just flipping the verdict.

The forecast observation in the previous comment stands unchanged: the line prices 5 lanes (cap x per-lane) while the line above says 0 open children, and it did so again at 2 open children. It is not referenced to what exists.

payload.description:
## Context

Surfaced while verifying the codex capability facts for basicly-lelg (2026-07-31, against the live
OpenAI docs). Not a defect — an unexamined opportunity, and a policy comment that may now be narrower
than it reads.

`src/basicly/agents.py:23-25` renders every subagent to `.claude/agents/<slug>.md` **only**, and the
comment gives the reason as "Single output root (basicly-2f4 policy): Claude Code reads only
.claude/agents". That statement is true *about Claude*, but it is not a statement about codex, and it
reads today as though the single root were settled for every agent family.

OpenAI now documents a repo-checked-in subagent surface: "add standalone TOML files under
`~/.codex/agents/` for personal agents or `.codex/agents/` for project-scoped agents", each defining
`name`, `description`, and `developer_instructions`. So there is a real second target for the subagent
tier that basicly does not project to.

Worth deciding rather than assuming, because the roster work (basicly-s2xf, v0.9.0) is where the
subagent tier gets its real content, and doubling the surface after that lands is more expensive than
deciding now.

Points the decision has to weigh:

- The format differs: our subagents render as markdown with frontmatter for Claude; codex wants TOML
  with a fixed field set. That is a new renderer and a new drift gate, not a second path in the same
  template.
- `agents-check` would need the same `--all-default-roots` treatment `skills-check` has, or it will
  pass while the codex root drifts (the failure mode basicly recorded for `.agents/`).
- Read the `2f4` decision first and check whether codex was considered and rejected, or simply not yet
  in scope. If it was a deliberate reject, close this and record the reason next to the comment so the
  next reader does not re-open it.
- No always-on cost either way: subagents are on-demand files, so this does not touch the AGENTS.md
  headroom problem.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given the 2f4 single-root policy and the documented codex project agents surface when this is decided then either subagents project to the codex root with a renderer and a drift gate covering it, or the decision to stay Claude-only is recorded with its reason beside the AGENTS_OUTPUT_ROOT comment so it is not re-opened

explicitly:

  "**Prompts, as catalog sources** (not agent-native subagent files — the factory is agent-agnostic)."

So the roster's roles are catalog-source prompts, deliberately NOT agent-native subagent files. Phase 5
will therefore never reach this question, and the `related` edge to s2xf is weaker than filed: the two

That also supplies a strong prior for the answer: the factory is agent-agnostic by design and the
roster deliberately avoids native subagent files, so "stay Claude-only and record the reason" is the
outcome the design principle points at. Confirm against the basicly-2f4 decision before recording it.

payload.acceptance_criteria: Given the harness after this epic closes when the full loop is driven in a consumer repo then no third-party product is invoked or required, the permitted libraries are pinned and declared, and a gate fails when a new runtime dependency is introduced without a recorded classification
payload.description:
## Context

**Corrected 2026-07-30 after the owner sharpened the criterion.** The first version of this epic
read the directive as "zero runtime dependencies" and set out to remove `jinja2`, `jsonschema`,
`pyyaml`, `rich`, `uv`, the pre-commit framework and node. That was wrong, and the correction
matters because it removes a large breaking change from the roadmap.

The axis is not external-versus-internal, nor binary-versus-package. It is:

> **Can we absorb this component's breaking change on our own schedule, or does it dictate terms
> to us?**

A **library or framework** is fine. It is versioned, we pin it, and when it ships a breaking
change we upgrade when ready and fix our own code. The blast radius is our source.

A **product** is not. `beads` is the case in point, and the evidence is already recorded in
`docs/design/work-tracker.md` section 2.10: crossing one of its schema migrations requires
*"exactly one designated clone"* to run `bd migrate` and `bd dolt push` while every other clone
installs the new binary and runs `bd bootstrap`. That is a coordinated, human-sequenced,
multi-machine operation sitting in our critical path. Worse, the upgrade is sometimes not
available at all: br's current main targets schema 17 and its reviewed migration accepts only
13-to-17 and 14-to-17, so a 0.2.19 database has no supported path forward from schema 16. A
dependency we cannot upgrade, and cannot decline to upgrade, is not a dependency we manage.

The compounding factor is that beads owns **our state** - every phase derivation, gate,
checkpoint, dependency edge, decision and run record. A library that owns no state can be swapped
in an afternoon; a product that owns the state cannot be swapped at all without a migration.

## The rule

**No third-party product may own basicly's state.** Libraries and frameworks are permitted and
pinned. An optional extension - existing skills, language or technology guidelines - is permitted
and must stay optional.

## Classification of every current dependency

| Component | Class | Verdict |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `jinja2`, `jsonschema`, `pyyaml`, `ruamel.yaml`, `rich` | library | **Keep.** Pinned, semver, owns no state. The catalog stays YAML - the stdlib-has-no-YAML-parser problem is no longer forcing a move to TOML. |
| `uv` | tool | **Keep.** Versioned, replaceable, owns no state. |
| pre-commit framework | framework | **Keep.** Dispatches our hooks; owns no state. |
| node (markdownlint hook) | tool | **Keep**, but it is the weakest entry - it is the only one whose absence has actually broken a commit path on this machine, and it earns a re-examination on its own merits rather than under this rule. |
| Python 3.14+ | language runtime | **Keep.** Not a product. Whether the floor should drop is an adoption question, not this one. |
| **`br` / beads** | **product that owns our state** | **Remove.** This is the whole of the directive. Tracked by `basicly-vkh0`. |
| **`bv`** | **product** | **Remove.** Measured at 0 of 141 surfaces used (`basicly-vkh0.2`), so this is a deletion rather than a replacement. |

## Why this epic still exists rather than folding into vkh0

`vkh0` removes the one product we have. This epic is the **policy** that stops the next one
arriving, which is the part that outlives the migration: the rule above written down where an
agent proposing a dependency will read it, the classification kept current, and a gate that
refuses a new runtime dependency it cannot classify.

## Success Criteria

- The dependency rule is stated in the architecture reference, every current dependency is classified against it, `br` and `bv` are gone from the runtime path, and a check refuses a newly added runtime dependency that is not classifiable as a library or framework

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given the harness after this epic closes when the full loop is driven in a consumer repo then no third-party product is invoked or required, the permitted libraries are pinned and declared, and a gate fails when a new runtime dependency is introduced without a recorded classification
payload.title: Own our state: no third-party product in the runtime path, libraries are fine

## Acceptance Criteria

Hit twice in one day (basicly-em9 in the authoring repo, term-m3a in the terminal consumer): when an issue is filed and immediately driven through the loop, the worktree branches from the last COMMIT, which predates the issue's .beads/issues.jsonl line — so the first commit in the worktree is rejected by beads-commit-msg (unknown id). Manual workaround each time: commit the filing in the base checkout, then `git checkout main -- .beads/issues.jsonl` inside the worktree.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. br create <issue> (jsonl dirty, uncommitted).
2. basicly loop advance ... through classify: worktree provisioned from HEAD.
3. Commit work in the worktree referencing the new id: beads-commit-msg rejects — the worktree's issues.jsonl lacks the id.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Loop worktree provisioning ensures the tracked issue's id is known inside the worktree: either the engine commits/requires a clean tracker state before branching (clear error naming the fix), or provisioning syncs .beads/issues.jsonl from the base checkout into the worktree.
- Regression test covering file-then-loop-immediately.

payload.description:
The commit-msg hook (.basicly/core/hooks/commit-msg.py) rejects any commit whose description contains characters outside [a-z0-9 space hyphen] — no capitals, no periods/dots. This is a stricter-than-spec house profile: Conventional Commits v1.0.0 itself places NO charset restriction on the description and its body is free-form (verified against the spec). The conventional-commits skill already documents lowercase-only and 'reword version strings', but it tells agents to REWORD out dotted/uppercase forms rather than move them to the free-form body, and it lacks the two real-rejection examples. The hook's error is also generic (does not name the offending character). Two real rejections in one session: 'Font Awesome v4' (capitals) and 'restamp the install to 0.2.0' (the dots in a version number).

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Attempt a commit with a capitalized proper noun (e.g. 'feat: add Font Awesome v4 icons') or a dotted version (e.g. 'chore: restamp the install to 0.2.0').
2. The commit-msg hook rejects it with a generic error that does not point at the offending char.
3. The skill offers no guidance that the exact version/proper-noun form can live in the commit body (which the hook does not validate).

## Acceptance Criteria

- conventional-commits/skill.yaml explicitly states the description charset (lowercase letters, digits, spaces, hyphens only) AND that exact version numbers/dots and proper-noun capitalization belong in the free-form commit body, not the subject; includes the Font Awesome and version-number examples.
- Guidance stays honest that this is stricter than the CC v1.0.0 spec (spec puts no charset limit on the description; body is free-form).
- commit-msg.py error output names the specific disallowed character(s) in the description.
- Catalog rebuilt; projected skill verified in sync (skills-check); commit-msg hook tests cover the char-naming; full suite green.
payload.title: conventional-commits skill omits the description charset rule the commit-msg hook enforces

payload.acceptance_criteria: Given the tier hook installer runs at project scope when it writes the settings command then the command contains no absolute interpreter path and no absolute repository path so the settings file stays committable and portable across machines and platforms, and given it runs at user scope then an absolute path is still written because that file is machine local, with tests that assert the project scope rendering carries neither
payload.description:
## Steps to Reproduce

From the root of this repository, at the installer's default scope:

    python3 .basicly/core/kit/install_hook.py --host claude

Observed, written into `.claude/settings.json`, a tracked and committed file:

    "/home/<user>/.local/bin/python3" "/home/<user>/development/basicly/.basicly/core/kit/claude_tier_hook.py"

Both halves are machine and user specific. Expected: a command that a team can commit and that
resolves on every teammate's machine and on all three supported platforms.

The suite did not catch it because every test in `tests/test_kit_install.py` writes into `tmp_path`,
where the settings file is never a tracked file.

## Root cause

`hook_command()` in `.basicly/core/kit/install_hook.py` renders `sys.executable` and
`Path(hook_path).resolve()` unconditionally, for both scopes. Its docstring justifies this with "a
relative path would break the moment a spawn happened in a subdirectory", and
`test_the_written_command_names_the_hook_by_an_absolute_forward_slashed_path` asserts the rendering
with the same rationale, which turned the defect into a pinned requirement.

Verified 2026-08-01 against the live hooks documentation at code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks. That
rationale is CORRECT, and the counter argument recorded on this bead is WRONG. The docs say handlers
run in the current directory, not in the project root, and the current directory changes during a
session. This repository has already observed exactly that failure on 2026-07-26: a directory change
made its own relative path hook fail with `can't open file
'<repo>/docs/.basicly/core/hooks/tool-usage.py'`. So a bare relative path is not the fix.

The documented fix is a placeholder that is neither absolute nor current directory dependent:
`${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR}` expands to the project root regardless of the working directory when the hook
runs. Present 18 times in the shipped 2.1.220 binary, against three positive controls and a negative
control that returned zero.

Interpreter, decided by the owner 2026-08-01 after the alternatives were measured: `uv run` rather
than a bare `python3`. Every committer to a basicly managed repo already needs uv on PATH because the
projected git hooks run `uv run python`, so for a basicly consumer this adds no dependency at all.
`--no-python-downloads` keeps the spawn path network free and makes it fail closed rather than
fetching an interpreter. Measured overhead about 117 ms, against a path far less frequent than the
Edit and Write hooks that already pay it. A bare `python3` was rejected because Windows ships no
`python3.exe` from the python.org installer and its App Execution Alias opens the Microsoft Store,
which is a worse failure than a clean one.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given the tier hook installer runs at project scope when it writes the settings command then the
  command contains no absolute interpreter path and no absolute repository path so the settings file
  stays committable and portable across machines and platforms, and given it runs at user scope then
  an absolute path is still written because that file is machine local, with tests that assert the
  project scope rendering carries neither
payload.title: Write a portable command when the tier hook installs at project scope

payload.text:
FOUND 2026-08-01 by exercising the just-landed wbsz.3 installer against this repository rather than a scratch one - the failure only appears when the target settings file is TRACKED, which no test covered because every test writes into tmp_path.

MEASURED. Running python3 .basicly/core/kit/install_hook.py at the default project scope in this repo wrote this command into .claude/settings.json:

  "<redacted:posix-home-path>" "<redacted:posix-home-path>"

Both halves are machine specific and user specific. .claude/settings.json is a committed file here and in any consumer repo that shares agent configuration across a team, so the installer as shipped makes a repo uncommittable without leaking a username and a home directory layout, and the entry is broken for every teammate and every other machine. This repo forbids committing a machine or user specific absolute path outright, so the change was reverted rather than committed and this bead carries the fix.

The user scope case is NOT affected and must not be changed: ~/.claude/settings.json is machine local by definition, so an absolute path is the correct rendering there. The bug is scope specific.

WHAT MAKES THIS SUBTLE, and why the test suite passed. tests/test_kit_install.py has test_the_written_command_names_the_hook_by_an_absolute_forward_slashed_path which ASSERTS the absolute path, with the stated rationale that a relative path breaks the moment a spawn happens in a subdirectory. That rationale is an assumption I did not verify against the host docs and it is what locked the defect in. Check it properly before fixing: basicly's own managed claude hook already ships a RELATIVE command, uv run python .basicly/core/hooks/protect-generated.py, and has worked for many sessions, which is strong evidence that claude code runs hook commands from the project root and that a repo relative hook path is fine at project scope. Confirm against the live hooks documentation rather than against that inference, then invert the test.

THE HARDER HALF IS THE INTERPRETER, not the path. basicly's own hooks say uv run python, but the kit may not require uv - that is the whole point of the kit. A bare python3 is absent on many Windows installs where the launcher is py. Options to weigh: emit python3 with a documented Windows caveat; probe for an interpreter at install time and record the choice while still writing something relative; or ship a tiny launcher the host can invoke directly. Do not pick silently - the answer decides whether the kit is genuinely cross platform, and the repo targets Windows, Linux and macOS.

Filed P1 rather than P2 because the shipped default scope is the one every consumer gets first, and the failure mode is leaking a username into a commit.

payload.acceptance_criteria: Given a lane is dispatched when the supervisor prints its dispatch line then that line names the issue the requested model tier the resolved model id and its source and on completion reports the models actually observed together with whether the requested tier was honoured
payload.description:
## Context

A dispatch line names the runner adapter and nothing about the model that will actually do the
work. From `_print_dispatch` in `src/basicly/cli.py` the operator gets:

```
dispatch: basicly-jr0l.40 via claude - finished; ready to land, context 106478 tokens
```

"via claude" is the adapter name, not a model. The operator cannot tell which tier was requested,
which model id it resolved to, or whether the host honoured it -- and tier resolution is the whole
point of the models map and the injection kit. A run that silently resolved to a cheaper or dearer
model than intended is indistinguishable from a correct one at the surface.

The data is partly there already. The run record carries `model`, `model_tier`, `model_source`,
`tier_honoured`, `model_mismatch` and `observed_models`. Measured on the 2026-08-01 supervised
run of basicly-jr0l.40, though, the declared half was empty and only the observed half had
content:

```
"model": null, "model_tier": null, "model_source": null, "tier_honoured": null,
"observed_models": ["claude-haiku-4-5", "claude-opus-5"]
```

So the record proves two models were used, and neither the dispatch line nor the record says
which tier was asked for. Note also that `observed_models` is only knowable after the run, while
tier and model id are knowable before it -- the two halves belong at different moments.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a lane is dispatched when the supervisor prints its dispatch line then that line names
  the issue, the requested model tier, the resolved model id and its source, and on completion
  reports the models actually observed together with whether the requested tier was honoured
payload.title: Report the requested tier and resolved model id on the dispatch line not just the adapter name

payload.description:
## Context

Found 2026-07-31 by the tool-name investigation (see basicly-8sxf's comments for the full measured
report). This is a hardening gap in our own validator, not in a third party.

`src/basicly/agents.py` defines `WRITE_TOOLS = frozenset({"Edit", "Write", "MultiEdit",
"NotebookEdit"})` and matches it by an exact, case-SENSITIVE set intersection to decide whether an
agent declaring a read-only posture is actually read-only.

Measured against GitHub's published alias table
(`docs.github.com/en/copilot/reference/custom-agents-configuration`): copilot's tool aliases are
explicitly **case insensitive**, and its `edit` primary accepts `Edit`, `MultiEdit`, `Write` and
`NotebookEdit`. So a catalog source declaring `edit`, `write`, `create` or `notebookedit` in lowercase
would:

- pass our read-only posture check, because none of those strings is in `WRITE_TOOLS`; and
- be granted real file-writing tools on copilot, because the alias resolves case-insensitively.

Our own authoring convention is PascalCase, and `catalog lint` plus review make a lowercase
declaration unlikely today, so this is latent rather than live. It is still the exact class of defect
the posture check exists to prevent, and the fix is small.

Two adjacent facts from the same investigation worth handling here or recording as out of scope:

- `MultiEdit` is **no longer** on Claude Code's published tool list, though copilot still accepts it as
  an alias. Keeping it in `WRITE_TOOLS` is harmless and still correct for copilot.
- `NotebookEdit` alone resolves on the copilot CLI to **both** `create` and `edit` - general filesystem
  write. So the narrowest notebook-only write tool on claude becomes full write on copilot. We do not
  ship it, and this check would reject it in a read-only agent, but the asymmetry is worth a comment so
  a future author does not assume tool breadth is preserved across families.

## Steps to Reproduce

- Author an agent source declaring a read-only posture and `tools: [Read, edit]` (lowercase `edit`).
- Run `basicly catalog lint`.
- Observed: the read-only posture check passes, because `"edit"` is not in `WRITE_TOOLS`.
  Expected: it fails, because the declared tool grants writes on at least one supported family.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given an agent source that declares a read-only posture and a write-granting tool named in any
  casing when the agent lint runs then it fails naming the tool and the posture, and given the same
  source with only read tools in any casing then it passes, with tests

payload.description:
## Problem

`basicly` projects its Claude hooks into every consumer's `.claude/settings.json` with a **relative**
script path, so each one fails whenever the agent's working directory is not the repo root.

`claude_settings._agent_hook_command` renders `uv run python <hooks_relpath>/<script>`, and its
docstring justifies the shape by mirroring the pre-commit entries. That precedent does not transfer:
a pre-commit hook always runs from the repo root, while a Claude Code hook handler runs in the
**current** directory. That is the exact fact `basicly-dukb` established from the vendor docs, and
`.basicly/core/kit/install_hook.py` already ships the correct form for the tier-injection hook —
`uv run --no-project --no-python-downloads python "${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR}/..."`, where the host
substitutes the placeholder as a plain string before any shell sees it, so it also works under
PowerShell.

So the repo fixed this for the kit and left its own two projected hooks — `tool-usage` (PostToolUse)
and `protect-generated` (PreToolUse) — on the broken form. Observed live in this repo: a `cd` into a
directory outside the root made the PostToolUse hook fail with
`can't open file '<other-dir>/.basicly/core/hooks/tool-usage.py': [Errno 2] No such file or
directory`. The PreToolUse case is worse in kind: `protect-generated` is a guard, and a guard that
cannot start is not protecting anything.

This has been survivable here only because an operator carried the workaround as habit ("never use a
bare `cd`"). A consumer inherits the broken hook and none of the habit.

## Steps to Reproduce

```sh
uv run python -c "
from basicly import claude_settings
from basicly.hooks import HookSpec
print(claude_settings._agent_hook_command(
    HookSpec(id='tool-usage', script='tool-usage.py', stage='post-tool-use'),
    '.basicly/core/hooks'))
"
```

Observed - `uv run python '.basicly/core/hooks/tool-usage.py'`, a relative path. Then, from any
directory other than the repo root, that command cannot find its script. Expected - the same
`${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR}`-qualified form the kit installer already uses, so the hook resolves from any
working directory and still contains no machine-specific absolute path.

Both hook scripts are stdlib-only (no `basicly` import), so `--no-project` is safe for them, matching
the kit.

## Scope

- src/basicly/claude_settings.py
- tests/test_claude_settings.py

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given basicly projects its managed Claude hooks into a repo when the agent's working directory is
  not the repo root then each hook still resolves and runs, the projected command contains no
  machine-specific absolute path, and re-running the projection over the previous relative-path form
  replaces it rather than leaving both
payload.title: Projected claude hooks use a relative script path so they break outside the repo root

Fix: when commit_tracker_state returns False in _on_ship (and the claim commit in _start_build_leaf), append an explicit warning to the AdvanceResult detail naming the foreign paths and the recovery (stash the foreign dirt and re-run, or commit it), instead of omitting the 'tracker state committed' suffix silently.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Leave an unrelated dirty file in the base checkout (for example an edit to `.gitignore`) so it is neither staged nor part of `.beads/**`.
2. Drive any tracked issue to its ship phase and run `basicly loop advance <issue>`.
3. The advance prints "worktree torn down and issue closed" and exits 0, but no `chore(beads)` commit was made - `git status` still shows the tracker export dirty, and a push at this point ships the code without the tracker state.

Expected: the advance detail explicitly warns that the tracker-state commit was skipped, names the foreign paths that blocked it, and states the recovery.

payload.acceptance_criteria: Given a dispatched lane when it completes then the record carries the context it actually consumed and given a small change to a large file when it is sized then the estimate is not the whole file grouping and merge coupling are unchanged and no completed lane is refused
payload.description:
## Steps to Reproduce

```
uv run python -c "
from pathlib import Path
from basicly import decompose
print(decompose.scope_read_cost(Path('.'), ['src/basicly/cli.py']))"
rg -n "read only the ranges you need" .basicly/core/fragments/
```

Observed - a scope naming `cli.py` costs its whole 91,839 characters, while the harness's own always-on guidance tells the agent not to read it that way. Expected - the estimate reflects the material a lane must reason over.

## Context

The ceiling half of `basicly-3w44` is closed. This is the measure half, and it is the one that unblocks chunking.

`decompose.scope_read_cost` is "tokenized size of the existing files matching the declared scope globs" - the whole of every named file. The band compares that against a budget of "material to reason over" (`config.py`). Those are the same quantity only if a lane reads every line of every file it names, and the repo's own `tool-usage` fragment forbids exactly that: "find files by name, localize with focused search, read only the ranges you need".

**Measured over 23 real headless lane transcripts** (off-repo, under the agent's own project directory, all `entrypoint: sdk-cli`):

| Measurement | Value |
| --- | --- |
| `Read` calls that are ranged | 75% |
| median fraction of a read file actually read | 0.207 |
| same, for files over 1500 lines | 0.078 |
| same, for `cli.py` | 0.027 |
| read material falling inside the declared scope | 37% |
| Bash output tokens vs Read output tokens | 443,860 vs 390,908 |
| estimate over measured, across 17 lanes with a declared scope | 0.17x to 4.65x |
| least-squares fit | `measured = 13464 + 1.075 x scope_read_cost` |
| measured material range (median) | 6k-99k (17k) |

Two consequences. The seed factors (3.0/2.0/1.5) are about **3x the empirical slope**, and there is a **~13.5k ambient term the formula has no slot for** - Bash output alone exceeds Read output and is unmodelled. And measured material is the same order as the original 64000 ceiling, which means the ceiling was roughly right and the **measure** is the defect. The 112000 raised by 3w44 (a) is therefore a compensating adjustment for a biased estimator, not a settled value; when the estimator is fixed the ceiling should come back down, and 3w44's gate is formula-relative so it will demand that on its own.

**Sub-file scope is dead on arrival.** Proven by running the real functions, not by reasoning: `globs_overlap('cli.py','cli.py:100-200')` is `False`, `scope_read_cost` of a ranged glob is `0`, and `merge._scope_covers` misses every diff path. Eleven consumers treat a scope glob as a set of paths with no filesystem access - grouping (`decompose.py:298`), collapsing paths (`:358`), merge coupling (`merge.py:749/797/831/870`), the loop scope-collision gate (`loop.py:798`), supervise found-info folding (`supervise.py:668/724`). Only the sizing chain treats it as a quantity. So changing the glob **grammar** breaks eleven consumers and would silently parallelize two lanes on one file while writing wrong permanent coupling edges; changing only the **function applied to globs**, or adding a second field, is safe.

**Telemetry is absent in-repo.** The `tool-usage` hook matches `Bash|Skill` only (`.basicly/core/hooks/tool-usage.py:3`) - 508 entries, zero file paths. `RunRecord` has no read or context field. Runner stdout is parsed in-process and discarded (`runner.py:226`). `decompose.py:702-706` already says so.

**Order matters.** Record `context_tokens` on `RunRecord` first: one additive field, gates nothing, and it is what both this bead and the ceiling need. Fitting a formula before the field exists is how the 216x build factor happened.

The counter-argument to the leading candidate, stated so it is not rediscovered: a per-file cap alone unblocks all six false refusals **but drops `basicly-kjc5.44` - one of the two lanes that actually failed, at 99,432 measured tokens - to 0.24x**, trading a visible false refusal for an invisible false admission of the exact lane that got SIGTERMed.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a dispatched lane when it completes then the run record carries the context it actually consumed so the estimator can be fitted to a measurement rather than a proxy
- Given a small change to a large file when its scope is sized then the estimate is not the whole file and decompose does not refuse it for size alone
- Given the scope globs when the measure changes then grouping scope-overlap collision detection and merge coupling attribution behave exactly as before and a test proves each
- Given the recorded lane outcomes when the new estimator is applied then no lane that completed is refused and no lane that failed for size is admitted

## Scope

- `src/basicly/decompose.py`
- `src/basicly/run_record.py`
- `src/basicly/runner.py`
- `src/basicly/config.py`
- `tests/test_decompose.py`
- `tests/test_runner.py`
- `CHANGELOG.md`
- `docs/design/factory-design.md`
- `docs/plan/implementation-plan.md`

Widened at build time. `runner.py` is the only dispatch site that can write `context_tokens`, `config.py` carries the ceiling the estimator derives, and `3w44`'s gate is formula-relative so it demands that re-derivation on its own.
payload.title: Scope read cost sizes whole files so a small change to a large module cannot be chunked

payload.text: Baseline recorded before this lane lands, per the measure-before-dispatching rule. basicly-ipx2 just produced four DISTINCT token quantities that this bead must not conflate - conflating quantities is the defect class the epic exists to fix. (a) banded scope estimate 62548, which is 2.0 x scope_read_cost + 2780; (b) context-window occupancy 124462, which tripped the 120000 ceiling (0.6 x 200000) and forced an early finalize; (c) metered API spend 3986470 tokens; (d) the read-plus-bash material this bead's least-squares fit is denominated in. Two consequences. First, the fit measured = 13464 + 1.075 x scope_read_cost predicts 45589 for ipx2 while observed occupancy was 124462, a 2.7x under-prediction - but that is NOT a refutation, because (b) and (d) are different quantities and occupancy includes the system prompt, instructions, tool results and the agent's own output. Do not fit (d)'s formula to (b)'s ceiling. Second, the two ceilings are compared against different things already: working_set_max 112000 against (a), context ceiling 120000 against (b). This lane's estimate is 94912, so a 1.99x estimate-to-occupancy ratio would predict roughly 189000 and an overrun, while the fit predicts 62985 and none. payload.title: Tracker-only commits trigger pointless builds - investigate and fix commit discipline

payload.text: [harness-policy] checkpoint=classify approved

INVESTIGATION (root cause, with evidence): tracker commits are separated from work commits structurally, not accidentally. (1) worktree provisioning copies the BASE WORKING-TREE issues.jsonl into the new worktree (worktree.py create, basicly-djt fix 32dc562) purely so the beads-commit-msg hook recognizes freshly filed ids; (2) merge.py _assert_base_ready requires a CLEAN base checkout at landing, so any base-side tracker mutation (claim, work type, checkpoint approvals - all recorded via br from base) must be committed before the landing advance; (3) the br daemon rewrites the full jsonl export in every checkout, so a harness branch that also commits issues.jsonl guarantees a rebase conflict at merge_worktree step 1 - br sync --merge (reconcile_beads) only runs AFTER a successful merge and cannot rescue the rebase; (4) the close cannot ride the last work commit because loop._on_ship closes the issue AFTER the merge commit exists (phase order: land at build->verify, then verify gate on base, then ship checkpoint, then close). Folding the close into a work commit is therefore impossible in the current two-checkout model; the tool-br rule (close folded into the resolving commit) applies only to non-loop base-checkout work.

DECISION: the pointless builds are a CI-trigger problem, not a commit-count problem - GitHub runs the workflows per push to main regardless of content, and the expensive job is the 3-OS quality-gates matrix (and in consumer repos like <redacted:private-consumer-repo>, the scaffolded basicly-gates workflow / their own verify build). Chosen fix: (a) add paths-ignore .beads/** to the push and pull_request triggers of basicly.yml and quality-gates.yml, and to the CONSUMER_CI_WORKFLOW template so new consumer installs get it; (b) keep tracker commits separate (structural, see investigation) but cut them to exactly two per track via skill discipline: ONE pre-provisioning chore(beads) commit folding claim+work-type+classify approval, and ONE closing commit after ship; (c) push discipline: push once per track after the closing commit, never push tracker-only commits alone. Trade-off accepted: a tracker-only push skips CI commit-message validation for those commits; the local commit-msg hooks are the deterministic floor and already validated them. REJECTED (for now): engine redesign folding the close into the merge commit (git merge --no-commit + stage jsonl) - it requires reordering the loop so landing happens AFTER verify+ship approval (today code lands on main BEFORE the ship checkpoint), would also remove the duplicate base re-verify, but changes governance and feature fan-in semantics; filed separately as a design bead. NOTE for existing consumers: install never overwrites the scaffolded CI workflow, so <redacted:private-consumer-repo> must add paths-ignore .beads/** to its own workflow manually.

payload.description:
## Context

Introduced by lane `basicly-hxnf.1` during the basicly-kjc5.22 dogfood run (2026-07-26) and found
in the post-run review of what the headless lanes wrote.

The lane rewrote the `python` skill's `description` to add its new trigger and dropped a
coordinating "or" while restructuring the list. Before:

    ...creating or changing .py files wiring up a subprocess call or chasing a test that
    passes on POSIX but fails only on Windows CI...

After:

    ...creating or changing .py files wiring up a subprocess call chasing a test that
    passes on POSIX but fails only on Windows CI ... or second-guessing syntax...

So it now reads "a subprocess call chasing a test", merging two distinct triggers into one
ungrammatical phrase. The body prose the lane added is accurate and well-sourced; this is only the
description field.

It matters more than a typo because a skill `description` is the always-loaded trigger text every
agent sees in its skill list, so a garbled trigger degrades retrieval for every session in every
consuming repo — and the always-on baseline is near its character cap
(see the always-on budget notes), which is why descriptions get restructured rather than extended.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. `rg -n "subprocess call chasing" .basicly/core/skills/python/skill.yaml`
2. Observed: the two triggers are run together with no conjunction.
3. Expected: "wiring up a subprocess call, chasing a test ... or second-guessing syntax ..." — three parallel triggers.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given the python skill description when it is read then its triggers are grammatically parallel and separated and the projections are regenerated with every gate passing

## Scope

- `.basicly/core/skills/python/**`
- `.claude/skills/python/**`
- `.agents/skills/python/**`

## Scope

- `.basicly/core/skills/python/skill.yaml`

payload.description:
## Steps to Reproduce

```
sed -n '648,656p' src/basicly/decisions.py
rg -n "capture_usage" src/basicly/decisions.py src/basicly/rubrics.py
uv run python -c "
from pathlib import Path
from basicly import run_record
h = run_record.dispatch_history(Path('.'))
print([{k: e.get(k) for k in ('phase','outcome','returncode','tokens','estimated')}
       for e in h.get('basicly-tcmy.11', [])])"
```

Observed - `decisions.py:655` calls `runner.run(spec, prompt, repo_root, timeout=...)` with **no** `capture_usage=True`, so the dispatch is recorded with `estimated: True` and a chars/4 floor. `rg` for `capture_usage` in that file returns nothing. Expected - a dispatch the grant meters reports adapter usage, or the grant does not treat it as unmeterable.

## Context

**This is the live root cause of the 2026-08-02 halt that `basicly-jr0l.64` was filed for, and `jr0l.64` does not close it.** That bead attributed the halt to a lane dispatch that died in pre-flight. The record it quotes is filed under `basicly-tcmy.11` but reads `phase: decide`, `outcome: executed`, `returncode: 0`, `duration_s: 10.01`, `tokens: 182`, `estimated: true` - it is the **decider agent** invoked on the escalation the failed lane enqueued, not the lane. `jr0l.64` correctly fixed the never-started case and said so in its own commit message rather than claiming the incident.

So the halt reproduces on any pass that delegates a single decision, whether or not a lane ever fails.

**The comment asserts the property the code does not have.** Directly above the call: *"Bounded and metered like every other dispatch (basicly-kjc5.31): without the timeout a hung decider hangs the pass forever, and without the run-record its tokens never count against the session's D3 grant ceiling."* The run record is written, so the second clause is half true - but the record carries an estimate, and under `session_spend` an estimated dispatch is an unmeterable one, which zeroes the remaining budget. A reader checking whether the decider is metered finds a comment saying yes. This is the `basicly-ipx2` defect class: a claim committed beside the thing it is wrong about.

**`rubrics.py:281` omits the flag deliberately and documents why** - `capture_usage` switches some adapters' stdout to JSON and the verdict is parsed as plain text. So the fix is not simply passing the flag at both sites; whatever is done must keep the decider's answer parseable. That constraint is the actual design problem and is why this is not a one-line change.

Options, none chosen here: capture usage on a second channel (the session store already serves copilot), exempt a decider dispatch from the unmeterable count and record it as a known-estimated class, or split the run so the verdict and the usage report are separate invocations. The first is cheapest if every target adapter has a store; the second is a policy change and needs the D3 argument re-made, because it deliberately spends grant budget it cannot see.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a pass that delegates one decision to the decider when the grant is checked afterwards then it is not halted for an unmeterable dispatch
- Given a decider dispatch when its run record is read then either the usage is adapter-reported or the record names the reason it is estimated and the grant treats that class deliberately rather than as an unknown
- Given the comment at the call site when it describes metering then it matches what the call actually does and a test fails if the flag and the prose disagree
- Given a decider invocation when usage capture is added then the verdict still parses and a test proves the answer survives the change

## Scope

- `src/basicly/decisions.py`
- `src/basicly/runner.py`
- `src/basicly/rubrics.py`
- `src/basicly/policy.py`
- `tests/test_decisions.py`
- `tests/test_runner.py`
- `tests/test_rubrics.py`
- `tests/test_policy.py`
payload.title: Every delegated decision halts an L2 grant because the decider dispatch is never metered

payload.text:
Fix shape decided 2026-08-03 by the owner-driving session, so the lane implements rather than chooses:

Add runner.result_text(spec, stdout) that unwraps an adapter's usage envelope back to the agent's own text - claude-json to the .result field, claude stream-json to the last result event, codex-jsonl to the last message, copilot-session-store unchanged because its --session-id flag never touches stdout. Then pass capture_usage=True at decisions.py:655 AND at rubrics.py:305, routing both through result_text before parsing.

Do NOT take the cheap path of exempting the decider from metering the way an unstarted record is exempted. The decider is a real agent run whose spend is real; exempting it keeps the grant meter wrong in the other direction.

Why the naive one-line fix fails, so it is not re-attempted: with capture_usage=True the claude adapter emits a JSON envelope on stdout, and decisions.parse_verdict (decisions.py:562) takes first-{ to last-} and json.loads it. It would parse the ENVELOPE, find no decision key, and fail closed to an abstention - every delegated decision would silently stop being delegated. rubrics.py:281 documents omitting the flag for exactly this reason, which is why both call sites move together.

Verification that the fix works, not merely that it runs: after the change, call policy.session_spend and policy.spend_status against the real record set and show unmetered_dispatches unchanged by a decider dispatch. A passing test suite is not evidence here - the defect is a fail-open meter, and jr0l.22 was shipped and inert for 67 percent of the tracker.

If the unwrapper cannot be made to hold for codex-jsonl (codex 0.146.0 reports no model anywhere and its jsonl shape is the least observed), write .basicly/usage/needs-input.json and stop. Do not invent a fallback.

[harness-info] Owner decision, 2026-07-26. Plan section 7.2 resolved.

DECIDED: scope test-isolation and subprocess-discipline. Keep catalog-authoring always-on.

Reasoning recorded because the call is per fragment and a future session must not re-litigate it. The github.com Copilot surface reviews pull requests; it does not run tests and does not spawn subprocesses, so test-isolation and subprocess-discipline do little work there and losing them costs little. Catalog-authoring is different: a pull request that edits catalog YAML is exactly what gets reviewed on that surface, so that guidance must keep being delivered there and stays always-on.

New input that sharpened the trade, measured under basicly-agzx.1: scoping does not merely fail to help Codex, it costs it. AGENTS.md grew 7014 to 8484 chars from one scoped fragment because codex inlines scoped fragments, so each fragment scoped is a real Codex increase against a Claude and Copilot decrease. Codex caps at 12000 rather than 9000, so there is headroom, but any claim that scoping cut the baseline must name the family.

Also relevant: basicly-agzx.1 refuted the strong cliff hypothesis, so this is a cost optimisation rather than a rescue. That lowers the urgency but does not change the answer.

payload.description:
## Context

Found by review while narrowing basicly-kjc5.26 (see the `[design-narrowing]` comment there).

`merge.record_coupling` writes a **gating** `blocks` edge and justifies itself with "A `blocks`
edge onto an already-landed lane gates nothing now (that lane is done)". In the supervisor that
premise is false: `_land_green` routes a landed lane `merged`, and it then parks in verify
awaiting a human ship approval - the bead is still open. `br blocked` therefore reports the
bounced lane as blocked, and `ready_lanes` drops it.

So the D5 bounce, whose whole purpose is to send a collided lane back to its own agent to
re-apply its intent, instead holds that lane behind a human ship approval on the lane it
collided with. At autonomy ceiling L0 (every ship checkpoint is a human stop) that is
indefinite. The lane also already spent a rework attempt on the way.

`kjc5.26` sidestepped this for the pre-emptive cancel path by publishing a `kind=coupling`
found-info record instead of an edge. The bounce path still writes the edge, and it is the
path that carries the design's "the graph learns" requirement - so the fix here has to keep
the graph learning without gating the lane that is supposed to re-run.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Two session lanes whose branches touch the same file with incompatible content.
2. Run one supervisor pass over both green outcomes: `supervise.route_outcomes(repo, session, (green_a, green_b))`.
3. Observed: lane A routes `merged` (open, parked in verify awaiting ship), lane B routes
   `bounced` and gains a `blocks` edge onto A, so `br blocked` lists B and `ready_lanes` omits it.
4. Expected: B is bounced *and still dispatchable* next pass, while the missed coupling is
   recorded for future decompositions.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a bounced lane whose collision is attributed to a lane that landed but has not shipped when the next pass derives its ready set then the bounced lane is dispatchable and the missed coupling is still recorded for future decomposition with tests

## Scope

- `src/basicly/merge.py`
- `src/basicly/supervise.py`
payload.title: A missed coupling edge gates the bounced lane it is meant to teach

payload.description:
From spike basicly-zv48 dimension 3. `basicly status --json` is single-repo and self-labelled (STATUS_SCHEMA_VERSION) "for fleet loops", and every dispatch drops a run-record into `.basicly/usage/`, but basicly does no aggregation across the housed repos of the dev workspace.

Add a read-only fleet rollup: `basicly status --fleet [--root PATH]` discovers the basicly-installed repos under the workspace root and rolls up, per repo, the `status --json` snapshot plus a run-record summary into one JSON payload. JSON-first, read-only, exit 0.

Rollup model (decided): in-process — call the current engine's `_status_report(repo_root)` on each discovered repo plus `run_record.load_run_records`; a per-repo failure is captured as an `error` field, never failing the whole rollup. Default root is the parent of the current repo; `--root` overrides. Reuses the existing single-repo status + run-record loaders (no new snapshot logic).

## Acceptance Criteria

- `basicly status --fleet` discovers the basicly repos (immediate subdirs of the workspace root containing a `.basicly/` dir), and emits a JSON payload `{schema_version, workspace_root, repos: [...], totals: {...}}`, sorted deterministically by repo name, exit 0.
- Each repo entry carries its name, the `status --json` payload (or an `error` string if the snapshot raises), and a run-record summary (total runs, counts by outcome, distinct agents/models, beads with runs).
- The command writes nothing anywhere (read-only) and returns 0 even when a repo is unreadable, has no `.basicly/`, or has no run-records.
- `--root PATH` overrides the discovered workspace root; the default is the parent of the current repo.
- Totals aggregate the per-repo run-record counts across the fleet.
- Full suite, ruff, ruff format, pyright, bandit, and the projection gates (basicly check / skills-check / agents-check / hooks-check) pass; verified by exercising the real command against this workspace (not just unit tests).

## Notes

- Cross-repo scope is READ-ONLY aggregation only (dimension 3's explicit ask); it respects the workspace boundary (no writes, no cross-repo mutation, no --add-dir).
- Human-formatted fleet table and a subprocess-per-repo execution model are out of scope (JSON-first, in-process).
payload.title: Observability: fleet rollup across housed repos

payload.description:
## Context

Three findings from the 2026-07-31 session retro, each traceable to a wrong statement that reached the
owner, and each preventable by one rule in an existing on-demand skill. Grouped because they are the
same class - how a claim becomes evidence - and because all three are skill edits, which cost **zero
always-on budget** (skills load on invocation). That matters: `copilot-instructions.md` has 974
characters of headroom, the tightest always-on surface, so none of this may become an
`applies_to: [all]` fragment.

### 1. A bead's third-party claim is not evidence -> `harness-loop` (build phase)

`basicly-kjc5.61`'s description asserted that models.dev "decisively" carries a `base_model` field
linking a provider serving id to the underlying model. Measured against the live endpoint before
implementing: present on **0 of 5911** records, and absent from the record schema entirely. Filed two
days earlier, so it was plausibly true once or never checked. A bead reads as authoritative because it
passed DoR, and dispatching on that text would have had an implementer build against a phantom field
and either fail or silently invent a fallback. The join that actually works is exact `name` equality
corroborated by `family`.
Rule to add: before implementing, re-verify any third-party API, CLI or schema claim the bead asserts,
and record the verification on the bead. Cheap, and it is what saved this lane.

### 2. A zero-finding scan needs a positive control -> `test-discipline`

While checking whether copilot CLI supports hooks, `strings` on the CLI binary found no hook
identifiers, and that was reported as evidence the capability was absent. A control then showed that
strings the CLI had been **directly observed emitting** (`allow-all-tools`, `premiumRequests`,
`modelMetrics`) also returned zero matches, because the JS payload is a compressed bundle. The method
was blind and the finding was retracted.
Rule to add: a search or scan that finds nothing is evidence only if the same method finds a
known-present control; without one, report the method inconclusive rather than the thing absent. The
repo already learned this shape once (a zero-finding tracker audit that had to be proved against a
known-bad item) but nothing distributes it.

### 3. Tracker semantics must be read through the engine -> `tool-br`

The owner was told `basicly-jr0l` carried an L1 grant with a 5M budget, read by regex over
`.beads/issues.jsonl`. The authoritative parse, `policy.active_grant`, reports **L3 with a 4M budget**,
because the last grant marker wins and the regex surfaced an earlier one. Same class as the existing
documented trap that `br` keeps one gate result per (gate, provider) so a gate must never be decided by
collapsing rows.
Rule to add: read tracker *semantics* - grants, gate results, derived phase - through the engine's own

payload.description:
## Context

Three tool behaviours cost an agent a wrong diagnosis or a stalled landing during the
2026-07-26 session, and none of them is written down in the skill that owns the tool. Each was
verified directly, not inferred, so the prose can state a fact rather than a caution.

1. **`python`** — this repo's floor is 3.14, where PEP 758 allows `except A, B, C:` with no
   parentheses. `src/basicly/decompose.py` uses that form. An agent reading it flagged it as a
   Python 2 syntax error and stopped to re-verify that the module imports at all.
2. **`tool-br`** — `br dep add` is idempotent (a repeat prints "Dependency already exists" and
   leaves exactly one row), and an existing edge's **type cannot be changed**: a later
   `dep add ... -t blocks` over a `related` edge is refused as a duplicate rather than upgraded.
   The second half is load-bearing for `supervise.propose_coupling_edges`, which now depends on
   whichever path records an edge first.
3. **`harness-loop`** — more than one agent session can share the one base checkout, and a
   landing mutates that shared tree. `merge._assert_base_ready` counts untracked files, so a
   second session's stray file blocks every landing, and clearing it is not the lander's call.

This is the acceptance-run subject for basicly-kjc5.22: three genuinely disjoint file scopes
(each skill projects only to its own `<skill>/` directories, verified by a projection probe), so
the governor can size them and the supervisor can run them as concurrent lanes.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given the three verified tool behaviours when the owning skills are read then each states the behaviour with its consequence and every projection gate passes

## Success Criteria

- Each of the three skills documents its behaviour and `basicly skills-check --all-default-roots` plus `basicly check` pass

payload.acceptance_criteria: Given a session tree containing a closed bead whose rework markers reached the cap when the lights out preconditions are computed then that bead contributes no violation and a covering L3 grant may delegate ship and given the same markers on an open bead then the violation still stands and ship returns to a human with tests
payload.description:
## Context

Found 2026-07-31 while landing basicly-kjc5.59 and basicly-kjc5.60. Every ship under the
basicly-kjc5 root demands a human confirm code despite an active L3 grant, and the reason the
engine prints is `rework escalation on basicly-kjc5.56 (gate verify: 2/2)`.

basicly-kjc5.56 is **closed**. It shipped 2026-07-27 with a human-answered ship checkpoint. Its
two verify-rework markers are resolved history from that landing.

`policy.lights_out_violations` walks `_session_issue_ids` (the root plus its whole transitive
parent-child tree) and, for each bead, counts `[harness-policy] rework gate=<g>` comment markers.
Once a bead reaches `max_rework` that count never decreases, because rework is recorded as
append-only comments and nothing marks an escalation resolved. So a **closed** bead's historical
escalation is read as a live session-wide violation forever.

Consequence: the L3 lights-out feature degrades permanently on any long-lived epic. The first
escalation anywhere in the tree drops every later child ship to a human for the rest of the
epic's life - basicly-kjc5 has 55+ children - and it degrades silently, since the operator only
sees that a human must approve. That is the opposite of what the D3 lights-out preconditions are
for, and basicly-u6jq.1 needs unattended operation to prove.

This is the same defect shape basicly-hsrs already fixed for grants: a grant on a **closed** root
issue is dead regardless of its markers. A marker on closed work is history, not live state.

**Not to be confused with the correct behaviour** it sits next to: an escalation on an **open**
bead is real unresolved work and must keep blocking a delegated ship. Only closed work is at
issue, so the fix must not widen what may be self-approved.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Take an epic with a child that once hit the rework cap on a required gate and has since been
   closed and shipped (basicly-kjc5 and basicly-kjc5.56 are a live example in this repo).
2. Hold an active L3 grant on the epic root with autonomy L3.
3. Drive any other child of that epic to its ship checkpoint with `basicly loop run <child> --root <epic>`.
4. Observed: ship refuses to self-approve, citing `rework escalation on <closed child> (gate verify: 2/2)`.
   Expected: a closed bead's resolved escalation does not count as a live violation, so ship
   delegates; an escalation on an open bead still refuses.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a session tree containing a closed bead whose rework markers reached the cap when the
  lights-out preconditions are computed then that bead contributes no violation and a covering L3
  grant may delegate ship, and given the same markers on an open bead then the violation still
  stands and ship returns to a human, with tests
payload.title: Stop a closed beads rework escalation from poisoning lights out forever

payload.acceptance_criteria: Given a pages deploy that failed at the deploy step when the documented recovery is followed then it re-triggers a fresh run rather than a rerun that cannot succeed and given a released tag whose published site still advertises the previous version then that divergence is detected rather than left to a human noticing it
payload.description:
## Context

Observed 2026-08-06 publishing `v0.7.1`. The site served the previous version for roughly two
hours after the release was tagged and published, so `README.md`, the GitHub release and the
landing page disagreed on the current version — on the three surfaces this repo holds to a
claim-accuracy rule.

Two separate defects, one of them self-inflicted by the obvious recovery command.

## 1. `gh run rerun` can never fix a failed pages deploy

Re-running the failed run produced:

```
Error: Multiple artifacts named "github-pages" were unexpectedly found for this
workflow run. Artifact count is 2.
```

`upload-pages-artifact` had already published a `github-pages` artifact on the first attempt;
the re-run added a second with the same name, and `deploy-pages` refuses to guess. So the
recovery is **deterministically impossible** by that route — it is not flaky, it cannot work —
and each attempt costs a full ~4-minute run before failing.

The correct recovery is a **fresh** run: `gh workflow run pages --ref main`. The workflow already
declares `workflow_dispatch`, so nothing needs adding. Confirmed working: run 31118489942
succeeded and the site moved to `v0.7.1`.

This is adjacent to a trap the workflow header already documents — a manual dispatch cancelling a
push-triggered deploy left the environment holding a deployment in `error`, which is why
`concurrency` is `group: pages, cancel-in-progress: false`. The artifact-collision variant is
recorded nowhere.

## 2. The deploy step has no retry, and pages got 13x slower

Measured durations for the same unchanged workflow:

| When | Duration | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 2026-07-31 | 19s | success |
| 2026-07-31 | 18s | success |
| 2026-08-02 | 20s | success |
| 2026-08-06 08:28 | 4m09s | success |
| 2026-08-06 14:18 | **10m19s** | **timeout** |
| 2026-08-06 16:04 | 4m28s | success |

Every run on 2026-08-06 exceeded four minutes against a ~20s baseline. The failing one reached
`in_progress` at 14:18:06 and was aborted at 14:28:20 — `deploy-pages` waiting on GitHub's Pages
API, with every build step green and the artifact uploaded.

**This is a dependency's behaviour, not a repo defect**, so treat it as requirements input rather
than something to fix upstream: `actions/deploy-pages` is given no `timeout-minutes` and no retry,
so a slow Pages API silently leaves the published site one version behind a released tag. Whether
the slowdown persists is unknown — three data points on one day is a trend, not a new baseline.
Re-measure before choosing a timeout value.

## Constraint on any fix

A longer timeout alone converts a failure into a slow success and hides the signal. Whatever
lands should make the *divergence* visible: a released tag whose site still advertises the
previous version is the condition worth detecting, and it is checkable in one request
(`curl -s <site> | grep -oE "v[0-9.]+"` against `__version__`).

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Let a `pages` run fail at the `actions/deploy-pages` step.
2. Run `gh run rerun <id> --failed`.
3. It fails with `Multiple artifacts named "github-pages"`, having spent a full run.
4. Run `gh workflow run pages --ref main` instead; it succeeds.

## Scope

- `.github/workflows/pages.yml`
- `.basicly/core/skills/release-process/skill.yaml`
payload.title: A failed pages deploy cannot be re-run and the deploy step has no retry

payload.acceptance_criteria: Given section 2.11 when it is read after this change then it records that the batch-then-bisect queue is unreachable code with the evidence states that basicly serial queue is ahead of what gastown runs withdraws the recommendation to build bisecting and names the readme-is-not-evidence failure that produced the original claim and the other six analysed repos each have a subsection with adopt and reject findings
payload.description:
## Context

`basicly-imnu.9` added section 2.11 to `docs/research/2026-07-26-sota-review.md` on 2026-07-30 and
put a factually wrong claim in it. The claim was written from gastown's README, fetched rather than
read from source:

> **Take - their merge queue is ahead of ours in one specific, adoptable way.** [...] Gastown
> *bisects* on verification failure [...] Bisecting is a pure throughput win with no new dependency
> and no LLM in the loop [...] worth filing against `merge.py`.

**The batch-then-bisect merge queue is dead code.** Verified in the clone at `649b832`:
`AssembleBatch` and `ProcessBatch` appear only at their own definitions
(`internal/refinery/batch.go:58`, `:211`) with no call sites outside tests; the config field that
would enable them is never read (`engineer.go:177-179`); `ProcessMRInfo` (`engineer.go:1321`) has no
callers at all including tests; and the Go merge engine is unreachable because the Refinery is a
Claude agent in a tmux session, with the Go-driven foreground mode returning a hard error -
*"foreground mode is deprecated; use background mode"* (`internal/refinery/manager.go:154-156`). The
agent runbook says it processes the queue **sequentially**
(`.claude/commands/patrol.md:126`). `README.md:96` and `:653-661` describe an algorithm the shipped
binary cannot run.

So the corrected conclusion inverts the original one: **basicly's strictly serial queue is ahead of
what gastown actually runs, and deterministic where gastown's is an LLM.** The full analysis also
computed bisection's break-even at a per-lane pass rate of about 0.86 for a batch of five, for
roughly 2,100 lines and a blame defect that would corrupt the coupling graph - so it should not be
filed as work, which is the opposite of what section 2.11 currently recommends.

The durable lesson is the one this repo already has a rule for and I broke anyway: a README claim is
not evidence. The first pass read gastown through a fetched README summary; every corrected fact
here came from reading source. Record that in the section rather than quietly fixing the text.

## Scope

Also absorb the other six repos from the 2026-07-30 analysis, which currently live only in
`reference-repos/_analysis/` outside the repo: `oh-my-agent`, `oh-my-openagent`, `symphony`, `ccpm`,
`Archon`, `hankweave-runtime`. One subsection each, adopt and reject, with the `file:line` evidence
that supports it - so the review is the synthesis input for the new implementation plan rather than
a set of files on one machine.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given section 2.11 when it is read after this change then it records that the batch-then-bisect queue is unreachable code with the evidence, states that basicly's serial queue is ahead of what gastown runs, withdraws the recommendation to build bisecting, and names the readme-is-not-evidence failure that produced the original claim, and the other six analysed repos each have a subsection with adopt and reject findings
payload.title: Correct the gastown merge-queue claim and absorb the seven-repo analysis

payload.description:
## Context

Owner decision 2026-07-30, after the seven-repo sweep put the question on the table: **the loop's
phases stay engine code. Declarative phases are rejected, not deferred.**

Two of the analysed projects had made phases declarative - Archon a Zod-validated node DAG in
`.archon/workflows/*.yaml`, Symphony an engine that knows only three predicates with the lifecycle in
`WORKFLOW.md` front matter - so the option was real and worth answering rather than ignoring.

Three reasons, in the order that decided it:

1. **The part that would have to move cannot move safely.** `derive_phase`
   (`src/basicly/loop_state.py:106-143`) is a five-rung predicate ladder, and most rungs are
   mechanical enough to express as data. The exception is the `verified` term -
   `gates.can_advance and (worktree is not None or has_children)`, plus ship's
   `(worktree is None or verified)`. That encodes the *landed* invariant found by incident
   `basicly-k35r`: approving ship before the landing wedged the phase with no route back to the
   merge. Expressed in YAML it becomes a boolean expression language, and the invariant lives where
   pyright cannot check it, the test suite cannot easily target it, and review will not catch a
   subtle edit. The general form of the cost is worth stating once: **every rule that moves from
   code to data leaves the type checker, the test suite, and code review.**
2. **Nobody has asked.** Zero beads request configurable phases, no consumer has raised it, and the
   eight phases were stable through the entire factory build. The repo rule is to solve the stated
   requirement rather than build a speculative abstraction.
3. **What a consumer would actually want to vary is already configuration** - `required_gates`,
   `max_rework`, the verify checks per mode, and the autonomy levels all live in `basicly.toml`.
   The demand that declarative phases would serve is largely already served.

Record honestly what the evidence does *not* show. It is tempting to argue that declarativeness
caused the determinism failures in those two projects; it did not. Archon's flaw is a disjunction in
a completion gate (`dag-executor.ts:4602`) and Symphony's is having no persistence at all. Both are
independent design errors in projects that also happened to be configurable. The correlation is not
causation, and the reason to reject is the typed-invariant argument above, not guilt by association.

Two things are adopted independently of this rejection and must not be lost with it:

- `basicly-m4zv.13` - Archon's evidence-artifact presence check, which needs no phase machinery.
- Symphony's three-predicate engine is worth reading as a **simplification prompt** for our own
  ladder rather than as a config feature: if an engine can drive a seven-stage lifecycle knowing
  only active/terminal/neither, our five rungs deserve a look for accidental complexity. Filed
  separately.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given the architecture reference and the implementation plan when each is read after this change then both record that phases stay engine code with the landed-invariant reason and the no-recorded-demand reason, both note that the correlation with those projects' determinism failures is not causation, and the plan states that declarative phases are not on the roadmap
payload.title: Record that phases stay engine code and declarative phases are rejected

payload.description:
## Context

The licence review of the seven repos swept on 2026-07-30 found **two rider-class restrictions that
the LICENSE file alone does not reveal** - the same class of finding as the `beads_rust` rider that
`references.md` section 2 exists to record. Analysis in
`reference-repos/_analysis/licenses.md`.

Five are clean stock licences: `gastown` MIT (Steve Yegge, 2025, diffed byte-exact), `oh-my-agent`
MIT, `openai/symphony` genuine stock Apache-2.0 with `NOTICE`, `ccpm` MIT (grant covers the markdown,
which matters because the reuse there is methodology and prose), `Archon` MIT. No licence file was
missing anywhere.

**`oh-my-openagent` is not open source.** `LICENSE.md` is the **Sustainable Use License 1.0**
(non-OSI): *"You may use or modify the software only for your own internal business purposes or for
non-commercial or personal use. You may distribute the software or provide it to others only if you do
so free of charge for non-commercial purposes."* Confirmed that the three files cited in review
section 2.12 - `model-resolution-pipeline.ts`, `category-model-requirements.ts`,
`model-settings-compatibility.ts` - all live under `packages/model-core/src/`, and **`model-core` has
no LICENSE of its own**, so the root SUL governs them. Only `pi-goal`, `pi-webfetch` and
`lsp-tools-mcp` carry their own; `omo-senpi/plugin/LICENSE` is a scoped MIT covering six named
portions only.

**`hankweave-runtime` carries a competition restriction through its `NOTICE.md`**, not its LICENSE:
*"By using Hankweave, you agree to Southbridge AI's Terms of Service"*, whose key provisions include
*"Competition restrictions on using Hanks to build competing products"* and *"Managed services
restrictions require prior written consent"*. basicly is a coding-agent harness and hankweave an
agent-orchestration runtime, so the restriction plausibly reaches us. Whether a NOTICE can bind at all
is genuinely unsettled - Apache-2.0 says notices are informational - and that is a question for
someone qualified, not for this bead to resolve.

## What is actually wrong in the repo right now

Two things were committed that these terms do not support, and both are mine:

1. **Review section 2.12** recommends the oh-my-openagent tier logic as *"about 400 lines of pure
   logic that ports to stdlib Python unchanged"*. Under the SUL that is not an available option.
2. **`basicly-vkh0.9`** and the **`basicly-kjc5.58` comment** carry the same recommendation shape -
   adopt these mechanisms, with source line ranges as the reference.

The sharp part: section 2.12 already contains the warning that *"reusing any of this text or deriving
an implementation from a quoted snippet requires reading that project's LICENSE first"* - written in
the same commit that then recommended derivation from two repos whose licences had not been read. The
warning was right and was not followed.

**What survives, and it is most of the value.** A licence restricts copying expression, not learning a
fact. The *measurements* stay usable and are the strongest findings: hankweave's own committed fixture
having 44.5% of events share a millisecond is a measured property of published data, not their code.
The *concepts* - declare a tier rather than a model id, return a provenance enum, clamp an unsupported
setting and record the downgrade, carry a running aggregate so the tail answers the common query - are
ideas. What must stop is treating their source as the implementation reference: no port, no snippet,
no line-by-line transcription, exactly the clean-room posture section 2.10 already sets for
`beads_rust`.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given references.md when it is read after this change then all seven repos appear in the section 1 table with revision and reuse verdict, the two restricted licences have their operative clause quoted and their consequence stated, and review section 2.12 and beads vkh0.9 and kjc5.58 no longer recommend porting or deriving from either restricted source while keeping the measurements and concepts that are unaffected
payload.title: Record the two restricted licences and withdraw the derivation recommendations

payload.acceptance_criteria: Given a written ceremony threshold when a change touches src or catalog sources then the harness loop is required and when a change is docs-only or tracker-only or config-only then a named lightweight path applies that skips the ceremony but never the hooks and the rule is stated as an imperative constraint rather than descriptive prose
payload.description:
## Context

Plan §7.1, resolved by owner decision 2026-07-26. The decision is made; this bead implements it.

DECIDED: the threshold is the touched path. The harness loop is required for any change touching `src/**` or catalog sources under `.basicly/**`. A docs-only, tracker-only, or config-only change may take a lightweight path.

Chosen because it is the only form of the rule that can be enforced rather than hoped for: a hook can check which paths a commit touches. The rule today mandates the loop for "non-trivial work", which is the agents own judgment call, so the rule is currently unenforceable - every loop decision this repo has made was an agent choosing to comply. A diff-size threshold was rejected as a poor proxy: a one-line change to a gate or a hook is exactly the kind of edit that most needs the ceremony.

The lightweight path skips the ceremony and never the hooks. That is the whole point of naming it - an unnamed escape hatch becomes "skip the loop" and then "skip the gates".

## Notes

The threshold belongs in the always-on Harness Loop fragment, and the recall measurement under basicly-agzx.1 is a reason to keep it short: content phrased as an imperative constraint is retrieved, descriptive prose is not - the one rule that scored 0/3 in both families was the only non-imperative line in the file.

Consider whether a hook can assert it, since that is the justification for choosing this form over the alternatives. If it cannot be asserted, say so rather than shipping an unenforceable rule in different words.

## Scope

- `.basicly/core/fragments/project/harness-loop.fragment.yaml`
- `docs/design/steering-surfaces-design.md`
payload.title: Write the ceremony threshold and the lightweight path below it
