payload.close_reason: Both skills authored and projected to all default roots; catalog lint, all five projection gates and verify --mode full green; always-on baseline unchanged because both landed as on-demand skills rather than fragments.
payload.description:
## Context

Three failures on 2026-08-06 were process errors the harness could have prevented, and
two of them recurred *within the same session* — which is the definition of knowledge
that belongs in the repo rather than in a head.

1. **`pgrep -f` / `pkill -f` self-match.** Both match the caller's own command line.
   `pkill -f "loop run <id>"` SIGTERMed the invoking shell (exit 144) while the target
   survived; later an `until ! pgrep -f "loop run <id>"` waiter matched itself, so its
   condition could never become true and it spun for 30 minutes **reporting a job as
   still running that had already succeeded**. The stale report is the damaging half.
2. **Monitoring commands were re-invented per lane** instead of reused, which is how the
   dotted-worktree-name trap (`basicly-jr0l.65` provisions `basicly-jr0l-65`) was
   rediscovered mid-session after it had already been observed.
3. **A valuable artifact was written to the scratchpad and destroyed.** An 846-line design
   document and the agent transcript that produced it both vanished between being written
   and being installed; only the conversation made them recoverable.

## What was done

Both rules landed as **skill** content rather than fragments, because the always-on tier
has no room: `AGENTS.md` measures 11 characters of headroom against its 12000 cap and
architecture already records that the next scoped fragment does not fit. A skill is
on-demand and costs the baseline nothing.

- `harness-loop` gains a *Watching a lane* section: the four canonical read commands, the
  dotted-name rule, the two self-match traps with their exact failure modes, and the rule
  to read a landing from its own summary rather than a filtered tail.
- `session-finish` gains two pickup-clean rules: no background process outlives the
  session, and anything worth keeping goes straight to its final path in the repo.

## What is deliberately not done, and why

No always-on fragment. The measured headroom forbids it, and forcing one in would push
codex over its cap — which is the tier that has no glob scoping and inlines everything.

## Follow-up worth considering separately

A deterministic check could catch the first class outright: a `pgrep -f`/`pkill -f` whose
pattern is not bracket-guarded is mechanically detectable in any shell a hook sees. Not
filed as part of this bead because it needs a home — the harness does not currently lint
the commands an agent runs, only the files it writes.

## Scope

- `.basicly/core/skills/harness-loop/skill.yaml`
- `.basicly/core/skills/session-finish/skill.yaml`
payload.title: Externalize the process traps that cost this session so they are harness rules not recollection

Any consumer without that stack fails every commit/push once hooks activate — release-blocking for the terminal-repo acceptance. The config-driven verify layer ([[verify.checks]] in basicly.toml, made consumer-appropriate in basicly-zrj.13.2) is what the hooks should run.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. basicly install in a non-Python repo (hooks activate).
2. Commit: pre-commit.py runs `uv run ruff check .` etc. — tool/venv missing, hook fails; push runs pytest on a repo without tests/.

## Acceptance Criteria

- pre-commit.py runs the basicly.toml [[verify.checks]] configured for mode "fast"; pre-push.py runs mode "full"; both stdlib-only (tomllib), no basicly import, standalone and manager-agnostic; empty/missing config passes with a note.
- A configured command missing from PATH fails with a one-line message (mirror verify.py's 127/126 contract), never a traceback.
- The authoring repo declares its full check set in its own basicly.toml (adds bandit and markdownlint entries) so dogfood coverage is unchanged — verified by running both hook scripts against this repo.

payload.acceptance_criteria: Given a lane runner killed by the wall clock with uncommitted changes in its worktree when the loop next advances then that work is committed on the harness branch and judged by the verify gate rather than discarded and re-dispatched as not-ready and the stall decision item is still queued so the timeout remains visible to a human with tests
payload.description:
## Context

Measured 2026-08-06 from `.basicly/usage/run-records.json` at 7bc44d0, after `basicly-m4zv.5`'s
lane died this way. **81 metered claude dispatches, 527,629,368 tokens, 413.95 USD.**

| | runs | tokens | share |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| executed | 68 | 474,355,290 | 89.9% |
| failed | 13 | 53,274,078 | 10.1% (41.99 USD) |
| *of which ran past 1100s* | **3** | **47,784,950** | **90% of all waste** |

Three runs account for nine tenths of every token this repo has spent on work that did not land.
Each was killed by `[runner] runner_timeout` after 20-30 minutes with **complete work sitting
uncommitted in its worktree**, and the harness discarded it - because committing is the *agent's*
last step, and the agent is what got killed.

```
basicly-o8p0     1801s  rc=None  21,517,477 tokens
basicly-m4zv.5   1801s  rc=None  16,387,353 tokens
basicly-kjc5.44  1201s  rc=None   9,880,120 tokens
```

`m4zv.5` is the one we can speak to directly: the work was **finished**, not partial. It passed 500
tests and 16/16 full checks unchanged, and was committed by hand with no edits. So 16.4M tokens
bought a correct change that the harness treated as a failed run.

## This is not the collision class, and fixing that did not fix this

Attempts 1-4 of the `basicly-u6jq.1` proof run failed on **shared-anchor landing collisions**;
`basicly-4746` removed the cause and `basicly-bdd4`/`basicly-m4zv.5` made the recovery converge.
That class is closed. This is a **second, unrelated** class that the same proof run now trips, and
it has no bead - the many "(context-ceiling overrun)" follow-ups are the *context* ceiling, a
different mechanism, already corrected to 1,000,000.

## The ceiling has no margin above the real work

`runner_timeout = 1800` (basicly.toml:292), deliberately below the 3600s default. Against the
measured distribution of *successful* lanes:

- longest success: `basicly-tcmy.34` at **1712s — 95.1% of the cap**
- 10 of 68 successes (15%) finished past 80% of the cap
- 2 of ~71 lanes that got past startup hit the wall clock outright (~3%)

So the ceiling sits inside the upper tail of legitimate work rather than above it. A lane 5% larger
than `tcmy.34` dies, and dies at maximum cost.

## Root cause: one timeout doing two incompatible jobs

The config comment says why 1800 was chosen: *"Lower than the 3600s default while an unsizeable
lane still defeats both dispatch cost gates (basicly-vz78): with no forward forecast, this timeout
is the only per-lane ceiling on a runaway run."*

So a **runaway guard** is standing in for a missing forecast, and it is the same number that bounds
a **legitimately long** lane. Nothing distinguishes them, so the guard cannot be loosened without
un-bounding the runaway case. Raising the number only moves the cliff.

## Fix shape — narrowed to preserving the work

**Scope narrowed 2026-08-06.** This bead originally proposed three steps. Steps 2 and 3 moved to
`basicly-lpsf` (retire the wall clock as the working bound), which is blocked on `basicly-rupz`
because today's activity probe cannot tell a thinking lane from a wedged one. What remains here
needs nothing new and recovers the loss on its own.

**Commit what the worktree holds when a lane is killed.** A timeout is the harness's decision, not
evidence against the diff, and the tree is already on disk. Commit it on the harness branch and let
the landing judge it — **verify is the right authority on a diff; a clock is not.**

Three properties make this the cheap half:

- **Agent-independent.** It needs no cooperation from a third-party CLI. `_kill_tree` terminates
  then SIGKILLs, and any scheme where the agent commits on a signal depends on `claude -p` treating
  SIGTERM as "commit now", which it does not promise. The salvage has to be harness-side.
- **It composes with what already shipped.** Today a killed lane leaves an uncommitted tree, the
  landing refuses `not-ready`, `_route_failed` charges the dispatch cap and re-dispatches — paying
  a second full run for finished work. A commit turns that refusal into a real *finding set*, which
  is exactly what `basicly-bdd4`'s brief and `basicly-m4zv.5`'s convergence check consume.
- **It cannot silently pass off unfinished work.** The commit is judged, not trusted: if verify is
  red the lane reworks with real findings; if green it lands. Either way the tokens bought
  something. Keep the stall queue item either way — a timeout is still a thing a human should see,
  and this bead must not turn one into a silent success.

Deliberately **not** in scope here: raising `runner_timeout` (that is `lpsf`, and alone it just
moves the cliff), and marking the commit in a way that lets ship close the bead without a human
seeing the timeout happened.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Dispatch a lane whose work needs more than `[runner] runner_timeout` seconds.
2. Watch the runner be killed at the deadline (`rc=None`, the run recorded `failed`).
3. Inspect the worktree: the edits are present and uncommitted.
4. Advance the loop. The landing refuses with "commit the work on `<branch>` before landing", the
   dispatch cap is charged, and the lane is re-dispatched - paying a second run for finished work.

Observed on `basicly-m4zv.5`, 2026-08-06, at 16,387,353 tokens.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/runner.py`
- `src/basicly/supervise.py`
- `basicly.toml`
- `tests/test_runner.py`
- `tests/test_supervise.py`
payload.title: A lane killed by the wall clock loses its whole run because it never commits

payload.text:
Investigated the implementation 2026-08-06 at 3269082. **The kill mechanism is not buggy** - it is
a careful piece of work - and saying so matters, because the defect is one layer up and a patch to
the mechanism would miss it.

`runner.run` (runner.py:1030-1056) spawns with `start_new_session` precisely so the dispatch is
killable as a *tree*, and on `subprocess.TimeoutExpired` it sets `timed_out`, nulls the returncode,
calls `_kill_tree` (killpg on POSIX, `taskkill /T` on Windows) and `_drain`s the pipes so buffered
output survives. `RunResult.timed_out` is a distinct field, not a returncode overload, and three
callers branch on it. All correct.

## What is actually wrong: terminal authority is on the uninformative signal

Two mechanisms watch a lane, and they have their powers backwards.

| | measures | knows if work is happening | power |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `runner_timeout` = 1800s | wall clock since spawn | **no** | **hard kill** |
| `StallWatchdog`, `stall_after` = 900s | `lane_activity` = commits + dirty tree | **yes** | flag only |

`StallWatchdog`'s docstring and config.py:1408-1410 both state the flag-not-kill choice
deliberately: *"a slow-but-working run is never cut short."* That instinct is right, but it left
the wall clock as sole executioner - and the wall clock cannot distinguish a working lane from a
wedged one. So the harness **hard-kills lanes that are demonstrably working** and **merely files a
queue item for lanes that are demonstrably wedged.**

That inversion is why the deadline ends up calibrated at 95% of the real work distribution: it is
carrying a job it has no information to do.

## Second defect, independent of the first: the salvage is asymmetric

On timeout the code rescues *buffered stdout* (`_drain`) and does nothing about the *worktree*,
which is where the run's entire value is. The routing then names the worktree explicitly -
loop.py:705 blocks with "inspect the worktree and re-dispatch", supervise.py:2395 queues a stall -
so the harness knows the tree matters and still never preserves it.

16.4M tokens of already-correct code was discarded while a few kilobytes of log was carefully
retained. That asymmetry, not the timeout value, is what makes the failure total.

## Why a cooperative fix will not work

`_kill_tree` terminates then SIGKILLs after `KILL_GRACE_S`. Extending that grace, or signalling
earlier so the agent can commit, depends on a third-party CLI treating SIGTERM as "commit now".
`claude -p` gives no such contract. **The salvage has to be harness-side** to be reliable.

## A blind spot in the probe that must be closed before the idle bound can kill

`lane_activity` (supervise.py:2136) hashes `git rev-parse HEAD` plus `git status --porcelain`. A
lane running a long test suite, or thinking, writes nothing and reads as **idle**. So making the
current probe terminal at 900s would trade one wrong kill for another - it would kill a lane
running our own 52s-to-14min gate set if it happened to be quiet.

Before the idle bound becomes terminal, the observed quiet-interval tail has to be measured and the
threshold set above it - the same discipline `basicly-m4zv.14` used for `-n auto`. The probe may
also need widening beyond git state.

Ordering against basicly-rupz, recorded because a blocks edge between them was filed and then corrected to related: **step 1 does not depend on streaming and should go first.** Committing a killed lane's worktree is agent-independent, needs no new measurement, and recovers the whole 47.8M loss on its own. **Step 2 does depend on rupz**: making the idle bound terminal is blocked on lane_activity's blind spot, and consuming the event stream is what removes it - an event is proof of life whether or not a file changed. And with per-turn usage in hand the better terminal bound is the D3 spend ceiling acting mid-dispatch, not the idle clock this bead originally proposed, so rupz partly supersedes step 2 rather than merely unblocking it. A blocks edge would have stranded step 1 behind a much larger change.

payload.description:
From spike basicly-zv48 dimension 2. `protect-generated.py` is a fail-open, Claude-specific PreToolUse hook: a tool-time bypass (or any non-Claude agent) can still stage a hand-edit to a basicly-generated file and reach a commit. Add a deterministic, agent-independent git backstop that catches it at commit time.

Design: a new pre-commit hook (`manager: git`, stdlib-only, companion to `protect-generated.py`) reads the projection manifest (`generated-manifest.json` -> `outputs` map of repo-relative path -> recorded sha256) and, for every staged generated OUTPUT whose staged blob no longer matches the hash the last `basicly build` recorded, blocks the commit. A legitimate rebuild stages the regenerated file AND the updated manifest together so hashes agree (pass); a hand-edit that skips the rebuild does not (block). Fail-safe: a missing manifest or unreadable git index exits 0 (a guardrail against accidents, not a security boundary — same stance as the PreToolUse guard).

## Acceptance Criteria

- A new pre-commit git hook blocks a commit that stages a basicly-generated output file whose staged content diverges from the projection manifest's recorded hash, naming the offending file(s) and pointing at the catalog-source + `basicly build` fix.
- A legitimate rebuild (regenerated output + updated manifest staged together) passes; a commit that stages no generated files passes; a staged deletion is not blocked (edits are the target).
- Fail-safe: a missing/unreadable manifest or a git-index read failure exits 0 (never locks a commit on the hook's own error).
- The hook is wired into `hooks.yaml` (`manager: git`, `stage: pre-commit`) and projected by `basicly hooks-build`; `basicly hooks-check` passes and the projected pre-commit config carries the entry.
- Full suite, ruff, ruff format, pyright, bandit, and the projection gates (basicly check / skills-check / agents-check / hooks-check) pass; verified by exercising a real commit (a hand-edited generated file is blocked; a clean tree commits).

## Notes

- The existing `protect-generated.py` PreToolUse guard stays as the first line (Claude tool-time); this hook is the deterministic commit-time backstop for all agents.
- Hash is compared over the staged blob bytes against the working-tree manifest (which reflects the last build); this mirrors `renderers.common.sha256_of_text` without importing basicly (hooks are standalone stdlib scripts copied to consumers).
payload.title: Guardrails: protect-generated git-stage manifest backstop

payload.acceptance_criteria: Given the calibrated build factor when it is removed then every class factor is its working-set-shaped seed the turn multiplier is applied in exactly one ratio and a regression test fails if a spend-derived factor is ever compared against the working set ceiling
payload.description:
## Steps to Reproduce

```
uv run python -c "
from pathlib import Path
from basicly import decompose, config
s = config.load_sizing_config(Path('.'))
print('seeds     :', s.build_factors)
print('calibrated:', decompose.calibrated_build_factors(Path('.'), s))
print('band max  :', s.working_set_max)
"
```

Observed - `{'task': 216.65, 'bug': 2.0, 'chore': 1.5}` against seeds `{'task': 3.0, 'bug': 2.0, 'chore': 1.5}` and a `working_set_max` of 64000. Expected - a factor in the same order as its seed, because the ceiling it is compared against did not change.

## Context

`decompose.calibrated_build_factors` computes `factor = entry["tokens"] / scope_read_cost`, where `entry["tokens"]` is the dispatch's **whole-lane cumulative token spend** and the result is multiplied by scope cost and compared against `working_set_max = 64000`, a **context-window** bound. The two are different units. The seed 3.0 models a working set; the calibration replaces it with a spend ratio, and spend is three orders of magnitude larger.

The 20 real samples on this tree, `tokens / scope`:

| class | samples | factors (min..max) | median | seed |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| task | 11 | 38.1 .. 2309.4 | **216.65** | 3.0 |
| bug | 7 | 198.0 .. 2310.1 | (seed kept) | 2.0 |
| chore | 2 | 432.2 .. 2013.0 | (seed kept) | 1.5 |

`calibration_min_samples` is 10, so only `task` has crossed the threshold. `bug` is at 7 - **three more bug dispatches and bugs are refused too**, then chore.

Consequences, all measured:

1. With factor 216.65 the largest scope that can pass is `64000 / 216.65` = about **295 tokens of scope read cost** before overhead. Every task-typed child with a scope beyond a couple of tiny files is refused permanently.
2. `basicly decompose <epic> --plan p.toml --dry-run` on a fresh 5-child epic (`basicly-uhiq`) returned `verdict: REFUSED` for 4 of 5 children. The only child that passed is the one typed `chore`, whose factor is still the seed.
3. The same factor feeds the spend forecast, which reported **$6408.66 and 13435 minutes** for a child whose real work is editing markdown.
4. The engine gets worse the more it is used: ten successful dispatches are what disabled the gate. This is a self-inflicted lockout, not a size problem.

This reframes the "size-debt deadlock" recorded in the handover. That deadlock was attributed to the size of `cli.py` (91,839) and `supervise.py` (71,222). For **bug**-typed work that attribution is right - `basicly-tcmy.9` sized at 75,648 = 37,082 x 2.0 + overhead, refused on file size alone. For **task**-typed work it is wrong: the refusals are the calibration, not the files.

Not a duplicate of `basicly-tcmy.5`, which covers the build factor's provenance and phase naming. This is a units defect in the calibration itself.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a calibrated build factor when it is computed then its numerator and the ceiling it is compared against are the same unit and a test fails if a spend-shaped numerator is compared to a working-set ceiling
- Given the twenty run records on this tree when the factors are calibrated then no class factor exceeds a bounded multiple of its seed and the bound is enforced rather than documented
- Given a five-child markdown-only epic when decompose dry-runs it then no child is refused for size and the forecast is within an order of magnitude of a real markdown lane
- Given a class that has not reached calibration_min_samples when more samples arrive then crossing the threshold cannot make a previously dispatchable child undispatchable without a recorded reason

## Scope

- `src/basicly/decompose.py`
- `src/basicly/config.py`
- `tests/test_decompose.py`
payload.title: The calibrated build factor divides whole-lane spend by scope cost so the size band refuses every task

payload.text:
BASELINE measured in base at 067ce1c BEFORE the fix, so the ACs are falsifiable at review.

DIAGNOSIS SHARPENED. forecast_spend's docstring states the invariant: 'the turn multiplier lives in exactly one ratio and the other two stay a price and a rate'. That ratio is tokens_per_working_set_token = 334. calibrated_build_factors computes whole-lane-spend / scope = 216, and whole-lane spend ALREADY contains the turn multiplier. So the multiplier is applied twice: 73603 x 216 x 334 = the 5.3 trillion token forecast. The calibration violates the invariant it was meant to serve.

The forecast PRICE is NOT defective - I initially divided cost by working set instead of by forecast tokens. Both children price at ~0.73 USD per million against a measured 0.848. Only the working-set estimate feeding it is wrong.

No run record carries a working-set measure (fields are tokens, cost, duration_s only), so the numerator cannot be corrected - hence delete rather than repair. Owner ruled: delete the calibration, keep the seeds.

BEFORE: factors {task 216.65, bug 2.0, chore 1.5}; task has 11 samples against calibration_min_samples 10; bug has 7 and chore 2, so both still hold their seeds. Three more bug dispatches breaks bugs the same way.

AFTER, predicted with seed factors against band max 64000 - THE FIX DOES NOT UNBLOCK EVERYTHING AND MUST NOT CLAIM TO:
  uhiq child0 de-reference code    scope  73603 x3.0 = 220809  STILL REFUSED
  uhiq child1 delete orphans       scope  12331 x1.5 =  18496  PASS
  uhiq child2 classify designs     scope 120667 x3.0 = 362001  STILL REFUSED
  uhiq child3 reconcile arch       scope  32519 x3.0 =  97557  STILL REFUSED
  uhiq child4 plan as index        scope  20311 x3.0 =  60933  PASS
Two of five pass. The other three refuse on honest scope read cost times seed factor - that is the real size-debt deadlock and it is a separate problem from this bead. An AC claiming the epic decomposes cleanly after this fix would be false.

z2wi's own scope is 46256 x2.0 = 92512, over the band, so this is a manual lane.

payload.description:
The tool-usage PostToolUse hook (.basicly/core/hooks/tool-usage.py) is meant to count each shell command's pipeline heads, but it also records argument words and here-doc/commit-message body words as if they were command heads. In a real session it logged tokens like 'Refine', 'musical', 'portable', '--description', 'G_MODEL' alongside git/gh/br. This pollutes 'basicly usage report' with non-commands and makes the never-used-skill culling signal unreliable.

Root cause: tools_in_command() splits the raw command on pipeline operators (| && ; and newline) with a regex BEFORE tokenizing, so operators and newlines that appear INSIDE a quoted string (a multi-line 'git commit -m' body, a 'gh --title/--body' with a semicolon) shatter the quoted text into fake segments whose first word is then counted as a command head. Heredoc bodies are already stripped (basicly-587); quoted-string bodies are not.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Run a command whose args include a multi-word quoted string with an operator or newline, e.g. 'git commit -m' with a multi-line body, or 'gh pr create --title "add x; ship it"', or a 'python3 - <<PY' heredoc.
2. Inspect .basicly/usage/tool-usage.json.
3. Observe body words (musical, portable, --description, ship) recorded as keys alongside the real commands.

## Acceptance Criteria

- tools_in_command() splits into pipeline segments in a quote-aware way: | && ; and newline that occur inside single/double quotes do NOT start a new segment, so quoted-string contents, flag values, and heredoc bodies are never counted.
- Only the real command at each pipeline head is counted; wrappers (uv/npx/...) still unwrap; builtins/env-assignments still skipped.
- Regression test covers a multi-line 'git commit -m' body AND a <<'PY' heredoc, asserting only the real commands are counted.
- Full test suite green.
payload.title: tool-usage hook counts heredoc/argument words as command heads

payload.acceptance_criteria: Given a fresh consumer repo with basicly installed and no operator memory when an agent is asked to drive a supervised run then every fact it needs is available from a command a skill or the projected instructions and no step depends on knowledge that exists only in an agent private memory
payload.description:
## Context

Owner, 2026-08-01: **"If you need to go search your memory to run basicly correctly, we are doing
it wrong."** A consumer who installs basicly inherits the engine, the projected instructions, the
skills and the hooks — and none of an operator's accumulated recollection. So any knowledge required
to run basicly correctly that lives only in an agent's private memory is an undocumented runtime
dependency, and the consumer hits the failure the operator learned to avoid.

Externalize in this priority order, owner-specified:

1. **Deterministic** -> a script, a command, or a gate. The engine answers it; nobody recalls it.
2. **Semi-deterministic** -> a script plus a skill (the skill carries the judgment and references
   the script).
3. **Non-deterministic** -> instructions and skills.

## Audit, 2026-08-01

An operator memory of 58 entries was classified against what the repo actually enforces. Three
groups came out.

**Group A - required to run basicly, NOT externalized.** These are the defects.

- The **supervised-run runbook** does not exist in the catalog. `loop supervise` appears only in
  `docs/design/factory-design.md` and `docs/architecture/architecture.md` (which describe the
  system, not how to drive it) and in the `harness-client` skill (which is about attaching as a
  second observer). The `harness-loop` skill, 271 lines, barely mentions supervise, grants or
  budget. Everything about starting a run - mint a grant, size the budget from measured cost, check
  the base is clean, know which runner will meter spend - was operator memory.
- **`FORCE_COLOR` breaks the piped-output test: zero mentions anywhere in the repo.** Pure memory.
- Budget sizing from measured per-lane cost: the numbers exist in run records, but nothing reads
  them and says "a 5-lane pass needs about this much".
- `br` read patterns: `br list --json` caps at ~50 and drops closed rows, so a whole-tracker
  question must read `.beads/issues.jsonl`. A zero-finding audit was silently wrong once because of
  this.
- The tracker export re-adds `source_repo_path` on every write, so a scrub is required before
  staging. Loop landings scrub automatically; an out-of-loop write does not, and the operator
  remembers.

**Group B - required, and ALREADY externalized.** The memory entry is redundant history, which is
fine and needs no work: the loop landing guards (`4psl`, `9niw`, `o0q3`), the commit-message rules
(the `commit-msg` and `beads-commit-msg` hooks plus `basicly commit`), the lint rules (ruff,
markdownlint), the deny-list, `--all-default-roots`.

**Group C - not about running basicly.** Agent working discipline and project state: verification
habits, session history, measurements, Claude-Code-specific facts. These legitimately stay in an
agent's memory or a handover, and are out of scope here.

## Scope

Children, one per tier. Filed separately so each can be prioritized on its own.

- **Tier 1, done in this session**: `basicly-f3mi` (projected Claude hooks used a relative script
  path, so every consumer's hook broke outside the repo root - the exact defect an operator was
  papering over with a "never use a bare cd" note) and `basicly loop preflight <root>`, a read-only
  command that answers the whole pre-run checklist and exits non-zero when a run would be blocked.
- **Tier 1, remaining**: environment preconditions the engine should assert rather than an operator
  recall - `FORCE_COLOR`, the node resolution that differs in non-interactive shells, and an
  automatic export scrub on the out-of-loop `br` write path.
- **Tier 2**: a `harness-supervise` runbook skill (or a `harness-loop` section) that carries the
  judgment around a run and points at `loop preflight` for the facts.
- **Tier 3**: fold the verification-discipline rules into `test-discipline` and `harness-loop`.

## Measuring it

`.scripts/recall_eval.py` already measures whether an agent recalls the always-on baseline **with
every file read denied**, which is the right shape for this question: can an agent operate correctly
from what the repo projects and nothing else? Extending it to cover the operational runbook, rather
than only the always-on rules, is how this epic gets a number instead of an opinion.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a fresh consumer repo with basicly installed and no operator memory when an agent is asked
  to drive a supervised run then every fact it needs is available from a command, a skill or the
  projected instructions, and no step depends on knowledge that exists only in an agent's private
  memory

payload.description:
## Context

Tier 3 of basicly-ze8z: non-deterministic, so instructions and skills.

Four rules earned by repeated real incidents are currently only in an operator's memory. Each is a general discipline rather than a basicly fact, which is why they belong in a skill rather than a gate:

- **A closed blocker is not a working gate.** A closed bead proves the code exists, not that the gate binds. `jr0l.22` was shipped, tested and inert for 67% of the tracker, and reading it as discharged risk cost a 36% grant overrun. Probe the gate's own functions against the real inputs first; a gate that fails open on missing input reports success indistinguishably from one that passed.
- **A broad test break is a layer error.** When one edit reddens many tests, read three of them before touching either side: they are collectively describing an invariant of the layer you reached into. Fourteen tests went red on a probe placed one layer too low; moving it fixed all fourteen with no assertion loosened.
- **Print the sample before choosing an estimator.** Two of three attempts at a spend bound were refuted by the data, not by argument: the population was bimodal, so any high quantile bounded cheap work using expensive work.
- **A capability fix can arm a pre-existing safety hole.** Removing a manual step removes whatever that step was implicitly authorizing. Letting the supervisor seed its own lanes put an ungranted session - which had no spend ceiling at all - one command from dispatching five metered agents.

Homes: the first three fit `test-discipline` and `harness-loop`; the fourth is a review habit and fits `harness-loop` or `session-finish`. Author as catalog YAML per the `catalog-authoring` skill, never a discoverable .md.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given an agent working in this repo when it verifies a claim or lands a change then these four rules reach it from a projected skill rather than from an operator memory and each one names the incident that earned it

payload.description:
The missing half of upgrade: `basicly install` must sync `.basicly/core/` to the bundled catalog version, not just materialize missing files. Core is managed/read-only (§4.2), so upstream wins there; the overlay is never touched. Uses the basicly-8fg provenance snapshot to distinguish upstream changes from user hand-edits.

Sync rules per bundled/on-disk/recorded hash triple:
- missing on disk -> write (new file)
- disk == bundled -> unchanged
- disk == recorded, bundled differs -> upstream change -> overwrite
- disk != recorded (or no snapshot) -> hand-edit -> warn + skip, `--force` overwrites
- on disk, not in bundle, disk == recorded -> upstream removed -> delete
- on disk, not in bundle, disk != recorded or unknown origin -> warn + keep (never delete unknown content)

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given an older installed core and a newer bundled catalog: changed core files are overwritten, upstream-removed core files are deleted, overlay fragments/overrides and basicly.toml are byte-for-byte untouched.
- A hand-edited core file (hash mismatch vs .basicly/state/install.json) is not silently clobbered: warn and skip by default, `--force` overwrites; both paths tested.
- Files present in core but unknown to both the bundle and the snapshot are kept with a warning, never deleted.
- After sync, install re-snapshots provenance and rebuilds artifacts so generated files match the new core.
- Tests cover: new/changed/removed upstream files, hand-edit skip and --force, unknown-file keep, overlay untouched.
payload.title: Core catalog upgrade sync: overwrite managed core from bundled catalog, prune removed files, protect hand-edits

payload.description:
Found while shipping basicly-zrj.12.1 (2026-07-15): creating a harness worktree runs pre-commit install from the WORKTREE venv, but git worktrees share .git/hooks with the base checkout, so the installed hook shims embed the worktree venv pre-commit path. Worktree teardown deletes that venv, leaving the base checkout with broken hooks (every commit fails with pre-commit not found) until basicly hooks-build is re-run manually.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. In the base checkout, run `basicly worktree create <name>` (or let `basicly loop advance` provision one) in an environment where `pre-commit` resolves via the worktree venv (`uv run` fallback in hooks.install_hooks with cwd=worktree).
2. Observe `.git/hooks/pre-commit` (shared common dir) now embeds `<repo>.worktrees/<name>/.venv/...` paths.
3. Tear the worktree down (`basicly worktree cleanup <name>` or loop ship).
4. Attempt any commit in the base checkout: the hook shim fails (pre-commit executable gone) until `basicly hooks-build` is re-run manually. Bit the team three times on 2026-07-15.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Creating and tearing down a worktree leaves the base checkout hooks working: a commit in the base checkout succeeds immediately after worktree cleanup.
- Either provision installs hooks in a worktree-safe way (e.g. core.hooksPath per worktree, or shims that resolve pre-commit from PATH/repo venv) or teardown reinstalls hooks from the base checkout.
- Regression test covering create -> teardown -> base-checkout hook run.

## Context

payload.description:
## Context

The harness enforces itself at **commit time**, through 14 projected git hooks. That is one
boundary, and it is the last one: a git hook fires after the agent has already spent the
tokens that produced the violation. The coding agent's own hook surface fires *during* the
work, which is where a cheaper refusal lives.

`factory-loop-requirements.md` section 3.3 argues exactly this for the plan gate — Shingo's
*"source > self-check > successive"* inspection placement, and Theory of Constraints'
"inspect before the constraint". A pre-tool-use hook is the source; a git hook is
successive.

## What must be established BEFORE building, because the docs disagree

Two documents contradict each other on whether the surface even exists:

```text
architecture.md:1871   "Agent hooks for Claude Code and Copilot | shipped"
tier-kit.md:55         on copilot 1.0.77 there is "no hook surface at all: no hooks
                        directory under ~/.copilot, no hook key in its settings.json,
                        no hook option in --help"  -- after three probes
```

`tier-kit.md`'s claim is a dated probe of a third-party CLI, so **both may now be stale**.
The first task on this bead is to re-establish the fact against each vendor's current
documentation and installed binary, per the `interface-facts` skill: never from recall, and
recording the probe so the next reader inherits it. If Copilot still has no hook surface,
this bead ships Claude-only and says so on a consumer-facing surface rather than
advertising parity it does not have — the failure `basicly-irrm` already caught once, where
the README advertised three agents and the ledger held dispatches for one.

## Shape, once the facts are in

Claude Code exposes lifecycle hooks (pre/post tool use, session start, stop). The harness
already owns the checks worth firing there: scope-collision detection, the module-size
ratchet, the plan gate's entry predicate, and the needs-input protocol. Projecting a subset
into the agent's own hook surface makes them refuse *before* the edit rather than at the
commit.

Constraints:
- **The git hooks remain the deterministic floor.** An agent hook is an additional,
  earlier surface, never a replacement — a consumer on a host with no hook support must
  still get the same guarantees at commit time. This mirrors the existing capability-tier
  problem (`basicly-imnu.3`): state the tier delivered, do not imply parity.
- **Projected from the catalog**, like every other surface, so a consumer receives them
  through `basicly install`.
- **No hook may be a silent no-op.** The repo's own root-cause finding is that an
  instrument built and never connected is its recurring defect class; a projected hook that
  the host never invokes is exactly that, so this bead owes a check that the hook fired.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a host whose hook surface is present, when a projected agent hook is installed and
  the agent performs the triggering action, then the hook runs - check: a test asserts the
  hook is invoked and its refusal reaches the agent, not merely that the file exists.
- Given a host with no hook surface, when the harness is installed, then the delivered
  capability tier is reported rather than assumed - check: `uv run basicly status` names
  which agent-hook surfaces are active and which are unavailable.
- Given the git hooks, when agent hooks are added, then the commit-time guarantees are
  unchanged - check: `uv run basicly verify --mode full` and the existing hook tests pass.

## Demonstration

`uv run basicly install` in a fresh consumer repo projects the agent hooks; performing the
triggering action in that repo produces the harness's refusal before the edit lands, and
`basicly status` names the tier delivered.

## Scope

- `.basicly/core/hooks/**`
- `src/basicly/hooks.py`
- `src/basicly/claude_settings.py`
- `tests/test_hooks.py`

## Plan

- integrity: `L3`
- budget: `120000`
- depends on: none
payload.title: Carry the harness gates into the coding agent hooks beside the git hooks

payload.text:
Copilot half re-probed and settled 2026-08-08 by the owner's question 'will you implement copilot CLI hooks?'. The answer is NO, and not on priority grounds - there is no surface to implement against:

    copilot --version                    GitHub Copilot CLI 1.0.77
    copilot --help | grep -i hook        (nothing)
    ls -a ~/.copilot | grep -i hook      (no hooks dir)
    grep -i hook ~/.copilot/config.json  (no hook key)

Three earlier probes of a repo-level .github/hooks/*.json also never fired it - on agent delegation, on a shell tool with --allow-all-tools, and on the same without it. Pinned to 1.0.77 because copilot self-updates.

So this bead ships CLAUDE-ONLY and says so. Three consequences for its acceptance criteria:

1. The capability tier must be REPORTED, not implied. basicly-imnu.3 already owns 'declare the tier install actually delivered'; this is the same defect one surface over. Advertising hook parity we do not have is what basicly-irrm caught once already, when the README advertised three agents and the ledger held dispatches for one.
2. The git hooks remain the deterministic floor for every family. An agent hook is an earlier surface, never a replacement - a consumer on a host with no hook support must still get the same guarantee at commit time.
3. Do NOT cite  on the copilot binary as evidence either way. It returns zero for preToolUse, modifiedArgs AND subagent_type - and subagent_type is a positive control that must be present, so the zero is a property of the probe (the 176M bundle is compressed), not of the binary.

What would reopen it: Copilot documents preToolUse with modifiedArgs, so the capability may exist SDK-only rather than CLI-only. payload.description:
## Context

Found 2026-08-07 by exercising `basicly-u6jq.2` on live work, hours after it landed. The
delegated decompose proposer is dispatched, produces a plan, and the plan is then refused or
lands a child that cannot be built - **because the prompt does not carry rules the
`harness-loop` skill states**. Two instances, same root cause.

Both are cheap to fix and both convert a delegated phase back into a human stop, which is the
exact thing the dark factory exists to remove.

## Steps to Reproduce

### Instance 1 - `shared` prose contradicts the output contract

1. Take a bead whose scope includes a shared anchor (a README or an architecture status
   table). `basicly-imnu.2` is one.
2. Run `basicly loop run basicly-imnu.2 --work-type feature --root basicly-imnu.2`.

Observed:

```
[blocked] classify -> classify: decompose needs an agent-proposed child plan; the proposed
child plan failed the plan schema: children[0] 'shared' entry
'docs/architecture/architecture.md' is not in that child's 'scope'; declare the path in
'scope' too, so the recorded scope stays the whole truth (needs input: children)
```

Expected: the plan validates, or the proposer is told the rule it must satisfy.

The cause is a contradiction inside one prompt in `src/basicly/loop.py`, about seven lines
apart. The prose:

> list under 'shared' any literal path the child touches **but does not own**

The output contract immediately below it:

> `"shared": ["<literal path already in scope>", ...]`

These say opposite things. A path a child "does not own" is precisely a path not in its
`scope`, and the validator enforces the second reading - `shared` must be a subset of
`scope`. A proposer that follows the prose, which is stated first and in natural language,
is refused every time.

`.basicly/core/skills/harness-loop/skill.yaml` has it right: "also list in `shared` any
literal path **from its `scope`** the child only appends its own entry to". The prompt's
prose diverged from the skill it implements.

### Instance 2 - the proposer types a leaf-shaped child as `feature`

1. Run the same proposer against `basicly-3ifz`.
2. It produced `basicly-3ifz.1` - a good plan, five well-formed acceptance criteria, correct
   scope - typed **`feature`**.

Observed: `basicly-3ifz.1` is a single coherent change (one new module, one CLI subcommand,
two test files) and a `feature` blocks at decompose demanding a child plan of its own,
provisioning no worktree. It had to be retyped by hand to `task` before it could be built.

Expected: the proposer classifies a child by shape.

The cause is that the prompt states the enum, `"type": "<bug|chore|task|feature>"`, and gives
no rule for choosing. The skill does give the rule: "classify by shape, not by ambition: one
coherent change is a `task`, and only work that genuinely fans out into separately landable
children is a `feature`. A `feature` blocks at decompose demanding a child plan and
provisions no worktree, so a leaf-shaped bead filed as one stalls before any code is
written."

## Cost

Measured this session: two proposer dispatches at 64,789 and 69,082 tokens. Cheap per
occurrence, but instance 1 blocks the lane outright and instance 2 lands a child that stalls
on its first dispatch. A shared anchor is the common case for a fan-out, not the rare one.

## Fix

Carry both rules into the prompt from the skill that already states them. For instance 1
correct the prose - it is the wrong half. **Do not relax the validator**, which is right for
the reason its own message gives: the recorded scope has to stay the whole truth, and a
`shared` path outside `scope` is a file the child writes without declaring.

Add a regression test that the prompt and the plan validator agree on the subset rule. A
contradiction between two strings in one prompt is caught by no existing gate, which is why
this reached live work.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given the decompose proposer prompt when it is generated then it states the shared-is-a-subset-of-scope rule exactly once and in one direction, carries the classify-by-shape rule for a child type, and a test fails if the prompt and the plan validator disagree on either rule

## Scope

- `src/basicly/loop.py`
- `tests/test_loop.py`
payload.title: The decompose proposer prompt contradicts its own plan schema

payload.description:
## Context

`basicly-r4jm` gave seven of the eight named artifacts a schema. `solution-design` is the
exception, and deliberately so rather than by omission.

D17 (`factory-loop.md:95`) decides it is **markdown with six machine-checked sections**, not a
JSON payload: 'Structured markdown is the only shape that is both readable and checkable - JSON is
unreadable and prose is unactionable.' Every other handoff artifact is a JSON payload validated by
`handoff.record` against a `<kind>.schema.json` and persisted as a compact `[harness-artifact]`
marker. Those are two different mechanisms.

So the question is not 'write the missing schema'. It is whether `solution-design` belongs to the
handoff family at all, and if it does, what validates it - a section checker like the DoR gate
already uses, or a JSON schema over a payload derived from the sections.

Also found while correcting the table: `factory-loop.md:139` still says 'the five
`solution-design` sections' while D17 was amended to six on 2026-08-08. One of the two is wrong.

## Steps to Reproduce

- Read `factory-loop.md` section 8's artifact table: eight artifacts named.
- `ls .basicly/core/schemas/`: seven of the eight have a schema; `solution-design` has none.
- Read D17: it specifies markdown sections, which `handoff.record` cannot validate.

## Scope

- `docs/requirements/factory-loop.md`
- `src/basicly/handoff.py`

CORRECTION to my escalation answer earlier today. I answered 'retry' calling this a transient gate failure of the basicly-55yh class. That was WRONG and a future reader should not inherit it. The retry reproduced the failure identically.

The real cause, with the gate's own output which I had not read when I answered:

  Missing layer in container 'basicly': module basicly.tuning does not exist.

This is basicly-69az's mechanism on a second config surface. Verified at main:
- .importlinter is the contract file, and this lane's diff adds tuning to a layer line ('policy | tuning | verify').

payload.description:
## Context

The merge queue already has the right mechanism for a generated artifact
(`basicly-lyro`): a path in `[worktree] generated_paths` is not merged, both sides are
discarded and `regenerate_command` rebuilds it from the tree the rebase produced. Measured
2026-08-08, it covers exactly one file:

```text
generated_paths    = [".basicly/generated-manifest.json"]
regenerate_command = ["basicly", "build"]
```

`docs/plan/implementation-plan.md` carries a second generated artifact - a
`<!-- docs-claims:begin plan-current-state -->` block written by `.scripts/docs_claims.py`
holding the module count, the test-file count and the verify-check counts. Every lane that
adds a module or a test file changes it, and it conflicted on the 2026-08-08 pass.

## Two reasons the one-line fix is wrong

1. **The file is only partly generated.** The rest is hand-authored ladder prose. The
   mechanism discards *both sides*, so declaring the whole path would destroy
   hand-written changes on any lane that also edited the prose.
2. **`basicly build` cannot rebuild it.** `.scripts/docs_claims.py` is referenced from
   `basicly.toml` as a `[[verify.checks]]` entry with a `fix_command`, and from **nowhere
   in `src/basicly/`** - so the declared `regenerate_command` is a no-op for this block.

So the block must move to its own included file (or the regeneration must become
block-scoped), **and** `docs_claims.py --fix` must be reachable from the regenerate path,
before the path is declared.

## Steps to Reproduce

```text
$ grep -n 'generated_paths' basicly.toml
103:generated_paths = [".basicly/generated-manifest.json"]

$ grep -rn 'docs_claims' src/basicly/
(no output - the declared regenerate_command cannot rebuild the block)
```

Observed on pass `basicly-u2hl:bc7cc925`, 2026-08-08: two lanes each added a source
module, the second rebased, `docs/plan/implementation-plan.md` conflicted on the
docs-claims counts, and the lane bounced back for a re-dispatch.

Expected: the block is a function of the tree, so the rebase should discard both sides and
rebuild it, as it already does for `.basicly/generated-manifest.json`.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given two lanes that each add a source module, when the second rebases onto the first,
  then the docs-claims block is rebuilt from the merged tree rather than bouncing the lane
  - check: a merge-queue test lands two branches that each add a module and asserts zero
  rework recorded and a block whose counts match the merged tree.
- Given a lane that edits hand-authored prose in the same file, when it lands, then that
  prose survives - check: a test asserts an edited prose line is present after the
  regeneration path runs.

## Demonstration

`uv run python .scripts/docs_claims.py --check` passes on the merged tree after a
two-lane landing that would previously have bounced.

## Scope

- `basicly.toml`
- `docs/plan/implementation-plan.md`
- `.scripts/docs_claims.py`
- `src/basicly/merge.py`
- `tests/test_merge.py`
- `tests/test_docs_claims.py`

## Plan

- integrity: `L3`
- budget: `80000`
- depends on: none

The lane landing basicly-5p49 hit a rebase conflict on exactly the block this bead names. Two lanes forked from the same base, both regenerated the generated block in `docs/plan/implementation-plan.md`, and neither value was correct after the merge:

```text
feje  87 modules, 157 test files, 24 checks
5p49  86 modules, 158 test files, 25 checks
truth 87 modules, 159 test files, 25 checks
```

I resolved it by deleting both sides and running `docs_claims.py --fix`, which is what `[worktree] generated_paths` would have done automatically for any path listed there. That list holds one entry, `.basicly/generated-manifest.json`, with `regenerate_command`.

payload.description:
## Context

`basicly usage report` names never-used catalog skills as culling candidates. The counter behind
it is the `tool-usage` PostToolUse hook, which counts **`Skill` tool invocations**.

`basicly-ey58` (shipped 2026-08-13) made a role's declared `skills:` reach its dispatch as
injected prompt content. An injected skill is never invoked through the Skill tool, so it never
increments the counter.

Measured on 2026-08-13, immediately after ey58 landed: the never-used list names
`validate-as-consumer`, `repair-in-place`, `decompose-plan` and `root-cause` - and all four are
declared by a loop role and delivered on every matching dispatch. The report recommends culling
skills that are actively used.

This is worse than a wrong number because of what the plan already records about the same
surface: the skill listing is budgeted at 1% of the context window and the host drops
descriptions **starting with the least-invoked skills**. A culling signal that under-counts the
role skills is a feedback loop pointed at exactly the skills the factory depends on.

The fix is not to count injection as invocation - they are different deliveries with different
adherence properties. The report needs a third state: delivered-by-injection, distinct from both
invoked and never used.

## Steps to Reproduce

- `uv run basicly usage report` and read the 'Never-used catalog skills' line.
- `grep -A4 '^skills:' .claude/agents/*.md` - five roles declare skills.
- Observed: four of the five declared skills appear as culling candidates. Expected: a skill a
  role declares is reported as delivered, not as unused.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/usage_report.py`
- `tests/test_usage_report.py`

payload.description:
## Context

The loop names a persona per state and a skill per phase. **Neither exists in code.**
Measured 2026-08-08:

```text
rg -n -w -i 'dana|kai|vera|remo|juno|lumi|tala' src/basicly/   ->  0 hits
```

Seven personas designed (`agent-roster-design.md:225-303`), zero implemented — one default
runner serves every phase (`factory-loop-requirements.md:249`, `loop.py:678`). Of the five
skills in `flr` section 7, only `python-guidelines` exists; `decompose-plan`,
`validate-as-consumer`, `repair-in-place` and `root-cause` are each marked
**"nothing (gap)"** in the design and absent from `.basicly/core/skills/`.

And the three agents we *do* vendor are inert: `.claude/agents/` holds `code-reviewer`,
`security-auditor` and `test-runner`, written by `agents.sync()`, and **no dispatch code
reads that directory** — its only other consumer is `cli.py:1261`, which globs it to delete
files.

## The ordering decision this reverses, and why

`implementation-plan.md:469` records personas as *"deliberately **not** filed yet: D5's
rule admits a persona only when it differs in tier, tools or artifact, and **the artifacts
do not exist**"*. That gate has now partly opened: `basicly-u2hl.18` shipped
`implementation-plan` and `change-summary` as typed artifacts, and `u2hl.20` added the
demonstration field. So Dana (produces `implementation-plan`) and Kai (produces
`change-summary`) now differ by **artifact** and satisfy D5's own admission test.

Vera, Remo, Lumi and Tala still do not — their artifacts (`validation-transcript`,
`release-record`) are unbuilt. **This bead admits only the personas that pass the test**,
and records the others as blocked on their artifact rather than filing them speculatively.
Admitting all seven would be the accretion R3 exists to prevent.

## Constraints that must hold

- **Catalog sources, never hand-written `.md`.** Author under `.basicly/core/agents/<name>/
  agent.yaml` against `schemas/agent.schema.json`, reusing `agents/blocks/*.block.yaml`;
  `basicly catalog lint` enforces it and `.claude/agents/` is projected output.
- **Vendored to consumers.** These must reach a consumer through `basicly install`, not
  exist only here. If agents are not currently vendored by install, that gap is part of
  this bead and must be stated rather than assumed.
- **Agent-agnostic.** `agent-roster-design.md:210` forbids role prompts being Claude
  subagent files. Whether that survives is `basicly-xjd2`'s question; until it is answered
  this bead authors catalog sources that project to every root, which is compatible with
  both outcomes.
- **Each judged role carries an explicit adversarial stance** and a role-specific list of
  how *that* role goes soft. The roster requires these be **derived from recorded verdict,
  rework and adjudication history**, not invented — a generic "be rigorous" instruction is
  a no-op that costs tokens. Where history is too thin, say the list is asserted.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given the projected catalog, when the agent roots are built, then each admitted persona
  is present in every root - check: `uv run basicly agents-build && uv run basicly
  agents-check` passes and each persona file exists under `.claude/agents/`.
- Given a dispatch for a phase that names a persona, when the prompt is built, then that
  persona's instructions are used rather than the default runner's - check: a test asserts
  the phase-to-role mapping resolves and the dispatch carries the role.
- Given a persona whose artifact does not exist, when it is proposed, then it is refused by
  D5's admission test - check: a test asserts a persona differing in neither tier, tools
  nor artifact cannot be registered.

## Demonstration

`uv run basicly loop run <feature>` at DECOMPOSE dispatches Dana with the decomposer's own
instructions, and `uv run basicly usage --json` attributes the spend to that role.

## Scope

- `.basicly/core/agents/**`
- `.basicly/core/skills/**`
- `src/basicly/loop.py`
- `src/basicly/agents.py`
- `tests/test_agents.py`
- `tests/test_loop.py`

payload.text:
Scope sharpened by the owner 2026-08-08; requirements/factory-loop.md section 6 was rewritten to match and is now the spec.

Three things this bead must honour that its description understated:

1. NAMED FOR THE ROLE, NOT THE PERSONA. The catalog source is .basicly/core/agents/<role>/agent.yaml where <role> is decomposer, implementer, validator, reviewer, decider, retrospector, curator - the same vocabulary the state table in section 3.1 uses. Dana/Kai/Vera/Remo/Juno/Lumi/Tala are display-only and carry no authority; the engine keys on the role id, which is the directory name.

2. TWO CLASSES, and only one is bound to a state:
   - loop agents: dispatched by the engine at a state boundary, bound to exactly one state (two for the implementer's repair mode). All seven are missing.
   - ad-hoc agents: invoked on demand, bound to nothing, the same relationship skills already have. The three that exist - code-reviewer, security-auditor, test-runner - are ALL ad-hoc.
   A missing loop agent means that state has no specialist and falls back to the default runner. A missing ad-hoc agent costs only its own convenience.

3. THE THREE EXISTING AGENTS NEED EVALUATING, NOT ASSUMING. Each must still pass D5's admission test (differ in tier, tools or artifact), and any overlap with a loop agent about to be authored must be resolved rather than left as two things with one job: code-reviewer against reviewer, test-runner against the deterministic verify gates.

AND THE HALF THAT IS NOT AUTHORING. Measured 2026-08-08: the projection works and nothing consumes it. .claude/agents/ is written by agents.sync() and NO dispatch-path code reads an agent root; the only other consumer is cli.py:1261, which globs the directory to DELETE files. Every dispatch ends at Popen of a CLI with a prompt built inline. So authoring the sources is necessary and not sufficient - the engine must also resolve a state to a role and dispatch it. Splitting that into its own child is likely the right call at decompose.

    loop.py:594   _run_agent(ctx, ctx.issue_id, cwd)          phase='build'  -> implementer
    loop.py:1642  _run_agent(..., phase='repair')             phase='repair' -> implementer
    loop.py:1758  _run_agent(ctx, subtask_id, cwd)            phase='build'  -> implementer

_run_agent signature is (ctx, issue_id, cwd, *, prompt=None, phase='build') at loop.py:709.
classify and decompose never call _run_agent at all, so decider and decomposer cannot reach an
argv through the engine no matter what ROLE_BY_PHASE says.

So the standing claim 'only 3 of 7 loop roles can ever be invoked - classify, decompose,
build/repair' is wrong. It is 1 of 7 - implementer - reached through 2 phases that map to the
same role. The other six are definitions with no caller.

Demonstrated the hard way: the decomposition for basicly-u2hl.54 was produced by dispatching
the decomposer agent BY HAND from the driving session, because `basicly loop advance` at the
decompose boundary reports 'decompose needs an agent-proposed child plan' and blocks. The
engine has the role, the agent file and the skill, and still cannot call it.

This is the recurring shape: a closed bead proves code exists, not that the path binds.

## Acceptance Criteria

- When the engine needs a work type at intake or classify, it shall dispatch through
  `_run_agent` with `phase='classify'` so `roles.resolve_role` places `--agent decider` on
  the runner argv, under a covering grant, instead of blocking for an agent-proposed value.
- When the engine needs a child plan at decompose, it shall dispatch through `_run_agent` with
  `phase='decompose'` so `roles.resolve_role` places `--agent decomposer` on the argv.
- Where the selected runner family cannot load the role from its projected agent root, the
  engine shall dispatch the default runner rather than emit a flag the host silently drops.
- Where no covering grant exists, the engine shall block for a human exactly as it does today,
  so this changes who is dispatched and not what may be self-approved.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/loop.py`
- `src/basicly/roles.py`
- `tests/test_loop.py`
- `tests/test_roles.py`
- `src/basicly/supervise.py`
- `tests/test_supervise.py`
- `changelog.d/basicly-4xmu.fixed.md`

## Steps to Reproduce

1. `uv run basicly loop advance <feature-id>` at the decompose boundary.
2. It blocks with 'decompose needs an agent-proposed child plan'.
3. `rg -n 'resolve_role' src/basicly/` returns one call site, inside `_run_agent`.
4. `rg -n '_run_agent\(' src/basicly/loop.py` returns three call sites, none for classify or
   decompose.

payload.description:
## Context

**A ratchet bounds a file. Nothing bounds the tree.**

Measured 2026-08-14: `src/basicly/` went from **36,641 lines to 42,966 in one week** - about +17% - with every structural gate live and green throughout:

```text
module-size       306 tracked modules within the 4000-token cap or their frozen baseline
comment-density   299 tracked modules within the 50% cap or their frozen share
noqa-debt         80 suppressions across 13 codes, each at its frozen count
vulture · wired-or-deleted · lint-imports · pyright (306 files, 0 errors)   all PASS
```

Every one of those is a **per-file or per-symbol** predicate. A tree can add fifty compliant modules and no gate notices, which is exactly what happened: the `factory-loop.md` section 9 baseline of "43 modules in a six-tier DAG" is now **86 modules**, and `basicly-tcmy`'s architectural findings were written against the smaller tree.

## Why this is not just another ratchet

The existing ratchets stop a file getting worse. They actively **reward** the growth this bead is about: the cheapest way to satisfy a module-size ratchet is to add a new module, which has no frozen baseline and starts clean. So the instrument that bounds file size is the instrument that drives module count, and nothing sits above the pair.

Note the interaction already paid for: extracting code out of an oversized module raises the remaining prose share and can trip comment-density, so an extraction only satisfies both gates when the extracted unit's prose share is above its origin's. A third signal on top of two that already fight each other must be designed with that in view, not bolted on.

## What it should measure

Deliberately open, because picking the metric before looking is how the six existing ratchets got their thresholds. Candidates, to be decided against this repo's own history rather than by preference:

- module count in `src/basicly/`
- total tracked tokens across all `.py`
- the ratio of the two, which is the one that discriminates *growth* from *redistribution* - splitting one module into two moves the first and leaves the third flat

Whichever is chosen, the requirement is the same: it must **not** be maskable by an action the per-file gates reward.

## What it must not be

Not a hard cap. The repo's own standing constraint is that a sizing control with no recorded correct firing becomes observability, and this signal has no firing history at all - it does not exist yet. So it ships **reporting and falsifiable**, recorded on the run and surfaced in the pass line, and earns the right to block only after it has refused something correctly. A prediction that blocks must be right; a prediction that reports costs nothing when it is wrong.

## Acceptance

- Given the current tree, when the signal is computed, then it reports a value and the window it was computed over, and does not fail any gate.
- Given a week in which N compliant new modules are added and no existing module grows, when the signal is computed, then it moves - so growth by addition is visible where the per-file ratchets are silent.
- Given a change that splits one module into two without adding code, when the signal is computed, then it distinguishes that from real growth rather than reporting them alike.
- Given the signal, when a supervised pass runs, then its value is recorded on the run and printed in the pass line, so it is falsifiable against the ledger.
- Given the signal has never refused anything, when it is evaluated, then it does not block - it is observability until it earns a firing.

## Scope

- `.scripts/`
- `basicly.toml`
- `tests/`

## Demonstration

`uv run basicly verify --mode fast` prints the tree signal and its window beside the existing per-file ratchet lines, and a seeded tree with added-but-compliant modules moves it.

payload.description:
## Context

**The merge queue can destroy committed work and report success.** Measured twice on
2026-08-08, on two different lanes, in one session.

A lane that hits a conflict mid-build resolves it the obvious way — `git merge main` —
which produces a **merge commit whose resolution content exists in neither parent**.
The merge queue then lands the lane with `git rebase`, and `git rebase` **skips merge
commits by default** (`--rebase-merges` is not passed). The resolution evaporates. The
rebase prints `Successfully rebased and updated refs/heads/<branch>` and exits 0.

## The two incidents

```text
basicly-u2hl.20   lost  src/basicly/handoff.py           demonstration field (D18)
                        .basicly/core/schemas/implementation-plan.schema.json
                        tests/test_handoff.py            incl. the control assertion
basicly-u2hl.14   lost  tests/test_artifact_record.py    the file its own gate needs
                        changelog.d/basicly-u2hl.14.added.md
```

## Why the test suite is not a backstop

**On `u2hl.20` the suite stayed green after the loss.** The feature and the tests that
covered it were in the same dropped merge commit, so removing both left a consistent,
passing tree that silently no longer did the thing the bead shipped. A gate cannot catch
this: there is nothing left to fail.

It was found only by pinning the pre-rebase tip and diffing:

```text
$ OLD=$(git rev-parse HEAD)          # before the rebase
$ git rebase main                    # "Successfully rebased"
$ comm -23 <(git ls-tree -r --name-only $OLD | sort) \
           <(git ls-tree -r --name-only HEAD | sort)
changelog.d/basicly-u2hl.14.added.md
tests/test_artifact_record.py
```

`u2hl.14`'s loss was load-bearing: the gate that bead ships is "one test file per source
module", and the dropped file was the test for a module main already carried, so the
lane would have shipped a gate its own tree fails.

## Steps to Reproduce

```text
1. Provision a lane worktree; commit work on the harness branch.
2. In the lane, `git merge main` and resolve a conflict by writing content that is in
   neither parent (any real conflict resolution).
3. `git rebase main` (what merge.py does at landing).
4. Observe: "Successfully rebased", exit 0, and the resolution is gone.
```

Expected: a landing either preserves the resolution or refuses, naming what it could
not carry. Never both drops it and reports success.

## Shape

Three candidates, and the choice is the design question:

1. **Detect and refuse.** Cheapest and safest: before rebasing, if the branch contains a
   merge commit, either bounce it back to the lane naming the merge, or take the
   diff-vs-first-parent route deliberately. Refusing is strictly better than silently
   dropping.
2. **`git rebase --rebase-merges`.** Preserves topology, but replays merges and can
   re-raise the same conflicts; needs its own conflict handling.
3. **Land by merge rather than rebase for branches that contain merges**, keeping rebase
   for the linear case.

Whichever is chosen, the **post-landing tree diff against the pre-rebase tip must become
a check**, because that is the only thing that actually caught this. A landing that drops
a tracked path present before the rebase and absent after, which main did not delete, is
a defect by construction.

Related but not the same: `basicly-3w51` (generated block bounces) is about *conflicts
recurring*; this is about a *resolution disappearing*.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a lane branch containing a merge commit whose resolution is in neither parent,
  when the merge queue lands it, then the resolution is present in the merged tree or
  the landing refuses naming the merge commit - check: a test builds exactly that branch
  shape, lands it, and asserts the resolution content is in the tree.
- Given any landing, when it completes, then no tracked path present before the rebase
  is absent after unless main deleted it - check: a test plants a file only in a merge
  commit and asserts the landing fails rather than silently dropping it.
- Given the failure mode, when it is reproduced, then the suite catches it without
  relying on the dropped code having surviving tests - check: the assertion is over the
  tree, not over behaviour.

## Demonstration

`uv run pytest tests/test_merge.py -k rebase_merge_commit` fails on the current
implementation and passes after the fix; a real landing of a merge-carrying branch
either preserves the resolution or prints a refusal naming the commit.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/merge.py`
- `src/basicly/supervise.py`
- `tests/test_merge.py`

## Plan

- integrity: `L3`
- budget: `110000`
- depends on: none
payload.title: Stop the merge queue rebase from silently discarding a lane conflict resolution

payload.text:
Fixed 2026-08-09. Shape 1 (detect and refuse) plus the mandated post-replay tree check.

## What shipped

New module src/basicly/rebase.py owns getting a branch onto base. Two guards:

- merge_commits() refuses BEFORE the rebase runs, so nothing is destroyed and the message
  names the commit. --rebase-merges was rejected: it replays the merge and can re-raise the
  same conflicts with no attended resolver, and landing by merge would put an unreviewed
  second parent onto base. Handing it back to the lane loses nothing.
- dropped_paths() is the general backstop over the result, because refusing a known cause
  only covers the cause that is known. It subtracts paths base itself deleted (present at the
  merge base, absent in base) or every landing onto a base that deleted a file would report a
  false drop. On a drop the branch is reset to its pre-replay tip - a restoration, not a
  discard, since the target is the exact commit the replay started from.

Statuses rebase-merge-commit and rebase-dropped-paths are in PRE_GATE_STATUSES (so a one-shot
gate override survives) and deliberately NOT in CONFLICT_STATUSES: a branch git would mangle
is a branch-shape defect, not a missed scope coupling, and routing it there would record a
 edge against a lane that collided with nobody.

## The extraction this forced, which was not optional

src/basicly/merge.py was frozen at 15,401 tokens and tests/test_merge.py at 19,737, so neither
could grow by a line. The seam taken is cohesive and related, not an unrelated refactor:
'getting the branch onto base' against 'merging it into base'. rebuild_generated_conflicts and
unmerged_paths moved with it (both were private to merge.py, no external callers), and
rebase.py does not import back - merge.py maps ReplayOutcome onto its own MergeResult.

Knock-ons all real, none optional: .importlinter is exhaustive so the new module needed a tier
(placed below merge, above config|worktree); the docs-claims generated block moved 79 -> 80
engine modules; the test-naming gate required tests/test_rebase.py.

## Deviation from this bead's stated demonstration

The bead names `pytest tests/test_merge.py -k rebase_merge_commit`. The tests are in
tests/test_rebase.py instead, because the test-naming gate refuses tests for a new module left
in the file named after the module it was extracted from. Five generated-conflict tests moved
there too and were rewritten against rebase.replay directly rather than through
merge_worktree, which is the layer that now owns the behaviour.

## Evidence

Tests are against a REAL git repo, deliberately: a stubbed git cannot skip a merge commit, so
a fake could only assert we called rev-list --merges, never that the thing being guarded
against happens.

- Positive control test_a_plain_rebase_really_does_discard_the_resolution reproduces the loss
  with the old path and asserts git exits 0 while doing it. If git ever stops skipping merge
  commits this fails and the guards become dead weight - the only way anyone would find out.
- test_replay_restores_the_branch_when_the_backstop_fires blinds guard 1 by injection to prove
  guard 2 independently catches and undoes the loss.
- test_dropped_paths_ignores_a_file_base_deleted is the discriminator for the subtraction; a
  guard that cries wolf gets switched off.
- The fixture had to be corrected mid-work: a lane whose OWN commits conflict does not
  reproduce this, it just bounces. The loss is silent precisely because the lane's commits
  replay cleanly and only the merge carries content, so the fixture uses git merge --no-commit.

Gates: basicly verify --mode full = 21/21 PASS. pytest 3611 passed (+7: 12 new, 5 relocated).

Exercised as a consumer, not only as a test - a real repo, a real git worktree, a real
merge-carrying branch, landed through merge.merge_worktree:

  status : rebase-merge-commit
  detail : harness/feat carries 1 merge commit(s) `git rebase` would skip, discarding any
           resolution held only there: c523ab05... Linearize the branch and re-land.
  branch unmoved: True   resolution intact: 'resolved: neither s

Correction to the comment above: line 22 reads " edge against a lane that collided with
nobody" because a backtick pair was eaten by the shell. It should read "a `related` edge
against a lane that collided with nobody" - COUPLING_DEP_TYPE, the non-gating dependency the
queue records for a missed coupling.

payload.description:
## Context

Agent hooks are projected per family by `hooks.yaml`'s `manager` field, and the two
families are **not** at parity [M 2026-08-08]:

```text
manager: claude    protect-generated      stage=pretooluse
manager: claude    tool-usage             stage=posttooluse
manager: copilot   tool-usage-copilot     stage=posttooluse
```

So a consumer on Copilot gets the telemetry hook and **not the guard**.
`protect-generated` refuses an edit to a generated file at tool time; on Copilot that
edit is caught only later, by the `protect-generated-commit` git hook. The git floor
still holds, so nothing is unsafe — but the earlier refusal, which is the whole point
of an agent hook (`factory-loop.md` section 3.3: source inspection beats successive),
is Claude-only.

## The premise that blocked this, and why it is gone

The repo believed Copilot had **no hook surface at all**. That claim was recorded in the
tier kit and repeated into `architecture.md`, and it was **wrong** — an artifact of a
probe that looked for a `hooks/` directory under `~/.copilot`, a hook key in a
`settings.json` that simply had none set, and a `--help` that does not enumerate config
keys. None of the three was a positive control.

Corrected and fetched from the vendor 2026-08-08:

```text
config          .github/hooks/*.json  |  settings.json "hooks"  |  config.json "hooks"
                config.json "disableAllHooks" turns them all off
events          sessionStart  sessionEnd  userPromptSubmitted
                preToolUse  postToolUse  errorOccurred
preToolUse      documented as able to APPROVE or DENY a tool call
```

`preToolUse` approving or denying is exactly what `protect-generated` needs, so this is
extension rather than invention — the projection layer already routes by `manager` and
already writes a managed `.github/hooks/basicly-<id>.json`.

## What this bead is NOT

**It does not resolve tier injection.** That needs a hook to *modify* a spawn's
arguments, not to approve or deny one, and no copilot hook has been shown to fire for an
agent spawn at all (three probes on 1.0.77, `basicly-wbsz`). Approve/deny and modify are
different capabilities; keep them apart. The tier kit's static fallback stands until
someone demonstrates a spawn-time rewrite.

## Constraints

- **The git hooks remain the deterministic floor.** An agent hook is an earlier surface,
  never a replacement — a consumer on a host without one must still get the same
  guarantee at commit time.
- **Parity is a claim on a consumer surface, so it must be exercised, not asserted.**
  `basicly-irrm` already caught this shape once when the README advertised three agents
  and the ledger held dispatches for one. A projected hook that never fires is the
  instrument-built-and-never-connected defect this repo keeps rediscovering.
- Event names are the vendor's and change without our involvement; treat the mapping
  from `stage` to a copilot event as data, re-probed rather than recalled.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a hook declared `manager: claude` with a stage that has a copilot equivalent,
  when the projection runs, then an equivalent copilot hook is written - check: a test
  asserts `protect-generated` produces a `.github/hooks/` entry on `preToolUse`.
- Given the projected copilot guard, when an agent edits a generated file, then the edit
  is refused before it lands - check: drive the hook with a real `preToolUse` payload
  naming a generated path and assert the deny response; and exercise it in a live
  session, since a projected hook that never fires is the defect this bead exists to
  avoid.
- Given a stage with no copilot equivalent, when the projection runs, then it declines
  and says why rather than writing a hook that cannot fire - check: a test asserts the
  decline path and its message.

## Demonstration

`uv run basicly hooks-build && uv run basicly hooks-check` writes and verifies a copilot
`preToolUse` guard, and `ls .github/hooks/` shows it beside the existing telemetry hook.

## Scope

- `.basicly/core/hooks/hooks.yaml`
- `src/basicly/hooks.py`
- `tests/test_hooks.py`

## Plan

- integrity: `L3`
- budget: `90000`
- depends on: none
