payload.description:
## What this record is

A completed research spike of 2026-09-04, filed as permanent memory rather than as work. Its
findings are actioned by basicly-hnnmk9.5, which carries the vocabulary decision.

The load-bearing result: the sentences themselves, each checkable against a file:line or a printed
measurement, plus a 15-term glossary flagging every word used in two senses, the naming ranking
where accuracy and communicability invert, and 15 claims not to make with the evidence that
refutes each. It also corrects two figures I had passed on wrongly: 16 of 22 unaddressed deepseek
items are harness, not 17, and the README phase list omitted validate.

---

# What `basicly` is — sentences you can say out loud

Written 2026-09-04. Read-only pass over `<repo>` at `bd5e7900`+.
Nothing in that repository was created, edited or deleted. No `pytest`, no `basicly verify`,
no `basicly check`, no `pre-commit`, no writing git command.

Every sentence below is either checkable against a `file:line` in this repo, against a
measurement whose command is printed, or against one of the four research reports of today
(cited as `[foundations]`, `[inventory]`, `[agentic]`, `[dsh]`). Sentences that could not be
grounded are not here.

---

## 1. One sentence

> `basicly` is a Python CLI that projects one YAML catalog into the instruction files,
> skills, subagents and hooks each coding agent reads, and runs a work loop whose phase is
> re-derived from an append-only event ledger on every command and whose advances are
> refused by gates.

Grounding: `src/basicly/cli.py` is the single entry point; `docs/architecture/architecture.md:113`
names the two halves ("distribution plane" / "execution plane");
`src/basicly/loop_state.py:31` is `PHASES`, `:140` is `derive_phase`;
`.basicly/core/kit/tracker/events.py` is the append-only log;
`src/basicly/policy.py:413` `classify_gates` is what an advance waits on.

---

## 2. Three sentences — the elevator version

> `basicly` is a harness for coding agents that a git repository installs with one command.
>
> It writes the guidance every agent family reads from one versioned YAML catalog, installs
> git hooks that refuse a bad commit at commit time, and drives one unit of work from intake
> to a merge over a graph of records in an append-only event ledger.
>
> It exists so the process and the state live in the repository instead of in a session or a
> vendor: the loop stores no phase, so a crashed, compacted or swapped session resumes by
> re-reading the ledger.

Grounding, in order: `README.md` install section; `docs/architecture/architecture.md:8-9`
("A workflow engine that drives a unit of work from an idea to a merge, over a tracked graph
of state"); `docs/architecture/architecture.md:344` (generated vs authored);
`src/basicly/loop_state.py:140` `derive_phase`; `docs/architecture/architecture.md:2453`
(§32.2, "A record's state is a **fold over its events**").

---

## 3. A paragraph, for an engineer who will use it

> You install `basicly` into a git repo with one command. It writes the guidance your agents
> read — `CLAUDE.md`, `AGENTS.md`, `.github/copilot-instructions.md`, skills, subagents,
> permissions — from one YAML catalog plus an overlay it never overwrites, and `basicly check`
> exits non-zero when a generated file was hand-edited. It installs git hooks at pre-commit,
> commit-msg and pre-push, so a rule is refused when you commit rather than after CI. Work is
> tracked in an append-only event ledger under `.basicly/ledger/`, committed with the code,
> with no external binary or database. `basicly loop` walks one record through intake,
> classify, decompose, build, verify, validate and ship. Build runs in a sibling git worktree,
> the build-to-verify landing is the only advance that touches git history, and phase is never
> stored — every command re-derives it.

(129 words.) Grounding: `docs/architecture/architecture.md:506-520` (three trees, one
write-owner each); `:548` (§11, the projection pipeline, total sort, byte-identical rebuild);
`:920` (§16, hooks); `:2453` (§32.2, the ledger); `src/basicly/loop_state.py:31` (`PHASES`);
`docs/architecture/architecture.md:1650` (§27.1, the worktree); `:1692` (§27.2, "the only
advance that touches git history"); `src/basicly/loop.py:1481-1550` (`_verify_and_land`).

---

## 4. The two cores, named honestly

### Core 1 — the execution process (the owner's "graph engineering")

**Plain name: dependency-ordered scheduling over an event-sourced work graph.**
Short form for speech: **"the work graph"**, which is the name the README already uses.

**The established disciplines it belongs to.** Two, not one, because the code does two
separable things.

| Half | Established discipline | Primary source (from the research) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| State is a fold over a log, never a stored cursor | **Event sourcing** | Martin Fowler, *Event Sourcing*, `martinfowler.com/eaaDev/EventSourcing.html`, 2005-12-12 — current state is a fold over the log; you can "discard the application state completely and rebuild it by re-running the events from the event log" `[foundations]` |
| Sibling work is ordered by declared constraints and everything unordered runs in parallel | **Topological scheduling over declared ordering constraints** | GNU make, *Types of Prerequisites*, `gnu.org/software/make/manual/html_node/Prerequisite-Types.html` — **order-only prerequisites** impose ordering and are "never checked when determining if the target is out of date" `[foundations]`. The sort itself is Kahn, CACM 5(11):558–562, Nov 1962 (bibliographic record only; ACM refused the fetch) `[foundations]` |

For contrast, the discipline the owner's *wording* describes is a third one: **derivation
edges over typed assets**, whose canonical implementation is Dagster, where an asset declares
"a set of upstream asset keys, which refer to assets that the contents of the asset definition
are derived from" — as opposed to Airflow, where "Tasks are entirely isolated" and an edge is
execution order only `[foundations]`.

**Two-sentence definition.**
> Every fact about a unit of work is an event appended to one log, and every value the loop
> acts on — the phase, the ready set, the blocked set, the dispatch rank — is a fold over that
> log rather than a field anyone wrote. Sibling units are ordered against each other by a
> `blocks` edge, and the default source of that edge is overlap of the write scopes the plan
> declared, not the flow of one unit's result into the next.

**Files that implement it.**

| Part | Site |
| --- | --- |
| the log, and the fold that is the authority | `.basicly/core/kit/tracker/events.py` |
| the phase ladder, derived on every read | `src/basicly/loop_state.py:31` (`PHASES`), `:140` (`derive_phase`) |
| the record graph: blocked set, cycles | `src/basicly/dependency_graph.py` |
| the ready set and the rank | `.basicly/core/kit/tracker/derivation.py:277`, `.basicly/core/kit/tracker/scheduler.py` |
| the parallel/serial decision | `src/basicly/decompose.py:303` (`serializes`), `:394` (`group_children`), `:431` (`chain_predecessors`) |
| the declared sibling edge | `src/basicly/decompose.py:89` (`ChildSpec.depends_on`), `src/basicly/plan_gate.py:16-19` |
| where both become one edge type | `src/basicly/decompose.py:2042-2049` |
| what actually gets dispatched | `src/basicly/supervise.py:1672` (`ready_lanes`), `:2174` (the thread pool) |
| the one place real files are checked | `src/basicly/loop.py:1328` (`_scope_block`) |

**"Graph engineering" should be replaced, and the change is free.** The phrase has no
literature: it was coined 2026-07-18 on a vendor blog and picked up by a second vendor two
days later, and a phrase-restricted search over arxiv.org, dl.acm.org, link.springer.com and
dblp.org returned nothing in this sense, against an identically shaped control search that
returned eight primaries `[foundations]`. **The cost of dropping it is zero in the tree:**
measured just now, `rg -il 'graph engineering' .` returns nothing (exit 1), while the positive
control `rg -il 'topological' .` returns four files — `docs/reference/cli.md`,
`docs/architecture/architecture.md`, `src/basicly/cli.py`, `src/basicly/decompose.py`. The
vocabulary already in the repo is the established one. The only cost is to sentences the owner
has already said out loud.

**The four candidate names, ranked.**

| Candidate | Accuracy | Communicability | Verdict |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **a workflow engine** (drop "with typed artifacts") | 1st | 3rd | Most accurate. It is the repo's own phrase at `architecture.md:8-9`, and it is what Airflow, Dagster, Temporal and Argo all call themselves, so an engineer places it instantly. **Drop "with typed artifacts":** 3 of 8 artifact kinds have a producer (`src/basicly/handoff.py:62-71`) and 5 carry a schema nothing writes (`architecture.md:3160`) |
| **a verification harness** | 2nd | 2nd | Accurate for the largest share of the code and for the differentiator the owner names, but it undersells the scheduler and the projection. Best second sentence, not the first |
| **a dependency-ordered work scheduler** | 3rd | 4th | Precisely right about the ordering decision and silent about the gates and the projection, which are more of the code. Use it for the specific question "what runs in parallel", never as the whole |
| **a gated pipeline** | 4th | 1st | Easiest to say and partly wrong. "Pipeline" implies a fixed linear path; the loop has a detour (validate returns to verify, `architecture.md:1359-1360`), rework is a self-loop that does not move the phase (`src/basicly/loop.py:481`), and there is no cursor to advance because phase is derived |

**Most accurate and most communicable differ.** Recommended pair of sentences:
"It is a workflow engine over a work graph in an append-only ledger" (accurate), followed by
"in practice, most of it is a verification harness" (communicable, and true — see Core 2).

### Core 2 — the harness

**Plain name: a projected guidance layer plus a gate stack.** Short form: **"the harness"**,
which is already the word in the code and the skills (`harness-loop`, `[harness-policy]`
markers, `basicly loop`).

**The established disciplines it belongs to.**

| Half | Established discipline | Primary source (from the research) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| One source rendered into every consumer's own file, byte-identically | **Deterministic build / declared-input reproducibility** | Bazel's action graph declares "required inputs and expected outputs … explicitly for each action"; Nix addresses outputs by hashing the derivation or the output contents `[foundations]`. `basicly`'s analogue: the projector's sort is total, so "two builds on identical sources produce byte-identical output" (`docs/architecture/architecture.md:568-570`) |
| A harness is the separable, replaceable layer around a model | **Named as such by the vendor** | Anthropic, *Managed Agents*, `anthropic.com/engineering/managed-agents`, 2026-04-08 — a stateless harness plus an interchangeable sandbox, motivated because "harnesses encode assumptions that go stale as models improve" `[agentic]` |
| Verification is the failure class a better model does not fix | **Multi-agent failure taxonomy** | MAST, arXiv 2503.13657v3 (1600+ annotated traces, κ = 0.88): incorrect verification 9.1%, no/incomplete verification 8.2%, and both "appear frequently even in successful runs" — so a green suite is not evidence the verification layer works `[agentic]` |
| A portable instruction unit | **The Agent Skills standard** | `agentskills.io/specification`, 46 listed clients including all three of `basicly`'s families; `basicly` already projects to it at `.agents/skills` (`src/basicly/skills.py`) `[agentic]` |

**Two-sentence definition.**
> The harness is everything an agent reads and everything that refuses it: one catalog
> projected into each family's own files, plus git hooks, a declared verify pipeline, ratchets
> on measured baselines, and integrity levels that decide which gates a change owes. The loop
> cannot run without it, because a dispatch's entire context is the projected output and every
> advance waits on a verdict the same checks compute.

**Files that implement it.**

| Part | Site |
| --- | --- |
| authored sources | `.basicly/core/` (fragments, skills, agents, hooks, targets, permissions, schemas, kit) |
| select and sort | `src/basicly/planner.py` |
| render and write-if-changed | `src/basicly/projection.py`, `src/basicly/renderers/` |
| per-surface projectors | `src/basicly/skills.py`, `agents.py`, `hooks.py`, `permissions.py` |
| the verify pipeline | `src/basicly/verify.py`, contract at `src/basicly/config.py:1066-1080` (`VerifyCheck`) |
| gate classification and who may write a result | `src/basicly/policy.py:413`, `src/basicly/config.py:253` (`ENGINE_GATE_PROVIDERS`) |
| integrity levels selecting the gate set | `src/basicly/integrity.py:48` (`LEVELS`), `:178` (`_SELECTIONS`), `src/basicly/validate_gate.py:76-99` |
| ratchets | `.scripts/` checks; specified at `docs/architecture/architecture.md:3597` |
| the dispatch adapters | `src/basicly/runner.py:273-312` |

**The interconnection the owner states is real and is in the document.** The two planes "meet
at two points and nowhere else": the loop dispatches an agent whose context is the projected
guidance, and the loop's verify step runs the same checks the git hooks run
(`docs/architecture/architecture.md:275-277`). That sentence is safe to say verbatim.

**Independent support that the harness is the larger half.** `[dsh]` mined a shipped
third-party agent runtime for portable mechanisms and split the unexploited residue by the
owner's own two cores. Its conclusion: that system "has almost nothing to say about the
execution process and a great deal to say about the harness".

**Reconcile the number before quoting it.** The report's UNADDRESSED list runs #1–#22. Its
harness set is explicit — "#2–#6, #9–#16, #18, #20, #22" — which is **16 items**. Its
execution set says "Only five items: #7 and #8 and #19 …, #17 and #21", then names **#1** as
execution too in the next sentence, so the execution set is **6**. 6 + 16 = 22, and the "17 of
22" figure in the brief is the "five items" sentence subtracted from 22, counting #1 twice.
**Say 16 of 22 are harness items, or say "most of it", but do not say 17.** The direction is
unaffected, and it is a reason to lead with "workflow engine" and follow with "verification
harness" rather than the reverse.

---

## 5. Glossary — the words `basicly` already uses

`docs/architecture/architecture.md:4942` (§39) is the authoritative glossary and it already
fixes most of these. Where a term is used in two senses, the flag says so.

| Term | One plain sentence | Defined at | Two senses? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **record** | One work item in the tracker — the thing that gets classified, built and closed. | `architecture.md:4950` (glossary: `issue`); state shape at `.basicly/core/kit/tracker/events.py` (`RecordState`) | **Yes, three.** The glossary reserves `record` for the work item, but the tree also has *run records* (`.basicly/usage/run-records.json`, one dispatch's telemetry) and a `release-record` artifact kind (`src/basicly/handoff.py:65`). Say "work record" when it matters |
| **lane** | One record being worked in its own worktree, from dispatch to landing. | `architecture.md:4951`; `src/basicly/supervise.py:472` (`AdoptedLane`) | No |
| **unit** | The same work item before it is dispatched — "one unit of work". | `architecture.md:4951`; `src/basicly/wip.py:41-44` | Minor: spend is summed in "micro-units" (`.basicly/core/kit/tracker/events.py:56`), always qualified |
| **phase** | One rung of the derived ladder: intake, classify, decompose, build, verify, validate, ship, done. | `src/basicly/loop_state.py:31` (`PHASES`), `:140` (`derive_phase`); glossary `architecture.md:4954` | **Yes.** The supervisor's own dispatch telemetry writes `"phase":"lane"` and `"phase":"decide"` — a different vocabulary in the same field name `[inventory]` |
| **gate** | A verdict engine code computes, and refuses on. | glossary `architecture.md:4956`; `src/basicly/policy.py:413` (`classify_gates`) | **Yes, in prose.** Only two providers count toward a required gate (`src/basicly/config.py:253`); anything else is `disregarded`. But the README and CI also call git hooks and workflows "gates", which is the broad sense |
| **checkpoint** | An approval marker a human (or a covering grant) writes; nothing is computed. | glossary `architecture.md:4957`; `src/basicly/config.py:391` (`CHECKPOINTS`); `src/basicly/policy.py:1215` | **Yes.** A typed `checkpoint` event kind is declared (`.basicly/core/kit/tracker/events.py:246`) and **zero were ever written**; all 823 real approvals are `[harness-policy] checkpoint=` comment markers (measured below). Separately, the ledger snapshot is called a "fold checkpoint" (`.basicly/core/kit/tracker/snapshot.py`) |
| **artifact** | A typed handoff payload one phase writes and the next may refuse on; eight kinds are declared. | `src/basicly/handoff.py:62-71` (`PRODUCERS`); `architecture.md:3130` (§33) | **Yes.** `architecture.md:518` calls the projected files "Generated artifacts" — an unrelated sense |
| **grant** | An autonomy marker on the session's root record, carrying a level and a token budget. | `architecture.md:2194` (§31.1) | No |
| **worktree** | A sibling git checkout at `<repo>.worktrees/<name>` on branch `harness/<name>` where a lane builds. | `architecture.md:1650` (§27.1); `src/basicly/worktree.py` | **Yes, externally.** The Claude Agent tool's `isolation: "worktree"` checks out *inside* the repo and poisons whole-tree gates — a different mechanism with the same word |
| **projection** | Turning authored catalog sources into the generated files agents read, deterministically and recorded in a manifest. | `architecture.md:548` (§11); `src/basicly/planner.py` (select/sort), `src/basicly/projection.py` (write-if-changed) | No |
| **catalog** | The authored YAML sources: the managed `.basicly/core/` plus your `.basicly-local/` overlay. | `architecture.md:506` (§10.1) | No |
| **ratchet** | A frozen measured baseline that may only fall, so a property nothing else measures cannot get worse in silence. | `architecture.md:3597` (§36.6) | No |
| **integrity level** | How far a defect could reach — L1 docs-and-tests, L2 engine, L3 consumer surface — assigned from the paths a change declares, and it picks the gate set, the model tier, the rework allowance and whether ship may be delegated. | `src/basicly/integrity.py:48` (`LEVELS`), `:178` (`_SELECTIONS`); `architecture.md:473` (§9.2) | **Yes, in spelling.** The document uses the names `docs-and-tests`/`engine`/`consumer-surface` while the code, the markers, `basicly.toml` and every `--autonomy` value still write `L0`–`L3` (`architecture.md:492`) |
| **rework budget** | The per-gate cap on repair attempts, default 2, with a lane-wide ceiling at twice it. | `src/basicly/config.py:138` (`max_rework`); `src/basicly/loop.py:2132` (`LANE_REWORK_CEILING_FACTOR = 2`); decision at `architecture.md:4251` (D-17) | **Yes, three names for one thing:** "cap", "allowance", "budget". `max_rework` is the field |
| **ledger** | The append-only JSONL event log under `.basicly/ledger/`, committed with the code; it is the only store there is. | `architecture.md:2453` (§32.2); `.basicly/core/kit/tracker/events.py` | No |

**Retired, per the glossary — do not use.** `node` (it once meant a record, a diagram element
and a JS runtime at once), `package` as a synonym for a landed lane, and `comment` as an event
kind. `architecture.md:4967-4971`. This matters for the naming question: **`node` is already a
retired word in this system**, which is another reason not to reach for a vocabulary whose
first two words are "node" and "edge".

**Measurements behind the two flags above** (commands run 2026-09-04, this repo's committed
ledger):

```
$ jq -r '.kind' .basicly/ledger/events-0001.jsonl | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
   3647 comment   1491 status   1300 edge   1204 created   569 field
    131 artifact     93 gate       20 dispatch    3 edge_retracted   1 tombstone
```
No `checkpoint` kind. Positive control: nine other kinds return non-zero, and
`KIND_CHECKPOINT` is declared at `.basicly/core/kit/tracker/events.py:246`.

```
$ jq -r 'select(.kind=="comment") | .payload.text // ""' .basicly/ledger/events-0001.jsonl \
    | grep -oE '^\[harness-policy\] [a-z-]+(=[a-z-]+)?' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
   467 checkpoint=ship   327 checkpoint=classify   29 checkpoint=decompose   (= 823 approvals)
   184 scope-violation   119 rework   88 grant   38 finding-set   17 needs-input
    16 rework-allowance   5 hold   5 gate-unreliable   4 convergence-refund
```

```
$ jq -r 'select(.kind=="artifact") | .payload.artifact' .basicly/ledger/events-0001.jsonl \
    | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
    71 change-summary   58 release-record   2 implementation-plan
```
Three of eight kinds have ever been written. Positive control satisfied: three non-zero rows,
so the five zeros belong to the population and not to the probe.

---

## 6. The reconciliation the owner must decide

### The disagreement, in plain language

The owner's framing says: **ask whether the next step consumes the previous step's result, and
order on that.** That is the definition of a true data dependency, and it is exactly Dagster's
edge semantics `[foundations]`.

The shipped default rule says something else. `src/basicly/decompose.py:303` `serializes(a, b)`
returns True — meaning "these two children must run one after the other" — when **any glob in
one child's declared write scope can match a common path with any glob in the other's**. It
never asks what either child produces or reads from the other. `group_children`
(`decompose.py:394`) takes the transitive closure of that relation with union-find, and
`chain_predecessors` (`:431`) turns each resulting group into a linear chain. The literature's
name for ordering imposed without data flow is GNU make's **order-only prerequisite**
`[foundations]`.

So: **the owner's rule orders on what flows; the code's default rule orders on what collides.**

Three further facts make the decision concrete, and they change what the right answer is.

1. **The code already has a channel for the owner's rule, and it is mandatory.** `depends_on`
   is a required plan field (`src/basicly/plan_gate.py:77` `PLAN_FIELDS`), and the plan gate's
   own docstring gives the reason in the owner's own terms: before it existed "the only
   ordering signal was scope overlap, which cannot express 'B needs A's decision' between two
   children that touch no common file" (`plan_gate.py:16-19`). A declared-empty list is an
   answer; an absent key is refused (`plan_gate.py:197-198`).
2. **The two rules are then flattened into one indistinguishable edge.** At
   `src/basicly/decompose.py:2042-2049` the declared `depends_on` targets and the computed
   chain predecessor are unioned, deduplicated, and written with the same call —
   `dep add <child> <dep> -t blocks`. Nothing records which rule drew a given edge. The live
   population holds 418 `blocks` edges and `[inventory]` states the declared/computed split
   over them **cannot be measured** for exactly this reason. The edge payload does carry a
   `provenance` key, but its values are migration provenance — `EXTRACTED` (275),
   `engine` (117), `dual-write` (26) — not dependency kind.
3. **A consumption edge between two siblings has no observable carrier today.** The engine can
   see a collision, because it can compare globs and, at the landing, the real diff
   (`src/basicly/loop.py:1328`). It cannot see a consumption, because no artifact kind is
   consumed by a sibling: the only consumers declared are "the BUILD fan-out" and "entry to
   VERIFY", both inside one record's own path (`src/basicly/handoff.py:62-71`,
   `architecture.md:3139-3147` (§33 table)). A lane's result reaches its sibling as a merged commit, and
   nothing records that the sibling read it.

### The ways to resolve it

**Option A — amend the framing.** Keep the code. Change the spoken and written explanation to:
"the graph orders two units when their declared write scopes overlap, and separately when the
plan declares that one needs another's result." Cost: one paragraph, and giving up the single
crisp sentence. Risk if not done: `[foundations]` states it plainly — if the consumption
framing is written into catalog guidance unamended, it will conflict with the code that
already implements the decision, and the code is the one under test.

**Option B — change the code so consumption is the primary rule.** Make `depends_on` the
ordering source and demote scope overlap to advice. Cost: this deletes the rule that produced
the system's measured protection, and the measurement exists. `src/basicly/contention.py:5-8`
records why the module was written — three lanes, provably disjoint scopes, `VERDICT: ready`,
and the third bounced twice on a `CHANGELOG.md` conflict and spent its whole rework budget.
Also, per fact 3, the engine has no way to observe a consumption it was not told about, so
Option B replaces a computed default with a declaration nothing can check. Not recommended.

**Option C — hold both, as two named edge kinds.** Keep both rules and stop flattening them.
Record on each computed edge that it came from scope overlap, and on each declared edge that it
came from `depends_on`. Cost: one payload field or one new edge type, plus the reader
(`.basicly/core/kit/tracker/derivation.py:136` currently reads exactly `blocks` as the
blocking type, so a new *type* would need vocabulary work while a new *field* would not).
Scheduling behaviour need not change at all.

### Recommendation

**Do Option C for the vocabulary, and Option A for the sentence — in that order.**

Reason: both concepts are already built and already required of every plan, so nothing needs
inventing; the only thing missing is that the ledger cannot tell them apart after the write,
which is why nobody can answer "how much of our ordering comes from data flow?" with a number
today. That is a one-field change that makes the owner's framing *measurable* instead of
merely arguable. Once the two edges have separate names, the honest sentence writes itself and
Option A costs nothing. Option B is the only one that trades away a measured protection for a
tidier story.

**This is the owner's call and it is not made here.**

---

## 7. What NOT to say

Each claim below sounds good, would be believed, and is not supported by the code as it stands
today. The refutation is next to it.

### About vendor neutrality

1. **"It runs Claude, Codex and Copilot."** Say instead: *"It projects into three agent
   families. Only Claude has ever been dispatched on this repo."* Measured 2026-09-04 over
   `.basicly/usage/run-records.json`: **735 run records across 399 work records — `agent` is
   `claude` 540 times and `manual` 195 times. Codex: 0. Copilot: 0.** Positive control: the
   field is populated and holds two distinct values, so the zeros are real. The ledger's
   `dispatch` events agree independently: claude 19, manual 1. Adapters for all three *are*
   declared (`src/basicly/runner.py:273-306`).
2. **"An agent family is interchangeable."** Not on the current adapter table. The `codex`
   spec carries no `agent_style` (`src/basicly/runner.py:285-296`), so a role cannot be
   selected on its argv — the architecture names this the field that "costs the most"
   (§29.1). Agent hooks are projected for two families, not three:
   `src/basicly/hooks.py:58` `AGENT_HOOK_HOSTS = {CLAUDE_MANAGER: "claude", COPILOT_MANAGER: "copilot"}`,
   while `codex-cli 0.146.0` reports `hooks` as a stable feature with a blocking `PreToolUse`
   `[agentic]`. And no schema-constrained result is available on all three: Copilot has
   neither `--output-schema` nor `--json-schema` `[agentic]`.
3. **"Mixing agents measurably helps."** There is no measurement, ours or anyone's. The
   closest published support for the mix-and-switch thesis is Cognition's report of running
   Claude and GPT together as "a capability router rather than a difficulty escalator", and it
   carries **no numbers** `[agentic]`. Meanwhile Tran & Kiela (arXiv 2604.02460v2) find single
   agents match or beat multi-agent systems on multi-hop reasoning **at equal reasoning
   tokens**, and Anthropic's own post says "most coding tasks involve fewer truly
   parallelizable tasks than research" `[agentic]`. The defensible claim is a *portability*
   claim, not a performance claim.
4. **"No cross-agent invocation standard exists."** This is a committed sentence at
   `docs/architecture/architecture.md:1964` and it is **refuted**: ACP v1 is a published
   JSON-RPC standard with 40+ listed agents, native `--acp` in Copilot CLI 1.0.82, and
   maintained adapters for claude and codex `[agentic]`. The *conclusion* — never guess an
   unknown binary's argv — survives. The premise does not. This one needs a documentation fix,
   not just a change of speech.

### About the graph

5. **"The graph decides what runs in parallel by what each step consumes."** It decides by
   write-scope overlap — `src/basicly/decompose.py:303`. See §6.
6. **"Parallel lanes are file-disjoint."** `architecture.md:1687` says the decomposer "marks
   lanes parallel-safe only when it can predict **file-disjoint** scopes", and the prediction
   is made from globs an agent declared, checked against reality only at the landing
   (`src/basicly/loop.py:1328`). Measured: **184 `scope-violation` markers; 22 named a
   colliding sibling and were refused; 162 recorded the contradiction and landed anyway**
   (commands in §5, re-derived independently of `[inventory]`, same figures). The supervisor
   never consults the contention module at all, and that module says so about itself:
   "nothing here refuses a pass" (`src/basicly/contention.py:22`).
7. **"The work graph holds gate results, checkpoints and evidence."** README:38-39 says this.
   Three of the five hold. Issues, dependencies and gate results are real typed data (1204
   `created`, 1300 `edge`, 93 `gate` events). Checkpoints are **not** typed graph
   data: the `checkpoint` kind has zero events and all 823 approvals are free-text comment
   markers (§5). "Evidence" is the weakest word in the sentence — `verification-evidence` and
   `validation-transcript` both have **no producer** (`src/basicly/handoff.py:68-69`), and the
   document already concedes that five of eight kinds "carry a contract that nobody can
   exercise" (`architecture.md:3160`).
8. **"Append-only means immutable."** Append-only here is enforced by audit, not by mechanism:
   `events.py` exposes no update or delete, and `LedgerLock` is a single-writer lock for
   concurrency, not immutability; nothing chains an event's bytes to a prior digest
   `[inventory]`. The proof it is not absolute is committed: `pyproject.toml:426-427` freezes
   `"basicly-vkh0.30/sequence-gap" = 1`, because "an append-only log has no undelete".

### About the gates

9. **"The gates cannot be bypassed"** / **"they fail closed."** Two fail-open paths are
   deliberate and documented in the code. An unreadable classification marker reads as
   unmarked, and `requires_validation(None)` is `False`, so the entire
   `validate-as-consumer` requirement silently disappears
   (`src/basicly/validate_gate.py:58-81`). A unit carrying **no** handoff artifact is admitted;
   only a present-and-invalid one refuses (`src/basicly/handoff.py:200-203`). Say: *"the
   deterministic gates refuse; two named admission checks are deliberately permissive when
   evidence is absent."*
10. **"An agent hook is a gate."** At the vendor boundary it is not reliably one. Claude Code's
    own docs warn that a mistyped hook path exits 127 and is treated as a **non-blocking**
    error, and that a timed-out hook does not block; Codex hooks are skipped until a per-hook
    trust hash is accepted, so a freshly cloned repo's gates are inert by design `[agentic]`.
    Every one of the three families fails open in at least one reachable way.
11. **"Tests passing means the verification layer works."** MAST measured incorrect
    verification at 9.1% and no/incomplete verification at 8.2%, and both "appear frequently
    even in successful runs" `[agentic]`. This is the repo's own always-on rule, and it is
    worth saying out loud rather than claiming the opposite.

### About the loop

12. **"The phases are intake, classify, decompose, build, verify, ship, teardown, retro."**
    That is README:34-35 and it is wrong three ways: it **omits `validate`**, it names
    `teardown`, and it names `retro` — and the architecture states "Repair and retrospective
    are not phases" (`architecture.md:1408`). The real set is `src/basicly/loop_state.py:31`:
    `("intake","classify","decompose","build","verify","validate","ship","done")`. Teardown is
    folded into the ship advance and the retro is a tracker comment. **This is a README defect
    to fix, not just a sentence to avoid.**
13. **"A serial merge queue."** True inside one supervisor process — the landing loop is
    single-threaded (`src/basicly/supervise.py:3390-3424`). It is not a lock over the merge:
    `base_lock.hold` wraps only the tracker-state roll-up commit (`src/basicly/merge.py:654`),
    while the rebase and `git merge --no-ff` (`src/basicly/merge.py:781`) run unguarded in the
    same base checkout, and the supervisor's singleton lock
    (`src/basicly/supervise.py:107`) excludes a second supervisor but not a hand-run
    `basicly loop advance`. Say "landings are serialized by the supervisor", not "by a lock".
14. **"A deterministic loop."** Be specific about what is deterministic. The projection is
    byte-identical on identical sources (`architecture.md:568-570`) and the phase is a pure
    function of five tracker values (`src/basicly/loop_state.py:140`). The work an agent does
    is not deterministic, and no part of the system claims it is. Do not let the adjective
    travel from the loop's bookkeeping to the dispatch.
15. **"We measure whether the guidance changes behaviour."** Not yet. The README's own roadmap
    carries it as `? researching — do entries change behaviour`, which is honest; a spoken
    claim that it is measured would not be. The four-failures table lists "Measure it" as the
    remedy for row four (`architecture.md:102`) — that is a remedy named, not a result
    reported.

### The safest capability sentences to say instead

Each of these is checkable today:

- "One catalog projects into three agent families' native files, and a drift gate in CI fails
  a hand edit." (`architecture.md:548`, `basicly check`)
- "Gates run at commit time through git hooks, not only in CI." (`architecture.md:920`, §16)
- "This repo declares 29 verify checks, and the loop's verify step runs the same checks the git
  hooks run." (`grep -c '^\[\[verify.checks\]\]' basicly.toml` → 29; the second clause is the
  document's own sentence at `architecture.md:277`. Note the check set is mode-selected —
  `src/basicly/config.py:1066-1080` — so "the same checks" means the same declarations, not
  necessarily the same subset on every invocation.)
- "Phase is never stored; every command re-derives it from the ledger, so a crashed session
  resumes by reading." (`src/basicly/loop_state.py:140`)
- "The work tracker is an append-only event ledger committed with the code — no binary, no
  database, no daemon." (`architecture.md:2453`; `README.md` committer requirements)
- "Lanes build in parallel in sibling worktrees and land one at a time, in dependency order."
  (`architecture.md:1685-1689`; `src/basicly/supervise.py:3390-3424`)
- "Integrity level is assigned from the paths a change declares, and it picks the gate set."
  (`src/basicly/integrity.py:48,178`)
- "Rework is capped per gate at 2 attempts, with a lane-wide ceiling at twice that."
  (`src/basicly/config.py:138`; `src/basicly/loop.py:2132`)

---

## What could not be established

- **Whether any of the 162 non-refused scope violations caused a downstream conflict.** The
  markers record the paths; joining them to `rework` events per record was not done — same
  gap `[inventory]` reports.
- **Whether the three projected agent families behave equivalently in practice.** Nothing was
  dispatched in this pass, and the run-record population holds no codex or copilot run to read.
- **The declared-versus-computed split over the 418 live `blocks` edges.** Not measurable, for
  the reason in §6 fact 2. This is a finding, not a gap in the method.
- **Runtime behaviour of anything here.** Per the task constraints no `pytest`, no
  `basicly verify/check`, no `pre-commit` and no whole-tree gate was run — live sibling
  worktrees exist under `<repo>.worktrees/`. Every claim rests on a
  file read, on a `jq`/`grep`/`rg` over the committed ledger and tree, or on one of the four
  research reports.

A correctness review found four retirement defects, three major: `_land_in_order` published `landing` per lane and retired it only when `route_outcomes` returned, so a `bounced` route left N lanes reading `landing` at once and falsified its own AC2; `record_pass_refusal` published for `counted` alone, empty whenever the forecast walk fails; the halted and ungranted returns published nothing; a band-refused lane kept `queued` because `live_lane` is the only site that pops it. The working path is `basicly policy checkpoint <id> ship --approve` then the same with `--confirm`, which reaches the guard with no advance in front of it. payload.description:
## Context

Owner, 2026-09-04: "do you have any suggestions how to prevent writting code against the
eplicitly stated rules, which will 100% bounce of the CI gates, rather than doing the current
loop: write code, write tests, try to commit, it bounces off."

Classified every gate refusal in that session. The expensive class was not rule violations: it
was the two size ratchets, 8 of 13 refusals. Those are not knowable from prose - the rule says
a gate exists, it cannot say that `supervise.py` has 456 tokens of headroom.

## The rule, the tool and the skill all already exist

- `.scripts/headroom.py` reports both ratchets' remaining room for a module. Its own docstring:
  "this is the read that lets a change be sized *before* it is written, which is the only point
  at which the information is cheap."
- `.claude/skills/python/SKILL.md:73` gives the command, and adds "a file with under ~200 tokens
  left wants the extraction decided now, not after the gate refuses."
- The skill is projected and available.

It was skipped anyway. `headroom.py`'s docstring records the same failure **three times in one
session on 2026-08-14** (basicly-co64), "every time by an agent who had measured tokens and not
prose". 2026-09-04 added three more. Six occurrences, all after the rule was written down.

So the guidance layer is not missing. It is advisory, and it has lost this argument six times.
`hooks.yaml` already states the remedy for exactly this shape, for `unsplit-loop-guard`: "The
always-on rule was in context and was violated anyway... Guidance that must bind becomes a hook."

## Design, with the vendor fact established rather than recalled

Verified against code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks.md on 2026-09-04: a PreToolUse hook's exit-0
stdout and stderr reach the debug log only and **never** the model. The one non-blocking outcome
that reaches the model is the JSON form with `hookSpecificOutput.permissionDecision = "allow"`
and `additionalContext`, capped at 10,000 characters.

So the hook allows every call and injects the figures. It does not block, which matters: blocking
to inform would be intrusive and would need a per-session escape hatch.

It fires only where `headroom.is_tight` already says an ordinary unit's edit would cross a bound.
Those thresholds are reused, not reinvented: `TIGHT_TOKENS = 615` and `TIGHT_POINTS = 1.0`,
measured over 44 rebaseline records.

Measured cost: 1.13s per invocation, three runs, on the `uv run --no-project` interpreter hooks
are launched with. `headroom.py` runs clean under it.

## Acceptance Criteria

- When an Edit or Write targets a tracked `.py` module that `headroom.is_tight` calls tight,
  then the hook allows the call and the module's remaining tokens and prose points are in the
  model's context before the write.
- When the module has room, then the hook is silent.
- When anything fails - a malformed payload, an unreadable baseline - then the call is allowed.

## Scope

- `.basicly/core/hooks/headroom-guard.py`
- `.basicly/core/hooks/hooks.yaml`
- `tests/test_headroom_guard.py`

payload.description:
## Context

The size ratchets are a **shared, unreserved, whole-tree budget**. Two lanes can each measure
headroom correctly, each pass their own gates, and whichever lands second bounces - because the
first spent the room in between. Neither graph models that contention, so the dependency graph
calls the lanes independent and they are not.

This is the failure the graph research names as false parallelism: nodes declared independent
that contend on a resource. See basicly-hnnmk9.9 for the inventory and basicly-zq9i2m.3 for the
file-scope half of the same gap.

## Measured, 2026-09-04, not hypothetical

`basicly-85cadb` measured its headroom correctly when it was written, and wrote the numbers into
its own `basicly.d` fragment: "`merge.py` had **0** tokens of module-size headroom, `checkout.py`
**15**, `supervise.py` **456** with **0.0** points of comment-density headroom, and
`tests/test_supervise.py` **488**."

The same fragment then declared: "`supervise.py` +296 fits inside its 456 and is not declared."

That lane sat unlanded. `basicly-ncday7` and `basicly-tjhjmk` then landed into the same two
modules and spent the room. When 85cadb was finally rebased its deltas were all stale and three
modules refused it: `merge.py` +62, `supervise.py` +297, `tests/test_supervise.py` +409. The
fragment's own sentence predicted the exact failure, and being right did not help, because the
measurement had no reservation behind it.

`merge.py` now reads `18746/18746 tokens (0 left)`. The next edit to it bounces, and nothing
tells the next lane that until it tries.

## What a reservation would do

A lane declares `## Scope` globs already, and `decompose` already compiles those into `blocks`
edges. The missing step is that a lane's declared scope should also **claim** the headroom of the
modules it names, at dispatch, so that:

- `loop preflight` refuses or serialises a second lane whose scope claims headroom already held.
- The claim is released when the lane lands or is killed, like the worktree binding.
- A lane rebasing onto a base that moved re-reads its claim rather than its stale measurement.

## Open questions a design must answer

- Where the claim lives. The worktree session record and the `basicly.d` fragment are both
  candidates; the fragment is committed and the session record is not.
- What is claimed. Whole-module headroom is coarse and would serialise more than necessary; the
  lane's own forecast delta is finer but is exactly the number lanes get wrong.
- Whether a stale claim is refused or merely reported. `contend:` is advisory today and was
  ignored - see basicly-hnnmk9.9, where 162 of 184 scope violations landed anyway.
- Whether this belongs to the ratchets or to the scheduler. Putting it in the ratchets makes
  every consumer repo pay for it; putting it in `supervise` keeps it to supervised passes.

## Acceptance Criteria

- When two ready lanes declare scopes whose modules have insufficient combined headroom, then
  `loop preflight` names the pair before the pass starts.
- When a lane lands, then the headroom it claimed is released.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/supervise.py`
- `src/basicly/contention.py`
- `src/basicly/decompose.py`
- `docs/architecture/architecture.md`

## Context

`basicly-a68ggd` split the loop region into a pass row over `lanes[]` and a backlog census over `units[]`, and added a `moved` mark so a reader can tell a working lane from a wedged one.

The mark is taken from `lanes[].state_since`, which is the only movement stamp the `harness-board/v1` contract declares. That field stamps the lane's **state** - `running`, `landing`, `waits-to-land` - and not its **phase**. So the mark answers "this lane did something within the beat", which is a proxy for the acceptance criterion the parent record actually wrote:

> WHEN a unit has moved phase since the previous beat, THAT MOVEMENT SHALL be visible, because a still picture of positions cannot distinguish working from wedged.

## Why the consumer cannot derive it

Two other sources were examined and both refused:

- `events[]` carries the transition, but only inside `text`, as this producer's own string (`id=... phase=ship`). `board_footer.events` joins event fields verbatim and parses none of them, and `board_render`'s own contract is that a foreign producer must render. Parsing `text` would be the first producer coupling in the consumer.
- A consumer-held previous snapshot would work, but `board_render.context` is a pure function of one document by design - "Passed rather than read so a page is a function of its inputs".

The producer knows when a unit changed phase. The consumer cannot.

## Acceptance Criteria

- WHEN the producer emits a lane whose phase changed, THE SNAPSHOT SHALL carry `lanes[].phase_since` as an RFC3339 instant, declared optional in `board-snapshot.schema.json`.
- WHEN `phase_since` is present, THE LOOP REGION SHALL take its `moved` mark from it rather than from `state_since`.
- WHERE a producer emits no `phase_since`, THE REGION SHALL fall back to `state_since` and SHALL NOT claim a phase transition it cannot see.
- WHEN the field is added, THE SCHEMA MAJOR SHALL NOT change, because the versioning rule is add-keys-only.

## Scope

- `.basicly/core/schemas/board-snapshot.schema.json`
- `src/basicly/board_snapshot.py`
- `src/basicly/board_loop.py`
- `tests/test_board_loop.py`
- `tests/fixtures/board/wall-v1.json`

## Plan

- integrity: `L2`
- demonstration: Start a supervised pass, let one lane cross a phase boundary, render the board and read the mark against the supervisor's own reported transition.

## Context

`basicly-ua9o5g` gave the board a region that draws a pending ask with the exact command and a prefilled form. It reads `asks[].actions[].basicly` to know which verb an ask offers.

**This producer never writes that key.** So the region is correct and unfed: on a real board it draws nothing, whatever is pending.

## Measured

```text
$ grep -c '"actions"' src/basicly/board_sections.py
0
$ grep -l '"actions"' src/basicly/board_asks.py src/basicly/board_regions.py
src/basicly/board_asks.py
src/basicly/board_regions.py
```

The zero is a controlled one: the same pattern finds both consumers, so it is absence and not a wrong probe. `board_sections.asks` builds `wait_id`, `kind`, `requested_at`, `issue`, `waiting_s`, and optionally `subject` and `question` — read the whole function; there is no `actions` branch.

Three fixtures (`wall-v1`, `dense-v1`, `full-v1`) carry `actions` because they were hand-authored against the schema. That is why `tests/test_board_action_wire.py` passes while the live board draws no form: its document is a fixture with the key supplied.

## Why it is one line of judgement, not one line of code

The verb is derivable from the ask's own `kind`, which `policy.record_wait_request` writes: `checkpoint` is answered by `policy checkpoint --approve`, `decision` by `loop answer`. What must not happen is a default — an ask of an unrecognised kind must carry no `actions`, so the schema's *"drawn without a button rather than refused"* rule applies rather than the board offering a verb that does not fit.

## Acceptance Criteria

- WHEN the producer emits an ask of kind `checkpoint`, IT SHALL carry one action offering `checkpoint-approve`.
- WHEN it emits an ask of kind `decision`, IT SHALL carry one action offering `loop-answer`.
- WHEN it emits an ask of any other kind, IT SHALL carry no `actions` key at all, and the consumer SHALL still draw the ask in the watch band.
- WHEN the board is served with a real pending checkpoint, THE PAGE SHALL carry a prefilled form for it — demonstrated against a live board, not a fixture.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/board_sections.py`
- `tests/test_board_sections.py`

## Plan

- integrity: `L2`
- demonstration: Queue a real checkpoint, serve the board, and read the form off the served page.

## Context

`docs/architecture/architecture.md:3018` — the R9 row of the requirements ladder — ends with:

> **One path is exempt by construction:** `fsck.rebuild` unlinks the target before writing, so the guard always meets an absent file and the rebuild that loses records is the one it cannot see

The code refutes it. `basicly-dx2ngn` closed that hole, and the fix carries its own comment saying so.

## Measured

`.basicly/core/kit/tracker/fsck.py:953-962`:

```python
    # Derived and compared before anything is deleted (basicly-dx2ngn). `write_snapshot`'s
    # shrink guard compares against the file on disk and the unlink below guarantees there is
    # none, so R9's refusal could never fire through this path. Taking it after the unlink
    # would destroy the records it exists to keep, so a refused rebuild removes nothing.
    produced = tuple((path, derive(covered)) for path, covered in derived_targets(ledger))
    for path, proposed in produced:
        loss = snapshot.shrinkage(path, proposed)
        if loss.refused:
            raise snapshot.SnapshotError(f"{path.name}: {loss.reason}")
    removed = tuple(snapshot.derived_paths(ledger))
```

The comparison happens **before** the unlink loop, and `tests/test_kit_tracker_fsck.py:832` asserts the refusal fires with `"0 records over a file holding 2"`.

So the ladder's most load-bearing row tells a reader the one gap that is closed is open. Found by the `curator` at `basicly-b2n2`'s ship, and confirmed against the code.

- WHEN the R9 row is read, IT SHALL NOT claim a path exempt from the shrink guard, because none is.
- WHERE the row describes `fsck.rebuild`, IT SHALL say the comparison is taken before the unlink and name the record that closed it.

## Context

The owner read the board and reported *"there is one failing pytest"*. The tree was green: `uv run pytest -q` gave 5262 passed, and `pytest -q -n 4 --durations=25` — the gate's own invocation — gave 5262 passed. The verdict on the page was **46 minutes old** and predated four merges.

The board invited the reading. Measured on the served document:

```text
snapshot generated_at : 2026-09-05T14:07:00Z
gates.recorded_at     : 2026-09-05T13:20:36Z   -> 46 minutes older
```

and the header drew both facts adjacent:

```text
gates 1 FAILING: pytest · mode full · recorded 2026-09-05T13:20:36Z
...                                                as of 5s ago
```

`as of 5s ago` is the *snapshot's* age. The gate verdict is a **bare absolute stamp** beside it, on a page whose vocabulary is otherwise ages throughout — `as of 5s ago`, `13 DAYS`, `since Sat 22 Aug 19:51 UTC`, `stale after 60s`. A reader has to notice that one figure is a different kind from every other and subtract by hand.

## This is the false-calm defect inverted

`basicly-2no50w` fixed the board saying nothing was waiting when something was. This is the board saying the tree is broken when it is not, and it costs the same thing: the reader stops trusting the region. `board_serve`'s own docstring states the principle — *"The board is as fresh as the producer that wrote its snapshot, and it always shows how old that snapshot is"* — and the `gates` section has a second, older freshness the page never states as an age.

## Why the stamp cannot just be reformatted

Two figures, two meanings. The snapshot age says how old the *document* is; the gate age says how old the *verdict* is, and the second can be arbitrarily older because it comes off `.basicly/usage/verify-run.json`, written whenever someone last ran `basicly verify`. A wall that has been up all day can be five seconds fresh and carry a verdict from breakfast.

## Acceptance Criteria

- WHEN the gate verdict is drawn, ITS AGE SHALL be stated in the same coarse unit the page uses elsewhere, not as an absolute stamp alone.
- WHEN the verdict is older than the document by more than the freshness window, THE REGION SHALL mark it stale, and a failing verdict older than that SHALL NOT be drawn in the alarm register.
- WHERE no verdict has been recorded at all, THE REGION SHALL say so rather than reading green.
- WHEN the age is drawn, IT SHALL come from the document's own `generated_at` and not from the reader's clock, so two viewers of one snapshot agree.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/board_footer.py`
- `.basicly/core/templates/board/board_page.html.j2`
- `tests/test_board_footer.py`

## Plan

- integrity: `L2`
- demonstration: Serve the board with a verify artifact an hour old and read the gates cell; then record a fresh pass and read it again.

## Context

`.basicly/usage/verify-run.json` recorded a `pytest` failure at `2026-09-05T13:20:36Z` under `basicly verify --mode full` in the base checkout. 38 of 39 checks passed; `pytest` returned 1.

It does not reproduce. Both invocations, on the same commit, minutes later:

```text
uv run pytest -q                          -> 5262 passed in 212.53s
uv run pytest -q -n 4 --durations=25      -> 5262 passed in 69.56s
```

So the tree holds an intermittent failure. One occurrence is known.

## The identity is unknown, and that is the finding

The artifact records this and nothing more:

```json
{"name": "pytest", "status": "fail", "returncode": 1,
 "detail": "output streamed rather than captured; reproduce with: pytest -q -n 4 --durations=25"}
```

**The gate streams pytest's output rather than capturing it, so a failure leaves no record of which test failed.** The 13:20 run's stdout went to `/dev/null` — an agent redirected it — and with it went the only copy of the failure. A reproduce hint is not evidence: this one is green.

That is the defect worth fixing first. A flake nobody can name is a flake nobody can fix, and this gate is the only place the suite's verdict is recorded for the board to draw.

## Two candidates, and no evidence chooses between them

- **A test that is not isolated under `-n 4`.** The gate runs four `pytest-xdist` workers, so two tests sharing a fixture, a temp path or module state can collide on a scheduling that a serial run never produces. `test-discipline` names this class.
- **A timing assertion.** The repo has several, and `timing-tests-wait-for-condition` records that the house rule is to poll a condition rather than a duration; a residual duration-based wait would fail under the load of four workers.

## Acceptance Criteria

- WHEN a `[[verify.checks]]` command fails, ITS OUTPUT SHALL be recorded in the run artifact, bounded, so the failure is diagnosable after the terminal is gone.
- WHERE a check streams by design, IT SHALL still capture on failure, because a streamed failure that nobody was watching is unrecorded.
- WHEN the suite is run repeatedly under the gate's own parallel invocation, THE FLAKING TEST SHALL be named, or the search SHALL report how many runs found nothing so the absence is bounded rather than assumed.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/verify.py`
- `src/basicly/verify_artifact.py`
- `tests/test_verify.py`

## Plan

- integrity: `L2`
- demonstration: Make one test fail deliberately, run `basicly verify --mode full`, and read the failing test's name out of `.basicly/usage/verify-run.json` rather than out of the terminal.

payload.text:
[measured 2026-09-05] The occurrence, and what is known about it.

WHEN: 2026-09-05T13:20:36Z, base checkout, `basicly verify --mode full --issue basicly-3qstvw --gate verify`, exit 1. 38 of 39 checks passed. The tree was at cf04cbb6.

WHAT: unknown, and unknowable from what was kept. The artifact holds only `{"name": "pytest", "status": "fail", "returncode": 1, "detail": "output streamed rather than captured; reproduce with: pytest -q -n 4 --durations=25"}`. The run's stdout was redirected to /dev/null by the agent that started it, so the only copy of the failure is gone. That is my error and it is also the record's point: a gate whose failure survives only in a terminal is a gate whose failures are lost by default.

DOES NOT REPRODUCE, on the same commit:
- `uv run pytest -q` -> 5262 passed in 212.53s
- `uv run pytest -q -n 4 --durations=25` -> 5262 passed in 69.56s

So the tree holds an intermittent failure at an unknown rate, with one known occurrence. A search is running; whatever it reports, the bound matters more than the result - four green runs is a rate under roughly one in four, not an absence.

[scope correction 2026-09-05] Two of this record's premises are wrong. Corrected before building.

FIRST, THE FIRST ACCEPTANCE CRITERION CONTRADICTS A STATED DESIGN DECISION. I wrote 'ITS OUTPUT SHALL be recorded in the run artifact'. `verify_artifact`'s module docstring refuses exactly that, with a reason: 'Verdict metadata only, never a check's output. Streaming is the contract a consumer watching a gate depends on, so nothing here captures anything; and the redaction rule run_record states holds the same way - a tool's stdout can carry a secret, a status and a return code cannot.' That decision stands. The corrected criterion is that the output must survive the terminal, not that it must land in THAT file.

SECOND, THE CHEAP FIX DOES NOT WORK. pytest already writes `.pytest_cache/v/cache/lastfailed`, so reading it looked like the whole answer. It is not a record of the last run - it ACCUMULATES across eras. Measured: 171 entries, of which 76 name files that no longer exist, `tests/test_br_adapter.py` alone holding 49 while `src/basicly/br.py` was deleted in db5619d6. So it cannot distinguish a failure in the last run from one months old, and a detail built from it would name deleted tests as current failures.

THIRD, THE DIAGNOSTIC RE-RUN CANNOT BE THE CAPTURE POINT EITHER, and this is the case that matters here. `verify.rerun_failures` already captures, but it is 'evidence, not a retry' - it re-runs after the fact, and a FLAKE passes on the re-run. The 13:20 failure would have produced no transcript through that path, which is why this occurrence has none.

THE DESIGN, then: tee rather than choose. Stream to the terminal exactly as now AND retain a bounded tail, on the first run. On failure write the tail through `redact` to a sibling file under the already self-ignored `.basicly/usage/`, and have the artifact's `detail` name that path instead of saying 'output streamed rather than captured'. The artifact stays verdict metadata only, streaming is unchanged, the secret rule is honoured by redaction plus a self-ignored path, and a flake leaves evidence.

payload.description:
## Context

`basicly-tyobdb` made the board state how far its gate verdict lags the document, and mark it stale past a window. **Age is a proxy.** The question a reader actually has is *"was this verdict taken at the head I am looking at"*, and the run artifact records no head.

So the board still cannot tell these two apart:

- a verdict from 20 minutes ago on a tree nobody has touched — **valid**, and now drawn as stale;
- a verdict from 3 minutes ago taken before two merges — **worthless**, and drawn as fresh.

The second is the dangerous one and the first is the noisy one. Both are wrong for the same reason: the artifact says *when* it ran, not *what* it ran against.

## Measured

`.basicly/usage/verify-run.json` holds exactly `mode`, `recorded_at`, `passed`, `checks`. The board's `repo` section already carries `head` and `dirty`, so the consumer has one half of the comparison and the producer never wrote the other.

## Why this is small

`verify_artifact.write_run_artifact` already takes the repo root. `checkout` and `merge` both read the head elsewhere in the tree, so nothing new has to be discovered — the head is one `git rev-parse` the artifact does not currently record, and `board_usage.gates` passes it through.

## Acceptance Criteria

- WHEN a verify run is recorded, THE ARTIFACT SHALL carry the commit it verified and whether the tree was dirty at the time.
- WHEN the board draws a verdict taken at a different head from the one it is showing, IT SHALL say which and SHALL NOT draw it in the failing vocabulary.
- WHEN the verdict's head matches, THE AGE ALONE SHALL NOT mark it stale, because an untouched tree does not go stale.
- WHERE the artifact predates this field, THE BOARD SHALL fall back to the age window `basicly-tyobdb` shipped, and say it is doing so.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/verify_artifact.py`
- `src/basicly/board_usage.py`
- `src/basicly/board_footer.py`
- `.basicly/core/schemas/board-snapshot.schema.json`
- `tests/test_verify_artifact.py`
- `tests/test_board_footer.py`

## Plan

- integrity: `L2`
- demonstration: Record a verify pass, make a commit, serve the board, and read the gates cell naming the head mismatch rather than a green tree.

## Context

Owner, reading the board 2026-09-05: *"i have no idea do we see what task are being worked on."*

They could not, and the page held the count three times over. Measured on the served document:

```text
THE LOOP    build 1
THE BACKLOG BUILD 1
BACKLOG     IN PROGRESS 1
RUNNING NOW (no cards)
```

Nine record ids are drawn on the page, all nine in `NEXT UP`, none of them the one in progress. A reader is told a record is being worked on three times and can never learn which.

## Why `RUNNING NOW` does not cover it

That region draws `lanes[]`, and a lane exists only where a supervised pass dispatched one. A record at `build` with no lane — picked up by hand, or a pass that ended without tearing down — is in progress by every count the page prints and absent from the only region that names work.

So this is not `basicly-9guj21`, which is about work the board *cannot* see. This is work the board **can** see, counts, and does not name.

## Acceptance Criteria

- WHEN a record is at a working phase with no lane, THE PAGE SHALL name it — its id, its title and its phase — and SHALL NOT report the count alone.
- WHEN such a record is drawn, IT SHALL be visually distinct from a dispatched lane, because it has no agent, no branch and no spend.
- WHEN a count on the page names a population of one or more, SOME REGION SHALL name at least one member of it, or the count SHALL say why it cannot.
- WHERE nothing is at a working phase, THE REGION SHALL collapse rather than reserve space.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/board_regions.py`
- `.basicly/core/templates/board/board_page.html.j2`
- `tests/test_board_regions.py`

- integrity: `L2`

## Context

Owner, 2026-09-05: *"even a graph on the page is a nice touch"*, in the same breath as *"is the work parallel or sequential"*.

The board cannot answer that second question and the data is already on the contract. `graph.edges` rides on every snapshot; the page draws it as **one number in the footer** — `DEP EDGES 843` — and as the feature heading on a ready row. The structure itself is never drawn.

`board_footer`'s own docstring states the intent the number falls short of: edges are *"the answer to why an item is not ready - the one question a count of blocked items raises and cannot settle"*. The page prints `BLOCKED 56` beside `DEP EDGES 843` and settles nothing.

## What a reader is asking

Not the whole graph. 843 edges over 291 active records is not a picture. The questions are:

- **is the next work parallel or sequential** — how wide is the ready frontier, and how deep is the chain behind the top of it;
- **why is this blocked** — for a named record, what holds it;
- **what unblocks the most** — which single record has the most dependents.

The third is what the scheduler already ranks on (`priority ASC, dependents DESC`), and the page never shows the second term.

## Acceptance Criteria

- WHEN the region renders, IT SHALL show the depth of the chain behind the ready frontier, so a reader can tell parallel work from a queue.
- WHEN a record is drawn anywhere on the page as blocked, THE REGION SHALL name what holds it, not merely that something does.
- WHEN one record unblocks more than any other, IT SHALL be named with its dependent count.
- WHERE the edge set is too large to draw, THE REGION SHALL state the bound it drew within and what it dropped, never a silent sample.
- WHERE `graph` is absent from the snapshot, THE REGION SHALL say so and SHALL NOT read as an unblocked backlog.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/board_graph.py`
- `src/basicly/board_render.py`
- `.basicly/core/templates/board/board_page.html.j2`
- `tests/test_board_graph.py`

## Plan

- integrity: `L3`

## Context

Owner, 2026-09-05: *"the diagram size and font does not fit the backlog 'next up' font size."*

Measured on the served document at 1920x1080. `max-height: 260px` against a `286`-unit viewBox scales the whole drawing by `260/286 = 0.909`:

| element | rendered |
| --- | --- |
| `NEXT UP` row title | **17px** |
| station name (`classify`) | **13.6px** |
| artifact and agent labels | **10px** |

So the region a reader looks at first carries type 20% smaller than the list beneath it, and its edge labels are the smallest text anywhere on the page. The hierarchy is inverted.

And the width is wasted. `preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid meet"` fits the drawing to the height and centres it, so it occupies **1091px inside a ~1900px region — 809px, 43%, is empty**.

## The cause is not the type sizes

Scaling the SVG scales the type with it, so raising a `font-size` inside the viewBox and leaving `max-height` alone changes nothing a reader can measure. The drawing has to be **wider and shorter** for its type to come out at the page's size — which is the same trade `basicly-6c97zx` already made twice, at `112px` when a pass runs and `display: none` under a 1000px wall.

## And it is spending that space on almost nothing

The live station counts are `1, 26, 1, 0, 0, 0` while the two terminals hold `263` and `936`. The census strip immediately below repeats all six numbers verbatim. So the page's largest region draws six near-zero figures twice.

That is the real finding: the diagram is oversized and under-typed because it has little to show. Any fix that only rescales it leaves a bigger drawing of the same six numbers.

## Acceptance Criteria

- WHEN the diagram renders, ITS STATION LABELS SHALL be at least the size of a `NEXT UP` row, measured on the rendered page and not in viewBox units.
- WHEN the diagram renders at a claimed width, IT SHALL use that width, and the unused fraction SHALL be under 10 percent.
- WHERE the diagram and the census draw the same figures, ONE OF THEM SHALL go, and the record SHALL say which and why.
- WHEN the region is changed, `check_render_overflow.py` SHALL report nothing clipped and nothing overlapped at 1440x900, 1600x1200 and 1920x1080, in both the idle and the running-pass states.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/board_diagram.py`
- `.basicly/core/templates/board/board_page.html.j2`
- `tests/test_board_diagram.py`

payload.description:
## Context

Owner, reading the board 2026-09-05: *"when will the work be done"*. The page cannot say, and the one figure that would start the answer reads `CLOSED TODAY not measured` — on a day eight records were closed.

`board_footer.throughput` is not wrong. It refuses to guess:

> **Absent, never nought.** A producer that records no `STATUS_KIND` row at all has not measured this and the cell says so; one that records them and closed nothing today is a measured zero.

The producer records none, ever.

## Measured

The consumer looks for `kind == "status"` (`board_footer.py:67`). `board_sections.events` builds its rows from **marker families** — `harness-run`, `harness-cost`, `harness-wait`, `harness-policy` — and `row.family.strip("[]")` is the `kind` it writes. A status change is a ledger event, not a marker, so no `status` row can ever appear there.

On the live document:

```text
events on the document: 6
kinds: {harness-policy: 1, harness-wait: 1, harness-run: 2, harness-cost: 2}
```

Eight records closed on 2026-09-05 and not one of them is in that tail.

## The same class as basicly-3qstvw, for the third time today

A consumer reads a field, the producer never writes it, and both sides' tests pass because each is asserted alone. The other two were `asks[].actions` (basicly-3qstvw) and this one. The pattern is worth a gate of its own, and that is filed separately.

## What it takes, and what it does not

The events tail is **capped at 50 by contract**, deliberately: *"an unbounded event list is how a derived, disposable document turns into the second source of truth this design refuses."* So the throughput figure must not be derived by lengthening that tail — a day's closes can exceed 50 rows, and the cap is not negotiable.

The honest shape is a **counted figure the producer computes**, the way `backlog` is: it folds the ledger once already, so counting distinct records closed on the document's own day costs nothing extra and lands as one integer.

## Acceptance Criteria

- WHEN the producer folds the ledger, IT SHALL emit the count of distinct records closed on the document's own day, as a figure and not as an event row.
- WHEN that figure is present, THE FOOTER SHALL draw it, and a day with no closes SHALL read as a measured zero.
- WHERE the producer does not emit it, THE CELL SHALL keep saying so rather than reading zero.
- THE EVENTS TAIL SHALL NOT be lengthened to carry it, because the cap is the contract.
- THE FIGURE SHALL be dated against the document's own `generated_at`, not the reader's clock, so a page opened after midnight does not report the producer's yesterday as an empty today.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/board_snapshot.py`
- `src/basicly/board_sections.py`
- `src/basicly/board_footer.py`
- `.basicly/core/schemas/board-snapshot.schema.json`
- `tests/test_board_snapshot.py`
- `tests/test_board_footer.py`

## Plan

- integrity: `L2`
- demonstration: Close a record on a scratch ledger, build the document, and read the count off the footer.

## Context

Three defects in one day, all the same shape: **a consumer reads a snapshot field the producer never writes, and every test on both sides passes.**

| record | the field | how it was found |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `basicly-3qstvw` | `asks[].actions[].basicly` | by grepping the producer after shipping the consumer |
| `basicly-tyobdb` (adjacent) | the gate verdict's age | by the owner misreading the page |
| filed alongside this one | `events[].kind == "status"` | by asking why `CLOSED TODAY` said `not measured` |

Each consumer was correct. Each producer was correct. The **seam** was never asserted, because the fixtures under `tests/fixtures/board/` are written against the *schema*, and a schema is a superset of what the producer implements. So an end-to-end test can serve a document more capable than anything the producer can emit — which is exactly what `tests/test_board_action_wire.py` did while the live board drew no form.

## The gate

For every key the board's consumer modules read out of a snapshot section, either the producer writes it, or the pair is declared as a gap with a reason. Both halves are mechanical:

- the consumer side is a literal-string scan of `src/basicly/board_{wall,regions,footer,loop,diagram,graph,asks}.py` for `.get("<key>")` and `["<key>"]` against a section reading;
- the producer side is the same scan over `src/basicly/board_{snapshot,sections,usage,facts}.py` for the keys it assigns.

A key the consumer reads and the producer never writes is either a defect or a declared foreign-producer affordance. The declaration is the point: `harness-board/v1` is deliberately a contract for producers that are not this harness, so some keys are legitimately unwritten here — and today nobody could tell those apart from the broken ones.

## Acceptance Criteria

- WHEN a consumer module reads a snapshot key this producer never writes, THE GATE SHALL name the pair and refuse, unless the key is listed as a foreign-producer affordance with a reason.
- WHEN the list is added to, THE ENTRY SHALL carry why this producer does not write the key, and the count SHALL be ratcheted as the waiver lists are.
- WHEN the gate runs on the tree as it stands, IT SHALL pass, and every key it excuses SHALL have been read rather than assumed.
- THE GATE SHALL NOT read the fixtures, because a fixture is written from the schema and is what hid all three defects.

## Scope

- `.scripts/check_board_seam.py`
- `basicly.toml`
- `tests/test_check_board_seam.py`

## Plan

- integrity: `L2`
- demonstration: Delete one key from `board_sections.asks` and watch the gate name it; then restore it and watch the gate pass.

payload.description:
## Context

Owner, 2026-09-05, restating a requirement they say they have given many times: *"the requirement was also to make the board interactive or a cockpit or a control panel where we can see and control the flow of work. Cool thing would be to be able to easily start, stop work, descope and so on."*

And the reason, in their words: *"One of the biggest issues with agentic development in the terminal alone is that human has no idea what is going on and when multiple parallel sessions and work is being done, it gets buried under. Terminal is fast and no one scrolls up, having multiple terminals does not help."*

And the test they set: *"if you as an agent look at the board, and only have access to the board, would you be able to see what is going on? what work is available, what work can start, is in progress? start work, stop work, inspect work (the info written in the record in a structured way)? descope work, scope work?"*

Explicitly **not** in scope: *"it is not about creating new records - that we can do via terminal. it is about work loop transparency and control."*

And the standing instruction: *"the board, even if it is a byproduct of basicly, it is essential and should grow with the basicly."*

## The gap, measured

Taken against the served board at 127.0.0.1:8788 on 2026-09-05, and against the snapshot it renders.

| the owner's question | answered today | by what |
| --- | --- | --- |
| what work is available | partly | `NEXT UP` draws 3 of 234 ready |
| what can start now | yes | `THE QUEUE`: 262 needs nothing, 24 waits on one, 8 waits on a chain |
| what is in progress | yes | `RUNNING NOW` and `CLAIMED, NO LANE` |
| what is blocked, and by what | yes | `THE QUEUE` names the top blockers and the longest chain |
| **inspect one record** | **no** | `units[]` carries `id, phase, priority, ready, status, title, type` and no body |
| **start work** | **no** | no action offers `loop run` or `supervise` |
| **stop work** | partly | `lane-kill` is in `ACTIONS`, but only reachable when an ask prefills it |
| **descope / scope** | **no** | no action changes status or priority |
| when will it be done | no | `basicly-hymq99` and `basicly-w6vbw61` |

So four of nine. The two channels that are missing are **inspect** and **control**, and they are missing for different reasons.

## The seam already exists

`board_actions.ACTIONS` is a closed table of three argv builders handed to the installed CLI as a subprocess. Its docstring states the design: *"The board is a renderer with a keyboard."* `.importlinter`'s `consumer-reads-only-the-snapshot` contract holds because the board never reads the tracker; it runs `basicly`.

That is the answer to inspect as well as control. A record's body does not have to enter the snapshot - 294 bodies would be a snapshot nobody can serve. The board runs `basicly tracker show <id>` the same way it runs `basicly policy checkpoint`, and renders what comes back. No contract moves.

`board_asks.pending` already prefills a row per implementable offer. What is missing is a surface for an action that no *ask* proposes - a ready record has no ask, so today nothing offers to start it.

## Acceptance Criteria

- WHEN an agent has the board and nothing else, IT SHALL be able to answer all nine questions in the table above, and a test SHALL enumerate them so the board cannot drift back into a report.
- WHERE a verb changes the flow of work, THE BOARD SHALL offer it on the row it applies to, not only where an ask happens to prefill it.
- THE BOARD SHALL NOT gain the ability to create a record: the owner keeps that in the terminal.
- `consumer-reads-only-the-snapshot` SHALL still hold: every new capability is an argv handed to the installed CLI.

## Plan

- integrity: `L2`
- children decompose this; each is a leaf a lane can build

payload.description:
## Context

Parent: basicly-lc2bd3v. The owner's words: *"inspect work (the info written in the record in a structured way)"*.

`units[]` carries seven keys and none of them is the record's body:

```
['id', 'phase', 'priority', 'ready', 'status', 'title', 'type']
```

So an agent holding only the board reads a title and stops. It cannot see the description, the acceptance criteria, the comments, the gate results, or which record blocks this one and why.

## The bodies do not go in the snapshot

294 open records with bodies is a snapshot no wall can serve, and the snapshot is a contract foreign producers implement - a required body field would break every one of them.

The board runs `basicly tracker show <id>` instead, as a subprocess, exactly as `board_actions` already runs `basicly policy checkpoint`. `consumer-reads-only-the-snapshot` is untouched: the board still reads no tracker.

## Acceptance Criteria

- WHEN a reader asks for a record by id, THE BOARD SHALL render its description, acceptance criteria, status, phase, priority, type, dependencies and comments, each under its own heading rather than as a JSON dump.
- WHERE the record does not exist, THE BOARD SHALL say so rather than draw a record whose every field is empty - `tracker show` returns `{"found": false}` and its `.fields.title` is null, which reads exactly like a record whose body was lost.
- THE RENDERED BODY SHALL be escaped: a description is producer text and reaches the page through autoescape like every other string.
- THE ACTION SHALL be read-only and SHALL NOT require a confirm code.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/board_actions.py`
- `src/basicly/board_serve.py`
- `.basicly/core/templates/board/`
- `tests/test_board_actions.py`

## Plan

- integrity: `L2`
- demonstration: open the board, ask for a record by id, and read its acceptance criteria off the page
