## Trigger

When a repository wants the append-only work tracker but not the rest of basicly, the only way in is `basicly install`, which converges a catalog, projections and hooks it never asked for, so I want each kit installable, updatable and removable on its own, so I can adopt the tracker in a repo that will never run basicly and take it back out cleanly.

## Context

Owner, 2026-09-08: the work tracker kit is one of the most essential parts of basicly and one that *people who do not use basicly will install standalone*, to get rid of a tracker whose records are edited in place - those conflict in git whenever more than one person or agent works the codebase in parallel. The model tier kit is the second such part: a repository may want control over which model runs which task without adopting anything else. Both are already kits, so a per-kit installer is the shape that matches what they are.

## Measured

Established by reading the CLI on 2026-09-08. Two kits exist:

| kit | files |
| --- | --- |
| `.basicly/core/kit/tracker` | 19 |
| `.basicly/core/kit/tier` | 5 |

`basicly --help` offers `install`, `uninstall`, `build`, `check` and 25 other commands. There is **no** `kit` command - `basicly kit --help` exits with `invalid choice: 'kit'`. `basicly install --help` mentions no per-kit selection; its only related flag records a technology selection. So the capability is absent rather than hidden, and the zero is trustworthy because the same `--help` probe did return the 29 commands that do exist.

## Why standalone matters, stated as the thing to protect

A consumer installing the tracker kit alone must get a tracker that virtually never conflicts under parallel work. basicly-aabirfj is the open finding that this is not yet true - the merge attribute the kit's own code is written for is not declared - and a standalone install is exactly the case where nobody will notice the omission until two agents collide. Whatever this record builds must carry that attribute into the consumer repository, or the standalone promise ships broken.

## Acceptance Criteria

- THE CLI SHALL install one named kit into a repository without installing the catalog, the projections or the hooks basicly otherwise converges.
- THE CLI SHALL update an installed kit in place, and SHALL report the version it moved from and to.
- THE CLI SHALL uninstall one named kit and SHALL leave no file it did not install, so a consumer can take it back out cleanly.
- THE INSTALLED KIT SHALL run in a repository where basicly is not installed and is never invoked, and a test SHALL drive it in such a repository rather than in this one.
- THE INSTALL SHALL carry every git attribute the kit's correctness depends on, including the event-log merge attribute basicly-aabirfj names, and SHALL fail rather than install a kit whose required attribute it cannot write.
- THE CLI SHALL list the kits available and which of them this repository has installed, so a consumer can tell an absent kit from a stale one.
- WHERE a kit is already installed at the requested version, THE INSTALL SHALL report that and change nothing.
- A TEST SHALL install, update and uninstall each kit in a throwaway repository and assert the tree returns to its original state.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/cli.py`
- `src/basicly/kit_install.py`
- `.scripts/kit_deployment.py`
- `.basicly/core/kit/README.md`
- `tests/test_kit_install.py`
- `docs/architecture/architecture.md`
- `changelog.d/<this-id>.added.md`

## Plan

- integrity: `L3`
- budget: `160000`
- depends on: `basicly-aabirfj`
- demonstration: in a throwaway git repository with no basicly installed, install the tracker kit, record and read an issue through it, update it, then uninstall it and confirm the tree is as it started

payload.text: Proposed fix from the consumer session that reported it, and it is better than treating this as a manifest problem: on first install, when a build target path already exists and carries no manifest entry, write the existing bytes to <path>.basicly-bak before overwriting. That reuses the convention --overwrite-scaffolds already established rather than inventing one, and it sidesteps the hard part entirely - install never has to distinguish its own stale output from user content, because the distinction stops mattering once the bytes survive either way. Acceptance should cover the three always-on outputs (.github/copilot-instructions.md, AGENTS.md, .claude/CLAUDE.md) and assert no backup is written on a repeat install, so the tree does not accumulate one per run.

payload.description: Reported by the terminal canary after a real 49-record import. tracker import preserves the source ids verbatim - term-* here - and says nothing about [tracker] prefix, which basicly.toml does not declare after an import. Reads and comments work; only minting a new ROOT record fails, with 'a create with no --parent needs an id prefix'. The harm is the ordering: the migration runbook's last step retires .beads/, and .beads/config.yaml (issue_prefix) is the only other place the string exists. Follow the runbook to the end and you delete the sole record of your own namespace, then discover it weeks later. The importer can derive the prefix from the ids it just landed - they all share it - and name it in the import report.

payload.description: Reported by the burndown-chart consumer before its first install. fragment.schema.json declares applies_to as an array of any string, catalog lint never mentions it, and the only enforcement is loader._validate_fragment, which refuses anything that is not all or a registered target. So the authoring loop is scaffold, validate against the shipped schema, pass, commit, and then discover at build time that the fragment was never loadable - 6 of their 8 overlay fragments. The values were rules quality style review security testing, every one a natural routing category, because the name reads as which contexts does this apply to and means which rendering target. build is step 10 of install, so steps 1 to 9 have already landed when it dies. A static enum in the schema is wrong because targets are registry files a consumer can add to; the fixes that hold are a message that names the registered set and points at tags, and a schema description that states the constraint.
payload.title: applies to passes the shipped schema and then hard fails inside build

payload.description: Reported by the terminal canary. install --overwrite-scaffolds writes name.basicly-bak siblings and nothing ignores them, so an upgrade leaves untracked files in a consumer tree and a landing refuses dirt outside the tracker. The tracker kit's derived folds are the same shape: SPEC section 4 says snapshot.jsonl is gitignored and never committed, this repo ignores it, and install never adds the entry - so a consumer who runs git add .basicly/ledger after an import commits the fold and recreates the dual store conflict the event log exists to escape. install already scaffolds the basicly.local.toml entry, so the seam exists and covers one file of four.

payload.description: Reported by the burndown-chart consumer on a real 702-record beads export. Every record refused and the dry run answered with 702 quoted ids, about 40KB of output, naming no constraint and no remedy. The cause is one rule and is the same for all of them: kit/tracker/ids.py _RECORD spells the prefix [a-z][a-z0-9]* with no hyphen, so burndown-chart-017 parses as prefix burndown with an illegal hyphen left in the suffix. Their prefix is burndown-chart. The maintainer decision is taken: the grammar does not widen, because ids.py:124 binds the prefix to the gate's first-hyphen split and the change would reach the commit-msg gate, evidence ids and child indices. So the refusal must say the constraint out loud, once, with the source prefix it found and the fact that a hyphenated prefix is not importable - instead of quoting every id. Also fixed here: preview never called _prefix_note, so the dry run could not name the id prefix at all.
payload.title: the import refuses every record and names no reason

payload.description: Reported by the burndown-chart consumer. Their ruff-format and prettier reached into .basicly/core and rewrote 75 files - 40 yaml, 1 yml, 1 css, 33 py - cosmetically, semantics preserved. basicly check then printed All generated files and manifest are up to date and exited 0. It is not silent: _report_provenance_notes prints a Note on stderr naming each drifted file. Reproduced here with a positive control - one mutated core file in a real 0.12.1 install gives exit 0, the up-to-date line on stdout, and the Note on stderr. The defect is that the summary contradicts the note printed beside it and nothing blocks, so over 75 files the note scrolls past and the consumer commits the rewrite. Owner decision taken: core drift refuses. Paired with shipping ignore snippets so a consumer's tooling leaves the vendored catalog alone.
payload.title: check says up to date over a vendored core a formatter rewrote

payload.description: Third identical data point for basicly-mmcqg8a and this one carries the mechanism. burndown-chart measures 41/46 = 89.1% on a fresh install, identical to this repo and to the terminal canary, with 13 overlay fragments of their own. routing_evals.routing_outcome builds descriptions from _model_invoked_descriptions and loads evals.yaml under the skill sources only, so consumer fragments are not in the corpus at all and cannot move the number. A fresh install therefore fails catalog lint until the consumer declares a floor defending a metric that measures our shipped skill catalog, that they cannot influence and are not responsible for. Worth deciding whether the gate should run in a consumer repo at all.

payload.description: Measured by the burndown-chart consumer on a first install with 13 overlay fragments: AGENTS.md 28221 chars 447 lines against a budget of 16000/320, .claude/CLAUDE.md 14278/221 against 9000/200, .github/copilot-instructions.md 14377/222 against 9000/200. payload.description: Reported by the burndown-chart consumer: a 52-byte uv.lock appeared at their repo root after install, named by no install output, in a repo that is pip plus pip-compile and not uv managed. Reproduced here with a positive control - a scratch consumer repo carrying a pyproject.toml, install, then one commit: uv.lock appears with version = 1, revision = 3, requires-python = >=3.14, byte-identical in shape to theirs, and protect-generated-commit then fails with files were modified by this hook. Cause: every projected hook entry is uv run python <script> (precommit_config._hook_entry and hooks._copilot_hook_config), and uv run treats any directory with a pyproject.toml as a project, resolving and writing a lock. Every hook script is stdlib only plus sibling imports, so --no-project is safe; pipe-status-guard.py in this repo already uses that form.
payload.title: the projected hooks run uv run without no project and write a uv lock

payload.description: Found while re-projecting the hooks in this repo. .pre-commit-config.yaml carries a markdownlint hook whose entry points at .basicly/core/hooks/markdownlint.py - a shipped catalog script with its own test - but hooks.yaml declares no such spec. precommit_config._is_managed treats any local hook whose entry contains the hooks relpath as basicly's, which is the prune that closed basicly-qdxxy0i, so hooks-build deletes it. managed_hook_mismatches only compares hooks that ARE in the spec list, so hooks-check stays green on a config build would change. Proved pre-existing rather than caused by the uv --no-project change: rendering HEAD's committed config through render_precommit_config with the old entry string also drops it. Two defects in one: a gate this repo runs on every commit is silently removed by our own build, and check is green on a config build would rewrite. The fix has a decision in it - declaring markdownlint in hooks.yaml with technologies node wires it for every node consumer, and the script needs markdownlint-cli2 present, so it could block commits in a consumer that has node but not that package.
payload.title: hooks build deletes a local hook that check reports as up to date

payload.text: The fix also carries the other half of the owner decision: install now names what it noticed and will not change on the repo's behalf - the exclusion line for a detected pre-commit, ruff, prettier or eslint config, the exclusion for a detected secret scanner (every imported record carries a sha256 import_digest and every scanner flags 64-char hex; a consumer's 702-record import gave them 702 hits), and a root CLAUDE.md now sitting beside the projected .claude/CLAUDE.md, which Claude Code loads as well.

payload.description: test_board_serve.py::test_the_record_route_answers_with_and_without_the_suffix failed once on 2026-09-11 and passed on re-run, and verify --mode full passed in the same minute. It asserts plain[1] == suffixed[1] over two separate GETs; the diff is one byte at index 11586, 0 against 1, which is a clock-derived value in the rendered page - an age or a timestamp - not a routing difference. The assertion is stronger than the property it means to hold. Compare the two responses with every time-varying span normalised, or assert the routing property directly. Pre-existing and unrelated to the v0.12.2 changes.
payload.title: a board serve test compares two pages rendered a moment apart

payload.description: The second half of basicly-vdlio8i, now confirmed in two consumer repos independently. hooks-check compares only the hooks that ARE in the current spec list, through managed_hook_mismatches, so anything build would ADD or REMOVE is invisible to it. Both canaries lost the projected markdownlint hook silently: terminal-05 greps their .pre-commit-config.yaml and finds no markdownlint entry at all, while hooks-check actively asserted health. They survived only because that repo duplicates the gate in its own .scripts/git-hooks/pre-commit.py, which is luck and not something the next consumer has. A consumer who relied on the projected hook had no signal whatsoever. The fix the reporter proposes is the right class - notice that a hook built before is no longer in the output - and there is a cheaper form already proved here: render_precommit_config over the current text diverges from the file on disk while hooks-check passes, so checking the render against the file catches adds, removes and reorders in one comparison. Watch the false-positive risk: the renderer preserves unmanaged blocks by position, so a byte comparison must be judged against a consumer's hand-maintained hooks before it becomes a refusal.
payload.title: hooks check is green on a config hooks build would rewrite

payload.description: A consumer whose source prefix carries a hyphen must rewrite it before importing, and nothing tells them the prefix appears outside the id field. In the burndown-chart export it appeared in id, title, description, notes and close_reason, and dependency edges are nested rather than top level. Rewriting only record[id] yields a ledger that imports clean and whose prose points at ids that do not exist - nothing fails, which is what makes it dangerous. The reporter supplied a verified shape: match the prefix WITH its trailing hyphen, never the bare prefix, because the repo name is the prefix and a bare match corrupts prose; recurse through dicts and lists so nested edges are caught; enumerate the touched fields by scanning before rewriting rather than assuming; accept on 702 of 702 matching RECORD_ID_PATTERN and 702 unique. The import refusal now names the constraint (basicly-iehbmvu), so a consumer meets the one-way door in time; this is the other half - what to do once they have met it.
payload.title: the migration runbook does not name the silent corruption a prefix remap causes

payload.description: Consequence of declaring markdownlint as a node-gated hook in v0.12.2 (basicly-vdlio8i), reported by burndown-chart from a real upgrade. Their .pre-commit-config.yaml now carries their own markdownlint-cli hook reading .markdownlint.json and ours running markdownlint-cli2, over the same files with two rule sets. Both pass, so nothing is broken - but ours no-ops in their tree because markdownlint-cli2 is absent, so the gate that passes is not the gate enforcing anything. Preserving their foreign hook is correct and they are not asking us to change that. What is missing is the notice: v0.12.1 to v0.12.2 is where the second gate silently appears, and the upgrade notes say nothing. Either say it in the notes, or have install name an existing markdown linter the way it now names a linter or secret scanner reaching into the managed core.
payload.title: a consumer that already lints markdown now runs two markdown gates

payload.text: Second consumer's recommendation, from a completed cutover on v0.12.2: do not run the rank-1 gate in a consumer repo at all. Their argument is the mechanism on basicly-6e8fzlz turned into a conclusion - a consumer cannot move the number, cannot be responsible for it, and blocking their first commit until they declare a floor for OUR catalog's routing quality teaches them only that the gate is noise. Their fallback if it stays: default the floor at install from the measured rate, which makes it a ratchet rather than a roadblock. Three repos have now measured 41/46 = 89.1%.

Correction from the reporter, and it strengthens the case rather than weakening it. This record said terminal-05 survived the silent deletion by duplicating the gate. They did not duplicate it as insurance: .scripts/git-hooks/ predates the basicly install there and always ran markdownlint, so the coverage that saved them belongs to a consumer who never depended on the projection at all. A repo that adopted basicly first and trusted the projected hook would have had nothing - no hook, and a hooks-check asserting health. Treat the two observed survivals as evidence about those two repos' pre-existing tooling, not as evidence that the blast radius is small. They also offer to be the test consumer for the false-alarm half of the render-vs-file check: their .pre-commit-config.yaml carries hand-maintained entries beside the managed ones, so a byte comparison against the render fires there on day one. That is the direction worth exercising.

Second data point, and it is the worse shape - it refutes the fix this record leans to. terminal-05's markdownlint is not a pre-commit entry at all: it is a step inside .scripts/git-hooks/pre-commit.py invoking node_modules/markdownlint-cli2. So a projected markdownlint hook collides with no entry install could detect by scanning .pre-commit-config.yaml, and nothing in the config would show the duplication - it simply runs markdown a second time, from a different harness, with its own file scoping. The proposal to have install name an existing markdown linter the way it names a linter or secret scanner therefore does not cover this case, which is the case that hides. Whatever lands has to work for a linter invoked inside a consumer's own hook script, or admit it only covers the visible half.

payload.description: Reported by burndown-chart from a real v0.12.1 to v0.12.2 upgrade and reproduced here as a consumer. .github/workflows/basicly-gates.yml is scaffolded only when absent, and it embeds five uvx --from git+...@vX.Y.Z pins built from the installing engine's own version (scaffolds.DIST_SOURCE). An upgrade converges and leaves all five at the old tag. The next push then runs the OLD engine against a catalog the NEW one installed, and the version-skew guard refuses: four of the five workflow steps fail. Positive control here - a scratch repo installed at 0.12.2, then uvx --from git+...@v0.12.1 basicly check exits 1 with Version skew: the core catalog was installed by basicly 0.12.2 and this is basicly 0.12.1. The guard is right; the interaction is the defect. install is the only thing that knows the new version, the workflow is the only place the pin lives, and install deliberately will not touch it after the first write. Nothing in the install output mentions it and the failure surfaces in CI as version skew rather than as anything a reader connects to the upgrade. .vscode/tasks.json carries the same five pins and the same latent shape - it does not break CI, it silently runs the old engine from a task. release.py already has the narrow machinery for this: PIN_FILES plus PIN_RE_TEMPLATE rewrite only the version substring.
payload.title: upgrading breaks a consumer CI because install will not move the pin it wrote

payload.description: Retro finding from the session of 2026-09-11, from a real user-visible wrong answer. A consumer asked whether the new .basicly-bak guard covers a root CLAUDE.md. I answered yes, reasoning that the guard runs over every planned output whatever its path - which is true and which I had verified. The conclusion did not follow: .basicly/core/targets/claude.yaml declares .claude/CLAUDE.md and root CLAUDE.md is not a planned output at all, so it was never at risk and no backup was written. The consumer caught it. Root cause: I verified the MECHANISM (path-agnostic iteration) and inferred the POPULATION (which paths are iterated) rather than enumerating it. The quality-gate fragment already says state only the scope actually exercised, and I did exercise the guard - the gap is narrower and is not covered: a guarantee's coverage is the list the code iterates, not the generality of the code that iterates it. Proposal for approval, not applied: one line in the quality-gate fragment - when claiming what a guarantee covers, name the list it iterates; generality of the mechanism is not evidence about membership.
payload.title: a coverage claim must enumerate the list a guard iterates

payload.description: Retro finding from the session of 2026-09-11. comment-density and module-size refused four times across the session - projection.py, tests/test_cli.py twice, .basicly/core/hooks/markdownlint.py - and each refusal arrived from a full pytest run, so the write-measure-trim loop cost about four minutes per iteration against a check that runs in about two seconds standalone. On markdownlint.py it took four trim cycles to get from 65.6 percent to under the frozen 62.7. The gates are right and the trims improved the prose; the feedback path is the defect. Both scripts take a path and answer immediately: uv run python .scripts/check_comment_density.py and .scripts/check_module_size.py. Proposal for approval, not applied: name those two as the fast local check in the python-guidelines skill, which already owns how to satisfy a size or complexity ratchet without gaming it, so the measurement happens while the docstring is being written rather than after the suite.
payload.title: a prose ratchet is a two second check run behind a four minute suite

payload.description: Quirks bullet proposed from an incident on 2026-09-11. Typing rg -rn <pattern> <path> reads as recursive plus line numbers by habit; ripgrep parses -r as --replace and consumes the next token as the replacement string, so the pattern is silently substituted in every printed line and no line numbers appear. Positive control run this session: rg -rn rank1_floor src/basicly/config.py printed catalog: Table(keys=frozenset({technologies, n, n_high_water})) - the searched term replaced by n - while rg -n on the same file printed 564: ... rank1_floor ... with the term intact. The failure is silent and the output looks like a real finding, which is what makes it worth a bullet: I nearly reported that config.py had no rank1_floor key. Proposal for approval, not applied: one bullet in the non-interactive-shell fragment, which already carries the zsh word-splitting and the count-the-sites-before-a-replace traps - rg -r takes a replacement, never recursion; ripgrep recurses by default, so -n alone is the form.
payload.title: rg -r takes a replacement so a bare -rn silently rewrites its own output

payload.description: Reported by the burndown-chart consumer as they closed their onboarding, and offered about our guidance rather than our code. They hit the zsh word-splitting trap the non-interactive-shell fragment warns about - a command prefix in a bare $VAR, exit 127 eight times in a row - and they had read the fragment first. Their point is the one worth keeping: stating the rule was not enough to stop a reader who had already seen it. They name the detectable signature, which is what makes this actionable rather than a complaint - a bare $VAR in command position. This repo's own principle is hook over note, and the same consumer had their other shell mistake caught by pipe-status-guard in the same session, which is the evidence that the instinct works. Proposal for approval, not applied: a PreToolUse guard on a bare $VAR appearing in command position, the way pipe-status-guard refuses a status read after head or tail. Check the false-positive rate first - a legitimate $EDITOR or $SHELL in command position is the population that decides whether it can be a refusal or only a warning.
payload.title: a bare VAR in command position is the signature of the zsh word splitting trap

That cost a round on v0.12.1. The re-record also caught two stale claims on that page, so do it by executing rather than by editing the numbers.

Correction found while applying this: the record says both scripts take a path. They do not. `uv run python .scripts/check_comment_density.py src/basicly/projection.py` and the same with `--help` both print the whole-tree summary (543 modules), and `grep -n 'argv|argparse|add_argument'` matches nothing in either script. The remedy stands on the timing rather than on narrowing: measured 2026-09-12, 1.30s and 0.12s wall clock against about four minutes for the pytest run that reports the same refusal. The bullet is written against what the scripts do.

Measured before building, as the record required. Population: 17358 Bash calls recorded across 214 transcripts for this repository. With the repo's own quote-aware splitter (shell_tokens.split_pipeline_segments), a bare unquoted $VAR head occurs in 4 calls (0.023%); three are recorded failing with exit 127 or '(eval):1: no such file or directory' and the fourth was permission-denied and never ran. A quoted "$VAR" head occurs in 54 calls (0.31%) and is always an executable path holding a space. $EDITOR, $SHELL and $PAGER in command position occur 0 times, so the population the record named as deciding refuse-versus-warn is empty. That makes it a refusal. The discriminator shipped is narrower still: the same command string must assign that variable a value holding whitespace, which cannot reach an environment variable the command never sets. Driven over the whole corpus the shipped guard fires on exactly those 4 and nothing else.

payload.description:
## Trigger

When a coding agent writes code it writes prose with it, and the prose then has to be kept true as the code moves, so the owner wants comments banned from code outright, enforced deterministically rather than by guidance, so the code is the only source of truth and a change to it can never leave a stale claim behind.

## Context

Owner, 2026-09-12: "ever since watermarking has been a part of the claude models, the comments in files have blown out of proportions". The rule is that the code is the authoritative source of truth, and the benefit is that changing code no longer obliges anyone to update a comment. This inverts the repository's current position, which is encoded in the `comment-density` ratchet, the `code-is-authoritative` rule and the comment sections of `python-guidelines` - all of which argue that prose carrying a why is evidence and must stay.

## Measured, 2026-09-12

Census over the tracked tree with `tokenize` and `ast`:

| population | count | chars |
| --- | --- | --- |
| prose `#` comments | 9926 lines | 710430 |
| docstrings | 9582 | 2489642 |
| functional directives | 332 lines | - |

Directives break down as `noqa` 122, `nosec` 108, `type: ignore` 48, `comment-density-waiver:` 25, `pragma: no` 14, `module-size-waiver:` 10, shebang 2, `fmt:` 3. Every one of these is read by a tool and must survive a strip, or the build stops. Docstrings are 78% of the prose mass.

Tracked file types: 554 `.py`, 3 `.html`, 1 each of `.sh`, `.ps1`, `.mjs`, `.css`, plus 12 `.j2`. So this repository exercises mainly Python; the kit must still cover the wider set a consumer has.

## The two docstring consumers, enumerated rather than assumed

- `.scripts/docs_claims.py:205` calls `ast.get_docstring` on each hook script to fill the Description column of the generated `catalog-hooks` table in `.basicly/core/hooks/README.md`. Strip docstrings and that column empties.
- Nine `.scripts/*.py` CLIs pass `description=__doc__` to `argparse`, so `--help` comes from the module docstring.

Both need a replacement before the strip: the hook description moves into `hooks.yaml` as a real field, and `description=__doc__` becomes a string literal. A string is code, not a comment.

## Owner decisions, 2026-09-12

- Docstrings are in scope; both comments and docstrings go.
- The `comment-density` ratchet, its 25 waivers, its frozen tables and its `basicly.d` entries are deleted, along with the guidance that argues for prose.
- The gate checks in CI and in pre-commit, and strips only on an explicit `--fix`. It never rewrites behind the committer.
- Covered: all code files - Python, shell, JS/TS, HTML, CSS, Java, C# and the other .NET languages. Excluded: config files, Markdown and docs.
- Packaged as a kit and distributed by `uvx` exactly as the tier and tracker kits are: its own package, vendor-by-default `init`, also runs direct, git-only channel until the v1.0.0 freeze.

## Acceptance Criteria

- THE KIT SHALL report every comment in a code file it supports, naming the file and line.
- THE KIT SHALL remove those comments only when `--fix` is given, and SHALL leave every functional directive in place.
- THE KIT SHALL refuse a file it cannot lex confidently rather than strip it, because a wrong strip corrupts source.
- WHERE the language is Python, THE STRIP SHALL be verified by re-parsing and comparing the abstract syntax tree with docstrings removed.
- THE STRIP SHALL be idempotent: a second pass over stripped output SHALL change zero bytes.
- THE STRIP SHALL NOT alter the content of any string literal.
- THE GATE SHALL run in CI as a `[[verify.checks]]` entry and at commit time as a hook.
- THE REPOSITORY SHALL carry no prose comment or docstring in a covered file once the migration lands, and the suite, `ruff` and `pyright` SHALL stay green.
- THE RUFF CONFIGURATION SHALL NOT select a rule that requires a docstring.
- THE KIT SHALL install into a repository that never runs basicly, by `uvx`, exactly as `basicly-tracker` and `basicly-tier` do.

## Plan

- integrity: `L3`
- demonstration: run the kit against a throwaway repository holding one file per supported language, check it reports every comment, fix it, and confirm the files still compile and the directives survive

## Trigger

Graph engineering is one of the key epics in the backlog and the ledger holds no prior art on it, so the owner supplied two sources and asked for the analysis banked before the epic is worked.

## Sources

- `https://adk.dev/2.0/` and its own markdown routes.
- `https://github.com/google/adk-python`, which the owner named as the authority for the API.
- A video transcript (Annie, "graph engineering"), supplied by the owner and treated as a set of claims to verify rather than as a source.

Verified 2026-09-12 against ADK Python **2.0.0** (GA 2026-05-19), cross-checked against **2.9.0**. Comparisons against LangGraph **1.2.11** and openai-agents **0.22.2**. Facts come from the unpacked wheel source or from code executed in a scratch venv **with no API key set**, so any model call would have raised.

## The term itself

**"Graph engineering" is the video's coinage. Google never uses it.** Zero hits across `graphs/`, `graphs/routes/`, `graphs/dynamic/` and `graphs/data-handling/`, with a working positive control ("prompt-based" hits 4x in `graphs.md`). The four-stage progression prompt -> context -> loop -> graph is unsourced framing. **Do not write the epic around the term as though it were established.**

## The transcript's claims, adjudicated

| Claim | Verdict |
| --- | --- |
| Agent and plain function in the same node list, same wiring | **VERIFIED, executed.** `NodeLike = BaseNode \| BaseTool \| Callable \| Literal["START"]`, `workflow/_graph.py:39` |
| Fan-out: parallel branches from one node | **VERIFIED, executed.** Several `edges` rows sharing a source |
| Join: waits for the slowest, bundles into a dict keyed by node name, no hand-written aggregator | **VERIFIED exactly, executed.** `JoinNode`; `outputs = {p: loop_state.node_outputs.get(p) for p in predecessors}`, `workflow/_workflow.py:697-706` |
| Router picks one downstream branch | **VERIFIED, executed.** `Event(route=...)` plus a `RoutingMap` edge row; `DEFAULT_ROUTE` fallback |
| Dynamic fan-out, branch count decided at runtime | **VERIFIED, executed** - `node(worker, parallel_worker=True)`, `workflow/_node.py:49-55`, `_parallel_worker.py:35-131` |
| Deterministic router when the set is closed, LLM when open | **PARTIAL.** The mechanism is real and node-type-agnostic (`_node_runner.py:288-290`). The closed-set/open-set *prescription* is the video's, not ADK's |
| 3 fetches + join + 1 strategist costs exactly one LLM call | **VERIFIED structurally.** `FunctionNode` and `JoinNode` make no model call; the count equals the `LlmAgent` nodes on the taken path |
| "Can you draw it before the input arrives?" is the decision rule | **CONTRADICTED in wording.** ADK's discriminator is control-flow complexity - loops, recursion - not input-dependence (`graphs.md:20-21`) |

## The API, and one place the code beats the docs

`google/adk/workflow/__all__`: `BaseNode, DEFAULT_ROUTE, Edge, FunctionNode, JoinNode, Node, NodeTimeoutError, RetryConfig, START, Workflow, node`. A plain callable in `edges` is auto-wrapped as a `FunctionNode` named after the function. A tuple row is a chain, a dict row is a router, fan-out is several rows sharing a source. A `Workflow` is itself a `BaseNode`, so graphs nest.

**`adk.dev/graphs/dynamic/` documents `parallelWorker` for TypeScript and Go only and shows Python an `asyncio.gather` workaround. The Python flag exists and works** - `workflow/_node.py:49-140`, executed. Caveat: it returns `_ParallelWorker`, underscore-private and absent from `__all__`, so it is a public keyword into a private type. Pin the version if we ever depend on it.

Status: **generally available**, Apache-2.0, Python >=3.10. Zero `experimental` markers under `workflow/` in 2.0.0, with a positive control (20+ other files in the same wheel do carry them). Symbol set identical in 2.9.0.

## Against the alternatives

| Shape | ADK 2.0.0 | LangGraph 1.2.11 | OpenAI Agents SDK 0.22.2 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Fan-out | several `edges` rows; `max_concurrency` | `add_edge(START, ...)` twice | none; write `asyncio.gather` |
| Join | **`JoinNode`, keyed by node name, zero user code** | no join node; fan-in without a reducer raises `InvalidUpdateError`, and with one you get an **unkeyed list** | none |
| Router | `Event(route=...)` + `RoutingMap` | `add_conditional_edges` | LLM `handoff` only |
| Dynamic fan-out | `parallel_worker=True` | `Send` | none |

The sharpest real difference: **ADK's join is keyed and free; LangGraph's needs a declared reducer and loses which node produced which value.** That is the transcript's strongest true claim.

## What this means for us

**The phase ladder is already a static graph in all but name.** `loop.py:1547` `_HANDLERS` is a 7-entry node table dispatched at `loop.py:1587`; the ladder is already drawn as a `stateDiagram-v2` at `architecture.md:1339-1362`. We already answered the video's own decision rule with "yes".

**The gap is that edges are not data.** ADK's `edges=[...]` is enumerable; ours are implicit in what each `_on_*` handler returns via `_moved(...)`. There is no object you can ask "what follows verify?".

Shapes we already have, and every router but one is deterministic:

| Site | Shape | Router |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `supervise.py:1215-1231` | fan-out via `ThreadPoolExecutor`, then a join already keyed by issue id into a tuple | n/a |
| serial landing, `architecture.md:1883-1895` | **a join ADK cannot express** - a conflicted landing bounces and the pass continues; `_parallel_worker.py:116-125` cancels every sibling and re-raises | n/a |
| `loop.py:1587` phase advance | router over a closed set of 7 | deterministic |
| admission, `architecture.md:1810-1834` | 6-gate router chain | deterministic |
| `loop.py:315-350` validate verdict | router on a judged verdict | **LLM**, and fenced by D-04 so it can never pass a required gate |
| `loop.py:200` decompose | **dynamic fan-out** - the agent proposes the shape, deterministic code applies it | ADK's own division of labour, already built |
| `loop.py:352-368` review lenses | **a fan-out that is not one** - a serial `for` over 2 independent LLM dispatches | deterministic |

## Adopting ADK: refused by four recorded non-goals

`architecture.md:412-433` refuses, as permanent: an LLM orchestrator in control of the tracker; an external daemon or dependency; agent-to-agent messaging; personas spawning personas (`ctx.run_node` is exactly that). Add **D-02**, which makes phase a derived function of five tracker values rather than held state - ADK's `Workflow` holds `_LoopState` in memory, which is the durable-phase field this repo removed on purpose.

Already tried and rejected, by name: a declarative phase table (D-02), an LLM router where a deterministic one would do (D-04), parallel verify and validate (D-05), a second LLM re-judging a verdict (`architecture.md:1874`, "the consensus-voting shape this design rejects"), nodes exchanging outputs directly.

## What is actually worth doing

1. **Parallelise the review lenses** (`loop.py:354`). A serial loop over two independent LLM dispatches, in a codebase that already owns a working `ThreadPoolExecutor` fan-out. No non-goal refuses it. **Check the inflight spend accounting first** - the researcher did not read it closely enough to say the two concurrent dispatches meter correctly.
2. **Key the lane join by name.** `dispatch_lanes` returns `tuple[LaneOutcome, ...]`; every consumer that wants one lane's outcome scans for it. ADK's `{name: output}` is the better shape and it is a pure refactor.
3. **Edges as data, but only succession.** Making the ladder enumerable would let the board draw it and let a gate assert the mermaid diagram matches the code. Any proposal must say plainly that it moves only *succession* to data and leaves `derive_phase`'s reachability in code - otherwise it re-litigates D-02 and should be refused on that ground.

## Could not establish

- Whether ADK's Python `parallel_worker=True` is intended public API (public keyword, private return type, no Python example found).
- Whether an ADK Python `LlmAgent` can emit a route directly; the mechanism is type-agnostic but only a Go example exists and executing one needs a live key.
- ADK's join behaviour when a predecessor fails; the docs warn about it (`graphs_routes.md:547`) but the failure path was not executed. This matters for the comparison with our bounce semantics and is one probe away.
- Whether "graph engineering" has currency outside the video; only Google's own docs were searched.
payload.title: research spike on graph engineering and google adk 2.0

Verified 2026-09-12 against ADK Python 2.0.0 GA with 2.9.0 as a cross-check, LangGraph 1.2.11 and openai-agents 0.22.2, from unpacked wheel source and code executed with no API key present. Six of the transcript's eight claims verified by execution, one partial, one contradicted in wording. Graph engineering is the video's coinage and Google never uses it. ADK's keyed JoinNode is genuinely better than LangGraph's reducer, and OpenAI's SDK has no graph at all. Adopting ADK is refused by four permanent non-goals plus D-02; what survives is three concrete items, of which parallelising the review lenses is the cheapest and needs the inflight spend accounting checked first.

## Trigger

When a repository installs a kit standalone it gets working code and nothing that tells an agent the code exists, so the agent never calls it, and I want each kit to ship its own skill and the instruction that triggers it, so a consumer without basicly gets the behaviour and not just the binary.

## Context

Owner, 2026-09-12, on the kit distribution landing: "the kit is not complete as it does not ship the dedicated skill at the least and instructions on how and when to call the skill in always-on instructions or at least scoped on when a coding file is created and edited, and a way on how to add this info to always-on instruction files if basicly is not installed in that repo. And this is also valid for all kits! Otherwise how would an agent in a consumer repo without basicly know when to use model tier and how, and when and how to use the work tracker."

The point is exact. `basicly-ssbkq5c` was written as an installer record and its acceptance criteria are all about files, attributes and idempotence. Every one of them is met and the kit is still not usable by an agent, because in this repository the guidance arrives through a channel the standalone install does not carry: fragments and skills projected by `basicly build`. A consumer who never runs `basicly` has neither.

## Measured, 2026-09-12

- Three kits ship: `comments`, `tracker`, `tier`. Each install writes only `.py` files, a README and, for the tracker, two git rules.
- Guidance for the comment ban exists in this repository as the `code-is-authoritative` fragment (path-scoped) and in the `python-guidelines` skill. **Neither travels with the kit.**
- Guidance for the tier kit is the `tier-injection` skill; for the tracker it is the `work-tracker` skill. **Neither travels either.**
- So a consumer repository that runs `basicly-comments init` has a hook-ready checker and no agent instruction anywhere that a comment is refused.

## Acceptance Criteria

- EACH KIT SHALL carry its own agent skill in its own directory, authored so it is not discoverable as a skill inside this repository.
- THE INSTALL SHALL write that skill into the agent skill roots a consumer actually reads, and `uninstall` SHALL remove exactly what it wrote.
- EACH KIT SHALL carry a short always-on block stating when to reach for the skill, and the install SHALL make it available to a repository that has no basicly.
- WHERE the consumer has an always-on instruction file, THE INSTALL SHALL be able to write that block into it inside a marked, idempotent region that `uninstall` removes, and SHALL NOT do so silently by default.
- WHERE the consumer has no such file, THE INSTALL SHALL print the block so a human can place it.
- THE SKILL AND THE BLOCK SHALL be the same text this repository uses, read from one source rather than written twice.
- A TEST SHALL install each kit into a throwaway repository, assert the skill and the block land where an agent reads them, and assert `uninstall` returns the tree to its original state.

## Plan

- integrity: `L3`
- depends on: `basicly-ssbkq5c` (closed)
- demonstration: in a throwaway repository with no basicly, install each kit and show the agent-facing files that appeared, then uninstall and show the tree is as it started
payload.title: each kit ships the skill and the instruction that make an agent use it

## Trigger

When a repository adopts the work tracker through `basicly install` its ledger gets no union-merge attribute, so two branches that each append an event conflict, and the promise the tracker exists to make is not delivered on the path most consumers take.

## Steps to Reproduce

Measured 2026-09-12 in a throwaway git repository with a real `basicly install`.

```
$ basicly install
basicly install complete: repo converged.
$ ls .gitattributes
".gitattributes": No such file or directory
$ git check-attr text merge -- .basicly/ledger/events-0001.jsonl
.basicly/ledger/events-0001.jsonl: text: unspecified
.basicly/ledger/events-0001.jsonl: merge: unspecified
```

The control, the same probe against a standalone `basicly-tracker init`:

```
tracker: added to .gitattributes: events-*.jsonl -text merge=union
$ git check-attr text merge -- .basicly/ledger/events-0001.jsonl
.basicly/ledger/events-0001.jsonl: text: unset
.basicly/ledger/events-0001.jsonl: merge: union
```

So the standalone installer is **more correct than the integrated one**, which is the wrong way round.

## Why no gate caught it

`grep -rn 'gitattributes|merge=union|check-attr' src/basicly/*.py .basicly/core/hooks/*.py` returns nothing. Positive control: the same grep for `gitignore` returns 10 files, so the probe discriminates. Repo-wide, `merge=union` appears in six files and exactly one of them **writes** it - `packages/basicly-tracker/basicly_tracker/__init__.py`, built 2026-09-12. `.scripts/kit_deployment.py` only checks it, and `.scripts/` does not ship to a consumer, so a consumer has neither the write nor the check.

basicly-aabirfj closed by declaring the attribute in **this repository's own hand-written `.gitattributes`** and gating it here. Its last acceptance criterion - "THE KIT SHALL install this attribute into a consumer repository" - was explicitly discharged to basicly-ssbkq5c, which built the standalone installer only. Nothing carried it into `basicly install`. The criterion was met for one of the two ways in.

## Blast radius

Every consumer that adopted the tracker through `basicly install`. The failure is silent until two branches append, and then it is a content conflict in a large JSONL file that a human must hand-resolve - the exact failure the append-only design exists to remove.

## Acceptance Criteria

- THE INSTALL SHALL write every git attribute and ignore rule the tracker kit's correctness depends on, reading the globs off `events.LOG_GLOB` and `snapshot.DERIVED_PATTERNS` rather than spelling them again.
- THE INSTALL SHALL refuse rather than converge where it cannot write them, matching the standalone installer.
- THE INSTALL SHALL be idempotent, and SHALL NOT disturb a rule the consumer already wrote.
- A CHECK THAT SHIPS TO THE CONSUMER SHALL report a ledger whose attribute is absent, since `.scripts/kit_deployment.py` does not travel.
- A TEST SHALL install into a throwaway repository and assert `git check-attr` reports `text: unset` and `merge: union`, with a control asserting the same history conflicts without them.
- THE TWO INSTALL PATHS SHALL agree, and a test SHALL assert that what `basicly install` guarantees for the tracker is what `basicly-tracker init` guarantees.

## Plan

- integrity: `L3`
- demonstration: install through basicly into a throwaway repo, build two branches that each append an event, merge them, and read every event present afterwards
payload.title: basicly install leaves the ledger without the union merge attribute

## Trigger

When a repository that already has basicly runs a standalone kit install, it ends up with two copies of the same kit at two different paths and nothing notices, so an agent may read one and a hook may run the other.

## Measured, 2026-09-12

`basicly install` materialises the catalog and the kit lands at `.basicly/core/kit/<name>/`. A standalone `basicly-<kit> init` vendors to `.basicly/kit/<name>/`. Both are plausible places to look, neither knows about the other, and the two can be at different versions.

Confirmed by running both into throwaway repositories and listing the trees.

## Why it matters more than tidiness

The kit is imported by path. A hook wired against one root keeps running the copy at that root after the other is updated, so an upgrade can appear to have landed and have changed nothing. That is the shape of failure this repository already pays for elsewhere - a stale copy that every diagnostic reports as installed.

## Acceptance Criteria

- WHERE a repository already carries the kit under the basicly-managed root, THE STANDALONE INSTALL SHALL say so and SHALL NOT write a second copy.
- WHERE a repository carries a standalone copy, `basicly install` SHALL report it rather than silently adding a second.
- THE MESSAGE SHALL name both paths and say which one the repository should keep.
- A TEST SHALL create each collision and assert the refusal names both paths.

## Plan

- integrity: `L2`
- demonstration: install through basicly, then run the standalone init in the same repository, and read what it says
payload.title: two install roots let a repo hold the same kit twice

payload.description:
## Trigger

When a repository adopts the comment ban through `basicly install` it gets the always-on rule and no skill, while a standalone consumer gets a full skill, so the integrated consumer has less guidance than the standalone one.

## Measured, 2026-09-12

`ls .basicly/core/skills/ | grep -i comment` returns nothing. The catalog ships `work-tracker` and `tier-injection` for the other two kits and nothing for the comment ban. The ban's guidance for a basicly consumer is the `code-is-authoritative` rule alone, which is a paragraph; the standalone consumer gets `.basicly/core/kit/comments/GUIDANCE.md`, which says where a fact goes now that a comment cannot hold it, which comments are directives that stay, and what the three proofs mean.

A second, smaller asymmetry: `basicly install` copies `GUIDANCE.md` and `INSTRUCTION.md` into `.basicly/core/kit/<name>/` and nothing projects them, so they sit inert in every basicly consumer.

## What must not happen

Two texts saying the same thing in two places is how a claim goes stale. Whatever lands must make the kit's skill and the catalog's skill one text with a gate on it, not a copy.

## Acceptance Criteria

- THE CATALOG SHALL carry a skill for the comment ban, so a basicly consumer is told the same thing a standalone consumer is told.
- THAT SKILL AND the kit's `GUIDANCE.md` SHALL be one text, and a gate SHALL fail where they diverge.
- THE KIT README SHALL say that `GUIDANCE.md` and `INSTRUCTION.md` are the standalone path's source and are not projected by `basicly build`, so a reader does not look for their output.
- A TEST SHALL assert the catalog skill exists, is discoverable by its description, and matches the kit text.

## Plan

- integrity: `L2`
- demonstration: install through basicly into a throwaway repo and show the comment-ban skill where an agent reads it

## Trigger

When a vendor retires a model the anchors keep naming it, so a declared tier resolves to something legacy or to nothing at all, and the tier kit ships that answer to every consumer.

## Measured, 2026-09-12, against models.dev

Four anchors were wrong at once, which is what a stale capture looks like:

| tier / vendor | was | now | why |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| maximum / anthropic | `claude-fable-5` | `claude-fable-5-1` | Anthropic lists Fable 5 under "Legacy models (still available)". Same 10/50 input/output, cache read falls 1.0 to 0.25 |
| low / moonshotai | `kimi-k2.5` | `kimi-k2.6` | k2.5 is gone upstream and `--check` refused by name. k2.6 is the cheapest remaining at 0.95/4 |
| maximum / openai | `gpt-5.6-sol`, collapsed onto high | `gpt-6-astra`, no collapse | Astra released 2026-09-04 at 10/50 and is served by BOTH `openai` and `github-copilot` at the same cost, which is the test the `-pro` models failed |
| high and maximum / google | unchanged | unchanged, now unavailable on the broker | github-copilot serves no Google Pro model at all any more, only the flash line |

OpenAI now publishes a genuine fourth class, so its `collapse` is removed rather than repointed. `gpt-6-astra-pro` is not served by `openai` directly, so it stays out for the reason the other `-pro` models did.

## What the fix had to include beyond the anchors

The generator's own `--check` passes against live models.dev, and that is not the suite. `tests/fixtures/modelsdev-api.json` is a 48 KB curated capture and still held `kimi-k2.5`, `gpt-5.6-sol` as maximum, and `kimi-k2-turbo-preview`, so sixteen tests failed on a green tool. The capture was rebuilt from live upstream keeping the same five providers, and `openai/gpt-4.1-mini` was added because the reasoning test needs a model with reasoning false that still passes the rule and the trimmed capture no longer had one.

## Acceptance Criteria

- THE ANCHORS SHALL name a model each vendor currently serves, and `generate_model_map.py --check` SHALL pass against live models.dev.
- WHERE a vendor publishes a genuine fourth class, ITS MAXIMUM TIER SHALL NOT declare a collapse.
- THE CAPTURED FIXTURE SHALL hold every anchor the tests resolve, so the suite fails when an anchor goes stale rather than passing against a snapshot.
- THE TIER KIT PACKAGE SHALL carry a new version, because the map it ships changed.
- THE STANDALONE KIT SHALL resolve the new maximum on both surfaces.

## Plan

- integrity: `L2`
- demonstration: run the resolver from a vendored standalone kit for maximum on claude and on copilot, and read the ids

## Trigger
The Anthropic prompting audit (2026-09-12) read `.basicly/core/fragments/security/secure-coding.fragment.yaml` and found four of five bullets state a prohibition with no reason and no alternative.

## Problem
Our own `catalog-authoring` skill requires every prohibition to carry a one-clause rationale and the alternative to take instead. The security fragment breaks that rule in four places, so the rule does not generalise past its literal case.

## Constraint

## Trigger
The owner, 2026-09-12: build a test that measures how much of the always-on instructions the model actually retains, comparing what the model generates against what the file says, and treat that as more important than a vendor doc.

## Why the old harness could not answer it
`.scripts/recall_eval.py` scored against a hand-maintained anchor list in `recall_rules.toml`. That list rotted: 9 rules had no anchors and 11 had stale text guards, and `--inventory` exited 1 on a clean tree. A hand-maintained inventory is the defect, not the symptom.

## What replaces it
`src/basicly/retention.py` derives the rules from the file itself, so there is no inventory to drift. Scoring is IDF-weighted content-word recall against every line and adjacent line pair of the response, taking the better of the whole rule and its imperative clause. Deterministic, stdlib only, no network.

`.scripts/retention_eval.py` dispatches a cell with the file and a no-guidance control, then reports the rate, the retention curve by position in the file, the per-section table, and each unretained rule beside the closest line in the response.

## Measured 2026-09-12, claude, n=1 per point
| lines | rules | retained | 1st half | 2nd half |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 152 | 59 | 94.9% | 93% | 97% |
| 266 | 74 | 91.9% | 92% | 91% |
| 700 | 130 | 82.3% | 89% | 75% |
| 1667 | 158 | 78.5% | 90% | 67% |

Control arm with no file: 5.1%, so the lift attributable to the file is +89.8 points.

The first half of a file holds near 90% at every length. Only the tail is lost, and the knee is between 266 and 700 lines.

## What bounds the claim
The probe cannot separate "forgot the rule" from "stopped enumerating": response length grew 111, 159, 178, 259 lines while rule count grew 59, 74, 130, 158. n is 1 per point. The scorer is lexical, with a calibrated false-negative near 1 in 6 on a distant paraphrase. The positional finding is a within-response comparison and survives all three caveats; the absolute rates are floors.

## Scope
- `src/basicly/retention.py`
- `.scripts/retention_eval.py`
- `tests/test_retention.py`

## Trigger
The owner, 2026-09-12, after the retention harness landed: build the in-session probe and the re-read remedy.

## What it is, and what it is not
The probe answers one question: is the instruction file in this session context. It is scoped that way deliberately.

It cannot measure retention. While the file is in context the answer is read from it, not recalled, and the probe output repeats every rule, so running it is itself a re-injection. It cannot measure adherence either: reciting a rule is not obeying one, and a gate or a PreToolUse hook is what enforces a rule.

It is a very good absence detector. The measured separation is 94.9% with the file against 5.1% without, a 90 point gap needing no tuning. Real causes of a true absent: a subagent never given the instructions, a session launched outside the repository root, a claudeMdExcludes pattern matching too much, a consumer where basicly install has not run. A compaction is not one; the host re-reads and re-injects the project root file after compact.

## Bands, all measured
loaded at or above 80 percent, absent at or below 30 percent, partial between, undersampled when the answer has fewer lines than the file has rules.

## Two defects found by running it rather than by testing it
The first real use scored 45 percent and read as degradation. The file was loaded and the answer had simply stopped early at 30 lines against 58 rules. Every genuine attempt measured wrote at least 1.17 lines per rule, including the arm with no file at all, so the undersampled band was added at 0.75 and the same run then read correctly.

The second: derive_rules took only the first line of a bullet, so every wrapped rule was truncated mid sentence. Bullets now join their continuation lines. The exhaustive self probe reads 91 percent loaded after both fixes.

## Scope
- `src/basicly/retention.py`
- `src/basicly/cli.py`
- `.basicly/core/skills/retention-probe/skill.yaml`
- `tests/test_cli_retention.py`

## Retro proposal, not applied

Session 2026-09-12. Awaiting the owner decision; a retro finding is never self-applied.

## The incident, twice in one session
Asked whether the bandit gate covers `packages/`, I ran `bandit -q -c pyproject.toml -r src .scripts packages` and reported a failure. The declared check is `bandit -q -c pyproject.toml -r .scripts .basicly/core/hooks .basicly/core/kit`. My invented path list produced a finding the real gate does not have, and I retracted it.

The same shape had already happened with the kits: `uv run --project packages/basicly-tier` reported all three kits broken, because that path reads the source tree where `force-include` has not run. Also retracted.

## Root cause, and why it is not a discipline failure
There is no way to run one declared check. `basicly verify` takes `--mode`, not a check name, so the only route to "run just this gate" is to retype its argv from `basicly.toml` - or, as happened, to approximate it.

Measured on `.basicly/usage/tool-usage.json`: `bandit` 19 direct invocations, `vulture` 67, `pyright` 267, `lint-imports` 140. `verify` appears once. The tools are run directly essentially always, and every direct run is an argv nobody checked against the declared one.

The `core-rules` fragment already says the authority is the code that reads it, not the docs. The authority here is `basicly.toml`, and the harness offers no way to obey it.

## Proposal
`basicly verify --only <name>` runs exactly one `[[verify.checks]]` entry with its declared argv, and refuses an unknown name by listing the ones that exist.

## Why this rather than a hook
A guard on hand-rolled invocations would fire on 493 recorded calls, most of them legitimate narrowing. The cheaper fix is to make the correct path exist, so the improvisation has a named alternative.

## Scope
- `src/basicly/cli.py`
- `src/basicly/verify.py`
- `tests/test_verify.py`

## Retro proposal, not applied

Session 2026-09-12. Awaiting the owner decision.

## The gap
`tests/test_kit_packages.py` proves two things and not the third. Two tests build a wheel and assert its `namelist()` carries the kit and the installer. Twenty-eight tests call `installer.run(...)` against the source module. Nothing installs a wheel and executes `init` from it.

So the packaging is checked and the logic is checked, and the join between them is not. A shim that cannot locate its kit at runtime, a `force-include` mapping that lands files at the wrong module path, an entry point that does not resolve - each would pass every test and break every consumer.

## How it surfaced
Only by hand. `uvx --from <wheel> basicly-tier init` in a scratch repository was the sole thing that exercised the path, and it is what proved both that the kits work and that the third skill copy was being written.

## Proposal
One test per kit: build the wheel, `uvx --from <wheel> basicly-<kit> init --into <tmp>` in a throwaway git repository, and assert the vendored kit, the two skill roots and the exit code. Slow, so mark it and keep it in `full` rather than `fast`.

## Why this and not more source-level tests
The source-level suite is already thorough. The defect class it cannot see is precisely the one that only appears once the wheel is built and installed, which is the state every consumer is in and no test was.

## Scope
- `tests/test_kit_packages.py`
- `basicly.toml`

## Observation
`tests/test_board_serve.py::test_a_stale_lock_hands_the_fold_back_to_the_viewer` failed inside the pre-push suite on 2026-09-12, refusing a docs-only push. The full suite had passed minutes earlier on the same tree.

```
assert None is not None
tests/test_board_serve.py:218: AssertionError
```

Line 218 is `assert served is not None`. Lines 215 and 216 passed, so `board.refresh()` had returned True and `board.refreshes` was 1.

## Not reproduced
Three runs of the test alone: pass. Three runs of the whole file under `-n 8`: 27 passed each time. Six attempts, zero reproductions.

## Hypothesis ruled out, recorded so nobody spends the same hour
The obvious read is a race between the two independent `live_holder` calls: `refresh` proceeds only when the holder is not live, and `payload` returns `_served` only when the holder is not live, otherwise reading a snapshot file that may not exist. That would explain a None.

It cannot happen. `live_holder` returns None once `age_s >= STALE_AFTER_S`, the test ages the lock to `STALE_AFTER_S + 1`, and an age only grows. The holder cannot become live between the two calls.

So `payload` returned `_served` and `_served` was None, while `refresh` had returned True on the branch that assigns it. Those two statements cannot both be true of one object, which is why this needs an instrument rather than another read.

## Suggested first step
Have the test print `board.failures`, `board._served is None` and the holder age at the point of failure, then leave it in the suite until it fires again. A cause guessed without a second observation is a guess.

## Why it matters
The pre-push suite is the gate before every push. A test that fails about once refuses work that is fine and trains people to re-run rather than read. This is the second timing-dependent test in this file: `basicly-gssz1qa` fixed a different one on 2026-09-12, which compared two pages against the clock.

## Scope
- `tests/test_board_serve.py`
- `src/basicly/board_serve.py`

The owner, 2026-09-12: "Four pillars, not a bundle of files" is a bad title, "The process is code, and so is the enforcement" should be written without the comma, and the hype should go. "Not everyone is American and it annoys 90% of people."

Five of nine section titles on the landing page used the same construction: a claim propped up by the thing it is not, or a comma splicing a second clause onto a title to add weight.

Four pillars, not a bundle of files. Read the design, not just the pitch. One command, into any git repo. Or take one piece, without the harness. The process is code, and so is the enforcement.

One body sentence did the same: "Plenty of projects ship an agent workflow. What is unusual here is that..." - a comparison with no measurement behind it.

Idiom and rhetorical construction are the part that does not survive a reader whose first language is not English. The repository already writes its answers in ASD-STE100 simplified technical english through the tired-engineer output style, and applied none of it to the prose a stranger reads first.

Six titles and one paragraph rewritten. The readme headings were checked and were already plain, so the site was the only offender.

`plain-english` is a new catalog skill, so it projects to the skill roots and ships to every consumer through `basicly install`. It names the constructions to delete with the real examples from this page, and separates its scope from `catalog-authoring`, which governs guidance a model reads under a character budget.

## Open, not filed as work
A skill fires on the model judging it relevant. A path-scoped fragment on `**/*.md` would fire whenever prose is touched, deterministically, at the cost of about a thousand characters of AGENTS.md, which inlines the scoped tier. The owner has the measurement to decide that.

SHIPPED: v0.13.0 and v0.13.1 both tagged, pushed and published with live release pages. Kits at tier 0.2.2, comments 0.2.1, tracker 0.2.1. Site live at v0.13.1. Tree clean, main level with origin.

THE SESSION GOAL IS MET AND WAS EXERCISED, NOT ASSUMED. All three kits install standalone from a built wheel into a fresh git repo: uvx --from <wheel> basicly-<kit> init exits 0, vendors the kit under .basicly/kit/<name>, and writes the skill to .claude/skills and .agents/skills. The tier wheel carries the model map byte-identical to ours. Testing them via uv run --project reports them broken and is the wrong instrument: force-include only runs at wheel build time.

THE OTHER BIG RESULT: always-on caps are measured, not guessed. retention_eval.py scores how much of an instruction file a fresh session returns. 152 lines 95 percent, 266 lines 92, 700 lines 82, 1667 lines 79, against 5 percent with no file. The first half of a file holds near 90 percent at any length; only the tail is lost, knee between 266 and 700 lines. Codex counts BYTES, which the old gate got wrong. always-on-size now refuses instead of warning. Limits: n=1 per point, the probe cannot separate forgetting from ceasing to enumerate, the scorer is lexical with a false negative near 1 in 6 on distant paraphrase.

OPEN, ALL AWAITING THE OWNER, NONE SELF-APPLIED, IN THE ORDER I WOULD TAKE THEM:
1. basicly-miwa0nj - the windows quality gate fails 13 of 39 runs, 33 percent, always the windows job while ubuntu and macos pass. A real windows regression would arrive looking exactly like the noise. First step is keeping the failing artefacts, because older logs expire before anyone reads them.

3. basicly-xhec56d - verify --only <name>. There is no way to run one declared check, so people hand-roll the argv; I did twice and reported two false failures. 493 direct gate-tool calls against 1 recorded verify.
4. basicly-wjx0soa - no test installs a wheel and runs init from it. Two tests check wheel contents, 28 run the installer from source, the join is untested and that is the state every consumer is in.
5. basicly-yj0pale - a board-serve test fails about once and refuses the push. The obvious race is recorded as ruled out.

ALSO OPEN: the semantic judge mode for the retention harness is not built; what shipped answers presence, never adherence. The plain-english skill ships to consumers and covers prose; the architecture document is 5045 lines and was not swept sentence by sentence, only corrected where it was factually stale.

NEXT: the owner's epics - visualization, work tracker, loop, deepseek research integration, graph engineering, architecture improvements.

payload.title: Research spike: pi and deepseek-harness against the subscription-bound headless runner

payload.text:
RESEARCHED 2026-09-13. All sources fetched live on that date. Nothing ported, nothing installed.

=== 1. A PREMISE OF THE QUESTION IS WRONG: `claude -p` IS THE AGENT SDK ===

Source: code.claude.com/docs/en/headless, fetched 2026-09-13. Its title is "Run Claude Code
programmatically" and its first line reads "Use the Agent SDK to run Claude Code programmatically
from the CLI, Python, or TypeScript." The same page: "To drive the same agent loop from another
language, run the CLI as a subprocess with the `-p` flag and `--output-format json`."

So `-p` is not a degraded mode beside an SDK. It is the sanctioned way to drive the SDK from a
language that is not Python or TypeScript. basicly is Python, so we could use the library; see
finding 3 for why we must not.

What `-p` already offers that we treat as missing:
- `--resume <session_id>` and `--continue` carry a conversation across dispatches.
- `--output-format json` returns `session_id`, `total_cost_usd` and a per-model cost breakdown.
- `--json-schema` returns schema-validated output in a `structured_output` field.
- `--append-system-prompt`, `--append-system-prompt-file`, `--system-prompt`, `--settings`,
  `--agents <json>`, `--mcp-config`, `--plugin-dir`.
- `--permission-mode auto|dontAsk|acceptEdits` and `--permission-prompts none` for unattended runs.
- `stream-json` carries `system/init` (model, tools, mcp_servers, plugin_errors, mcp_server_errors)
  and `system/api_retry`.

AND WE ALREADY RESUME. src/basicly/runner.py:350 emits `--resume <id> --fork-session`;
`RESUME_FORK_FLAGS` at line 66 and `record_session_seed` at line 322 persist a seed per feature and
family. The claim "we throw context away on every dispatch" is false for the claude adapter. What is
true is the price: a prior measurement in this repo put `--fork-session` at about ten times the cost
on a corpus because the forked prefix is not cache-shared.

=== 2. A DATED COST EVENT IS ALREADY SCHEDULED AGAINST US ===

Same source, on `--bare`:
  "Set ANTHROPIC_API_KEY before running it, because bare mode doesn't use your subscription login."
  "In bare mode, Claude Code never reads OAuth credentials or the system keychain."
  "`--bare` is the recommended mode for scripted and SDK calls, and will become the default for `-p`
   in a future release."

Read those three together. The day `--bare` becomes the default for `-p`, every basicly dispatch
stops billing the subscription and starts billing the API, silently, at API rates. Our runner does
not pass `--bare` today and does not pin against it either. This is the single most actionable
finding in the spike and it is a scheduled regression, not a hypothetical.

Secondary consequence: `--bare` also skips hooks, skills, subagents, plugins, MCP and CLAUDE.md.
Our whole guidance projection is exactly what bare mode refuses to load. If we ever adopt bare mode
for determinism we must pass the catalog back in by flag, which is what the page's own table
describes.

=== 3. THE AGENT SDK LIBRARY CANNOT SPEND A SUBSCRIPTION ===

Source: code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/overview, fetched 2026-09-13, verbatim:
  "Unless previously approved, Anthropic does not allow third party developers to offer claude.ai
   login or rate limits for their products, including agents built on the Claude Agent SDK. Use the
   API key authentication methods described in the Quickstart instead."

So the move "leave `-p`, adopt the Python Agent SDK, manage context properly" buys nothing we do not
already have and costs the subscription. The subprocess CLI is the subscription path. That resolves
the owner's "`-p` is a mistake" concern in the opposite direction from the one expected.

=== 4. PI (earendil-works/pi, was badlogic/pi-mono; the old name redirects) ===

MEASURED 2026-09-13 with `gh api repos/earendil-works/pi`: MIT, TypeScript, 104,554 stars, pushed
2026-09-13, not archived. Sources: the repo page and packages/coding-agent/README.md and
packages/ai/README.md, all fetched 2026-09-13.

Packages: `pi-coding-agent` (interactive CLI), `pi-agent-core` (agent runtime, tool calling, state
management), `pi-ai` (unified multi-provider LLM API), `pi-telemetry`, `chord`.

CONTEXT. Sessions auto-save to `~/.pi/agent/sessions/` as JSONL. "Each entry has an id and parentId,
enabling in-place branching without creating new files." Compaction is manual with `/compact
<instructions>` and automatic on overflow. Stated honestly: "Compaction is lossy. The full history
remains in the JSONL file; use /tree to revisit." Resume with `pi -c`, `pi -r`, `--session <path|id>`.
This is the same shape as Claude Code's transcript plus resume. It is not better; it is open.

AUTH, THE REASON THIS SPIKE EXISTS. 30+ providers. Resolution order: explicit per-request credential,
then a `CredentialStore`, then environment variables, then ambient sources such as AWS profiles or
gcloud ADC. Verbatim: "Every provider owns its auth: how API keys resolve ... and, where supported,
OAuth login/refresh flows."

THREE providers support subscription OAuth through `/login`: Anthropic Claude Pro/Max, OpenAI
ChatGPT Plus/Pro for the Codex models, and GitHub Copilot. That is the capability the owner asked
about: one harness, open models by API key AND the existing subscriptions by OAuth.

TOOLS. Four built-ins: read, write, edit, bash, plus grep, find, ls and powershell on Windows.
`pi.registerTool({ name: "deploy", ... })` from a TypeScript extension, and an extension may replace
a built-in outright. CLI selection with `--tools`, `--exclude-tools`, `--no-builtin-tools`,
`--no-tools`.

SKILLS. The Agent Skills standard, loaded from `~/.pi/agent/skills/`, `.agents/skills/`,
`.pi/skills/`. WE ALREADY PROJECT TO `.agents/skills`. A pi target in our catalog is close to free.

EXTENSIONS. Custom tools, subagents, plan mode, custom compaction and summarization, permission gates
and path protection, git checkpointing and auto-commit, sandbox execution, MCP. Event hooks with
`pi.on("tool_call", async (event, ctx) => {...})`.

WHAT PI REFUSES TO DO, in its own Philosophy section: "No built-in to-dos. They confuse models. Use a
TODO.md file, or build your own with extensions." No work tracking. No acceptance-criteria
verification. And from the repo page: it "does not include a built-in permission system", with
containerization recommended instead.

RISK, NOT RESOLVED: pi's Anthropic OAuth is precisely what the Agent SDK page says third-party
developers may not offer "unless previously approved". Whether pi holds that approval is NOT
ESTABLISHED by this spike, and pi's own documentation carries no terms-of-service note either way.
Do not make a product commitment to pi's Claude login before asking Anthropic directly. Its API-key
and open-model paths carry no such question.

=== 5. DEEPSEEK HARNESS (deepseek-ai/deepseek-harness, CLI `dsh`) ===

MEASURED 2026-09-13 with `gh api repos/deepseek-ai/deepseek-harness`: MIT, TypeScript, 222,129 stars,
pushed 2026-09-11. Published 2026-08-13 per secondary reporting, which is the one figure here that is
not primary. Sources: README.md, AGENTS.md, docs/architecture.md and eleven package READMEs read
through the GitHub contents API on 2026-09-13.

ARCHITECTURE. Built on Cordis: "plugins contribute services, typed events, and reversible effects to
a shared context." There is no privileged core. The model adapter, the tool registry, the session log
and the agent loop itself are each a replaceable plugin. Composition is by profile and bundle:
`dsh-base` plus `dsh-web-app`, `dsh-headless`, `dsh-sdk-app`, `dsh-acp-app`. Config is `cordis.yml`
with validated fields and "no hardcoded tunables in plugins".

THE SESSION INVARIANT, THE BEST IDEA IN EITHER PROJECT. From AGENTS.md, verbatim: "Model-visible
<=> logged: anything

=== 6. WHAT NEITHER HARNESS SHIPS, WHICH IS WHAT BASICLY IS ===

Both pi and dsh stop at the session boundary. Their state is per session, on one machine, under a
home directory. Neither ships any of the following, and I looked for each by name in the package
list and the docs index:

- A work record in the repository carrying acceptance criteria that a gate reads. dsh's `goal` is
  the nearest thing and it is one objective per session, not a graph the repo owns. pi refuses the
  category outright.
- Verification and validation bound to that record, so a phase cannot advance without evidence.
- Commit-time git hooks. Both gate the agent. Neither gates the artefact, so neither holds for a
  human, for a second agent, or for CI. basicly has 24 hook scripts under .basicly/core/hooks.
- One catalog projected into several agent families. pi and dsh each configure themselves.
- Install and upgrade convergence that preserves a consumer's overlay.

This is the same verdict recorded for claude-code-harness on basicly-u2hl.38 on 2026-08-09, reached
against two much larger projects: a live competitor on the gating and orchestration axes, a
non-competitor on the tracker and projection axes.

It is also the third and fourth independent instance of the design we chose on 2026-07-30 and
recorded at architecture.md:86-106 - phases as engine code, not configuration. dsh makes the agent
loop a plugin; pi makes it an extension point. Neither derives a phase from a committed graph.

=== 7. THE ECONOMIC QUESTION, RESTATED SO IT CAN BE ANSWERED ===

The owner's figure, that the API costs 10x to 20x a subscription for the same work, is the owner's
estimate and is NOT MEASURED in this spike.

Today there are exactly three ways to spend a subscription on agent work:
  a. the interactive CLI, which agent teams now cover well and which cannot run unattended;
  b. `claude -p` without `--bare`, which is what we do, and which finding 2 puts on a clock;
  c. a third-party OAuth login such as pi's, whose permission is unresolved per finding 3.

Only (c) also reaches open-weight models, and (c) is the one with legal exposure. That is the whole
trade, stated plainly.

The comparison that actually decides the product is NOT "subscription versus Anthropic API". It is
"subscription versus an open-weight API". An open-weight model bought by API key has no subscription
to lose, so the 10-20x multiplier does not apply to it at all. We have a lane measured at about
33.2M tokens; priced against DeepSeek or another open-weight endpoint that becomes a number instead
of an argument. That measurement is not done and is the first follow-up below.

=== 8. FOLLOW-UPS. NONE OF THIS WAS DONE; NO DEVELOPMENT IN THIS SESSION ===

a. Pin the runner against the announced `--bare` default flip, and add a gate that fails if a
   dispatch would bill the API. This is a dated cost regression with our name on it. Highest value,
   smallest change, do it first.
b. Price one real lane's measured token count against an open-weight API endpoint, next to the
   subscription. Until that number exists, harness portability is a preference, not a decision.
c. Establish whether pi holds Anthropic's prior approval for Claude Pro/Max OAuth. Ask Anthropic;
   do not infer it from the fact that pi ships it.
d. Decide whether the runner seam should gain `dsh` as an adapter. dsh is a library with a documented
   plugin seam, not a CLI, so it is a different kind of adapter from codex and copilot. Note that
   our runner has never once dispatched codex or copilot: `basicly health` on 2026-09-13 measures 561
   claude runs and 200 manual runs, and zero for both. Adding a fourth unexercised adapter repeats a
   mistake rather than fixing one.
e. Adopt two dsh ideas regardless of which harness wins, because both are ours to build and neither
   requires leaving Claude: `spill` (return a locator and retrieval guidance instead of inlining a
   large tool result) and the invariant "model-visible <=> logged".

=== LIMITS OF THIS SPIKE ===

- No code was run from either project. Every claim about pi and ds
