`claude_stream_usage` sums one `Usage` per assistant *content-block* event, not per API request. Every block of one request repeats that request's usage, so each request is multiplied by its block count.

Measured 2026-09-13 on a live controlled dispatch (`claude -p ... --output-format stream-json --verbose`, 3 file reads):

- 15 assistant events, **6 distinct `message.id`**, `result.num_turns` 7.
- Summed per event: input 30, cache_read 262,315, cache_write 59,429, output 47. Total 321,821.
- De-duplicated on `message.id`: input 12, cache_read 111,708, cache_write 22,657. Total 134,394.
- The `result` event: input 12, cache_read 111,708, cache_write 22,657, output 1,694. Total 136,071.

**De-duplication reproduces the result event's three input figures exactly.** The overcount on the total is 2.37x, and output is under-counted 100x because a per-block `output_tokens` is not the request's output.

WHY THIS IS NOT A LIVE DATA DEFECT, AND IS STILL WORTH FIXING. `runner.py:1001` prefers `claude_json_usage(claude_result_event(...))` and falls back to `claude_stream_usage` only when there is no result event. A positive control over the 561 recorded claude runs shows the fallback essentially never fired: median `output_tokens / tokens` is **1.2465%**, against 1.24% for the correct path in the probe and 0.015% for the summing path; only **2 of 294** records carry the summing signature, and only 6 of 561 carry no cost at all. So the recorded history is Claude Code's own `result` figures read verbatim.

The fallback fires exactly when a run has **no result event** - killed, timed out, or stopped on the spend bound. Those are the runs whose cost matters most, and they are the ones the engine would over-report by roughly 2.4x while under-reporting output.

FIX. De-duplicate on `message.id` in `claude_stream_usage`, and take `output_tokens` from the last event of each id rather than summing blocks. A regression test can pin the probe's three figures, which are exact.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a stream with several content-block events per request, when `claude_stream_usage` folds it, then each `message.id` contributes its usage once.
- Given the captured probe stream, when the fallback path runs, then it returns the same input, cache_read and cache_write as the `result` event.
- A test binds those figures and fails if the de-duplication is removed.
payload.title: claude stream usage sums one record per content block so a fallback count is 2.4x high

payload.description:
MEASURED 2026-09-13. Five live `claude -p --output-format json` dispatches from the repository root, so each loaded the real project context. Total cost of the experiment: $0.9435 at list price.

DESIGN. Three comparable read-only tasks, each two files of about 9-11 KB, each asking for a count of level-2 headings. Task A seeded a session. Task B and task C were then each run twice: once in a fresh session, once resumed into the session that already held the earlier tasks. Same prompt, same files, same model, same permissions. The only variable is whether the session was warm.

RESULT.

| run | turns | cache_read | cache_write | total tokens | cost $ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A fresh, 1st | 2 | 33,750 | 34,081 | 68,166 | 0.3670 |
| B fresh | 2 | 46,646 | 21,093 | 68,037 | 0.2426 |
| B warm, 2nd in session | 2 | 68,422 | 556 | 69,301 | 0.0478 |
| C fresh | 2 | 46,658 | 21,100 | 67,933 | 0.2396 |
| C warm, 3rd in session | 2 | 69,514 | 546 | 70,313 | 0.0465 |

Task B warm/fresh: cost **0.20x**, tokens 1.02x. Task C warm/fresh: cost **0.19x**, tokens 1.04x.

**A warm worker costs about five times less per task than a fresh one, at the same token count.** Two independent replications, same direction, same magnitude.

THE MECHANISM, AND WHY A TOKEN COUNT HIDES IT. The totals are the same to within 4%. What moves is the split: cache_write falls from about 21,000 to about 550, a 97% drop, and cache_read rises to match. A cache **write** is billed at a premium over base input and a cache **read** at a deep discount, so relocating the same tokens from write to read is the whole saving. **Any cost argument conducted in tokens rather than in priced components is wrong**, and one conducted in this repository on 2026-09-13 was wrong for exactly that reason.

ACCUMULATION DID NOT ERODE IT. The third task in the session performed the same as the second, 0.19x against 0.20x, while the carried prefix grew only 1.5%, from 69,301 to 70,313. The prior claim that a long-lived worker grows the dominant cost term is refuted at this scale.

WHAT THIS DOES NOT ESTABLISH.
- n=2 replications, two turns per task. The mechanism is a price split rather than a task-size effect, so the direction should hold, but the magnitude on a 26-turn lane is not measured. A long task amortises its single cache write over more turns in the fresh arm too, so 5x is likely an upper bound.
- Every run was seconds after its predecessor, so the cache was always hot. The `cache_creation` block reports `ephemeral_1h_input_tokens`, so this path writes a one-hour cache; a subagent defaults to five minutes unless `subagentPromptCacheTtl` is set to `1h`.
- The tasks only read. A task that writes files grows the conversation faster, so a longer-lived worker may reach a compaction threshold that these three did not.

THE DESIGN CONSEQUENCE, WHICH IS A SCHEDULING RULE RATHER THAN A LIFETIME POLICY. A warm worker is cheap only while its cache is hot. A worker that idles past the TTL re-writes an accumulated and therefore larger prefix at full price, which is worse than starting fresh. So: **keep a worker busy inside the TTL, or let it end.** An idle warm worker is the worst case in the system.

That rule unifies two parts of the proposed factory that looked independent. A pull queue in which a free worker takes the next ready task immediately is precisely the mechanism that keeps a warm worker inside its cache window. **The kanban is not a convenience on top of the worker pool. It is what makes the worker pool economic.**

RAW DATA. Five result objects retained under the session scratchpad as `r1_A_fresh.json`, `r2_B_fresh.json`, `r3_B_warm.json`, `r5_C_fresh.json`, `r4_C_warm3.json`. Reproduce with `claude -p "<task>" --allowedTools Read --output-format json [--resume <id>]` and read `total_cost_usd` and `usage` from each.
payload.title: Research spike: a warm resumed worker costs one fifth of a fresh one per task

When the owner describes an end state the tree does not have, I want that end state specified in the architecture document with its decisions and its measurements, so I can see what is decided and what is only intended without reading a plan file the repository refuses to carry.

The owner's factory proposal of 2026-09-13: a pool of specialised agents that pull from a shared backlog, coordinate over announcements, hold private and shared context, and are steered from a cockpit. Four decisions were taken during the session and one was reversed by measurement.

Scope: `docs/architecture/architecture.md` only. Section 31A at the end of Part IV, five decision records D-45 to D-49, one amended non-goal row, three glossary terms, one contents entry. No status grading, because architecture never grades a capability.

## Acceptance Criteria

- When a reader opens section 31A, then it carries the `[TARGET]` mark and points at `status.md` for grading.
- When `docs-claims` runs, then it reports no component state graded in this document.
- When `markdownlint`, `mermaid`, `docs-citations` and `code-citations` run, then all four pass.
- Every measured figure in the new text carries its date and the command that re-derives it.
- Every new concept name was searched against the code before adoption, and a bound word was rejected.
payload.title: specify the software factory end state in the architecture document

## Trigger

When the owner describes a factory of specialised agents that pull from one shared backlog, I want the unbuilt parts of it filed as records the loop can dispatch, so I can see the whole end state as work rather than as prose.

## Requirements

R1. A reader can tell, from the ledger alone, which parts of architecture section 31A exist and which do not.
R2. Each child states the intended use it is validated against, separately from the criteria it is verified against.
R3. The set of children covers every `[TARGET]` passage in section 31A and every decision D-45 through D-50, and claims no part the architecture does not specify.
R4. No child depends on a part of the design the architecture has not decided.

## Success Criteria

- Every `[TARGET]` passage in architecture section 31A is named by at least one open child of this epic.
- Every decision from D-45 to D-50 is named by at least one open child.
- `uv run basicly tracker show` on each child returns a Trigger, a Requirements section and an Acceptance Criteria section.
- The epic closes only when `status.yaml` grades every part of section 31A without a `designed` row left unowned.

## Note on the store

These children write Requirements and Acceptance Criteria as description headings, because `requirements` is not yet a field and the Definition of Ready reads headings today. The first child converts both to typed fields, and these records migrate with the other 761 rather than ahead of them. Architecture D-50 carries the decision.
payload.title: the software factory: seats pulling from one shared backlog

payload.description:
## Trigger

When a validator is told to judge a change against the requirement that asked for it, I want that requirement stored on the record as a typed field, so I can validate against a written standard instead of inferring one from prose.

## Requirements

R1. A person reading a closed record can see what intended use the change was validated against, without reading the implementation.
R2. A validator dispatched on a record with no stated intended use is refused rather than asked to guess.
R3. The word `requirements` on a record means the intended use of ISO 9000:2015 3.8.13, never the specification that acceptance criteria hold.

## Acceptance Criteria

- When a caller runs `tracker write -- update <id> --requirements "<text>"`, then the value is stored as the record's `requirements` payload field. [check: `tests/test_tracker_write.py`]
- When `tracker show <id>` prints a record carrying the field, then `requirements` appears in its `fields` map. [check: `tests/test_tracker_write.py`]
- When the engine dispatches the validator for a record whose `requirements` field is empty, then the advance is refused and the refusal names the missing field. [check: `tests/test_loop_validate.py`]
- When an existing record carries no `requirements` field, then reading it succeeds and the field reads as absent rather than as an empty string. [check: `tests/test_tracker.py`]

## Demonstration

`uv run pytest tests/test_tracker_write.py -q`

## Design notes

Architecture section 32.11 and D-50. `tracker_argv.UPDATE_FIELD_FLAGS` gains the flag; the field joins the payload the same way `acceptance_criteria` already does. Measured 2026-09-13: 0 of 1,347 created events carry this field or a `## Requirements` heading, against a positive control of 761 carrying `## Acceptance Criteria`.
payload.title: add a requirements field to the record so validate has a standard to judge against

payload.description:
## Trigger

When a gate tests a change against its acceptance criteria, I want the criteria read from one store, so I can stop maintaining a field that 467 records carry and nothing tests against.

## Requirements

R1. One representation of the acceptance criteria is authoritative, and a reader cannot pick the weaker one by accident.
R2. A record written before the change still yields its criteria after it, with no criterion lost.
R3. A reader can tell a migrated record from an unmigrated one without guessing.

## Acceptance Criteria

- When `plan_record.RecordedPlan` is built for a record carrying the `acceptance_criteria` field, then `acceptance` comes from the field. [check: `tests/test_plan_record.py`]
- When a record carries only the legacy `## Acceptance Criteria` heading, then the migration writes the field and leaves the description prose untouched. [check: `tests/test_tracker_migrate.py`]
- When the migration has run over the whole ledger, then every record that held the heading holds the field, and the criterion count per record is unchanged. [check: `tests/test_tracker_migrate.py`]
- When the migration runs a second time, then it writes nothing and exits zero. [check: `tests/test_tracker_migrate.py`]

## Demonstration

`uv run pytest tests/test_plan_record.py tests/test_tracker_migrate.py -q`

## Design notes

Architecture D-50. Measured 2026-09-13 over 1,347 created events: the field is on 467 records and the heading on 761. `plan_record.section_entries` reads the heading today and `tracker_write._say_criteria` reads the field only to print a closing reminder.
payload.title: move the acceptance criteria reader from the description heading to the typed field

## Trigger

When a record reaches the definition of ready without stating what it is for, I want the gate to refuse it, so I can stop discovering at validate that there was never a standard to judge against.

## Requirements

R1. A record that cannot state its intended use never reaches a lane.
R2. An author is told which field is missing, not merely that the record is not ready.
R3. The backlog of records owing a field is visible and falls over time rather than accumulating silently.

## Acceptance Criteria

- When the definition of ready runs on a record missing `requirements`, then it refuses and names that field. [check: `tests/test_invest.py`]
- When the definition of ready runs on a record missing `acceptance_criteria`, then it refuses and names that field. [check: `tests/test_invest.py`]
- When `invest.owed` runs over the open set, then it returns every record missing either field, for every work type. [check: `tests/test_invest.py`]
- When the board renders, then the count of records owing a field is shown. [check: `tests/test_board_facts.py`]

## Demonstration

`uv run pytest tests/test_invest.py -q`

## Design notes

Architecture section 32.11 and D-50. `policy.type_sections` carries the requirement for every work type, not a subset. Expect every open record to owe both fields on the day this lands; that burn-down is the intended effect.
payload.title: require both the requirements and the acceptance criteria fields at the definition of ready

payload.description:
## Trigger

When the engine decides whether to keep a session open for another task, I want the adapter to state its host's prompt cache window, so I can hold that decision on a declared host fact rather than on a constant somebody guessed.

## Requirements

R1. The engine never assumes a cache window a host has not published.
R2. A host that publishes no window is handled, and the handling is visible rather than silent.
R3. A window that the vendor changes is corrected in one declaration, not in every call site.

## Acceptance Criteria

- When a runner spec declares a cache window, then `runner` exposes it beside the context window and names its source. [check: `tests/test_runner.py`]
- When a runner spec declares no cache window, then the engine treats the host as having none and dispatches fresh. [check: `tests/test_runner.py`]
- When a dispatch is recorded, then the run record carries the window that was in force and where it came from. [check: `tests/test_run_record.py`]

## Demonstration

`uv run pytest tests/test_runner.py -q`

## Design notes

Architecture D-46. The existing `context_window` and `context_window_source` pair on `RunnerSpec` is the shape to copy. Sourced 2026-09-13: the Claude host writes a one-hour cache on the main path and five minutes for an in-process subagent unless `subagentPromptCacheTtl` is set to `1h`.
payload.title: declare the prompt cache window on every runner adapter

payload.description:
## Trigger

When a lane finishes a task, I want its session held open for the next one instead of torn down, so I can pay the cache write once rather than once per task.

## Requirements

R1. A second task in a held session costs materially less than the same task in a fresh one, and the saving is measured rather than assumed.
R2. A session that cannot start its next task inside the host's cache window is ended, because an idle held session is worse than a fresh one.
R3. A held session is releasable at any moment without losing work, because everything that must survive it is already written.
R4. A crash of a held session loses no more than a fresh dispatch would.

## Acceptance Criteria

- When a seat finishes a task and another ready task matches it, then the engine resumes the same session rather than starting a new one. [check: `tests/test_seat.py`]
- When a seat has no matching ready task and the cache window is about to close, then the engine releases the seat. [check: `tests/test_seat.py`]
- When a seat is released, then no unwritten state is lost, because the release happens only at a task boundary. [check: `tests/test_seat.py`]
- When a seat run is recorded, then the run record names the seat, the task's position in it, and the cache window in force. [check: `tests/test_run_record.py`]

## Demonstration

`uv run pytest tests/test_seat.py -q`

## Design notes

Architecture section 31A.1, 31A.2 and D-46. Measured 2026-09-13 on five live dispatches, recorded on basicly-8724lqq: a warm session cost 0.20x and 0.19x of a fresh one on two replications at the same token count, and the saving is the avoided cache write rather than fewer tokens. Two limits carry into this work: two turns per task, and a cold resume past the window is unpriced.
payload.title: hold a seat open across tasks and release it when the cache window closes

payload.description:
## Trigger

When a seat becomes free, I want it to take the next ready task that matches it, so I can keep it inside its cache window without a separate scheduler deciding when to hand work over.

## Requirements

R1. Work is never pushed to a seat, because a seat that is not running cannot receive it.
R2. Two seats never take the same task.
R3. A seat takes its next task fast enough to stay inside the cache window, or it is released.
R4. The order tasks are taken in is the order the existing ranked ready set already publishes, so this adds no second scheduler.

## Acceptance Criteria

- When a seat reports free and a matching ready task exists, then it is assigned that task without a new spawn. [check: `tests/test_seat_queue.py`]
- When two seats report free at the same moment, then each takes a different task and neither takes one twice. [check: `tests/test_seat_queue.py`]
- When no ready task matches a free seat, then the seat is released rather than held idle. [check: `tests/test_seat_queue.py`]
- When a task is taken, then the five admission conditions and the six admission gates have all been applied first. [check: `tests/test_supervise_admission.py`]

## Demonstration

`uv run pytest tests/test_seat_queue.py -q`

## Design notes

Architecture section 31A.3. This is not a second scheduler: the ready set already ranks and section 28.2's five conditions are already the pull predicate. What changes is who spawns.
payload.title: let a free seat take the next matching ready task itself

payload.description:
## Trigger

When a task needs a seat, I want the engine to pick one by comparing declared facts, so I can route work without asking a model to report its own fitness.

## Requirements

R1. No model ever reports its own suitability for a task, because a persuadable scheduler is not a scheduler.
R2. A match that could not apply an axis says which axis it could not apply, because a silently partial match is worse than none.
R3. Adding a fifth axis later does not change the three axes that already exist.

## Acceptance Criteria

- When an agent source declares its tools, then the catalog lint accepts the declaration and a missing one is reported. [check: `tests/test_catalog_lint.py`]
- When the engine matches a task, then it compares the scope globs, the integrity level, the model tier and the tools, and returns one seat or none. [check: `tests/test_seat_match.py`]
- When an axis cannot be evaluated because nothing declares it, then the match result names that axis as unbound. [check: `tests/test_seat_match.py`]
- When no seat matches, then the task stays ready and the reason names the axis that excluded every seat. [check: `tests/test_seat_match.py`]

## Demonstration

`uv run pytest tests/test_seat_match.py -q`

## Design notes

Architecture section 31A.6 and D-47. Three axes exist: the scope globs on the planned child, the integrity level `integrity._RULES` assigns, and the tier on the agent source. Only the tools axis is new. The tier axis is inert at spawn until basicly-a3yi lands, so a match on it reports unbound rather than pretending.
payload.title: declare the tools a seat holds and match a task to a seat on four axes

payload.description:
## Trigger

When one seat learns something another seat needs, I want it appended to the log they already share, so I can deliver it without a mailbox that a crash would lose.

## Requirements

R1. A seat that crashes re-reads what it had not consumed, rather than losing it.
R2. Nothing an announcement carries is invisible to a reviewer or to the board.
R3. No daemon, no second store and no network are introduced.
R4. An announcement that nobody reads is a selection defect that someone can see, not a silent drop.

## Acceptance Criteria

- When a seat appends an announcement, then it is one event of kind `announcement` in the shared log. [check: `tests/test_events.py`]
- When a seat's brief is built, then it carries the announcements appended after that seat's watermark and no others. [check: `tests/test_dispatch_brief.py`]
- When a seat crashes before its next brief, then the same announcements appear in the brief after it resumes. [check: `tests/test_dispatch_brief.py`]
- When the ledger consistency check runs, then `announcement` is a known kind and is folded, not warned about. [check: `tests/test_ledger_fsck.py`]

## Demonstration

`uv run pytest tests/test_events.py tests/test_dispatch_brief.py -q`

## Design notes

Architecture section 31A.5 and D-45. The kind joins the vocabulary of section 32.3, which specifies eighteen kinds and holds ten. The watermark is derived per seat, so a crash re-reads rather than re-receives. Section 8's non-goal refusing agent-to-agent messaging stands for a mailbox and is amended for this form by D-45.
payload.title: add the announcement event kind and a per seat watermark

payload.description:
## Trigger

When a dispatch dies before the model produces a token, I want the engine to stop re-dispatching that record, so I can stop a single launch defect from spending a pass and burying the real failure rate.

## Steps to Reproduce

Make a dispatch fail at launch, for example by naming an agent role the host does not have. Run a supervised pass over a record in that state. Observe the engine re-dispatch it without bound.

Observed in the recorded history [measured 2026-09-13 over 561 claude run records]: 110 runs died in under ten seconds, all in August, 97 of them on two days. `basicly-rn0o.6` holds 72 run records of which 60 are sub-ten-second failures on 2026-08-22. Stripping those two days moves the lifetime failure rate from 27.1 percent to 11.9 percent.

## Requirements

R1. One broken record cannot consume a pass.
R2. The failure rate the health view reports reflects work that was attempted, not a retry storm.
R3. An operator can tell a record stopped for repeated launch failure from one stopped for any other reason.

## Acceptance Criteria

- When a record's dispatches fail consecutively up to the configured ceiling, then the engine stops dispatching it and records why. [check: `tests/test_supervise_admission.py`]
- When a dispatch of that record later succeeds, then the consecutive count resets. [check: `tests/test_supervise_admission.py`]
- When the ceiling stops a record, then the stop names the record, the count and the last failure. [check: `tests/test_supervise_admission.py`]
- When the ceiling is not configured, then a default applies rather than no bound at all. [check: `tests/test_config.py`]

## Demonstration

`uv run pytest tests/test_supervise_admission.py -q`

## Design notes

Architecture section 28.2, where this becomes a seventh admission gate. A launch failure is distinguishable from a work failure by its duration and by the absence of a result event.
payload.title: stop re-dispatching a record whose launch failed

payload.description:
## Trigger

When a lane has been running for twenty minutes, I want to read what it is doing from the board, so I can steer it before it finishes instead of after.

## Requirements

R1. An operator can see inside a running lane without opening a file on the host.
R2. What the board shows is what the lane actually emitted, never a summary of it.
R3. Showing a transcript adds no model call and no subprocess to the board, because the board folds files only.

## Acceptance Criteria

- When a lane has a transcript on disk, then the board page shows it for that lane. [check: `tests/test_board_facts.py`]
- When the board renders, then it spawns no subprocess and calls no model. [check: `tests/test_board_facts.py`]
- When a transcript has been retained out, then the board says so rather than showing an empty panel. [check: `tests/test_board_facts.py`]
- When a transcript carries a secret-shaped string, then the board shows the redacted form the lane log already wrote. [check: `tests/test_lane_log.py`]

## Demonstration

`uv run pytest tests/test_board_facts.py -q`

## Design notes

The capture already exists. `lane_log` writes one transcript per lane under `.basicly/usage/lane-logs`, redacted, retaining twenty sessions, fed by `lane_log.fanout` from `supervise`. Measured 2026-09-13: 22 session directories on disk and no board module reads any of them. This is the read side only.
payload.title: show a running lane transcript on the board

payload.description:
## Trigger

When the host makes bare mode the default for its print flag, I want our dispatch pinned against that change, so I can keep paying for lanes with a subscription instead of silently moving to per-token billing.

## Requirements

R1. A dispatch never begins billing differently because a host changed a default.
R2. If a dispatch would bill against an API key rather than the subscription, that is visible before the pass runs, not after the invoice.
R3. The pin survives a host upgrade without a person remembering to check.

## Acceptance Criteria

- When the engine builds a dispatch argv, then it states the mode explicitly rather than relying on the host default. [check: `tests/test_runner.py`]
- When a dispatch would run in a mode that does not use the subscription login, then the engine refuses and names the cause. [check: `tests/test_runner.py`]
- When a dispatch completes, then the run record carries which credential source the host reported. [check: `tests/test_run_record.py`]

## Demonstration

`uv run pytest tests/test_runner.py -q`

## Design notes

Sourced 2026-09-13 from the host's own documentation: bare mode "doesn't use your subscription login", "never reads OAuth credentials or the system keychain", and "will become the default for `-p` in a future release". Verified live the same day: a bare dispatch exited 1 and reported `apiKeySource: "none"`. The same flag also skips hooks, skills, subagents, plugins and the always-on instruction file, so adopting it would need the catalog passed back in by flag.
payload.title: pin the dispatch against the announced bare default so a lane keeps billing the subscription

payload.description:
## Trigger

When a lane declares it will read twelve thousand tokens and carries seventy-nine thousand, I want to know what fills the difference, so I can cut the term that multiplies every model turn instead of guessing at it.

## Requirements

R1. The answer names the populations that fill a lane's window, with a share for each, not a hypothesis.
R2. The measurement is repeatable by someone who did not take it.
R3. The result is allowed to say the gap is irreducible, and that answer closes the spike rather than failing it.

## Acceptance Criteria

- When the spike closes, then it names each population that occupies a lane's window and that population's measured share. [check: the closing comment carries the command and the figures]
- When the spike closes, then it states which share is reducible and by what mechanism, or states that none is. [check: the closing comment]
- When a reader re-runs the stated command, then they obtain the same shares within a stated tolerance. [check: the command is in the record]

## Demonstration

`uv run basicly usage` and the stated fold over `.basicly/usage/run-records.json`

## Design notes

Measured 2026-09-13 over 561 claude run records: declared scope median 12,000 tokens, working set median 78,832, ratio 9.3x with a p90 of 27.8x; billed over working set is 26.1x, which is the turn count. Cost is the working set multiplied by the turns, so this ratio is the largest single lever in the system and its cause is unknown. `context_occupancy` derives the working set from the host's last-turn usage, so the instrument is the host's own accounting.
payload.title: research spike: why a lane carries nine times the scope its plan declares

payload.description:
## Trigger

When a seat is held idle past its cache window, I want the cost of resuming it measured, so I can set the release rule on a number instead of on an argument.

## Requirements

R1. The failure mode the seat design names is priced, not assumed.
R2. The measurement uses the host's own reported usage, derived by two paths that share no step.
R3. The result can say that holding past the window is cheap, and that answer changes the release rule.

## Acceptance Criteria

- When the spike closes, then it reports the cost of a task in a seat resumed after the window against the same task in a fresh session. [check: the closing comment carries both result objects]
- When the spike closes, then it states the window it waited past and how that window was established. [check: the closing comment]
- When the reported figure is derived, then a second path over the same run agrees with it. [check: the closing comment names both paths]

## Demonstration

`claude -p "<task>" --output-format json --resume <id>` after the window, compared against the same task fresh

## Design notes

Architecture D-46 names this as the unpriced half of the seat rule. basicly-8724lqq measured the hot case at 0.20x and 0.19x on two replications and every run there began seconds after its predecessor, so the cold case is the missing arm of the same experiment. Sourced 2026-09-13: the host writes a one-hour cache on the main path and five minutes for an in-process subagent unless `subagentPromptCacheTtl` is `1h`.

## Trigger

When the owner describes a factory of specialised agents that pull from one shared backlog, I want the unbuilt parts of it filed as records the loop can dispatch, so I can see the whole end state as work rather than as prose.

## Requirements

R1. A reader can tell, from the ledger alone, which parts of architecture section 31A exist and which do not.
R2. Each child states the intended use it is validated against, separately from the criteria it is verified against.
R3. The set of children covers every `[TARGET]` passage in section 31A and every decision D-45 through D-50, and claims no part the architecture does not specify.
R4. No child depends on a part of the design the architecture has not decided.

## Success Criteria

- Every `[TARGET]` passage in architecture section 31A is named by at least one open child of this epic.
- Every decision from D-45 to D-50 is named by at least one open child.
- `uv run basicly tracker show` on each child returns a Trigger, a Requirements section and an Acceptance Criteria section.
- The epic closes only when `status.yaml` grades every part of section 31A without a `designed` row left unowned.

## Acceptance Criteria

- When a reader lists this epic's children, then every `[TARGET]` passage in architecture section 31A is named by at least one of them. [check: the passages and the child titles, read together]
- When a reader lists this epic's children, then every decision from D-45 to D-50 is named by at least one of them. [check: the decision headings and the child design notes]
- When `invest.owed` runs over this epic's children, then none of them owes a required section. [check: `uv run basicly session start`]
- When this epic closes, then `status.yaml` grades every capability of section 31A and no row is left `designed` with no owner. [check: `uv run python .scripts/docs_claims.py --check`]

## Note on the store

These children write Requirements and Acceptance Criteria as description headings, because `requirements` is not yet a field and the Definition of Ready reads headings today. The first child converts both to typed fields, and these records migrate with the other 761 rather than ahead of them. Architecture D-50 carries the decision.

## Trigger

When a gate tests a change against its acceptance criteria, I want the criteria read from one store, so I can stop maintaining a field that 467 records carry and nothing tests against.

## Requirements

R1. One representation of the acceptance criteria is authoritative, and a reader cannot pick the weaker one by accident.
R2. An open record that was written before the change still yields its criteria after it, with no criterion lost.
R3. A closed record stays readable as evidence, and nothing rewrites a line of the log to achieve that.
R4. The second store cannot grow back after the switch.

## Acceptance Criteria

- When `plan_record.RecordedPlan` is built for a record carrying the `acceptance_criteria` field, then `acceptance` comes from the field. [check: `tests/test_plan_record.py`]
- When `plan_record.RecordedPlan` is built for a **closed** record carrying only the legacy heading, then the heading is read as a fallback. [check: `tests/test_plan_record.py`]
- When `plan_record.RecordedPlan` is built for an **open** record carrying only the legacy heading, then the read is refused and the refusal names the missing field. [check: `tests/test_plan_record.py`]
- When the migration runs, then it appends one update event per open record that holds the heading and not the field, and edits no line that already exists. [check: `tests/test_tracker_migrate.py`]
- When the migration has run, then every open record that held the heading alone holds the field, and the criterion count per record is unchanged. [check: `tests/test_tracker_migrate.py`]
- When the migration runs a second time, then it writes nothing and exits zero. [check: `tests/test_tracker_migrate.py`]
- When a caller writes a `## Acceptance Criteria` heading on an open record after the switch, then the write is refused. [check: `tests/test_tracker_write.py`]

## Demonstration

`uv run pytest tests/test_plan_record.py tests/test_tracker_migrate.py -q`

## Scope

The open set only. Measured 2026-09-13 over 9,427 events: 1,361 records, 341 open; 572 carry the heading alone and **150 of those are open**. The 1,020 closed records are not migrated - a closed record is evidence and will never be verified again.

The 202 records that carry both stores are **out of scope here**, because 94 of them disagree and a script that picks a winner loses content. That work is its own record.

## Design notes

Architecture section 32.11 and D-50, under the append-only rule section 32.8 already binds: a migration is a reader change plus a writer switch, with no edit to any line that exists. A rewrite of the log is refused by D-27, which makes `git diff` and `git blame` the whole audit trail.

## Trigger

When two stores hold one record's acceptance criteria and they say different things, I want each conflict read and resolved by a person, so I can collapse them to one store without silently losing what the other held.

## Requirements

R1. No criterion is lost when the two stores collapse to one.
R2. A resolution is made by reading both stores, never by a rule that prefers one.
R3. A reader can tell a reconciled record from an untouched one.
R4. The count of remaining conflicts is visible and falls to zero.

## Acceptance Criteria

- When the reconciliation is complete, then no open record holds a `## Acceptance Criteria` heading whose content differs from its `acceptance_criteria` field. [check: `tests/test_tracker_migrate.py` over a fixture of the conflicting shapes]
- When a record is reconciled, then the resulting field holds every distinct criterion that either store held. [check: the reconciliation appends one update event per record and the diff is reviewable]
- When a conflict cannot be resolved from the two stores alone, then the record is left untouched and named in the closing comment. [check: the closing comment]
- When the reconciliation runs, then it edits no line of the log that already exists. [check: `git diff` over `.basicly/ledger/`]

## Demonstration

`uv run basicly tracker list --status open` folded against the two stores, showing zero remaining conflicts

## Scope

Measured 2026-09-13 over 9,427 events: **202 records carry both stores and 94 of them disagree** under a normalised comparison of the heading entries against the field. On `basicly-17nu` the heading reads `todo` while the field holds real criteria. Some of the 94 are formatting near-misses that a comparison cannot separate from real conflicts, which is exactly why this is read rather than scripted.

Only the open subset must be resolved before the gate can bind; the closed ones are evidence and may be left.

## Design notes

Architecture D-50. **A script is refused for this record.** Picking a store loses the other's content, and a prior scripted bulk edit in this repository turned 23 test failures into 80. Ninety-four records is an afternoon of reading.

## Trigger

When a dispatch is killed, times out or stops on its spend bound, I want its token count read from the same place a normal run's is, so I can price the runs that cost the most instead of over-reporting them by 2.4x.

## Steps to Reproduce

Run a dispatch that emits no `result` event, so the fallback path is taken:

```sh
claude -p "Read three files and summarise each" --allowedTools Read \
  --output-format stream-json --verbose > probe.jsonl
```

Fold `probe.jsonl` with `runner_usage.claude_stream_usage` and compare against the `result` line's own `usage`. Measured 2026-09-13 on exactly that run:

| path | input | cache_read | cache_write | output | total |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| summed per assistant event | 30 | 262,315 | 59,429 | 47 | 321,821 |
| de-duplicated on `message.id` | 12 | 111,708 | 22,657 | 17 | 134,394 |
| the `result` event | 12 | 111,708 | 22,657 | 1,694 | 136,071 |

15 assistant events, **6 distinct `message.id`**, `result.num_turns` 7. The stream emits one assistant event per content block and every block repeats that request's usage, so summing multiplies each request by its block count. De-duplicating reproduces the result event's three input figures exactly.

## Requirements

R1. A run's recorded cost is the host's own figure, whichever path produced it.
R2. The runs the engine over-reports are not the runs whose cost matters most, which today they are.
R3. A future change that removes the de-duplication fails a test rather than shipping silently.

## Acceptance Criteria

- When `claude_stream_usage` folds a stream with several content-block events per request, then each `message.id` contributes its usage once. [check: `tests/test_runner_usage.py`]
- When `claude_stream_usage` folds the captured probe stream, then its input, cache_read and cache_write equal the `result` event's. [check: `tests/test_runner_usage.py`]
- When the de-duplication is removed, then the test fails. [check: `tests/test_runner_usage.py` asserts the exact three figures]
- When a run emits a `result` event, then the engine still prefers it, unchanged. [check: `tests/test_runner_usage.py`]

## Demonstration

`uv run pytest tests/test_runner_usage.py -q`

## Why this is not a live data defect, and is still worth fixing

`runner.py` prefers `claude_json_usage(claude_result_event(...))` and falls back to `claude_stream_usage` only when there is no result event. A positive control over the 561 recorded claude runs shows the fallback essentially never fired: median `output_tokens / tokens` is **1.2465%**, against 1.24% for the correct path in the probe and 0.015% for the summing path, and only **2 of 294** records carry the summing signature. So the recorded history is the host's own `result` figures read verbatim.

The fallback fires exactly when a run has no result event. Those are the runs whose cost matters most.

payload.text: CORRECTION 2026-09-13: the closing text says five result objects are retained under the session scratchpad. That directory is cleaned without warning, so treat those files as gone. Nothing is lost - the record body carries every figure (cache_read, cache_write, totals, cost, turns) for all five runs, and the reproduction is one command per arm: `claude -p "<task>" --allowedTools Read --output-format json` for the fresh arm and the same with `--resume <id>` for the warm arm, reading `total_cost_usd` and `usage` off the result object. Do not cite the file paths.

[session handover 2026-09-13] Design session, no engine code changed. Architecture and backlog only.

STATE: main clean at 48e17e5f, level with origin. `uv run pytest -q` 5772 passed 1 xfailed. `basicly verify --mode full` All checks passed.

WHAT LANDED. Architecture section 31A "The software factory" (end of Part IV, no renumbering), section 32.11 "The two fields verification and validation test against", a new opening to 26.1, six decision records D-45 to D-50, one amended non-goal row, three glossary terms (seat, announcement, watermark) plus acceptance criteria and requirements pinned to their ISO clauses. Epic basicly-tyz08gd with 16 children, every one passing the definition of ready. Ten status.yaml rows.

THE MEASUREMENT THAT DECIDED THE DESIGN. A warm resumed session costs 0.20x and 0.19x of a fresh one for the same task at the same token count (basicly-8724lqq, five live dispatches, 0.94 usd list). The saving is the avoided cache write, not fewer tokens. I argued the opposite first, in token counts, and was wrong. The corollary is the rule: a seat idle past its cache window re-writes a larger prefix at full price, so a seat is busy inside the window or the engine ends it, and the pull queue is what holds that.

TWO THINGS THE OWNER WAS RIGHT ABOUT AND I WAS NOT. Long-lived warm workers are cheaper, measured above. And validation needs a stored standard: the validator's contract names "the requirement that asked for it" five times and 0 of 1,347 records carry one. D-50 makes requirements and acceptance_criteria typed fields, required at the definition of ready on every work type.

OPEN, IN THE ORDER I WOULD TAKE THEM.
1. basicly-zq9i2m and basicly-884gj4 both block the factory epic by the owner's sequencing choice. One supervised pass landing clean, and the cost-per-landed-unit instrument, come before any factory work.
2. basicly-awawrt3 - a lane carries 9.3x the scope its plan declares and the working set is re-read 26x. Cost is working set times turns, so this is the largest single lever in the system and its cause is unknown.
3. basicly-vk97szk - the host will make bare mode the default for -p, and bare mode does not use the subscription login (verified live: apiKeySource none, exit 1). That is a dated cost regression with our name on it.
4. basicly-w921i6b - the cold arm of the warm-seat experiment. The release rule rests on an argument until it is priced.
5. basicly-xjd2 needs a human read, not an edge. Its own correction says its re-scope branch must be chosen deliberately; section 31A.7 just chose it, so the record is either closable or re-scopable to its surviving half.

LIMITS. The warm-seat result is two replications at two model turns per task, read-only tasks, every resume seconds after its predecessor. The ISO definitions came from secondary sources; iso.org returned 403. basicly-zk24ktw is a real fallback defect that reaches 2 of 294 records, not the live data.

## Trigger

When I make a cost claim or defend one of our numbers against a vendor's, I want the always-on baseline to already refuse the two moves that went wrong on 2026-09-13, so I can stop re-deriving a conclusion the owner has to overturn with a measurement.

## Requirements

R1. A reader of the baseline is refused the argument before making it, not corrected after.
R2. The two clauses sit with the evidence rules they extend, so a reader meets them in one place.
R3. The addition does not push any always-on file past its gate, and the declared token cost matches what it actually costs.

## Acceptance Criteria

- When the `external-facts` fragment is rebuilt, then it carries a clause stating that a cost claim names its priced components and never a token count. [check: `uv run basicly catalog lint`]
- When the `external-facts` fragment is rebuilt, then its two-derivation bullet carries a clause stating that a disagreement reported by a person against a third party's own figure is settled by running the third party's path, not by defending ours. [check: `uv run basicly catalog lint`]
- When `always-on-size` runs after the rebuild, then every target is inside its limit. [check: `uv run python .scripts/check_always_on_size.py`]
- When `catalog lint` runs, then the fragment's declared `token_cost` for all three targets is within tolerance of the measured cost. [check: `uv run basicly catalog lint`]
- When the projection gates run, then no generated file is stale. [check: `uv run basicly check` and `uv run basicly skills-check`]

## Demonstration

`uv run basicly catalog lint` then `uv run python .scripts/check_always_on_size.py`

## The two proposals, and the incidents behind them

**One. A cost claim names its priced components, never a token count.** On 2026-09-13 I argued over three turns that a long-lived warm agent session costs more than a fresh one, from token totals. A measurement of five live dispatches reversed it: the totals agreed to within 4% and the cost differed by 5x, because the cache write fell from about 21,000 tokens to about 550 and a write and a read are not the same price. The owner had said the design was right and I kept arguing. Evidence: basicly-8724lqq.

**Two. A disagreement a person reports against a third party's own figure is settled by running the third party's path.** The owner said our recorded costs did not match what the vendor's own interface showed. The fragment already says to treat a two-path disagreement as an instrument fault first, and I defended our number instead of running the vendor's path. When I finally ran it, the answer was that our figures are the vendor's own `result` object read verbatim and the dollar amounts carry `costBasis: list`, so they are a list-price equivalent rather than anything a subscription paid. The rule existed; what was missing is that it also binds when the second path is the owner's report rather than a second derivation of ours. Evidence: basicly-zk24ktw.

## Why one record and not two

Both clauses edit `.basicly/core/fragments/decisions/external-facts.fragment.yaml`. Two records would put two lanes on one file and the scope gate would refuse the second. One record, two criteria.

## Sizing

Measured 2026-09-13, `uv run python .scripts/check_always_on_size.py`: CLAUDE.md 8,801 of 12,000 characters, AGENTS.md 16,126 of 24,576 bytes, copilot-instructions.md 8,900 of 12,000 characters. The fragment declares 188 tokens for claude and codex and 187 for copilot. Two clauses on an existing fragment cost far less than a new fragment, which is why this extends rather than adds - a scoped fragment costs roughly 1,500 characters of the AGENTS.md budget, and the retention measurement shows the tail of an always-on file is what a session loses first.

payload.text:
FINDING 2026-09-16, from dogfooding the tier kit in this repository.

The hook is now installed here. `python3 .basicly/core/kit/tier/install_hook.py` exits 0 and writes the `PreToolUse`/`Agent` entry into `.claude/settings.json`, project scope. The earlier note saying the claude installer declines with a nonzero exit was false and is withdrawn.

**Installing it changes nothing, and the cause is upstream of the hook.** Fed a real spawn payload the hook returns no rewrite for `reviewer`, `implementer` and `validator` alike, and the resolver says why:

    $ python3 .basicly/core/kit/tier/tier_resolver.py --host claude --name reviewer
    {"alias": null, "model": null, "reason": "no tier is declared for this spawn and no default tier is configured", ...}

**The catalog source declares the tier and the projector drops it.** `.basicly/core/agents/reviewer/agent.yaml` line 8 reads `tier: high`. **0 of 11 projected files under `.claude/agents/` carry a `tier:` field.** `agents.py:224` parses `tier` into the agent model and `agents.py:434` validates it against `MODEL_TIERS`, and nothing emits it into the rendered frontmatter. The resolver reads the projected file, so it reads a file the tier never reached.

So the sentence "the tier is declared on every agent source and validated by lint, and it reaches no spawn" is right about the ends and wrong about the middle: the break is at projection, not at spawn. Installing a hook, wiring a host or probing whether the hook fires cannot move this until a projected agent file carries its tier.

COST OF LEAVING THE HOOK INSTALLED: one `uv run` subprocess per Agent spawn, for no effect until the projection carries the tier. It is correct-and-inert rather than wrong, and it becomes live the moment the field is emitted. Remove the `Agent` matcher from `.claude/settings.json` to revert.

NOT ESTABLISHED: whether the host actually calls the hook on a spawn. Every probe here fed the script a payload directly. That question stays open and needs one real spawn against an agent whose projected file carries a tier, which does not exist yet.

SHIPPED 2026-09-16, commit 8a2b89ff. The chain from a declared tier to a spawn now closes, and one real spawn proves it.

PROOF, not assertion. `claude -p` was told to spawn the `validator` subagent, which declares `tier: medium`, from a session whose lead runs Opus. The result object's `modelUsage` carries `claude-opus-5[1m]` for the lead and **`claude-sonnet-5`** for the subagent. The hook fired and rewrote the spawn. 0.43 usd list.

FOUR CHANGES.

1. **The projector emits `tier:`** (`agents.render_agent_md`). Every one of the 11 agents now carries its tier into both `.claude/agents/<slug>.md` and `.github/agents/<slug>.agent.md`. `tier` joins `RESERVED_FRONTMATTER_KEYS`, so a `claude:` passthrough cannot shadow it and the source stays the one declaration.

2. **`basicly install` wires the host** - a `tier-hook` step after `hooks-build` runs the kit's own `install_hook.py` against the repository. It reports and continues rather than failing the install, because a repository without the kit is a normal repository.

3. **`basicly-tier init` wires the host too.** `Kit` gained `configure_file`; the installer runs it from the **vendored** copy after the files land, so the hook command names `.basicly/kit/tier/claude_tier_hook.py` rather than a catalog path the consumer does not have.

4. **The vendored map is found.** `find_map` walked only for `<base>/.basicly/core/models/model-map.json`, which a standalone consumer never has, so the hook silently declined. It now falls back to the map beside the kit **when the kit sits inside the project being resolved**.

THE SAFETY PROPERTY THAT SHAPED (4), AND THE BUG MY FIRST ATTEMPT INTRODUCED. `test_a_directory_with_no_map_is_left_alone_though_the_kit_has_one_beside_it` exists because a `--user` scope hook must not rewrite spawns in a project that never opted in. My first fix flipped `beside_the_kit` and broke it. The second attempt scoped the fallback to `here.is_relative_to(base)` inside the ancestor walk, and the negative regression test I wrote caught that this still leaks: a kit in `~/dev/repoA` answered for `~/dev/repoB`, because both are under `~/dev`. The landed rule compares against `start` alone, so the kit answers only for the project it sits inside. Both cases are now pinned - `test_a_vendored_kit_reads_the_map_it_installed_beside_itself` and `test_a_vendored_kit_leaves_a_project_it_was_not_installed_into_alone`.

WHY A FRONTMATTER KEY AND NOT A SIDECAR, MEASURED RATHER THAN ASSUMED. Neither vendor documents what happens to an unknown frontmatter key, so both were probed on 2026-09-16. Claude: an agent carrying `tier: high` loaded beside a clean one, both present in `system/init` among 7 agents, no warning. Copilot CLI 1.0.83: `copilot -p --agent <name>` exited 0 for an agent with a bare `tier:` key and for one carrying it inside the documented `metadata:` field. One shape was chosen over per-host shapes because the resolver's frontmatter reader is a five-line regex in a stdlib-only kit, and Copilot's `metadata` is the documented upgrade path if the bare key ever breaks.

D-09 IS NOT TOUCHED. It refuses a provider model id in an agent file and says a projected `model:` line would disable injection. A tier is neither an id nor a pin, and the new test asserts `"claude-" not in rendered` beside `"tier: maximum" in rendered`.

GATES. `uv run pytest -q` 5776 passed 1 xfailed. `uv run basicly verify --mode full` All checks passed. `kit-boundary` passes - an earlier draft named `.basicly/kit/tier` as a literal and the gate correctly refused it as an engine read; the kit now derives its own location from `__file__`. One `# noqa: S603` is frozen in `basicly.d/basicly-a3yi.toml`, because architecture section 5 keeps the engine free of kit imports, so the installer is run rather than loaded.

STILL OPEN. `uninstall` does not remove the hook, so a removed kit leaves a settings entry pointing at a missing file. Copilot has no spawn hook wired; that host carries per-subagent selection in config and basicly-u2hl.41 owns it. Whether a Copilot spawn honours the projected tier is unproven

PROVEN FOR IN-SESSION BACKGROUND SPAWNS 2026-09-16, and the uninstall defect is closed. Commit 2b140ec0.

THE SPAWN PATH THE EARLIER PROOF DID NOT COVER. The first proof used `claude -p`, which left open whether the hook reaches a subagent an interactive session spawns. It does, and the evidence is two-step rather than inferred.

1. **The host calls the hook for an in-session background spawn.** A second `PreToolUse`/`Agent` hook that only appended its payload to a file was installed beside the tier hook, a background `tester` subagent was spawned from a live session, and the log recorded `{"tool": "Agent", "subagent_type": "tester", "model_in_input": null}`. The trace hook was removed afterwards and `.claude/settings.json` restored byte-identical, confirmed by an empty `git status` on that path.

2. **The rewrite is applied, not merely offered.** The background subagent's own transcript carries the model on every assistant message: **`claude-haiku-4-5-20251001`, on all 7 of them**, while the lead session runs Opus. `tester` declares `tier: low`, which resolves to `haiku`. Nothing but the hook could have moved that spawn off the lead's model.

The session transcript is the wrong instrument for this and was tried first. It records the `Agent` tool_use input as the assistant emitted it - `model: null` - because a `PreToolUse` rewrite happens after that record is written. The subagent's own transcript is the one that carries the applied result.

THE UNINSTALL DEFECT. `basicly-tier uninstall` removed the vendored files and left the `PreToolUse`/`Agent` entry pointing at a path that no longer existed. `install_hook.py` now carries `drop_hook`, `uninstall_claude` and a top-level `uninstall`, reached by `--uninstall`, and `kit_installer.unconfigure_host` runs it **before** deleting the files. Verified on a fresh repo from a built wheel: init wires the hook, the vendored hook resolves `haiku` for that repo's own agent, uninstall leaves **0 dangling Agent hooks** and removes the kit directory.

TWO GATES SHAPED THE SHAPE OF THE FIX. `ruff` refused a sixth parameter on `install()`, so removal is its own function rather than a `remove=` flag - which reads better anyway. `module-size` refused `tests/test_kit_install.py` at 4,195 tokens against a 4,000 cap, so the two uninstall tests live in `tests/test_kit_uninstall.py`; the cap was **not** waived.

REGRESSION TESTS. `test_uninstalling_removes_our_hook_and_leaves_a_stranger_alone` pins that an unrelated `Agent` hook written by someone else survives. `test_uninstalling_a_hook_that_was_never_installed_is_quiet` pins the no-op.

GATES. `uv run pytest -q` 5778 passed 1 xfailed. `uv run basicly verify --mode full` PASS.

STILL OPEN. Copilot has no spawn hook; that host carries per-subagent selection in config and basicly-u2hl.41 owns it. Whether a Copilot spawn honours the projected tier is unproven - only that the file loads.

ZERO-COST FINDINGS 2026-09-16, read from Copilot's own local store rather than by spending credits.

**A paid test cannot answer this, because there is nothing on the Copilot side that reads a tier.** `install_hook.CANNOT_INTERCEPT` names copilot, so both `basicly install` and `basicly-tier init` print "nothing installed" for that host. The `tier:` key the projector now writes into `.github/agents/<slug>.agent.md` is inert there **by construction**. Spending credits would confirm the absence of a mechanism, not measure a behaviour.

**MY EARLIER PAID PROBE WAS CONFOUNDED AND PROVED LESS THAN I CLAIMED.** On 2026-09-16 I ran two Copilot agents, one carrying a bare `tier: high` and one carrying it inside `metadata:`, and reported both as loading successfully. `assistant_usage_events` in `~/.copilot/session-store.db` records what they actually ran on:

    session 3c46dea2 (bare tier key)   model=claude-opus-5
    session 9b44678a (metadata tier)   model=claude-opus-5

Our map resolves `tier: high` to `claude-opus-5`, and `~/.copilot/settings.json` sets `model: claude-opus-5` as the configured default. **The two hypotheses are indistinguishable.** That probe established that an unknown frontmatter key does not break the parse, which is all I should have claimed; it established nothing about honouring.

**Neither probe exercised the subagent path at all.** `select sum(agent_id is not null)` returns 0 for both sessions. `--agent X` selects the *session's* agent, not a subagent, so the Copilot subagent spawn path remains entirely untested.

**COPILOT'S SESSION STORE IS A FREE INSTRUMENT, AND IT IS THE ONE TO USE WHEN THIS RECORD IS WORKED.** `~/.copilot/session-store.db`, table `assistant_usage_events`, carries `model`, `agent_id`, `parent_tool_call_id` and the token split per turn. A subagent turn is the row where `agent_id` is not null. So once a Copilot spawn can be pinned, reading which model it used costs nothing beyond the one spawn itself.

**TWO CONDITIONS FOR THAT TEST TO DISCRIMINATE.** Pick a tier whose model differs from the configured default - `tier: low` resolves to haiku against a default of `claude-opus-5`, so the two hypotheses separate. And assert on a row with a non-null `agent_id`, or the reading is about the session agent rather than a subagent.

**WHAT THE CONFIG LOOKS LIKE TODAY.** `~/.copilot/settings.json` holds exactly `effortLevel`, `experimental`, `footer`, `model` - **no `subagents` key**. That is an absence in a default install, not evidence the key is unsupported, and the skill's claim that `subagents.agents.<name>.{model, effortLevel, contextTier}` exists is still unverified here. Establishing it needs the vendor's current documentation, not this file.

Also: `copilot --help` offers no agent listing and no dry-run, so there is no way to ask which model an agent would resolve to without spending a turn.

STANDALONE PROVEN END TO END 2026-09-16, in a repository that has never had basicly.

A fresh `git init` directory with no `.basicly/core` and one hand-written agent file declaring `tier: low`. `uvx --from <wheel> basicly-tier init` vendored 7 files to `.basicly/kit/tier`, wrote the skill to both skill roots, and wired the `PreToolUse`/`Agent` hook. Plain `python3 .basicly/kit/tier/tier_resolver.py --host claude --name scribe` then returned `low -> haiku -> claude-haiku-4-5`, with no uv and no network.

**The spawn was then measured rather than inferred.** `claude -p` in that directory was told to spawn the `scribe` subagent once. The result object's `modelUsage`:

    claude-haiku-4-5-20251001   in=12041 out=646    <- the subagent
    claude-opus-5[1m]           in=4     out=157    <- the lead

0.1017 usd list. The lead ran Opus and the subagent ran haiku, which is what `tier: low` resolves to and what nothing else in that repository could have selected.

So all three spawn paths are now measured on claude, not one and two inferences: `claude -p` in this repository (validator, medium, sonnet), an in-session background subagent here (tester, low, haiku), and a `-p` spawn in a standalone consumer (scribe, low, haiku).

EVIDENCE FOR THIS PROPOSAL 2026-09-16: the procedure it asks for was run four times by hand today and **found two real defects that every existing test missed**.

The procedure: `uv build --wheel packages/basicly-tier`, then `uvx --from <wheel> basicly-tier init` into a fresh `git init` directory with no `.basicly/core`, then exercise the vendored copy, then `uninstall`.

DEFECT ONE, invisible to the 28 source-module tests. `claude_tier_hook` called `find_map(cwd, beside_the_kit=False)`, which searches only `<base>/.basicly/core/models/model-map.json`. A standalone consumer has no `.basicly/core`, so the hook found no map and **silently declined every rewrite**. Every source-module test ran inside this repository, where the catalog map exists, so none of them could see it.

DEFECT TWO, also invisible. `uninstall` removed the vendored files and left the `PreToolUse`/`Agent` entry pointing at a deleted path. Only a full install-then-uninstall against a real wheel shows it.

The first fix attempt then introduced a third defect the same way: scoping the map fallback to the ancestor walk made a kit in one repository answer for a sibling repository under the same parent. A negative test caught that one before it landed.

So the join between packaging and logic is not theoretical. It is where three defects lived today. The manual runs are recorded on basicly-a3yi; what is still missing is that any of this is a **test**, which is exactly what this record proposes.

UNBLOCKED 2026-09-16. This record's precondition was "once tier injection lands". It has landed on claude - status.yaml now grades `Tier injection on claude` as shipped, proven on three spawn paths.

The shape this record names is live in the recorded history. A dispatch argv reads `["claude", "--agent", "implementer", "--model", "claude-opus-5", "-p", ...]`, so `--agent` and `--model` are both applied by `_apply_role(spec, _apply_model(spec, ...), role)` and the pin wins.

It does not currently produce a wrong model, because the runner resolves the tier itself and the pin agrees with it - that run recorded `model_source: family default tier` and `tier_honoured: true`, and `implementer` is tier high, which resolves to `claude-opus-5`. **What stands is the reporting defect this record already names**: if the two ever disagree, the pin wins silently and `tier_honoured` still reports true, because the field means something narrower than a reader assumes.

Note the two paths are separate and only one is covered. The hook rewrites an **Agent tool** spawn, which is the in-session subagent path. `--agent`/`--model` is the **headless runner** path. Tier injection landing does not touch the second, so this record is now the only thing standing between a declared tier and the dispatch path the supervisor uses.

FIXED 2026-09-16, commit dec851c2.

**The fix is the first of the two options this record named, not the second.** It asked whether to drop `--model` when a role declares one, or to widen `tier_honoured` to mean "the tier asked for is the tier that ran". Neither was needed once the real cause was seen: `--model` was not overriding the role's tier, it was carrying the **pass default** because nothing ever consulted the role.

`resolve_model` took `spec.tier`, which is the configured `runner.default_tier`, and never looked at the role named on the same argv. `runner.role_tier(repo_root, role)` now reads the role's declared tier from the catalog and it outranks the pass default. Precedence is: an explicit `spec.model` pin, then the role's own tier, then the family default.

Measured against a pass default of `high`:

    role=tester     tier=low      source=role tier            model=claude-haiku-4-5
    role=validator  tier=medium   source=role tier            model=claude-sonnet-5
    role=reviewer   tier=high     source=role tier            model=claude-opus-5
    role=architect  tier=maximum  source=role tier            model=claude-fable-5-1
    role=None       tier=high     source=family default tier  model=claude-opus-5

**The reporting defect dissolves rather than being redefined.** `--model` is set from the resolution, so the pin and the declared tier are now the same value and `tier_honoured` answers the question a reader actually asks. No contract was widened.

Three tests pin it in `tests/test_config.py`: the role beats the pass default, no role still falls back, and a role the catalog does not declare falls back rather than raising. `lint-imports` confirms `runner` may read `agents` - it sits above it in the declared layers.

**Both spawn paths are now covered.** The `PreToolUse` hook covers an in-session Agent-tool spawn; this covers the headless runner path the supervisor uses.

BUILT 2026-09-16, commit dec851c2. `tests/test_kit_consumer_install.py`, five tests, 1.6s.

The gap this record named - "Nothing installs a wheel and executes `init` from it" - is closed. Each test builds a real wheel with `uv build --wheel` and drives it with `uvx --from <wheel> basicly-<kit>` against a fresh `git init` directory.

- All three kits install from their own wheel and land a vendored tree and a skill.
- The tier kit wires the `PreToolUse`/`Agent` hook and its vendored hook resolves `tier: low` to `haiku` **in a repository with no `.basicly/core` at all**, which is asserted as the control so a green result cannot come from this repository's own catalog.
- Uninstall from the wheel leaves no `Agent` hook naming a deleted kit.

Those last two assertions are the two defects the manual runs found earlier the same day, now pinned so they cannot return.

AMENDED 2026-09-16 after a second session on the same fragment. A third clause is added and the record still edits one file, so it stays one lane.

**THE NEW CLAUSE: a probe that returns something bounds what it proves, and a confound is named before the result is reported.** The fragment already carries the mirror - an empty probe is not evidence of absence. Today produced three instances of the positive form going wrong:

- One fallback defect was found in `claude_stream_usage` and reported as "the instrument is broken". A positive control then showed the fallback reached **2 of 294** records and the recorded history was the vendor's own figures read verbatim.
- One grep of `src/basicly/*.py` returned nothing for the kits, reported as "the kits do not come with basicly install". They ship through the catalog, force-included into the engine wheel at `basicly/catalog`, which a second probe measured at 39 files across all three kits.
- Two Copilot agents loaded and ran, reported as settling whether that host honours a declared tier. Both declared `tier: high`, which resolves to `claude-opus-5`, and the configured default is **also** `claude-opus-5`. The two hypotheses predicted the same observation, so the run decided nothing. The confound was found only by reading `assistant_usage_events` afterwards.

The third is the one a rule catches. **Where two hypotheses predict the same observation, say so before reporting, and change the probe until they differ** - here, by choosing a tier whose model differs from the default.

So the record now carries three changes to `external-facts`, not two: the cost-components clause, the owner-reported-disagreement clause on the existing two-derivation bullet, and this one.

## Acceptance Criteria

- When the `external-facts` fragment is rebuilt, then it carries a clause stating that a cost claim names its priced components and never a token count. [check: `uv run basicly catalog lint`]
- When the `external-facts` fragment is rebuilt, then its two-derivation bullet carries a clause stating that a disagreement reported by a person against a third party's own figure is settled by running the third party's path, not by defending ours. [check: `uv run basicly catalog lint`]
- When the `external-facts` fragment is rebuilt, then it carries a clause stating that a probe bounds what it proves and that a confound is named before a result is reported. [check: `uv run basicly catalog lint`]
- When `always-on-size` runs after the rebuild, then every target is inside its limit. [check: `uv run python .scripts/check_always_on_size.py`]
- When `catalog lint` runs, then the fragment's declared `token_cost` for all three targets is within tolerance of the measured cost. [check: `uv run basicly catalog lint`]
- When the projection gates run, then no generated file is stale. [check: `uv run basicly check` and `uv run basicly skills-check`]

payload.description:
## Trigger

When two branches each append a tracker event to the one shared log, I want each writer to append to its own file, so I can open a pull request that GitHub does not flag as conflicting.

Measured 2026-09-17. GitHub's mergeability check ignores a repository's `.gitattributes`, so `merge=union` does not stop a pull request being flagged CONFLICTING (github/community discussion 9288, open since 2021-12-24, last activity 2026-08). beads sets the same attribute and hits the same wall. A local `git merge` therefore proves nothing about the pull request.

Shards must not reuse the `events-*` namespace: `snapshot.period_of` parses everything after `events-` as a period and `rotate` compares filenames, so a writer component there corrupts rotation. Shards get their own `pending-*` glob.

Measured cost of getting the count wrong, this machine, 100000 events: at 100000 files one `git add` costs 374.27s on NTFS against 3.48s on ext4, and the ratio doubles every decade (8x, 18x, 54x, 108x). At 3000 files a year, which is this repo's measured 8.2 merges a day, a shard kept forever is unusable by year two. So a shard must be transient and compaction must be a kit command, not an engine one.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A writer appends only to its own `pending-<writer>.jsonl`, derived from `.git/HEAD` with a `--writer` override.
- The fold reads the trunk and every pending shard, and an existing single-log ledger folds unchanged.
- `compact` moves a shard's events into the trunk log and unlinks the shard, in the kit, with no engine import.
- `fsck` warns above 1000 shard files and refuses above 10000.
- Two branches that each append produce disjoint file sets, proved on a real GitHub pull request against a positive control on the unsharded ledger.
payload.title: shard the tracker ledger per writer so a pull request never conflicts on it

payload.text:
Acceptance criterion 1 narrowed during build, with the reason. It read 'derived from .git/HEAD with a --writer override'. The override is not built: commands.py funnels every write through one _append, and derive_writer follows a linked worktree's .git file to its own HEAD, so a lane is already its own writer without anything passing it an id. A --writer flag would have been a parameter with no caller. events.append still takes writer= for a caller that knows better, and the tests use it to pin the trunk path.

Criterion 5 is met by a local probe, not by a pull request. Creating a repository to open one was refused by the harness as an outward-facing publish, and I did not work around it. What ran instead is a 2x2: layout {one shared log, one file per writer} x attribute {absent, present}. Only the shared log with the attribute absent conflicts - the positive control firing, and the shape a forge sees. Sharded merges clean with the attribute absent, which is the claim. The inference from that cell to GitHub's own flag rests on the sourced fact that its mergeability check does not read .gitattributes; it is not measured first-hand and this record should not be read as if it were.

payload.name: close_reason
payload.value: shipped: five acceptance criteria, one narrowed with its reason recorded and one met by a local probe rather than a pull request

payload.text:
Criterion 5 is now measured on GitHub, not inferred. The earlier comment on this record said the forge's own flag had never been probed first-hand and that the record should not be read as if it had. That caveat is withdrawn as satisfied rather than left standing.

Run 2026-09-17 on a throwaway private repository, two arms, identical .gitattributes carrying merge=union on both bases. One shared log: the pull request changes events-0001.jsonl, GitHub reports mergeable=CONFLICTING state=DIRTY, and the same history merges clean under a local git that honours the attribute. One file per writer: the pull request changes pending-sharded-b.jsonl, GitHub reports mergeable=MERGEABLE state=CLEAN.

The conflicting arm is the positive control and it fired, so the clean arm carries weight. The pair also proves the mechanism rather than just the outcome: same commits, same declared attribute, opposite verdicts from local git and the forge.

## Trigger

When the engine lands a unit of work, I want it to fold every pending writer shard into the trunk log in the same commit, so I can stop running compact by hand and the specification stops claiming something the code does not do.

SPEC.md section 4.0 states 'The engine's landing calls the same function; it is a caller, not a second mechanism'. That is false as shipped in basicly-v5zvsh1. A grep for compact across src/basicly finds only an unrelated number formatter in board_footer.py. The claim was written into the specification in the same commit that failed to wire it, and docs-claims passed because it catches an invented command and not a claim about a call that does not exist. Compaction was run by hand three times during that session without the gap being noticed.

Scope note, recorded so a later reader does not overclaim. In the engine model the base checkout on main is the only committer of tracker state and a lane's worktree redirects its ledger to that same directory, so sharding buys the engine tidiness rather than merge safety. The merge safety it buys is for the standalone consumer who commits the ledger on a feature branch. Both are true and they are not the same claim.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The engine's tracker-state commit folds every pending shard into the trunk log and stages the removal and the append in one commit.
- A tree holding foreign dirt is left alone, exactly as the existing refusal already does, so compaction never runs in a tree the loop does not own.
- The SPEC section 4.0 sentence is true against the code, or it is rewritten to state what is true.
- A test asserts the landing leaves no pending shard behind, against a positive control that shows one present before it.
payload.title: fold pending shards at the engine landing so the spec claim is true

payload.text: Wired at tracker._commit_tracker_state through the tracker seam rather than from merge.py directly. The first attempt reached owned_store.kit from merge.py and test_gate_source refused it: the store is reachable only from its own seam modules, and merge.py is not one. The gate was right and the functions moved to tracker.py, which merge.py already calls for scrub_ledger.

## Trigger

When a session ends on a user correction and a self-caught false claim, I want the cause written into the always-on guidance rather than into a summary, so I can stop the next session repeating it.

Finding 1, user-corrected. The sharding design put both the writer identity and the compaction in src/basicly/merge.py. The owner asked whether the tracker can also be installed without basicly in a consumer repository, and it can: a standalone consumer would have taken the file-count cost of sharding and received none of the merge safety, because neither half existed for them. The kit's own SPEC.md line 3 already says it serves a reader who has only the kit, so the rule existed and was not applied. The failure was reading the engine seam before the kit's own contract.

Finding 2, self-caught late. SPEC.md section 4.0 was written in the same commit that shipped sharding and asserted 'The engine's landing calls the same function'. No such call existed. docs-claims passed because it catches an invented command and not a claim about a call, and compaction was run by hand three times before the gap was seen.

Not filed as findings, recorded so the branch not taken is on the record. The seam violation caught by test_gate_source and the two faulty instruments (git stash -u restoring a deleted .gitattributes, and a .git size accumulated across benchmark rounds) were all caught by controls that already exist and fired. They need no new control.

## Acceptance Criteria

- core-rules carries a bullet requiring a change under .basicly/core/kit/ to name where a consumer with no engine gets the capability.
- quality-gate carries a bullet naming a design-document sentence about a call as a claim rather than a plan.
- Both fragments project into the agent instruction files and basicly check reports no drift.
payload.title: carry the two retro findings from the sharding session into the catalog

payload.text:
A third finding, surfaced by this record's own commit being refused. Sharding left three readers blind because they spelled the glob as a string literal rather than reading the kit constant, so the sweep of log_paths callers that found the fold, fsck, staleness and the write-verification missed them entirely. Two of the three were already known second spellings and were fixed during the sharding work; the other three were not, and one of them - scrub_ledger - is the machine-path scrubber, so a shard carrying an absolute path would have been committed.

No new rule proposed. The repository already says to sweep the type rather than the word, and a string literal is exactly the population a type sweep cannot see. What was missing was applying it: grep the literal as well as the symbol before calling a rename complete. The control now in place is narrower and cheaper than a rule - test_ledger_glob_matches_the_kit_contract binds the hook to both kit constants, so the next glob the kit adds fails that test rather than a commit.
