## Trigger

When work is running that the board's `running now` region cannot see, I want the region to name only the population it actually draws, so I can trust it will not imply it is showing everything.

## Context

Owner question, 2026-08-22: *"I also understand that the only things that are shown on the board are the ones started by supervisor. what about other subagents or background agents - are they also shown on the board?"*

The answer is **no**, and it is structural rather than an omission in the producer.

## Measured

A board lane comes from one place: `board_facts.lane_facts` calls `supervise.derive_session(...)` and reads `state.adopted` (`src/basicly/board_facts.py:237-238`). An `AdoptedLane` (`src/basicly/supervise.py:466-474`) is *"one in-flight lane re-adopted from its br worktree binding"* and carries a required `loop_state.WorktreeBinding`.

So a thing appears on the board if and only if it has **a tracker record carrying a `worktree:` external_ref**. A subagent spawned through a host's own agent tool has neither. A background shell job has neither.

`rg -n 'subagent|sub-agent|background|spawn' src/basicly/board_*.py` returns two hits and both are prose in unrelated docstrings, saying the producer *spawns* nothing. Positive control: `rg -c 'lane' src/basicly/board_facts.py` returns 30, so the probe reaches the files and the absence is real.

## Why this matters more than it looks

The region is headed `RUNNING NOW`. A reader takes that as *what is happening in this repository*, and on 2026-08-22 the true answer included four read-only investigation subagents and two background shell jobs that the board could not see and did not mention. The heading over-claims: it means *what the supervisor dispatched*, and nothing says so.

That is the same class as `basicly-a68ggd`, where a region headed `THE LOOP` shows the whole backlog. A heading that names more than its producer can see is a defect whichever direction the gap runs.

## What is genuinely hard here

A subagent is **not** a lane and should not be drawn as one. It has no tracker record, no worktree, no branch, no acceptance criteria, and no landing. Giving it a lane card would invite a reader to expect a merge that will never come.

It also may not be observable at all. A lane is a subprocess this engine spawned and metered, so its stream is readable; a subagent of the *host* is inside the host's own process tree and the engine has no handle on it. Whether it can be counted at all is the first question this record has to answer rather than assume - and if the answer is that it cannot, then the honest fix is the heading and not a new section.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/board_regions.py`
- `.basicly/core/templates/board/board_page.html.j2`
- `tests/test_board_regions.py`

## Plan

- integrity: `L3`
- budget: `120000`
- depends on: `basicly-ibzr0f`
- demonstration: Run a supervised pass while separately running work the engine did not dispatch, then read the board and check that nothing on it claims to be showing that second population - and if the design admits it, that it is drawn as something other than a lane.

## Steps to Reproduce

Run any agent without the supervisor - a bare claude session in this checkout, or `basicly loop run` before its worktree binds - then open the board: the lanes region names only records carrying a worktree external_ref, and `running now` counts more work than any visible lane, with nothing on the page saying the difference exists.

payload.name: requirements
payload.value: The `running now` heading shall name only the population it actually draws, not implying it shows all running work. Whether a host subagent or a background job is observable by this engine at all shall be established and recorded with evidence. Where such work is observable and drawn, it shall be visually distinct from a lane and carry none of a lane's affordances.

## Trigger

When the board header shows a run id with no title, an unlabelled progress bar, a stale-looking gates cell, and lifetime machine spend on the run's own line, I want every header cell to carry a labelled figure, so I can read the header without tripping on any of its measured defects.

## Context

Owner, 2026-09-02: "header is still confusing." Third time the header is raised; basicly-jbd80w and basicly-v8jwf0 moved rows and fixed the alarm band, and the owner still cannot read it. This record states what the header holds today, so the next change is against a measurement and not a feeling.

Measured on the live page at 1712x1345, three lines left and one cell right:

```text
basicly  REPO basicly · main · 1687bc87   RUN basicly-k6tpep · open · L3 [bar] 43%
GATES [GREEN] mode full · recorded 2026-09-01T19:38:28Z   SPEND machine-local · 2,032.19 usd · 36.59 usd largest · 1.4B in · 8.7M out
CLOSED TODAY not measured
                                   as of 11s ago / 2026-09-02T09:18:28Z · stale after 60s · [●] producer basicly · 0.11.0
```

Seven things a reader trips on, each verifiable against the snapshot:

1. `RUN basicly-k6tpep` is an id with no title. The snapshot's `units[]` holds the root's title; the header does not use it.
2. `L3 [bar] 43%` names no figure and no denominator. `session.spent_tokens` 42,966,175 of `token_budget` 100,000,000, and `spent_tokens_live` 55,722,904 already reads higher than the committed figure the bar uses.
3. `GATES GREEN` beside `recorded 2026-09-01T19:38:28Z` says the green is yesterday's, and nothing says whether that is fine.
4. `SPEND machine-local · 2,032.19 usd` is the lifetime spend of this machine, not the run's. It sits on the run's line and reads as the run's cost.
5. `1.4B in · 8.7M out` are lifetime token counts with no reader action attached.
6. `CLOSED TODAY not measured` is a standing row that says nothing, the shape basicly-ibzr0f removed from the cards.
7. The right cell repeats the time three ways (`as of 11s ago`, the timestamp, `stale after 60s`) and carries the boxed glyph from the sibling record.

## Raised a fourth time, 2026-09-06

Owner, on the same header: *"another thing that i do not like is the header top right corner
banner. there we can improve the visualization."* That is defect 7 above, unchanged, and the
fourth session in which this header has been raised. Priority moved to P1 on that ground
alone: a complaint a person repeats four times is a requirement with no gate behind it.

Measured again on the 2026-09-06 wall, the same cell now reads:

```text
                    as of 2s ago
2026-09-06T14:39:36Z - stale after 60s - producer basicly - 0.11.0
```

Still three renderings of one instant, still boxed in green so it competes with the alarm band
directly beneath it, and still carrying the producer name and version - two facts no operator
acts on - in the wall's most valuable corner.

Two figures on the left have moved since this was filed. The grant bar now reads `103%` with
no numerator and no denominator, which is defect 2 having crossed its own budget. And
`CLOSED TODAY 4` finally measures something, which retires defect 6.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/board_regions.py`
- `src/basicly/board_render.py`
- `src/basicly/board_footer.py`

## Earlier acceptance text (the acceptance field is authoritative)

- WHEN the header renders, LINE ONE SHALL answer which checkout and which run: repo, branch, short head, the root's title with its id beside it, and the run status.
- WHEN a grant is live, THE HEADER SHALL print `spent of budget tokens` as two figures with the bar, using the live figure where the producer holds one and naming the committed figure as such otherwise.
- WHEN the gates cell renders, IT SHALL carry the verdict and the age of the record in the same phrase form as freshness (`recorded 14h ago`), and SHALL colour amber past the same stale threshold the freshness cell uses.
- Lifetime spend and lifetime token counts SHALL move to the footer beside `agents`, and the header SHALL carry the run's own spend only.

## Trigger

When a prompter names a concrete model that a host cannot run, I want the spawn to fall back to the same-tier model the host does support, so I can honour the intent behind the request instead of failing it outright.

## Context

Owner requirement 2026-07-31. A human prompter writes something like "spawn an agent that uses
gpt-5.6 sol and send it to analyze this document". The expectation: on copilot it succeeds literally,
because copilot serves that model; on claude it cannot, so it should fall back to the model of the SAME
TIER that the host can actually run. This is the reverse of basicly-kjc5.61's forward lookup and needs
its own mechanism plus catalog guidance, because the agent acting on the request is the thing that has
to do the resolving.

Verified constraint: **claude code cannot run a GPT model at all.** Its subagent `model` field accepts
`sonnet`, `opus`, `haiku`, `fable`, a full claude model id, or `inherit` - every value is Anthropic. So
a literal cross-vendor request is impossible there and substitution is the only non-failing option.
Copilot by contrast serves 6 vendors (measured: 29 models spanning OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Microsoft,
Moonshot AI, xAI), so it can honour most such requests literally.

## The sharp problem: reverse lookup is AMBIGUOUS

In the anchor set, `gpt-5.6-sol` occupies BOTH `high` and `maximum`, because OpenAI ships a three-class
ladder and the top class serves both tiers (docs/design/agent-roster-design.md R5). So resolving
"sol" backwards yields two tiers, and on claude they substitute differently: `high` gives
`claude-opus-5`, `maximum` gives `claude-fable-5` - which is double the input price and five times the
output price. A naive implementation picks whichever row it hits first and no one notices.

The same collapse applies to Moonshot (`kimi-k3`) and Google (`gemini-3.1-pro-preview`) in the derived
map, so this is the normal case, not an edge case.

## Two hard rules, both inherited from existing decisions

1. **Substitution must be VISIBLE.** If the prompter asked for `gpt-5.6-sol` and the agent spawns on
   `claude-opus-5`, that must be stated back to the prompter. basicly-kjc5.59 already establishes
   "record that the tier was not honoured rather than implying it was"; this is the same rule at the
   prompt surface. An invisible model swap is worse than a refusal because the prompter believes the
   request was honoured.
2. **An ambiguous reverse lookup is resolved by a documented rule or REFUSED, never guessed.** Options
   worth weighing: prefer the lowest tier that maps to the named model (cheapest, least surprising, and
   errs toward not overspending); or refuse and ask which tier was meant. Fail closed either way -
   "cannot tell" must never read as "safe to proceed". Whatever is chosen must be written down.

## Delivery shape

Per the owner, this needs distributing as guidance, not only as engine code: instructions and/or a skill
that teach an agent to (a) recognise a prompt naming a concrete model, (b) resolve it through the
committed map, (c) substitute tier-preserving where the host cannot honour it, and (d) say what it did.
It must work for custom agents and ad-hoc prompts, not just catalog-shipped agents - so it pairs with
basicly-wbsz's no-harness-required kit.

Mind the always-on budget: the baseline is at its soft cap, so this belongs in a skill or a path-scoped
fragment, not another `applies_to: [all]` fragment (see basicly-a3ab.1 and the headroom table in
docs/architecture/architecture.md section 7).

Depends on basicly-kjc5.61 for the map. Related: basicly-izda (ordered preference lists),
basicly-wbsz (portable kit), basicly-a3yi (emission), basicly-5xcj (tier-choice guidance, which this
should not duplicate).

payload.value: When a prompt names a model the current host cannot run, the agent shall spawn on the same-tier model the host does support, and shall report the substitution naming both the requested and the actual model. When a named model's reverse lookup maps to more than one tier, the documented disambiguation rule (interactive: ask; non-interactive: price parity, then task class, then higher tier as last resort) shall apply, or the request shall be refused rather than a tier being guessed.

```python
    produced = tuple((path, derive(covered)) for path, covered in derived_targets(ledger))
```

## Trigger

When a salvage commit is rejected, I want the reported cause to name the hook that actually failed, so I can fix the real defect instead of re-dispatching a lane that already holds the fix.

## Context

A lane that hits the runner timeout tries a salvage commit. When that commit is rejected, the advance prints a **passing** hook line as the reason, so an operator reading the message goes to the wrong gate.

Observed 2026-08-17 on basicly-wpc8.1, verbatim:

    [blocked] classify -> classify: runner 'claude' stopped on runner_timeout after 3600s
    in worktree 'basicly-wpc8-1'; the salvage commit was rejected:
    protect-generated-commit.................................................Passed;
    inspect the worktree and re-dispatch

`protect-generated-commit` passed. So did every hook in that list. The actual cause was one stale citation, found by running the commit by hand and reading the whole output:

    docs/requirements/factory-loop.md: 1 stale citation(s); this document has no recorded debt
      - line 85: merge.py:509 - past end-of-file or a blank line

The lane had moved a function in `merge.py`, so a parenthetical line reference in another document landed on a blank line. A one-line fix, hidden behind a message naming a gate that was fine.

## The defect

The reporter appears to take the **last** line of the hook output rather than the failing one. A pre-commit run ends with its passing hooks after the failing one has already printed, so the last line is almost always a pass. The message is therefore not merely unhelpful, it is reliably wrong whenever more than one hook runs.

## Why it costs more than it looks

A timed-out lane is already the expensive case: the tokens are spent and the work is uncommitted. The operator's next decision is whether to salvage by hand or re-dispatch, and that decision needs the real cause. Pointing at a passing gate argues for re-dispatch, which pays the whole lane cost again to arrive at the same one-line fix.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/runner.py`
- `src/basicly/loop.py`
- `tests/test_loop.py`

When several hooks run and one fails, the report names the failing hook even though a passing hook printed after it. When no hook output can be attributed to the failure, the message says so instead of quoting an unrelated line.

## Trigger

When uncommitted changes sit in the base checkout but touch no file the incoming merge changes, I want the advance to proceed, so I can run parallel work in one checkout without every landing waiting on it.

## Context

`loop run` refuses to advance when the base checkout has **any** uncommitted change, including changes in files the incoming merge cannot touch. So one piece of unrelated work in progress blocks every lane landing, and the operator's only remedies are to commit work that is not ready or to discard it.

Observed 2026-08-17. basicly-wpc8.1 was green in its worktree — 4295 passed — and committed at 89a5436. The build-to-verify advance, which is the only step that merges, refused:

    base checkout has uncommitted changes; commit or stash first:
    M .basicly/core/kit/tracker/differential.py
    M src/basicly/cost_rollup.py
    ... 13 more, none of them in the lane's commit

Not one of the dirty paths appears in the lane's commit, so `git merge` itself would not have refused. The precondition is broader than the operation it protects.

## Why the broad form was chosen, and why it is still worth narrowing

The broad check is safe and cheap, and it prevents a class of confusion where a landing silently mixes an operator's work into a lane's merge. That reason is real. What it does not distinguish is dirt that **could** conflict from dirt that provably cannot.

The narrowing is checkable rather than judged: the merge's own file set is known before it runs, and so is the dirty set. Refuse on the intersection, on the engine tracker paths the advance itself commits, and on anything the rebase would regenerate. Admit the rest, and say in the advance detail which dirt was admitted, so nothing is silent.

## The operating cost this has today

Parallel work in the base checkout serialises against lane landings. An operator running several agents in one checkout - which is the obvious way to keep a backlog moving while a lane runs - discovers only at the landing that none of it may land until all of it is committed. The repo's own answer is a sibling worktree per unit of work, and that answer is right; the point here is that the precondition makes the failure appear at the worst moment rather than at the start.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Take a lane green in its own worktree and committed on its harness branch.
2. Dirty one tracked file in the base checkout that the lane's commit does not touch - any
   file at all, since the check does not look at which:

       git -C <base> status --short

3. Run the advance that merges:

       uv run basicly loop advance <lane-id>

4. Read the refusal, then check the claim it rests on by intersecting the two sets by hand:

       git -C <base> diff --name-only
       git -C <base> log --format= --name-only <base-branch>..harness/<lane-id> | sort -u

5. Read the precondition itself:

       rg -n 'uncommitted changes; commit or stash first' src/basicly/merge.py

Observed - this record's measurement 2026-08-17 on `basicly-wpc8.1`, green at 4295 passed
and committed at 89a5436:

    base checkout has uncommitted changes; commit or stash first:
    M .basicly/core/kit/tracker/differential.py
    M src/basicly/cost_rollup.py
    ... 13 more, none of them in the lane's commit

Step 4's two lists had an empty intersection, so `git merge` itself would not have refused.

## Trigger

When a document citation names a file and line that has drifted onto real but unrelated code, I want the citation gate to catch it, so I can trust a passing gate as proof the citation still points at what it claims.

## Context

The citation ratchet reports a stale `file:line` only when the cited line happens to be **blank or past end of file**. A citation that has drifted onto a different line of real code passes, and stays passing.

Measured 2026-08-17 on one block, `docs/plan/implementation-plan.md` around line 124, which tabulates three call sites:

| Cited | Actually at | Off by | Gate said |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `loop.py:869` `_run_agent` | 858 | 11 | passed |
| `loop.py:1119` `_run_proposer` | 1108 | 14 | **stale**, but only after an unrelated edit shifted it onto a blank line |
| `supervise.py:2651` `_dispatch_lane` | 2651 | 0 | passed, correctly |

Two of the three were wrong. The block was written 2026-08-15 in f8f6d34, so both survived two days and an unknown number of gate runs. The one the gate caught, it caught by luck: a three-line comment added elsewhere in `loop.py` pushed line 1119 onto a blank line.

## Why this is the worse failure mode

A citation pointing at nothing is an obvious defect. A citation pointing at the **wrong but existing** line reads as verified and is not — the same class the architecture rewrite hit, where three section references pointed at a real but wrong section. A reader who follows one lands on unrelated code and has no signal that the pointer, rather than their understanding, is what is wrong.

## What would fix it

The convention already exists and this repository states it: name the symbol, not the line. A symbol citation is checkable by search and survives every edit above it. The three entries above already name their symbol in the next column, which is why dropping the numbers cost nothing — that is the repair applied to the two stale ones in 1f3162b.

So the gate's own rule can be stronger: a `file:line` citation in a document is refusable on sight when the same entry names a symbol, and checkable against the symbol's definition line when it does not. What it must not do is treat a line's non-blankness as evidence.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Run the gate over the tree and read its summary line:

       uv run python .scripts/check_docs_citations.py

2. Take a `file:line` citation the gate just passed and resolve the symbol it names:

       rg -n '^def _dispatch_validation|^def _repair_in_place|^def _run_subtask' src/basicly/loop.py
       rg -n '^def _dispatch_lane' src/basicly/supervise.py

3. Read what actually sits at each cited line:

       sed -n '507p;1655p;1813p' src/basicly/loop.py
       sed -n '2651p' src/basicly/supervise.py

4. Read the staleness rule the gate applies:

       rg -n 'past end-of-file or a blank line' -B2 .scripts/check_docs_citations.py

Observed, measured 2026-08-19 against the block at `docs/plan/implementation-plan.md` around
line 124. Step 1 printed:

    [docs-citations] 33 citation(s) in 17 document(s), 10 checkable against a named symbol,
    0 stale; no document is above its [tool.docs_citations.frozen] baseline

**That `0 stale` is the positive control as well as the defect** - the gate parsed 33
citations, so it is reading the documents; it simply reports none of these as stale:

| Cited | Symbol is at | Off by | The cited line actually holds | Gate |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `loop.py:507` `_dispatch_validation` | 507 | 0 | the `def` | passed, correctly |
| `loop.py:1655` `_repair_in_place` | 1641 | 14 | `left where that dispatch reads it instead.` | **passed** |
| `loop.py:1813` `_run_subtask` | 1799 | 14 | `cwd = Path(session.worktree_path)` | **passed** |
| `supervise.py:2651` `_dispatch_lane` | 2626 | 25 | an f-string inside a different function | **passed** |

Three of the four are wrong and all three pass, because step 4 shows the only test is
`if at > len(lines) or not lines[at - 1].strip()` - non-blank and in range is treated as
evidence. A reader following `supervise.py:2651` lands 25 lines inside another function with
no signal that the pointer rather than their understanding is what is wrong.

Expected: a `file:line` citation whose entry also names a symbol is refused on sight, and one
that names no symbol is checked against the symbol's definition line. A line's
non-blankness is never accepted as evidence that the citation is live.

## Scope

- `.scripts/check_docs_citations.py`
- `tests/test_check_docs_citations.py`

payload.name: requirements
payload.value: When a citation entry also names a symbol, the gate refuses the line reference and checks the symbol's definition line instead. When a citation names only a line and that line no longer holds the cited construct, the gate reports it stale, whether or not the line is blank. The gate never treats a non-blank line as evidence that a citation is live.

When a test in `tests/test_supervise.py` or `tests/test_rubrics.py` passes `Path()` as the repository root, I want it to use a temporary directory instead, so I can be sure the test can never write to the real ledger.

## Context

Roughly 45 places in tests/test_supervise.py and 3 in tests/test_rubrics.py pass Path() as the repository root, so the engine under test resolves to the developer own checkout rather than a temp directory.

They pass today because they never reach the store. That is the whole risk: each is one seam change away from writing to the real ledger. Measured rather than reasoned - during the flip repair a traceback showed repo_root PosixPath(.) reaching owned_write.append, and the only thing between the test and a write to the live ledger was an invalid record id. The fix is mechanical - tmp_path rather than Path() - and the value is that a test can no longer write to the repository it is testing.

This record was minted by a probe of the owned create path and repurposed rather than tombstoned.

- `tests/test_rubrics.py`

## Trigger

When a repository document asserts a third-party interface behaviour with no adjacent source, version and date, I want a gate to refuse it, so I can stop an unpinned claim from being believed for months.

## Context

Nothing refuses a repository document that asserts a third party interface behaviour with no source, no version and no date. Four recurring memory entries are the same shape, and the cost is asymmetric: a wrong fact about our own code fails a gate, a wrong fact about someone elses interface is committed as prose and believed for months.

`.scripts/check_docs_citations.py` is the precedent. It walks documents for a `file:line` citation into code and holds each document at a frozen count, so an existing population does not fail the tree on day one while a new claim does.

## What the gate reads

A claim about an external interface, adjacent to a source URL, a version and a date it was verified at. The skill `interface-facts` already states the pinning rule and its own examples carry versions without dates, so the gate has a live population to bind on.

## What it must not do

It must not attempt to check that a fetched URL was the vendors. No gate can, and one that tried would fail open. Route correctness stays documentation tier; only the presence of source, version and date is mechanical.

## Scope

- `.scripts/`
- `pyproject.toml`
- `basicly.toml`
- `tests/`

## Trigger

When `sync_agents` or `sync_skills` removes a projection, I want the printed reason to match the real cause, so I can tell whether the file returns later or is retired for good.

## Context

Found by the `basicly-e2mz.8` lane 2026-08-14 and confirmed by hand at main after the merge.

`cli.py:1808` hardcodes one reason for every path `agents.sync_agents` returns:

```text
cli.py:1808   print(f"Removed {...} (excluded by technology selection)")
cli.py:1693   the identical string on the skills path
```

`e2mz.8` gave `sync_agents` a second reason to remove a file - a projection whose catalog source was
deleted. The path printed is correct; the parenthetical is not. A consumer watching an upgrade is
told a technology selection removed the file when the source was deleted instead.

## Why this is not cosmetic

The two causes have different consequences for a reader. *Excluded by technology selection* means the
file will come back when the selection changes, so nothing is lost. *Orphaned* means the source is
gone and the artifact is retired. A consumer who reads the first and means the second will wait for a
return that never comes.

It is also the same defect class this session has now paid for three times: one string standing for
two facts. `basicly-9rv0` was two predicates that disagreed, `basicly-7jb5` was one gate name spelled
three times, and this is one message covering two causes.

## The skills path already had it

`cli.py:1693` prints the same string for resources `_prune_orphans` removed **because they left the
source**, so this is a pre-existing shape rather than one `e2mz.8` introduced. That matters for the
fix: correcting only the agents site would leave the skills site lying, which is how a defect class
survives its own bead.

`check_synced_agents` already returns `(path, reason)` pairs and words them correctly - the check half
is right and only the build half is wrong. The reason vocabulary therefore already exists; nothing
needs inventing.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Read the two print sites and the seam that already carries a reason:

       rg -n 'excluded by technology selection' src/basicly/cli.py
       rg -n -A2 'def sync_agents' src/basicly/agents.py
       rg -n -A3 'def check_synced_agents' src/basicly/agents.py

2. In a scratch copy of a repo carrying projected agents, force the *technology* removal:
   record a selection that excludes one agent's technology and rebuild.

       uv run basicly install --technologies python
       uv run basicly agents-build

3. In a second scratch copy, force the *orphan* removal instead: leave the selection alone,
   delete the catalog source behind a projected agent, and rebuild.

       rm -r .basicly/core/agents/<name>
       uv run basicly agents-build

4. Read the `Removed ...` line each rebuild printed and compare the two parentheticals.
5. Repeat steps 2 and 3 against a skill and `uv run basicly skills-build`, which is the
   second site.
6. Run the check half over the same trees and compare its wording with the build half's:

       uv run basicly agents-check

Observed, re-checked 2026-08-19: step 1 shows `sync_agents` typed
`-> tuple[SyncResult, list[Path]]` - paths only, no reason - while `check_synced_agents` is
typed `-> list[tuple[Path, str]]` and words its reasons correctly already. Both build sites
hardcode the same string, `cmd_agents_build` at `src/basicly/cli.py:1858` (cited in this
record as `cli.py:1808`, since drifted) and `cmd_skills_build` at `src/basicly/cli.py:1743`
(cited as `cli.py:1693`). So step 4 prints `(excluded by technology selection)` in **both**
scratch copies, and it is true in only one of them.

Expected: the two lines differ and each is true. *Excluded by technology selection* means the
file returns when the selection changes; *orphaned* means the source is gone and the artifact
is retired, and a consumer who reads the first while the second is true waits for a return
that never comes. The vocabulary already exists on `check_synced_agents`, so nothing needs
inventing - and `cli.py:1743` must be corrected in the same change, because fixing only the
agents site leaves the skills site lying.

## Acceptance

- When `sync_agents` removes a projection, then it returns the reason it removed it rather than the
  path alone, and the command line prints the returned reason.
- When `sync_skills` removes a resource, then the same holds on that path.
- Given a consumer whose technology selection excludes an agent and a second whose source was
  deleted, when each upgrades, then the two removals print different reasons.
- When the check half runs on the same trees, then its wording and the build half's agree.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/cli.py`
- `src/basicly/agents.py`
- `src/basicly/skills.py`
- `tests/test_agents.py`
- `tests/test_cli_catalog.py`

## Demonstration

Install into two fresh scratch repos, deselect a technology in one and delete a source in the other,
upgrade both, and read the two lines. They must differ and each must be true. Read the output; do not
assert it.

payload.name: requirements
payload.value: `sync_agents` and `sync_skills` return the reason each removal happened, and the command line prints that returned reason instead of one fixed string. A removal caused by a technology exclusion and a removal caused by a deleted source print different reasons, and each is true. The check half's wording (`check_synced_agents`) agrees with the build half's wording on the same trees.

## Trigger

When a lane is dispatched to build a unit of work, I want it to receive the requirement, scope and any recorded plan the engine already holds, so I can stop paying a lane to rebuild context a session already read.

## CORRECTED 2026-08-13 — read this before the text below
The defect holds verbatim: `loop.py:867-879` still passes only the issue id, with no
requirement, scope, plan or prior finding. **The evidence and the remedy are both stale.**

**The 254x is two incomparable populations.** Re-measured over 346 records on 2026-08-13 it is
now 320x - and it compares a `decide` dispatch averaging **12 seconds** to a `lane` averaging
**979 seconds**. That is a one-turn classification against a multi-hour build, so it cannot
isolate briefing from work type. This repo's own recorded lesson is "a cost prior from the
wrong population"; do not cite this ratio as the cost of a short prompt. The causal claim that
a ~1.1M-token floor is "bought by the instruction" has **no instrument behind it**: there is no
per-lane split between context acquisition and implementation.

**Two mechanisms are now recorded as if they were one fix.** `factory-loop.md` section 8.3
still names the engine-assembled durable brief. `implementation-plan.md:224` substitutes
`--resume --fork-session`, calling the floor "a cache miss, not tokens". These are different
designs with different costs and the choice must be made explicitly, not inherited.

**The fork figure does not hold in our shape.** Probed on claude 2.1.231, 2026-08-13: 19.06x
same-directory, but the denominator is the ~21k-token host floor, not a repo corpus - against a
lane's 8.66M mean that floor is 0.24% of a lane. And a fork from a **different working
directory degrades to 5.4x**, because cwd and a git-status snapshot sit inside the cached
prefix, worktrees of the same repository included. Every lane is dispatched at
`cwd=worktree_path` (`supervise.py:2623`), so fork-per-lane plus worktree-per-lane **is** the
degraded case. See `basicly-w20y` for the documents-side correction.

**Acceptance criterion 3 was unmeasurable when written** and is now measurable:
`basicly-i4gg` (closed 2026-08-13) landed the claude cache split that a before/after ratio
needs.

---

## Context

**A dispatched lane is told to go and read; a dispatched decider is handed its corpus. The
same model on the same repo costs 254x more for the first.** Measured 2026-08-08 over the
whole of `.basicly/usage/run-records.json`:

```text
phase    n    mean tokens   mean $   mean s   failed
lane    77      8,124,617    6.28      942    16/93 = 17.2%
build   28     11,564,149    8.70     1163     4/153 =  2.6%
decide  24         31,991    0.23       14     5/29  = 17.2%
```

`loop.dispatch_prompt` (`loop.py:858`) is ~90 words and passes **only the issue id**:

```text
"You are in a git worktree dedicated to the tracked issue <id>. Read AGENTS.md for the
 repo rules, run `br show <id>` for the requirement and acceptance criteria, implement
 the work, and commit it on the current branch referencing that issue id. ..."
```

No requirement text, no scope, no plan, no architecture, no prior finding. The prompt
*instructs* the agent to rebuild what the dispatching session already holds, and the
~1.1M-token floor every lane pays before its first edit is bought by that instruction.

Observed cost of the same waste twice in one session: `u2hl.15`'s lane independently
re-derived pyright's dot-directory behaviour that had been measured, written down and
committed to its own bead an hour earlier.

Per unit of output, the floor dominates small work: `u2hl.16` cost **\$0.077 per changed
line**, `u2hl.14` **\$0.010**.

## What this bead is NOT

It is **not** "make the prompt longer". `factory-design.md` §D6 records a deliberate
decision that every dispatch pays fresh context priming, grounded in Laban et al.'s
measured **-39% on multi-turn** degradation. That decision is about *conversation* history,
not about *facts the engine already knows*, and this bead must not overturn it by accident.

The docs already contain the shape that resolves the tension: the **report file**
(`agent-roster-design.md:664-670`, `gates-and-rework-design.md:219-235`) — an agent
inherits through a durable, structured artifact rather than through a replayed window.
`basicly-u2hl.18` already shipped two such artifacts (`implementation-plan`,
`change-summary`) as typed records, so the mechanism exists and has a schema.

## Shape

Give the dispatch prompt a **brief assembled by the engine** from what it already has:
the bead's requirement and acceptance criteria (already read to gate it), the declared
scope, the plan artifact, and any finding recorded on the bead. Every one of those is a
tracker read the engine performs anyway.

Two constraints from this repo's own measurements:
- **Selection, not serialisation** (D21): `br ready --json` costs 36.9% of a lane and its
  five-field projection costs 1.7%. Assemble the brief from named fields, never by pasting
  a payload.
- **Our own vocabulary, not `br`'s** (D22): `br` is being removed; the brief names our
  record fields so only the adapter changes at the flip.

## Demonstration

`uv run basicly loop run <bead> --runner manual` prints the brief the lane would receive,
and it contains the bead's acceptance criteria and scope rather than an instruction to go
and read them.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/loop.py`
- `src/basicly/br.py`
- `tests/test_loop.py`

## Plan

- integrity: `L3`
- budget: `120000`
- depends on: none

## Earlier acceptance text (the acceptance field is authoritative)

- Given a dispatched lane, when its prompt is built, then the requirement, acceptance
  criteria, declared scope and plan artifact are present in the prompt - check: a test
  asserts each field appears in `dispatch_prompt` output for a fixture bead.
- Given the same bead dispatched twice, when the briefs are compared, then they are
  identical - check: a test asserts prompt determinism, preserving D9's diffability.
- Given a measured pair of lanes before and after, when mean tokens-to-first-edit are
  compared, then the briefed lane is lower - check: recorded on the bead from
  `run-records.json`, with the before figure taken in base first.

## Trigger

When a claude dispatch reads a cached prefix, I want its run record to show the cache it actually read, so I can measure whether a briefing remedy moves the quantity it claims to move.

## Steps to Reproduce

```
python3 -c "
import json
d=json.load(open(\".basicly/usage/run-records.json\"))
recs=[r for v in d.values() for r in v if isinstance(r,dict)]
have=[r for r in recs if \"cache_read_tokens\" in r]
```

Observed - 361 records, 206 carry `cache_read_tokens`, and **3 of those 206 are non-zero**,
all on claude. Expected - a claude dispatch that reads a cached prefix records what it read.

## Context

`factory-loop.md` section 15.5 makes the cache split the gate on everything else: without
it "a 40% apparent saving that actually broke a cached prefix is indistinguishable from a
real win". The document still says "0 of 297 dispatch records carry a cache split", which is
stale in the direction that hides this - the extractor now writes the field, so a reader
checking presence concludes the gap closed. Presence is not population.

This blocks the measurement `ejdm` exists for. The `--resume --fork-session` mechanism is
priced entirely in cache reads - 19x on a hit against a cold seed, ~10x on a corpus once the
denominator is corrected - so `ejdm.4`, which measures the briefed lane against the unbriefed
one, has no instrument for the quantity its remedy moves.

Not established here: whether the extractor drops the numbers or the dispatch shape genuinely
misses the cache. `claude -p` opens a fresh session per lane and this repo passes no
`--resume`, so a near-total cache miss may be the true reading rather than a parser fault.
Deciding which is the first work, and a positive control is available - a hand-run
`--resume --fork-session` dispatch is known to return a non-zero read.

- `src/basicly/runner_usage.py`

Anthropic's own `total_cost_usd`, not the token figure - `CLAUDE_TOKEN_KEYS`
(`runner_envelope.py:71`) sums `cache_read_input_tokens` at full weight while cache reads
bill at 0.1x, so the token column overstates spend by roughly 3-10x.

```text
bead        dispatches   cost   lines changed   $/line
u2hl.16          1      $ 1.47        19        0.077   <- worst
u2hl.12          1      $ 6.29         -            -
u2hl.15          3      $10.43         -            -
u2hl.23          2      $27.07     1,736        0.016
u2hl.14          4      $25.62     2,575        0.010   <- best
```

**The small lane is the wasteful one.** A dispatch pays a fixed floor of roughly 1.1M
processed tokens / $1.47 - repo rules, always-on guidance, the skill index, the bead,
orientation, plus `uv sync` and `npm install` on a fresh worktree - before it edits
anything. A long lane amortises that against a stable cached prefix and gets cheaper per
line; a short one does not.

## The gap

`supervise._band_verdict` already computes a floor verdict -
`under the floor - dispatches, but merge it with a sibling` - and **the floor never
refuses; only the ceiling does**. So nothing stops a 19-line change from being dispatched.

It cannot simply be made binding as it stands, because the band is measured on
`decompose.scope_read_cost` - the cost of *reading* the scope, not of *changing* it -
and read cost did not predict change cost here either: `u2hl.16` measured 15,199 tokens
(above the 8,000 floor, so it dispatched) and produced 19 lines, while `u2hl.14` measured
78,709 and produced 2,575.

`basicly-tcmy.34` closed 2026-08-05 on the forecast unit, and `_band_verdict`
(`supervise.py:1387`) still reads a `WorkingSetAdmission` - a scope *read* figure. So the
floor was never in that bead's scope and does not inherit its fix; the measurement above
is fresh evidence taken 2026-08-08, not a restatement of it.

## What this bead does, and what it defers

Bind the floor on a **forecast of change size**, not read size, and record the rule in the
`harness-loop` skill so a driving session applies it before `supervise` is even called:
a unit expected to change under roughly 200 lines is done in session, not dispatched.
Calibrating the change-size forecast itself stays on `basicly-tcmy.34`.

## Demonstration

`uv run basicly loop preflight basicly-u2hl` prints an under-floor refusal for a seeded
19-line child instead of `in band`.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/supervise.py`
- `src/basicly/decompose.py`
- `.basicly/core/skills/harness-loop.skill.yaml`
- `tests/test_supervise.py`

## Plan

- integrity: `L2`
- budget: `90000`
- depends on: none

## Earlier acceptance text (the acceptance field is authoritative)

- Given a child whose forecast change size is below the floor, when a pass is planned,
  then the band refuses it naming the in-session route rather than dispatching - check:
  `uv run basicly loop preflight <epic>` prints a refusal row for a seeded under-floor
  child, and a test asserts `_band_verdict` returns the refusing verdict for it.
- Given the same child, when a human overrides, then the override is recorded - check: a
  test asserts the override path writes a marker naming who allowed it.

payload.value: When a child's forecast change size is below the floor, the band refuses to dispatch it and names the in-session route instead. When a human overrides that refusal, the override is recorded and names who allowed it.

When a loop subcommand is invoked, I want its handler to resolve from a dedicated console module, so I can read the command-line module without it also carrying the whole factory operations console.

## Context

Found by the lane-C survey 2026-08-14. The largest item in the backlog and the last in its chain.

After the owned extractions land, the command-line module still cannot be named without the word and. It is the projection and distribution command surface, lines 125 to 1930, and an interactive factory operations console.

```text

session rendering           cli.py:3441-3560

parser wiring               cli.py:4048-4910, about 860 lines
```

The module is 4,911 lines and 51,691 tokens, frozen at 54,336 against a 4,000 cap.

## The seam is a responsibility, not a metric

The loop console has its own state, its own vocabulary and its own test files. The layering contract is exhaustive with the command-line module alone at the top tier, so the new module needs a declared tier between it and the supervisor. It imports the supervisor, the loop, the decisions module and the policy module, and only the command-line module imports it.

## The ratchet arithmetic

The command-line module is frozen on size and not on prose share, so it has prose headroom below the cap. The loop console is printer-heavy code, so the extraction raises the remainder's prose share. Measure both before choosing the exact cut. Record the shrink through the delta mechanism, never by editing the frozen line.

- `.importlinter`

## Depends on

## Demonstration

`uv run pytest tests/test_cli_loop.py -q` and a diff of `uv run basicly loop status` output against the pre-split output.

## Trigger

When a lane writes itself a scratch note under the gitignored `.basicly/usage/` directory, I want the markdownlint hook to skip it, so I can write a working note without blocking my own commit on a file that can never be committed.

## Context

Found 2026-08-21 while recovering two lanes the spend bound stopped mid-flight. Both had committed-quality work staged and neither could commit:

```text
markdownlint............................................Failed
.basicly/usage/scratch/rn0o-3-plan.md:22 MD022/blanks-around-headings
.basicly/usage/scratch/rn0o-3-plan.md:23 MD032/blanks-around-lists
```

`.basicly/usage/.gitignore` holds `*`, so nothing under it is tracked or committable. The markdownlint hook globs `**/*.md !.venv/** !node_modules/**`, which reaches it anyway. A lane that writes itself a plan note - which the guidance encourages, and four of the five worktrees in this pass did - blocks every commit in its own worktree on a file that can never be committed.

One lane said so in its own transcript: *"I violated the scratch-file rule and it just bit me."* The rule it names is a prose rule; the gate is what actually fires, and it fires on the wrong population.

## Why this is the gate and not the lane

A machine-local, gitignored working file is not repository content. Linting it is the instrument reading outside its own population - the same class as counting a census file as part of its own census. The remedy is the glob, not more prose telling agents where to write.

Note the interaction with `basicly-jr0l.71`, which records a nested `node_modules` poisoning the same gate. Both are the same defect: the glob does not follow the ignore rules.

## Scope

- `.basicly/core/hooks/markdownlint.py`
- `.markdownlint-cli2.jsonc`
- `.pre-commit-config.yaml`
- `tests/test_hooks_markdownlint.py`

## Plan

- budget: `70000`
- depends on: none
- demonstration: Write a deliberately malformed markdown file under `.basicly/usage/scratch/` and commit successfully, against a control malformed file at the repository root that the hook still refuses.

When a new session starts, I want to answer where the work is, what is in progress and what is planned from the tracker alone, so I can stop cross-checking three stores that disagree with each other.

## Context

Owner directive 2026-08-28: there is no single point of truth. A session found three stores that disagree: the gitignored `HANDOVER.md`, `docs/plan/implementation-plan.md` with `docs/requirements/`, and the ledger. The 2026-08-20 release decision lives only in a ledger comment on basicly-7phc and claims to be recorded in the plan document; it is not. `docs/plan/` and `docs/requirements/` are declared obsolete by the owner. The ledger is the authority for current, in-progress and planned work, and `docs/architecture/` must be cross-checked against the code (basicly-atrqcd).

For the ledger to be the authority its write path must be honest and its read path must be exact, for a human and for an agent alike. Today a write can report recorded when it did not land (basicly-vkh0.50, basicly-wu4w8v), a valid status is refused with exit 0 (basicly-bj8kks), a field cannot return to a value it held (basicly-z9bggw), a whole-file rewrite takes no lock (basicly-cqu7i3), a record can never be removed (basicly-vkh0.34), every count off `tracker show` is inflated by duplicate edges (basicly-vkh0.52), and 44 open records carry single-character labels written by a string-as-list defect.

- Every architecture claim basicly-atrqcd names is either corrected or bound to a tripwire.

## Trigger

When someone asks how this system should be described, I want the README and the architecture overview to use one agreed, accurate pair of sentences, so I can stop reaching for a coined phrase or an unsupported claim.

## Context

Owner asked how to describe basicly in concise sentences. Research established that the phrase
"graph engineering" has no literature: coined 2026-07-18 on a vendor blog, picked up two days later
by a second vendor which concedes the provenance is unsettled, both selling the remedy. A
phrase-restricted search over arxiv.org, dl.acm.org, link.springer.com and dblp.org returned nothing
in this sense, against an identically shaped positive control that returned eight primaries.

Dropping it costs nothing in the tree. `rg -il "graph engineering" .` returns nothing, exit 1;
positive control `rg -il topological .` returns four files. The phrase exists only in speech.

A sharper reason not to reach for node/edge vocabulary: `node` is already a **retired** word in this
system own glossary (`docs/architecture/architecture.md:4967-4971`), because it once meant a record,
a diagram element and a JS runtime at once.

## The naming result

Accuracy and communicability rank in opposite directions, so two sentences beat one word.

| candidate | accuracy | communicability |
| --- | --- | --- |
| a workflow engine | 1st | 3rd |
| a verification harness | 2nd | 2nd |
| a dependency-ordered work scheduler | 3rd | 4th |
| a gated pipeline | 4th | 1st |

Recommended pair: "a workflow engine over a work graph in an append-only ledger", then "in practice
most of it is a verification harness". The first is already this repo own phrase at
`docs/architecture/architecture.md:8-9`.

Two things to drop. "Typed artifacts" - see basicly-hnnmk9.2, only 3 of 8 kinds have a producer.
And "pipeline" - the loop has a detour (validate returns to verify,
`docs/architecture/architecture.md:1359-1360`), rework is a self-loop that does not move the phase
(`src/basicly/loop.py:481`), and there is no cursor to advance because phase is derived.

## Three shapes to name apart, because conflating them is what a graph framing gets wrong

| layer | real shape | what makes it terminate |
| --- | --- | --- |
| the plan a decomposer emits | a DAG | acyclicity, checked at the plan gate |
| the loop a lane executes | cyclic, with rework back edges | the rework bound |
| the ledger | append-only, monotone | nothing needs to; it only grows |

## A claim to stop making

"It runs Claude, Codex and Copilot" is not supportable. Measured over
`.basicly/usage/run-records.json`: 735 run records across 399 work records, `agent` is claude 540
and manual 195, **codex 0 and copilot 0**, with the field populated as its own control. The ledger
`dispatch` events agree independently, claude 19 and manual 1. Adapters for all three are declared
at `src/basicly/runner.py:273-306`. The honest sentence is "it projects into three agent families;
only Claude has ever been dispatched here" - a portability claim, not a performance claim.

Also unsupported: "mixing agents measurably helps". There is no measurement, ours or published.
Tran and Kiela (arXiv 2604.02460v2) find single agents match or beat multi-agent systems on
multi-hop reasoning at equal reasoning tokens.

## Scope

- `README.md`
- `docs/architecture/architecture.md`

## Earlier acceptance text (the acceptance field is authoritative)

- The README and the architecture overview use one agreed pair of sentences.
- The vendor-neutrality claim states portability, and names that only one family has been
  dispatched.
- No consumer surface uses "typed artifacts" while basicly-hnnmk9.2 is open.

## Trigger

When a validate gate passes and the ledger records the pass, I want the console to report the same outcome, so I can trust the printed line without a second check.

## Context

Found while shipping four records on 2026-09-06. The console said a gate failed; the ledger recorded that it passed. The ledger is right.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Take an L3 record at `verify` whose validate gate is required.
2. `basicly loop run <id> --root <epic-with-a-grant>` or `basicly loop advance <id>`.

Observed, on two records independently:

```
[blocked] validate -> validate: the validator recorded validate-as-consumer failed;
the unit stays in validate (needs input: validation)
```

Measured against the ledger immediately after, counting every `gate` event for each record:

```
basicly-zq9i2m.6: 2 gate event(s) -> [('verify', True), ('validate-as-consumer', True)]
basicly-62h3x9:   2 gate event(s) -> [('verify', True), ('validate-as-consumer', True)]
```

There is **no failed gate event for either record**. `basicly policy gate <id>` agrees: `required passed: ['verify', 'validate-as-consumer']`, `advance: ALLOWED`. Both records then shipped with no rework and no second validator run.

Expected: the line names the state the ledger holds, or says nothing.

## Why this is worth a record rather than a shrug

It is not a fail-open - the gate is honest and the store is correct, which is the reassuring half. It is the surface disagreeing with the record, and that has a cost this session measured twice over: an operator who reads `failed` on a gate that passed learns to distrust the console, exactly as an operator who runs the board's offered command and watches it stop one step short learns to distrust the board (`basicly-lc2bd3v.3`).

The two defects are the same disease in two surfaces. A harness whose narration and whose store disagree cannot be operated by reading either one.

## What is not yet established

Which of three this is: a message composed before the gate write lands and never re-read; a message keyed on the validator's own exit status rather than on the recorded gate; or a message about the *reviewer* dispatches that follow the validator, mislabelled as the validator's. The reviewers do run in this phase - both records carry `[harness-review] lens=correctness` and `lens=security` comments - so the third is not idle speculation and the three are distinguishable by reading the emitter.

Settle that before writing the fix: the remedy differs for each, and a message patched without knowing which would still be wrong in the other two cases.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/loop.py`

## Trigger

When an operator watches many agents work unattended, I want the board to state what each agent does and whether it needs the operator, so I can run the factory from the page alone.

## Context

Owner directive 2026-08-22, after reading the live wall while four lanes were building: *"We need improvements all over the board. I give you the autonomy to iterate and build an enterprise professional board that is informative to humans so that agents can work unattended and we always know what is going on and on what thing are agents working."*

Seven complaints were named. Each was traced to code and filed as its own record. This record exists because nine independent patches on the present layout would not add up to the board the directive asks for. It is the design those nine build toward, and it is approved.

## The question the board must answer

**What is happening right now, and does it need me?**

Everything on the page earns its space against that question. A reader arriving cold must learn, without a second source: whether the factory is running, what each agent is working on this second, whether anything is stuck, and what a stuck thing needs from them.

## The principles

**The reader is an operator, never a producer author.** No word on the page may name a role the reader does not hold. `producer`, `emitted`, `section`, `withheld` and `renderable` are engine vocabulary and do not appear. A diagnostic a producer author needs is reachable, and it is not a standing row.

**A state is worth one channel, not three.** The present design gives every state a glyph, a border style and a colour for the same fact, and says so at `board_wall.py:14-15`. Colour plus a word replaces all three.

**A quantity is stated once, in one unit.** The present band states one wait as `6 DAYS` and as `160h 16m`.

**Colour means severity, not existence.** The page's alarm channel fires today whenever an ask exists. A five second wait and a six day wait must not paint the same.

**Space is spent on what is uncertain.** A green state is a word. An exception expands. This continues the principle `basicly-7ogfbq` landed rather than replacing it.

**Every figure names its own denomination.** A live token estimate and a recorded token figure are different quantities. Where both exist, both are shown and each is named.

## The layout, top to bottom

**1. Status line.** Repo, branch, head, the gate verdict as `GATES n/n`, and how fresh the document is. One line, recessive.

**2. The alarm, only when there is one.** Its severity comes from the wait duration against declared thresholds. It states in plain words what has stopped, that a person is what stops it, how long, and the command that answers it. Absent when nothing waits.

**3. RUNNING NOW - the hero region.** One card per adopted lane, carrying: the unit id, the feature it serves, its phase, the agent and model running it, how long it has run, what it has spent, and **the last thing it said**. That last field is what tells a working lane from a wedged one, and no other field can.

**4. The grant.** One bar: live spend against the budget, with the live figure named as an estimate that reads high, and the recorded figure named as the one that lands at completion.

**5. NEXT UP, grouped by the feature each row serves.** A heading per epic with its ready count, rows beneath. Units attached to no feature form their own group with a count, because that count is itself a finding - 45 of 190 today. Depth is spent on the highest-priority features and the row budget is computed from the viewport, not fixed.

**6. Footer.** Backlog totals, agent health, lifetime spend. No producer diagnostics.

## What was built and measured

A working mockup was generated from the live `/snapshot.json` and the supervisor's own terminal line, and every figure in it is real. It renders clean at 1200, 1440 and 1920 - `.scripts/check_render_overflow.py` reports neither overflow nor overlap at any of the three.

Two fields in it come from the supervisor's terminal rather than the document, and that is exactly what `basicly-0hxck3` fixes. The grant bar reads 20.7% where the live board reads 0%, and that is `basicly-wctp0g`.

## The children

- `basicly-eaw1dy` the feature name on a row
- `basicly-v8jwf0` the alarm band's severity and wording
- `basicly-jbd80w` the producer diagnostics leaving the human surface
- `basicly-ffm2yp` the row budget computed from the viewport
- `basicly-a68ggd` the loop region showing the pass rather than the backlog
- `basicly-wctp0g` the spend meter that can move while a lane runs

- `src/basicly/board_facts.py`
- `src/basicly/board_render.py`
- `.basicly/core/templates/board/board_page.html.j2`

The page shall render with no overflow and no overlap at 1200, 1440 and 1920 pixels wide.

## Trigger

When a record page's destination path is a symbolic link, I want the writer to refuse it, so I can stop a planted link from overwriting a file the board's user can write.

## Context

Found by the security reviewer the engine dispatched at VALIDATE on `basicly-62h3x9`, 2026-09-06, with a probe it ran rather than an argument it made. The code is on main.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Pick an output directory a second party can write to, which `basicly board --out` creates itself.
2. Plant a symlink at `record/<any-id-in-units>.html` pointing at a file the board's user can write.
3. Run `basicly board --out <that directory>/board.html`.

Observed, from the reviewer's probe:

```
written,refused: (1, 0)
target head: <!doctype html>|<html lang="en">|  <head
```

The target file lost its content. Expected: the write refuses a path that is a symlink and reports it as refused.

## What is and is not being claimed

**Not path traversal.** `board_record.SAFE_ID` is anchored at both ends and holds; the path stays inside `record/`. `board_serve`'s `/record/<id>` route reaches no filesystem at all - it is a dict lookup - and `board.record("../../etc/passwd", ...)` returns `None`.

**What changed with `basicly-62h3x9`.** The class is pre-existing for the two files `board --out` already wrote. That record made the names **predictable and numerous** - one per record in `units`, 297 today - and made the tool create the directory itself. An attacker plants rather than guesses.

**Exposure is low and stated as low.** The reviewer's own words: *"high that the write follows the link, low that anybody runs the board with a shared output directory outside the demonstration line."* This is filed because the fix is small and the finding is demonstrated, not because the risk is pressing.

## Also unverified, deliberately left as a note

A Windows device name - `CON`, `NUL`, `COM1` - passes `SAFE_ID` and would become `record/CON.html`. The reviewer was on Linux and could not run it, so it is stated as unverified rather than filed as a finding. Settle it on Windows before treating it as either.

## Trigger

When a repository has an active grant and no supervisor holds a lock, I want the header to still name the granted root, its level, its budget and its spend, so I can see the grant state without a running process.

## Context

Third instance of one root cause, found 2026-09-06 by watching the header go blank the moment a supervisor exited cleanly.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Work a repository with `basicly loop run` only, so no supervisor lock is ever taken.
2. `uv run basicly board --out /tmp/board.html` and read the header's run line.

Observed:

```
RUN not emitted by this producer
NOT DRAWN  session - not in this snapshot
```

Expected: the run's record, its grant level, its token budget and its spend, which are facts about the repository and not about a process.

## Cause, and why it is a pattern

`board_serve.session_facts` returns None unless `supervise.read_holder` finds a lock file. `board_facts.session_facts` adds the grant on top and inherits the same gate. So the run line, the grant level, the budget bar and the spend figure all exist only while a supervisor process holds a lock.

This is the **third** capability keyed on that lock rather than on the work:

| capability | record | state |
| --- | --- | --- |
| lane rows in `RUNNING NOW` | `basicly-kqh9dj8` | fixed 2026-09-06 |
| the six lane states `LANE_STATES` ships | `basicly-ncday7` | shipped, then unreachable, reached by the fix above |
| the run line: record, grant, budget, spend | **this record** | open |

Each was built for the supervised pass and each is absent on the single-lane path, and in every case the absence rendered as an absence of *work* rather than an absence of *a supervisor*.

## Why nobody noticed until now

A stale lock kept it alive. `read_holder` returns the holder whatever its age and the caller marks it `stale = age_s > STALE_AFTER_S`, so a lock left by a dead session still fed the header - the board drew `RUN basicly-k6tpep - open - L3 - 103%` all day with no supervisor anywhere. A detached `loop supervise` run then took that lock and released it cleanly on exit, which removed it, and the header went blank.

So the header was not working; it was being fed by a corpse. That is worse than it having been blank all along, because the figure it drew - a grant bar at 103% - was the only warning anywhere that the session had gone human-only.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/board_serve.py`
- `src/basicly/board_facts.py`
- `src/basicly/board_regions.py`

When an agent writes a test after the fix it pins, I want the test-discipline guidance to demand proof that the test fails against the pre-fix code, so I can stop a test that passes for the wrong reason from standing as a regression guard.

## Context

Session retro 2026-07-25. Two concurrency tests written for basicly-kjc5.17 passed with the fix removed - they proved nothing. One used an Event that returns immediately for the thread that set it, so the intended interleaving never happened; the other was accidentally serialized by the GIL because the fake tracker does no IO. Both were caught only because the agent chose to disable the lock and re-run, which nothing asked it to do.

The test-discipline skill says to add the regression test that would have caught the bug first, which assumes test-first ordering and prevents this. In practice a test is often written after the fix, and then passing is not evidence of anything. The missing rule is explicit: when a test is authored after the fix it claims to pin, prove it red against the pre-fix shape - revert the fix, watch it fail for the stated reason, restore. ## Trigger

When a merged diff changes the code that scores a landing, I want the report to state that the pre-merge code produced the verdict, so I can avoid a wasted rework attempt on a fix that already works.

## Problem

`basicly loop run` executes from the base checkout. Python imports `merge`/`verify`/`loop` from base's files at process start, then the landing merges the harness branch into base *during that same process*. Modules are never reloaded, so the landing is scored by the code as it was **before** the merge it just performed.

For most work this is invisible. For a change to the landing logic itself it is actively misleading: the fix looks broken on its own landing, and the run spends rework attempts proving it.

Observed on basicly-kjc5.56, which added signature-based unreliable-gate scoring. Commit timestamps on main:

    23:29:53  fix v1 merged  (singular-only signature register)
    23:30:14  merge commit
    23:34:20  attempt 2 process starts - imports base modules from disk
    23:34:26  fix v2 merged  (adds the plural br message shape)
    23:34:47  merge commit

Attempt 2 therefore ran v1's matcher against a message only v2 recognises, did not match, and escalated at rework 2/2. Base's code forgives that exact message when called afterwards, so the fix was correct the whole time. The bead spent its entire rework budget on the defect it fixes.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Change the scoring logic in `merge._verify_for_landing` or `verify`.
2. Commit it on the harness branch and run `basicly loop run <id>`.
3. Observe the landing merges the change and then scores itself with the pre-merge code.

Observed: the new behaviour does not apply, and a failure it would have forgiven charges rework.
Expected: either the landing scores itself with the code it merged, or it says plainly that it did not.

## Notes

Not obviously worth making the engine re-exec itself - that is a real complexity cost for a narrow case, and re-exec mid-landing has its own failure modes. The cheap and honest option is to name it: when the merged diff touches the landing-scoring modules, print that the verdict was produced by the pre-merge code and that a re-run will use the new logic. Then nobody spends a rework budget rediscovering it.

Related: basicly-55yh (the re-run mitigation), basicly-kjc5.56 (the signature register), basicly-4tjt (clearing a rework counter after an escalation).

## Scope

- `src/basicly/loop.py`
- `src/basicly/merge.py`
- `tests/test_integration_loop.py`

payload.value: When the merged diff touches the landing-scoring modules, the verdict report shall state that the pre-merge code produced it and that a re-run applies the merged logic. A test shall cover a diff that touches those modules and a diff that does not.

## Trigger

When basicly nears its 1.0.0 release, I want the five consumer surfaces frozen and guarded by a deterministic gate, so I can promise stability instead of adding capability at the last release.

## Context

`docs/plan/implementation-plan.md` §7 names the `v1.0.0` row of the release ladder as "stabilize and declare": `1.0` is a promise, so the last release proves it instead of adding capability. On 2026-08-27 no tracker record existed for any §7 item (search of 254 open records for semver, surface, acceptance test, breaking, forward-version, compatibility: zero hits on the §7 work). The row carries seven items; two are already recorded elsewhere (`basicly-tcmy.24` error-path polish, open; `basicly-u2hl.46` scope precedence, closed) and are referenced, not duplicated.

The exit criteria are the §7 exit criteria verbatim: the acceptance test passes on a machine that has never seen this repo; the compatibility policy is published; a surface-breaking commit without a `!` marker fails deterministically; `v1.0.0` is tagged by `basicly release` with both pushes owner-approved.

## Success Criteria

- The five consumer surfaces are enumerated in one machine-readable place and frozen: CLI commands and flags, `basicly.toml` plus the `.basicly-local/` overlay contract, the catalog source schemas, the generated-file contract, and the owned ledger event format.
- A commit that changes a frozen surface without a `!` marker is refused by a deterministic gate (hook and `basicly verify`), with a test that trips it.
- A published compatibility policy states what `1.x` promises for each surface and how a break is announced.
- A fresh consumer repository (git plus a uv-provisioned interpreter, nothing else) installs basicly, runs every gate green, and drives one unit of work to a landed commit; this runs as a test, not as prose.

## Trigger

When a `pages` deploy fails at the `actions/deploy-pages` step, I want the recovery to trigger a fresh workflow run instead of a rerun that can never succeed, so I can restore the published site without wasting a run.

## Context

Observed 2026-08-06 publishing `v0.7.1`. The site served the previous version for roughly two
hours after the release was tagged and published, so `README.md`, the GitHub release and the
landing page disagreed on the current version — on the three surfaces this repo holds to a
claim-accuracy rule.

Two separate defects, one of them self-inflicted by the obvious recovery command.

## 1. `gh run rerun` can never fix a failed pages deploy

Re-running the failed run produced:

```
Error: Multiple artifacts named "github-pages" were unexpectedly found for this
workflow run. Artifact count is 2.
```

`upload-pages-artifact` had already published a `github-pages` artifact on the first attempt;
the re-run added a second with the same name, and `deploy-pages` refuses to guess. So the
recovery is **deterministically impossible** by that route — it is not flaky, it cannot work —
and each attempt costs a full ~4-minute run before failing.

The correct recovery is a **fresh** run: `gh workflow run pages --ref main`. The workflow already
declares `workflow_dispatch`, so nothing needs adding. Confirmed working: run 31118489942
succeeded and the site moved to `v0.7.1`.

This is adjacent to a trap the workflow header already documents — a manual dispatch cancelling a
push-triggered deploy left the environment holding a deployment in `error`, which is why
`concurrency` is `group: pages, cancel-in-progress: false`. The artifact-collision variant is
recorded nowhere.

## 2. The deploy step has no retry, and pages got 13x slower

Measured durations for the same unchanged workflow:

| When | Duration | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 2026-07-31 | 19s | success |
| 2026-07-31 | 18s | success |
| 2026-08-02 | 20s | success |
| 2026-08-06 08:28 | 4m09s | success |
| 2026-08-06 14:18 | **10m19s** | **timeout** |
| 2026-08-06 16:04 | 4m28s | success |

Every run on 2026-08-06 exceeded four minutes against a ~20s baseline. The failing one reached
`in_progress` at 14:18:06 and was aborted at 14:28:20 — `deploy-pages` waiting on GitHub's Pages
API, with every build step green and the artifact uploaded.

**This is a dependency's behaviour, not a repo defect**, so treat it as requirements input rather
than something to fix upstream: `actions/deploy-pages` is given no `timeout-minutes` and no retry,
so a slow Pages API silently leaves the published site one version behind a released tag. Whether
the slowdown persists is unknown — three data points on one day is a trend, not a new baseline.
Re-measure before choosing a timeout value.

## Constraint on any fix

A longer timeout alone converts a failure into a slow success and hides the signal. Whatever
lands should make the *divergence* visible: a released tag whose site still advertises the
previous version is the condition worth detecting, and it is checkable in one request
(`curl -s <site> | grep -oE "v[0-9.]+"` against `__version__`).

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Let a `pages` run fail at the `actions/deploy-pages` step.
2. Run `gh run rerun <id> --failed`.
3. It fails with `Multiple artifacts named "github-pages"`, having spent a full run.
4. Run `gh workflow run pages --ref main` instead; it succeeds.

## Scope

- `.github/workflows/pages.yml`
- `.basicly/core/skills/release-process/skill.yaml`

payload.name: requirements
payload.value: Given a failed pages deploy, the documented recovery shall trigger a fresh `pages` workflow run rather than `gh run rerun`, which fails on a duplicate `github-pages` artifact. Given a released tag whose published site still shows the previous version, the workflow shall detect that divergence rather than rely on a human to notice it.

## Trigger

When the catalog eval's four arms are undesigned and the safety tier's status is undecided, I want the arms declared and the gate-or-metric question answered, so I can measure a guidance change without a contaminated or unfalsifiable result.

## Context

Plan section 10's second owed owner decision, **taken 2026-08-14: design the arms now.** It had been
owed since the plan was rewritten on 2026-08-08 and had no owner; architecture section 14.4 names the
shape and nothing is built.

The owner chose this over deferring it past v1.0.0.

## What is owed

Two things, and the second is the sharper one.

**The four arms.** Architecture section 14.4 names the shape of a catalog eval but not the arms
themselves. An arm is a cell whose guidance configuration is declared, so a measured difference
between arms is attributable to that configuration and to nothing else.

**Whether the safety tier is a gate or a metric.** A metric reports; a gate refuses. This repository
has a recorded rule for exactly that call - D23: a control with no recorded correct firing becomes
observability, and one that has earned a firing keeps its teeth. A safety tier that has never fired
starts as a metric under that rule, and the decision is whether safety is the exception.

## The constraints this design must honour, each already recorded

- **The isolation assertion is the whole instrument.** Plan section 11 names the risk: *"a measurement
  is uninterpretable because an arm was contaminated"*, and the remedy already written is that the
  harness reads back what guidance is live in the cell and fails if it does not match the arm's
  declaration. Without that, every number the eval produces is unfalsifiable.
- **Stage by adding entries to the enforced set, never by lowering a threshold.** Also plan section 11.
  Tier-1 failure from the start.
- **8 of 34 skills had ever been exercised** when last measured, and that figure is now unsound
  (`basicly-4grf`) because `ey58` injects a role's skills into the dispatch prompt, so the never-used
  report cannot tell an uninvoked skill from an injected one. **The eval needs a sound exercised-count
  before it can measure anything about guidance**, so state whether this bead depends on `4grf` or
  routes around it.
- **An unmeasured behavioural claim costs context every turn** - the plan's third invariant. That is
  the argument for the eval and it is also the standard the eval itself is held to.

## Acceptance

- When the four arms are declared, then each names its guidance configuration and what a difference
  between it and its neighbour would establish.
- When an arm runs, then the harness reads back the guidance live in that cell and fails if it does not
  match the declaration.
- When the safety tier is decided, then the decision states whether it gates or reports and cites the
  rule that decided it.
- When the design lands, then it states what it depends on for a sound exercised-count and does not
  assume the 8-of-34 figure.

## Scope

Design only. `docs/architecture/architecture.md` section 14.4 is the target of the write-up; the
implementation is decomposed after.

## Demonstration

The four arms are readable by someone who was not in the room, and for each one a reader can say what
result would falsify it. A design nobody can falsify is the thing this eval exists to catch.

## Trigger

When a change touches `src/**` or a catalog source under `.basicly/**`, I want the harness loop required and a named lightweight path for everything else, so I can enforce the ceremony by the touched path instead of by an agent's own judgement.

## Context

Plan §7.1, resolved by owner decision 2026-07-26. The decision is made; this bead implements it.

DECIDED: the threshold is the touched path. The harness loop is required for any change touching `src/**` or catalog sources under `.basicly/**`. A docs-only, tracker-only, or config-only change may take a lightweight path.

Chosen because it is the only form of the rule that can be enforced rather than hoped for: a hook can check which paths a commit touches. The rule today mandates the loop for "non-trivial work", which is the agents own judgment call, so the rule is currently unenforceable - every loop decision this repo has made was an agent choosing to comply. A diff-size threshold was rejected as a poor proxy: a one-line change to a gate or a hook is exactly the kind of edit that most needs the ceremony.

The lightweight path skips the ceremony and never the hooks. That is the whole point of naming it - an unnamed escape hatch becomes "skip the loop" and then "skip the gates".

## Notes

The threshold belongs in the always-on Harness Loop fragment, and the recall measurement under basicly-agzx.1 is a reason to keep it short: content phrased as an imperative constraint is retrieved, descriptive prose is not - the one rule that scored 0/3 in both families was the only non-imperative line in the file.

Consider whether a hook can assert it, since that is the justification for choosing this form over the alternatives. If it cannot be asserted, say so rather than shipping an unenforceable rule in different words.

`uv run pytest -q` and a search showing one meaning per name.
