## Trigger

When an agent has only the board and nothing else, I want it to answer all nine of the owner's operator questions and offer the verbs that change the flow of work, so I can see and control the loop without a session transcript.

## Context

Owner, 2026-09-05, restating a requirement they say they have given many times: *"the requirement was also to make the board interactive or a cockpit or a control panel where we can see and control the flow of work. Cool thing would be to be able to easily start, stop work, descope and so on."*

And the reason, in their words: *"One of the biggest issues with agentic development in the terminal alone is that human has no idea what is going on and when multiple parallel sessions and work is being done, it gets buried under. Terminal is fast and no one scrolls up, having multiple terminals does not help."*

And the test they set: *"if you as an agent look at the board, and only have access to the board, would you be able to see what is going on? what work is available, what work can start, is in progress? start work, stop work, inspect work (the info written in the record in a structured way)? descope work, scope work?"*

Explicitly **not** in scope: *"it is not about creating new records - that we can do via terminal. it is about work loop transparency and control."*

And the standing instruction: *"the board, even if it is a byproduct of basicly, it is essential and should grow with the basicly."*

## The gap, measured

Taken against the served board at 127.0.0.1:8788 on 2026-09-05, and against the snapshot it renders.

| the owner's question | answered today | by what |
| --- | --- | --- |
| what work is available | partly | `NEXT UP` draws 3 of 234 ready |
| what can start now | yes | `THE QUEUE`: 262 needs nothing, 24 waits on one, 8 waits on a chain |
| what is in progress | yes | `RUNNING NOW` and `CLAIMED, NO LANE` |
| what is blocked, and by what | yes | `THE QUEUE` names the top blockers and the longest chain |
| **inspect one record** | **no** | `units[]` carries `id, phase, priority, ready, status, title, type` and no body |
| **start work** | **no** | no action offers `loop run` or `supervise` |
| **stop work** | partly | `lane-kill` is in `ACTIONS`, but only reachable when an ask prefills it |
| **descope / scope** | **no** | no action changes status or priority |
| when will it be done | no | `basicly-hymq99` and `basicly-w6vbw61` |

So four of nine. The two channels that are missing are **inspect** and **control**, and they are missing for different reasons.

## The seam already exists

`board_actions.ACTIONS` is a closed table of three argv builders handed to the installed CLI as a subprocess. Its docstring states the design: *"The board is a renderer with a keyboard."* `.importlinter`'s `consumer-reads-only-the-snapshot` contract holds because the board never reads the tracker; it runs `basicly`.

That is the answer to inspect as well as control. A record's body does not have to enter the snapshot - 294 bodies would be a snapshot nobody can serve. The board runs `basicly tracker show <id>` the same way it runs `basicly policy checkpoint`, and renders what comes back. No contract moves.

`board_asks.pending` already prefills a row per implementable offer. What is missing is a surface for an action that no *ask* proposes - a ready record has no ask, so today nothing offers to start it.

## Redefined by the owner, 2026-09-06 — the cockpit is a development environment

> *"the board is the human instrument for implementation of new features. the human will set
> up the backlog with the agent using terminal, and then it will view and control the
> implementation via the board. That is why this board design must look like a development
> environment for a human, where he sees what is going on and can react on it."*

And the reason, which is the same one they have given all session in different words:

> *"I have asked you many times during implementation, and several times in this session,
> where are we now. that is because I cannot see clearly where we are."*

**This supersedes the wall framing.** The board was built as a glance surface read from across
a room, and every design decision followed from that: cap the lists, prefer counts to members,
draw a diagram rather than a backlog. Those were right for a wall and are wrong for a cockpit.
`basicly-a68ggd` is the clearest case - it is closed, and its title is *"the loop region shows
the whole backlog binned by phase instead of the running pass"*. The region was deliberately
made **not** a list of what sits in each phase. The owner is now asking for exactly that list.
It is a reversal on a new requirement, not a regression, and it is recorded here so nobody
re-closes `a68ggd`'s finding on top of it.

**The division of labour, stated by the owner:** the backlog is set up *with an agent in the
terminal*. The cockpit is where a human **views and controls the implementation**. So the
cockpit does not need record creation - it needs seeing and reacting.

**Two surfaces, not one page:**

1. **The loop** - what is happening now, as a kanban of phase columns in the shape Linear and
   Jira use, where each phase names its members and a member is reachable.
2. **The backlog** - what is planned, ordered, with the controls to shape it.

**Titles carry the meaning, ids are the address.** The owner: *"the real titles of features and
tasks are more important than IDs. IDs should be there but focus is on titles, description,
priority, and dependency."* The board leads with ids in most regions today.

**And the case nothing is designed for: N sessions on one repository.** The owner:
*"4-5 terminals, each with an open session, are working on the same repository."* Shared
branch, shared worktrees. `basicly-kqh9dj8` shipped worktree visibility, which is one agent's
answer to "who is inside a lane"; it says nothing about which *session* holds what, whether two
are about to collide, or what a fifth terminal joining should be told.

**Priority:** the owner has made visualization number one, on the ground that the cockpit is
*"the 1st thing a user will see when starting basicly after installation in their repo"*.

## Plan

- integrity: `L2`
- children decompose this; each is a leaf a lane can build

payload.name: requirements
payload.value: The board lets a viewer inspect a record's body, start a ready record, stop a running lane, and descope or reactivate a record, each as an action on the row it applies to. The board draws two surfaces: a loop view of what runs now by phase, and a backlog view of what is planned, ordered, with controls to shape it. Every capability stays an argv handed to the installed CLI, so `consumer-reads-only-the-snapshot` still holds.

## Trigger

When the quality-gate guidance says only to run the repository's checks, I want it to name the one command that runs every gate and the pass line to confirm, so I can stop a hand-picked subset from being reported as the whole gate.

## Context

Session 2026-08-14, and this is a user-visible mistake rather than a near miss: I reported "all
gates green" before committing `basicly-ejdm.2`, then the commit was **refused**. What I had run
was `pytest` plus five checker scripts I picked by name. What I had not run was the gate, which
then failed on `pyright` and `projection-skills`.

The `quality-gate` fragment says: *"Run the repo's checks on anything touched, re-run after the
final edit"*, and *"Point at gates, don't restate them."*

## Root cause, and it is in the wording

"The repo's checks" is a **set an agent has to assemble**, and an agent that has just run five
checkers has evidence it assembled it correctly. There is no moment at which a hand-picked subset
announces that it is a subset - it looks exactly like the whole.

The repo already has the one command: `.basicly/core/hooks/pre-commit.py` runs all 20 and prints
`checks passed: 20/20`. Nothing in the guidance names it, so the fragment describes an outcome
where it could name a command - which is the inversion of section 3.1, the rule that guidance
points at the enforcement rather than restating it.

## Proposed change, for a human to apply

Amend the `quality-gate` fragment so the check step **names the command** rather than the set:
run the repo's own gate runner, and confirm the pass line it prints. The count in that line is
what makes a subset visible - `18/20` cannot be misread as green, while five green scripts can.

D25 forbids an agent amending the catalog, so this is filed rather than applied.

## The second half, which the wording cannot fix

I also reported the result before running the gate. The fragment already carries
*"Confirm success from the explicit pass/fail summary line; truncated output hides failures"* -
that rule was right and I did not follow it. Only the first half is a guidance defect.

payload.name: requirements
payload.value: The `quality-gate` fragment's check step must name the command that runs every gate, not describe a set an agent assembles itself. The fragment must name the exact pass-line format to confirm, such as a count of checks passed against the total.

## Trigger

When a pass changes nothing and re-dispatches a decider for an item a human already routed, I want the supervisor to stop re-deciding it and end the session with a stalled narrative, so I can stop paying for identical passes that buy no progress.

## Context

Observed 2026-08-27 on `basicly loop supervise basicly-zq9i2m --tier high --max-passes 8`. Passes 4 to 8 were identical: `carried: basicly-2kh170 - landing without a new dispatch`, then `routed: basicly-2kh170 -> rework` on the same scope collision, then the pass spend gate refused (`89259646 tokens forecast; 87452222 remaining`), then `decider: basicly-zq9i2m#3018546b66 [escalation] to human` with a fresh decider rendering each time. The ledger holds 5 `[harness-run] phase=decide` records for that one decision id. Nothing changed between the passes: no lane dispatched, no landing succeeded, the queue held the same item. The session ended `stopped: --max-passes 8 reached`, so five of eight passes bought nothing and the operator read a full pass count as work.

Two defects share the root that a pass has no notion of "this pass changed nothing":

1. `record_pass_refusal` is idempotent per (issue, kind, question), so the queue item was correctly re-enqueued once, but the decider was dispatched again on every pass for an item it had already routed to a human. A human-routed item is pending until a human answers; re-deciding it spends a decider run per pass and cannot change the answer.
2. A pass whose only outcomes are a repeated landing refusal and a repeated queue item is a stall. The supervisor kept looping until `--max-passes`, and a session without that flag would loop until the operator noticed.

## Steps to Reproduce

Root with one carried lane whose landing bounces on a stable cause (a scope collision with a live sibling), and ready children whose forecast exceeds the remaining grant. `basicly loop supervise <root> --max-passes 4`. Observed: 4 identical passes, 4 decider runs on one decision id. Expected: after the first pass that changes nothing, the session ends with a `stalled:` narrative naming the pending decision and the bounced lane, and the decider runs at most once per queue item.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/supervise.py`
- `src/basicly/decisions.py`
- `tests/test_supervise.py`
- `tests/test_decisions.py`
- `changelog.d/*.md`

payload.name: requirements
payload.value: When the next pass finds a queue item the decider already routed to a human still pending, no new decider dispatch must run for it, and the pass narrative must name it as pending on a human. When a pass dispatches no lane, lands no lane, and enqueues no new item, the supervisor must end the session with a stalled narrative naming every pending item and bounced lane, and exit non-zero. When a pass dispatches or lands at least one lane, the session must continue as today.

## Trigger

When a suppression list cites the wrong file or carries a stale hit count, I want each citation to resolve to its suppressed condition and each count checked for staleness, so I can trust the exemption tables instead of auditing the wrong module.

## Context

Found by the lane-E cross-cutting survey 2026-08-14. Three defects in the lists' own claims, each verified.

```text
pyproject.toml:90   says the two false positives sit at hooks.py:280 and :282
                    they are at precommit_config.py:127 and :129
                    hooks.py:280 is now a different function
pyproject.toml      says two of them are true false positives
                    a third is: tb, a protocol parameter at tracker_usage.py:286
.ruff.toml          records 111 hits for one ignored rule
                    measured today: 187
```

A maintainer who follows the first citation audits the wrong module.

The rule with the stale count keeps its rationale, which survives. What rots is the number, and nothing ratchets the growth of an ignored family. A second recorded count still measures correctly, so the rot is per entry rather than systemic.

## A fourth of the same class

`tracker_surface.py:51` points at a function in `tracker_usage`. The function lives in `tracker_invocation.py:62`. And `tracker_surface.py:52` re-spells a constant from `tracker_invocation.py:30`. The concept a token that can be a tracker surface word has two definitions.

## Re-measured 2026-08-19, two of the four halves are moot

Two files this record named do not exist: a tracker surface module and a tracker invocation module. So the finding that two definitions of the surface-word concept had drifted apart is **gone with the modules**, and two of the four declared scope entries went with it.

What survives is the suppression-list half, and it is still live: the project file cites a hook module for names that live elsewhere, and the lint configuration carries a count that no longer matches its population.

This is one instance of a general rule filed as `basicly-twfj` and re-measured under `basicly-e2mz.48.2`: every exemption list is machine validated against the population it exempts from. Five of this repository's exemption tables already report a stale entry and several do not. Prefer folding this record into that work over fixing two citations by hand, because the hand fix leaves the next drift undetected.

## Scope

- `pyproject.toml`
- `.ruff.toml`

## Trigger

When a live tracker record cites a `file:line` or a scope glob that has drifted, I want a check that re-resolves the cited symbol and reports the drift by name, so I can stop building against a citation that silently points at the wrong place.

## Context

An audit of 24 live work items on 2026-08-13 checked every `file:line` citation it relied on.
**14 of 14 had drifted.** This is one missing mechanism, not fourteen defects:

```text
runner.py:141-142        -> :151            basicly.toml:512 / :568   -> :619
supervise.py:2700        -> :2727           cli.py:3582               -> :3589
merge.py:466 / :520      -> :475 / :529     cli.py:3265               -> :3314
policy.py:560            -> :673            run_record.py:605         -> :742
supervise.py:1286        -> :1222           loop.py:327               -> moved module
supervise._band_verdict  -> working_set.py:285
```

Why it matters more than tidiness: a citation is how a work item makes its claim checkable, and
the repo's own rule is "re-check a cited `file:line` before fixing it"
(`implementation-plan.md`, section 1 item 2). When every citation is stale, that rule costs a
re-derivation per item and readers stop performing it - which is how `basicly-4xmu`'s
reproduction came to omit `_run_proposer`, and how a P0 was nearly built against a remedy the
plan had replaced.

Two live items show the failure in its worst form, where the **symbol** moved rather than the
line: `basicly-esxp` cites `supervise._band_verdict`, now `working_set.py:285`; and
`basicly-o40x`'s declared `## Scope` names `.basicly/core/skills/harness-loop.skill.yaml`, a
path that **matches no file** (the real one is `harness-loop/skill.yaml`). A scope glob matching
nothing is what `basicly-a3ab.3` exists to catch for catalog entries, and nothing catches it for
a bead's own scope block - `basicly policy dor` warns only when a `## Scope` heading parsed to
zero globs, not when a declared glob matches zero files.

## Why a line number is the wrong thing to store

The durable identifier is the symbol, not the offset. A check that re-resolves
`module.function` and reports where it now lives survives every refactor; a check that compares
stored line numbers fails on the first unrelated insertion above them.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Pick any live bead older than a week that cites a `file:line`.
2. Open the cited line. Positive control before reporting drift: confirm the file exists and the
   symbol is findable elsewhere in it, so "wrong line" is distinguishable from "deleted".
3. Observed: 14 of 14 sampled citations pointed at the wrong line or a moved module.

## Demonstration

`uv run python .scripts/check_bead_citations.py` names the drifted citations across the live
tracker and exits non-zero, and `--strict` or a per-bead argument reports one item.

## Scope

- `.scripts/check_bead_citations.py`
- `tests/test_check_bead_citations.py`
- `basicly.toml`

## Earlier acceptance text (the acceptance field is authoritative)

- Given a live work item citing a symbol that has moved, when the check runs, then it names the
  item, the stale citation and the symbol's current location - check: a test plants a bead
  citing a known-moved symbol and asserts all three appear.
- Given a work item whose declared `## Scope` carries a glob matching no file on disk, when the

## Trigger

When the tree-growth signal only prints during a `basicly verify` run, I want it recorded on the run and surfaced in the supervised pass line, so I can read a trend without running the gate again.

## Context

`basicly-5p49` shipped the tree-growth signal and met four of its five acceptance criteria. This bead is the fifth.

The signal prints from `basicly verify`. It is not recorded on the run and it does not appear in the supervised pass line, so it is visible to whoever runs a gate and invisible to whoever reads a pass afterwards.

## Why the lane stopped rather than reaching

Two reasons, both stated by the implementer rather than discovered later.

The scope globs on `basicly-5p49` were `.scripts/`, `basicly.toml` and `tests/`. The pass line comes from `supervise._report_coverage`, beside the existing band and spend lines, and the run fields come from `run_record`. Both are outside those globs.

And there is a hard blocker. `src/basicly/supervise.py` is frozen by the module-size ratchet and may only shrink, so adding a report line to it fails the gate today. That is the same shape `basicly-r343` hit: a ratchet refuses a change to a file, and the real fix is a split that has nothing to do with the change.

## What that makes this bead depend on

`basicly-wotk` extracts the outcome routing sink out of `supervise.py` and is the item that gives that file headroom. Doing this one first means either a second waiver or a refactor bolted onto a reporting change.

## Why it is worth doing at all

The standing rule is that a demoted or advisory number must still be recorded on the run, surfaced in the pass line and kept falsifiable against the ledger. A signal that only prints during a gate run satisfies none of those. It also cannot earn the right to block, because earning it requires a firing history and nothing records one.

- `src/basicly/run_record.py`

`basicly-wotk`, which gives `supervise.py` the headroom this needs.

Run a supervised pass and read the tree-growth line beside the band line, then read the same value back out of the run record.

## Trigger

When a lane adds a module and declares it in the import contract, I want the landing to check the contract against the tree under test instead of the pre-merge base package, so I can land a change the lane's own worktree already verified clean.

## Steps to Reproduce

Measured 2026-08-07 landing `basicly-3ifz.1`, **hours after `basicly-69az` shipped**
(`a90585f`). That fix reads the lane tree's `config.py` schema via `ast` so a lane can add
a `basicly.toml` key and declare it in one commit. It covers exactly one config surface.
Here is the same mechanism on a second one.

1. A lane adds `src/basicly/tuning.py` and declares the module in `.importlinter`'s layer
   contract (`policy | tuning | verify`) in the same commit.
2. `basicly verify --mode full` inside the lane worktree passes: 16 gates PASS,
   `Contracts: 2 kept, 0 broken`.
3. `basicly loop run <id>` lands it from the base checkout.

Observed - the merge gate fails, twice, identically, and the convergence detector escalates:

```
Missing layer in container 'basicly': module basicly.tuning does not exist.
merge failed: verify full failed: lint-imports
```

Expected: a lane that adds a module and declares it in the import contract can land.

## Cause: same as 69az, different config surface

The landing runs verify from the **base** checkout, so `import_linter` resolves the
`basicly` package base has installed - which has no `tuning` module - while reading the
**lane tree's** `.importlinter`, which declares one. The contract names a module the
analyzed package lacks.

This is `69az`'s exact shape: a declaration in the lane's tree referencing something only
the lane's code provides, validated by the pre-merge process. `69az` fixed it for
`basicly.toml` by resolving the schema from the tree under test. `.importlinter` was not in
that fix's scope and resolves the package, not a schema, so the same remedy does not
transfer unchanged.

**The trap that makes this expensive**: running the gate inside the worktree passes,
because `uv run` there resolves the worktree's own package. So the lane, and any human
checking by hand, both see green. Only the landing sees it, and it reads as a flaky gate. I
diagnosed it as transient on the first occurrence and was wrong; the correction is recorded
on `basicly-3ifz.1`.

## Cost

Two full rework rounds plus one escalation on `basicly-3ifz.1`, then a hand landing. The
convergence detector fired correctly both times - "this round changed nothing it reports" -
which is right and still leaves the lane stuck, because the lane cannot fix a failure that
does not exist in its own tree.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/verify.py`
- `.importlinter`
- `tests/test_verify.py`

payload.name: requirements
payload.value: When a lane's commit adds a module and declares it in `.importlinter`, the landing's `lint-imports` check must analyse the tree under test, not the pre-merge base package. A regression test must first prove the bare missing-layer refusal red, then prove the fix green.

When an agent follows the non-interactive-shell fragment's flag bullet to delete a directory recursively, I want the fragment to name the allowed spelling, so I can avoid a command the permissions deny-list blocks.

> Use non-interactive flags (`cp -f`, `mv -f`, `rm -f`, package-manager `-y`, ...) for ops that

For the common case - removing a scratch **directory** - following that literally produces

notes from an earlier session, so the guidance has now mis-steered at least twice.

and the deny-list agree.

recursive delete uses `rm -r` and that the force variants are denied, e.g. "... for ops that can
hang on a prompt - but a recursive delete is `rm -r`, never `rm -rf`, which the deny-list blocks

chars on all three surfaces; headroom at the time of filing was CLAUDE.md ~1060,

## Trigger

When a consumer module in the board reads a snapshot key its own producer never writes, I want a gate that catches the mismatch, so I can tell a real defect from a declared foreign-producer affordance.

## Context

Three defects in one day, all the same shape: **a consumer reads a snapshot field the producer never writes, and every test on both sides passes.**

| record | the field | how it was found |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `basicly-3qstvw` | `asks[].actions[].basicly` | by grepping the producer after shipping the consumer |
| `basicly-tyobdb` (adjacent) | the gate verdict's age | by the owner misreading the page |
| filed alongside this one | `events[].kind == "status"` | by asking why `CLOSED TODAY` said `not measured` |

Each consumer was correct. Each producer was correct. The **seam** was never asserted, because the fixtures under `tests/fixtures/board/` are written against the *schema*, and a schema is a superset of what the producer implements. So an end-to-end test can serve a document more capable than anything the producer can emit — which is exactly what `tests/test_board_action_wire.py` did while the live board drew no form.

## The gate

For every key the board's consumer modules read out of a snapshot section, either the producer writes it, or the pair is declared as a gap with a reason. Both halves are mechanical:

- the consumer side is a literal-string scan of `src/basicly/board_{wall,regions,footer,loop,diagram,graph,asks}.py` for `.get("<key>")` and `["<key>"]` against a section reading;
- the producer side is the same scan over `src/basicly/board_{snapshot,sections,usage,facts}.py` for the keys it assigns.

A key the consumer reads and the producer never writes is either a defect or a declared foreign-producer affordance. The declaration is the point: `harness-board/v1` is deliberately a contract for producers that are not this harness, so some keys are legitimately unwritten here — and today nobody could tell those apart from the broken ones.

## Scope

- `.scripts/check_board_seam.py`
- `basicly.toml`
- `tests/test_check_board_seam.py`

## Plan

- integrity: `L2`
- demonstration: Delete one key from `board_sections.asks` and watch the gate name it; then restore it and watch the gate pass.

## Trigger

When an operator's private memory is required to run basicly correctly, I want every deterministic, semi-deterministic and non-deterministic fact externalized into a command, a skill or the projected instructions, so I can run a supervised pass with no fact that exists only in an agent's memory.

## Context

Owner, 2026-08-01: **"If you need to go search your memory to run basicly correctly, we are doing
it wrong."** A consumer who installs basicly inherits the engine, the projected instructions, the
skills and the hooks — and none of an operator's accumulated recollection. So any knowledge required
to run basicly correctly that lives only in an agent's private memory is an undocumented runtime
dependency, and the consumer hits the failure the operator learned to avoid.

Externalize in this priority order, owner-specified:

1. **Deterministic** -> a script, a command, or a gate. The engine answers it; nobody recalls it.
2. **Semi-deterministic** -> a script plus a skill (the skill carries the judgment and references
   the script).
3. **Non-deterministic** -> instructions and skills.

## Audit, 2026-08-01

An operator memory of 58 entries was classified against what the repo actually enforces. Three
groups came out.

**Group A - required to run basicly, NOT externalized.** These are the defects.

- The **supervised-run runbook** does not exist in the catalog. `loop supervise` appears only in
  `docs/design/factory-design.md` and `docs/architecture/architecture.md` (which describe the
  system, not how to drive it) and in the `harness-client` skill (which is about attaching as a
  second observer). The `harness-loop` skill, 271 lines, barely mentions supervise, grants or
  budget. Everything about starting a run - mint a grant, size the budget from measured cost, check
  the base is clean, know which runner will meter spend - was operator memory.
- **`FORCE_COLOR` breaks the piped-output test: zero mentions anywhere in the repo.** Pure memory.
- Budget sizing from measured per-lane cost: the numbers exist in run records, but nothing reads
  them and says "a 5-lane pass needs about this much".
- `br` read patterns: `br list --json` caps at ~50 and drops closed rows, so a whole-tracker
  question must read `.beads/issues.jsonl`. A zero-finding audit was silently wrong once because of
  this.
- The tracker export re-adds `source_repo_path` on every write, so a scrub is required before
  staging. Loop landings scrub automatically; an out-of-loop write does not, and the operator
  remembers.

**Group B - required, and ALREADY externalized.** The memory entry is redundant history, which is
fine and needs no work: the loop landing guards (`4psl`, `9niw`, `o0q3`), the commit-message rules
(the `commit-msg` and `beads-commit-msg` hooks plus `basicly commit`), the lint rules (ruff,
markdownlint), the deny-list, `--all-default-roots`.

**Group C - not about running basicly.** Agent working discipline and project state: verification
habits, session history, measurements, Claude-Code-specific facts. These legitimately stay in an
agent's memory or a handover, and are out of scope here.

## Scope

Children, one per tier. Filed separately so each can be prioritized on its own.

- **Tier 1, done in this session**: `basicly-f3mi` (projected Claude hooks used a relative script
  path, so every consumer's hook broke outside the repo root - the exact defect an operator was
  papering over with a "never use a bare cd" note) and `basicly loop preflight <root>`, a read-only
  command that answers the whole pre-run checklist and exits non-zero when a run would be blocked.

  recall - `FORCE_COLOR`, the node resolution that differs in non-interactive shells, and an

When an agent verifies a claim or lands a change, I want the four discipline rules earned by past incidents to reach it from a projected skill, so I can stop relying on an operator's private memory for them.

## Context

Tier 3 of basicly-ze8z: non-deterministic, so instructions and skills.

- **A closed blocker is not a working gate.** A closed bead proves the code exists, not that the gate binds. `jr0l.22` was shipped, tested and inert for 67% of the tracker, and reading it as discharged risk cost a 36% grant overrun. - **A broad test break is a layer error.** When one edit reddens many tests, read three of them before touching either side: they are collectively describing an invariant of the layer you reached into. - **Print the sample before choosing an estimator.** Two of three attempts at a spend bound were refuted by the data, not by argument: the population was bimodal, so any high quantile bounded cheap work using expensive work.
- **A capability fix can arm a pre-existing safety hole.** Removing a manual step removes whatever that step was implicitly authorizing. Letting the supervisor seed its own lanes put an ungranted session - which had no spend ceiling at all - one command from dispatching five metered agents.

## Trigger

When main advances mid-pass because a tracker write dirties the base, I want a lane behind its own base to reach a committable state without a human decision, so I can avoid an escalation for a record it has no relationship to.

## Context

Six lanes in one pass on 2026-08-22 were each blocked from committing by the `release-notes` gate reporting changelog entries that belong to **other** records and are present on main. The gate is right every time and none of the lanes did anything wrong.

## The loop, and it closes

```text
the supervisor requires a clean base to land          (base: clean, checked every round)
  -> a tracker write dirties the base                 (.basicly/ledger/events-*.jsonl)
  -> so the tracker write must be committed to main
  -> main advances
  -> every in-flight branch is now behind main
  -> release-notes reports main's changelog entries as missing from the branch
  -> the branch cannot commit
  -> it needs a rebase, which is on the explicit-confirmation list
  -> so it escalates to a human
```

Every step is correct in isolation. The cycle is the defect.

## Measured on this pass

Thirteen commits reached main while six lanes were in flight. Five landings were held behind a pass-level flag set by the first failure. Two lanes escalated a decision asking permission to rebase - `basicly-fi1i7z` explicitly, and `basicly-6oa3mt` hit the same wall while committing. Two branches additionally acquired a merge commit from trying `git merge main` instead, which `rebase.merge_commits` refuses at landing, so that route strands the lane rather than saving it.

The gate already distinguishes the two cases correctly and says so in its own words: *this tree is behind, not in debt. Rebase. Never declare it invisible - such an entry is true at a branch point and false on arrival.* So the diagnosis is not the gap; the **remedy is gated on a human** and the human is the same actor whose commits caused it.

## Three candidate cuts, and the evidence for each

**Rebase a lane's own branch without a human.** A rebase of an unlanded, unpushed, lane-owned branch onto its own base rewrites no shared history. The confirmation rule exists for published history and for destructive resets. Narrowing it to exclude this case removes the escalation entirely. Against: the rule is currently spelled by shape rather than by reach, so narrowing it needs the reach to be checkable - unpushed and unlanded are both testable.

**Let the landing rebase.** The engine already rebases at landing (`rebase.merge_commits` is its own refusal), so the capability is present; what is missing is doing it *before* the lane's own commit rather than at the merge queue.

**Stop advancing main during a pass.** The tracker's own writes are the only thing forcing it. If the base's cleanliness check ignored the ledger - which the engine commits itself at provisioning, landing and ship - a session's tracker writes would not have to reach main mid-pass at all.

The third is the root cut and the first is the cheap one. They are not exclusive.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Start a supervised pass with two or more lanes.
2. While they run, close any record whose `## Scope` names a shipped path, write its `changelog.d/<id>.<category>.md`, and commit that to main.
3. Wait for a lane to finish and attempt its own commit.

**Observed 2026-08-22.** The lane's commit is refused by `release-notes` naming a changelog file it has never heard of, its verify reports 31 of 32, and it can neither commit nor rebase without a human.

**Control.** The same lane on a branch forked after that commit passes `release-notes` unchanged, so the refusal is the base gap and not the lane's own debt.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/supervise.py`
- `src/basicly/loop.py`
- `tests/test_supervise.py`

## Plan

- integrity: `L3`
- budget: `130000`
- depends on: none
- demonstration: Run a two-lane pass, advance main mid-pass with a closed record carrying a changelog entry, and watch both lanes reach a committed state with no human decision, against a control run on the current engine where they do not.

payload.name: requirements
payload.value: A lane whose branch is behind its base and owes nothing itself can reach a committable state without a human decision, and it cannot do so by creating a merge commit the landing gate will later refuse. The cost of the base advancing during a pass is bounded, and a lane is not refused for a record it has no relationship to. Where the ledger alone dirties the base, the base's cleanliness check stops requiring a session's tracker writes to reach main mid-pass, because the engine already commits the ledger at provisioning, landing and ship.

## Trigger

When a caller relays a confirm code to `loop run` for a ship checkpoint the grant has declined, I want the invocation to consume that code, so I can approve the checkpoint instead of losing it to an advance step run first.

## Context

Measured 2026-09-04 while the ship checkpoint for `basicly-qwqd35` was approved by hand, after
the `basicly-k6tpep` L3 grant reported `token_budget spent (104485469/100000000 tokens under
this grant; 191034258 lifetime)` and returned every checkpoint to a human.

`basicly loop run <id> --confirm <code>` refused four separately issued codes in a row, each
seconds after issue, with `checkpoint ship: REFUSED - invalid or expired confirm code`.

## Steps to Reproduce

With a record at phase `verify`, `advance ALLOWED`, and a grant that has declined the ship
checkpoint:

1. `uv run basicly loop run <id> --root <root> --runner manual` prints a code and stores it.
   Verified equal: printed `6a96a6d8`, and
   `.basicly/usage/checkpoint-confirms.json` held `{'code': '6a96a6d8'}`.
2. `uv run basicly loop run <id> --root <root> --runner manual --confirm 6a96a6d8` refuses.
3. Read the store again. It now holds a different code, `9256fa79`.

## Cause

`loop run` resolves the phase boundary before it consumes the relayed code. The advance step
hits the same ship checkpoint with `confirm=None`, so `policy.approve_checkpoint_guarded`
takes the `if confirm is None` branch at `src/basicly/policy.py:1402` and calls
`_issue_confirm_code` at `:1408`, which overwrites the store entry keyed
`<id>:ship` (`policy.py:1288-1299`). The later `_consume_confirm_code` at `:1413` then
compares the caller's code against the code the same invocation just wrote, and rejects at
`:1417`.

The two steps share one key and run in the wrong order, so the relayed code is always stale
by the time it is read.

## Why it was not seen before

The bug needs a grant that declines. With a live grant the advance delegates the checkpoint
and no code is ever issued. `basicly-mfavrh` shipped through `loop run` earlier the same
session for exactly that reason.

## The path that works

`uv run basicly policy checkpoint <id> ship --approve` then the same command with
`--confirm <code>` (`src/basicly/cli.py:2784`) reaches the guard with no advance in front of
it. Printed and stored codes matched, and the approval was recorded:
`checkpoint ship: APPROVED (basicly-qwqd35)`.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/loop.py`
- `src/basicly/policy.py`
- `tests/test_policy.py`
- `tests/test_loop.py`

## Earlier acceptance text (the acceptance field is authoritative)

- When a caller passes `--confirm` to `loop run`, then the invocation consumes that code
  without issuing a new one for the same checkpoint key.
- When the grant has declined a checkpoint and a code is relayed to `loop run`, then the
  checkpoint is approved.
- A regression test drives `loop run --confirm` on a record whose grant has declined, and
  fails if the store entry changes during the invocation.

## Trigger

When `decompose` writes a `blocks` edge between two children, I want the edge to record whether it came from a declared `depends_on` or from computed scope overlap, so I can measure how much ordering comes from real data flow rather than file collision.

## Context

The owner states the ordering rule as "does the next state consume the previous state result".
That is a true data dependency, and it is Dagster asset-edge semantics. The shipped default rule
is different: `src/basicly/decompose.py:303` `serializes(a, b)` returns True when any glob in one
child declared write scope can match a common path with any glob in the other. It never asks what
either child produces or reads. `group_children` (`decompose.py:394`) takes the transitive closure
with union-find and `chain_predecessors` (`:431`) turns each group into a linear chain. The
literature name for ordering imposed without data flow is the GNU make order-only prerequisite.

So the owner rule orders on what flows and the code default orders on what collides. Both are
legitimate and both are already built.

## The defect

`depends_on` is a mandatory plan field (`src/basicly/plan_gate.py:77` `PLAN_FIELDS`) and the plan
gate own docstring gives the reason in the owner terms: before it existed "the only ordering
signal was scope overlap, which cannot express B needs A decision between two children that touch
no common file" (`plan_gate.py:16-19`).

At `src/basicly/decompose.py:2042-2049` the declared `depends_on` targets and the computed chain
predecessor are unioned, deduplicated and written with the same call, `dep add <child> <dep> -t
blocks`. Nothing records which rule drew a given edge. The live population holds 418 `blocks`
edges and the declared/computed split over them cannot be measured. The edge payload does carry a
`provenance` key but its values are migration provenance, EXTRACTED 275, engine 117, dual-write 26,
not dependency kind.

The consequence: nobody can answer "how much of our ordering comes from data flow" with a number,
so the owner framing is arguable rather than measurable.

## Not recommended, and why

Making `depends_on` the primary rule and demoting scope overlap deletes a measured protection.
`src/basicly/contention.py:5-8` records why that module exists: three lanes with provably disjoint
scopes, `VERDICT: ready`, and the third bounced twice on a CHANGELOG.md conflict and spent its
whole rework budget. The engine also cannot observe a consumption it was not told about, because
no artifact kind is consumed by a sibling.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/decompose.py`
- `.basicly/core/kit/tracker/derivation.py`
- `tests/test_decompose.py`

## Earlier acceptance text (the acceptance field is authoritative)

- When `decompose` writes a `blocks` edge, then the edge records whether it came from a declared
  `depends_on` or from computed scope overlap.
- A read surface reports the split over the live edge population as two counts.
- Scheduling behaviour is unchanged.

payload.value: Each `blocks` edge `decompose` writes records whether it came from a declared `depends_on` dependency or from a computed scope-overlap chain. A read surface reports the split over the live edge population as two counts. Scheduling behaviour stays unchanged.

## Trigger

When the supervisor selects lanes for a pass, I want it to consult the file contention graph it already compiles, so I can stop it admitting two lanes whose declared scopes collide on the concurrency integer alone.

## Context

An inventory of every graph this repo maintains found nine, composing at exactly one point:
`decompose.decompose` compiles the file contention graph into `blocks` edges on the record
dependency graph, once, at plan time (`src/basicly/decompose.py:2041-2048`). After that the record
graph never learns anything more about files.

Established, each with its own probe:

- The edges are never re-derived against an amended scope. `_scope_block` records a violation and
  never adds an edge (`src/basicly/loop.py:1361`).
- Hand-filed siblings get no edges at all. `src/basicly/contention.py:14-18` says so outright.
- The supervisor never asks. `rg -n contention src/basicly/supervise.py` returns 3 hits, all prose
  about store contention. Positive control on the same file: `rg -c "merge\."` returns 21.
  Contention is reachable only from three CLI sites.

`.importlinter` permits `supervise -> contention` (tiers 6 and 10, higher may import lower), so the
missing edge is a choice and not a structural constraint.

## Measured consequence

184 `scope-violation` events across 160 distinct records. 22 named a colliding sibling and were
refused. **162 recorded the contradiction and landed anyway.**

Parallelism is decided twice, neither time by looking at real files: once at plan time from
agent-declared globs, then continuously from a bare integer, `[worktree] concurrency`. Real files
are consulted only at the landing, after the concurrency is already spent.

## Observed by hand, 2026-09-04

The record graph reported basicly-ncday7, basicly-glosgv, basicly-qwqd35 and basicly-2no50w as
four independently ready siblings. Reading the four bead bodies showed basicly-glosgv edits
`board_wall.STATES` and the per-state CSS block, which is the exact structure basicly-ncday7 has to
extend. A human dropped glosgv and paired qwqd35 instead. The system offered no signal.
`loop preflight` did print `contend: no append-only path declared`, which is the advisory half.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/supervise.py`
- `src/basicly/contention.py`
- `tests/test_supervise.py`

## Earlier acceptance text (the acceptance field is authoritative)

- When the supervisor selects lanes for a pass, then it refuses or serialises a pair whose declared
  scopes collide, rather than admitting both on the concurrency integer alone.
- `loop preflight` names each colliding pair in the selected set before the pass starts.

## Trigger

When two ready lanes each measure a module's size-ratchet headroom correctly at plan time, I want the engine to reserve that headroom at dispatch, so I can stop the lane that lands second bouncing on room the first lane already spent.

## Context

The size ratchets are a **shared, unreserved, whole-tree budget**. Two lanes can each measure
headroom correctly, each pass their own gates, and whichever lands second bounces - because the
first spent the room in between. Neither graph models that contention, so the dependency graph
calls the lanes independent and they are not.

This is the failure the graph research names as false parallelism: nodes declared independent
that contend on a resource. See basicly-hnnmk9.9 for the inventory and basicly-zq9i2m.3 for the
file-scope half of the same gap.

## Measured, 2026-09-04, not hypothetical

`basicly-85cadb` measured its headroom correctly when it was written, and wrote the numbers into
its own `basicly.d` fragment: "`merge.py` had **0** tokens of module-size headroom, `checkout.py`
**15**, `supervise.py` **456** with **0.0** points of comment-density headroom, and
`tests/test_supervise.py` **488**."

The same fragment then declared: "`supervise.py` +296 fits inside its 456 and is not declared."

That lane sat unlanded. `basicly-ncday7` and `basicly-tjhjmk` then landed into the same two
modules and spent the room. When 85cadb was finally rebased its deltas were all stale and three
modules refused it: `merge.py` +62, `supervise.py` +297, `tests/test_supervise.py` +409. The
fragment's own sentence predicted the exact failure, and being right did not help, because the
measurement had no reservation behind it.

`merge.py` now reads `18746/18746 tokens (0 left)`. The next edit to it bounces, and nothing
tells the next lane that until it tries.

## What a reservation would do

A lane declares `## Scope` globs already, and `decompose` already compiles those into `blocks`
edges. The missing step is that a lane's declared scope should also **claim** the headroom of the
modules it names, at dispatch, so that:

- `loop preflight` refuses or serialises a second lane whose scope claims headroom already held.
- The claim is released when the lane lands or is killed, like the worktree binding.
- A lane rebasing onto a base that moved re-reads its claim rather than its stale measurement.

## Open questions a design must answer

- Where the claim lives. The worktree session record and the `basicly.d` fragment are both
  candidates; the fragment is committed and the session record is not.
- What is claimed. Whole-module headroom is coarse and would serialise more than necessary; the
  lane's own forecast delta is finer but is exactly the number lanes get wrong.
- Whether a stale claim is refused or merely reported. `contend:` is advisory today and was
  ignored - see basicly-hnnmk9.9, where 162 of 184 scope violations landed anyway.
- Whether this belongs to the ratchets or to the scheduler. Putting it in the ratchets makes
  every consumer repo pay for it; putting it in `supervise` keeps it to supervised passes.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/supervise.py`
- `src/basicly/contention.py`
- `src/basicly/decompose.py`
- `docs/architecture/architecture.md`

## Earlier acceptance text (the acceptance field is authoritative)

- When two ready lanes declare scopes whose modules have insufficient combined headroom, then
  `loop preflight` names the pair before the pass starts.
- When a lane lands, then the headroom it claimed is released.

## Trigger

When an agent dispatches a lane with `basicly loop run`, I want that dispatch to carry the same stall watchdog and dispatch bounds a supervised dispatch carries, so I can flag a stalled lane for a human rather than relying on the wall clock alone.

## Context

Owner, 2026-09-06: *"lanes should not be killed if they are doing work. lanes must be inspected to determine if they hang, and conditions to kill them must be fulfilled. for example a timeout which we set is a poor condition on its own, because an agent can sometime work for hours on a task."*

**The engine already agrees with that, in writing.** `runner.DispatchBounds` says of the wall clock: *"it is the one signal that carries no information about whether work is happening"*, and `runner.StallWatchdog` is documented as *"A flag, not a kill - and deliberately the earliest of the three bounds, so a human learns about a wedge while it is still theirs to intervene in... A slow-but-working run is never cut short here."*

The defect is that none of it reaches a lane started with `basicly loop run`.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. `basicly loop run <id> --work-type task` on any record.
2. Read what bounds the dispatch it starts.

Measured 2026-09-06:

```
$ rg -n "StallWatchdog\(" src/basicly
src/basicly/supervise.py:2670

$ rg -n "DispatchBounds\(" src/basicly
src/basicly/supervise.py:2688

$ rg -n "runner_timeout|bounds|watchdog" src/basicly/loop.py
loop.py:891    timeout=config.runner_timeout,
loop.py:911    timeout=config.runner_timeout,
loop.py:1138   timeout=config.runner_timeout,
```

Both informed bounds are constructed in exactly one file, and it is not the one the single-lane path uses. `loop.py` passes the wall clock and nothing else.

Expected: the same three bounds, in the same order, whichever verb started the lane.

## Not hidden - stated, three times, and never closed

`loop.py` already documents its own gap:

* `loop.py:188` - *"the spend gate, the watchdog and the stream meter that only exist there"*
* `loop.py:524` - *"names the session as its grant root but has no watchdog or stream"*
* `loop.py:684` - *"watchdog or stream meter of its own"*

So this is a known asymmetry carried as a comment rather than as a record. It is the same shape as `basicly-kqh9dj8`, where lane *visibility* was keyed on the supervisor and a `loop run` lane was invisible: a capability built for the multi-lane path, absent on the single-lane one, with the difference written down and never gated.

## What this costs, measured today

Every lane driven this session used `loop run`. Each therefore ran with the poor condition alone and no stall flag. Three of them died, and the cause each time was the *host* killing the shell they were children of - which is a fourth failure mode none of the three bounds covers, and which the operator could only diagnose by reading a git worktree by hand.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/loop.py`
- `src/basicly/runner.py`
- `src/basicly/supervise.py`
- `tests/test_loop_dispatch_bounds.py`
- `tests/test_runner.py`
- `changelog.d/<this-id>.fixed.md`

## Working Set

- `src/basicly/loop.py`
- `src/basicly/runner.py`
- `src/basicly/supervise.py`
- `tests/test_runner.py`

## Plan

- integrity: `L2`
- budget: `90000`
- depends on: none
- demonstration: start a lane with `loop run`, watch it idle past `stall_after`, and read the flag raised for a human while the lane is still alive - then let a working lane run past the same bound untouched.

payload.value: A `loop run` dispatch carries the same `StallWatchdog` and `DispatchBounds` a supervised dispatch carries, and a quiet lane whose event stream, commits or worktree dirtiness has changed is not stopped. When the stall bound is reached, the engine flags it for a human and does not terminate the lane, and the wall clock stays the backstop rather than the first bound reached. A test asserts that the bounds a `loop run` dispatch receives equal the bounds a supervised dispatch receives, and a lane that dies because its parent process was killed is recorded as such.

## Trigger

When a hand-built fixture encodes the format its author believes in rather than the format itself, I want `test-discipline` to require a test that drives a live capture where one exists in the tree, so I can catch a parser defect a hand-built fixture cannot see.

## Context

Session 2026-08-14, `basicly-ejdm.2`. Nine unit tests over hand-built transcript turns all passed
against a pairing rule that was **wrong on every real transcript**. The demonstration caught it,
not the suite.

The rule paired a turn's tokens against the immediately preceding line. A real claude transcript
forwards the tool result as a `user` event carrying no usage, which sits between the call and the
turn that pays for the answer:

```text
assistant  tokens= 26234 tools=[Agent]   <- the call
user       tokens=     0 tools=[]        <- the forwarded result, no usage
assistant  tokens=     0 tools=[]
assistant  tokens= 26635 tools=[]        <- the turn that pays for the answer
```

So the rule reported a real captured lane as **100% unattributed** - a confident figure measuring
nothing. Every hand-built fixture had an assistant turn adjacent to its predecessor, because that
is the shape a person writes when they are thinking about the rule rather than the format.

## Why the existing guidance did not catch it

`test-discipline` covers isolation, order-independence and asserting on observable behaviour. All
nine tests satisfied every one of those and were still blind, because the defect was in the
**shape of the input**, not in the shape of the test.

The repo already had the evidence: `tests/test_runner_subagent_stream.py` holds a stream captured
from a live Claude Code 2.1.226 dispatch, with a comment saying every field is verbatim from that
capture. Driving it took one scratch script.

## Proposed change, for a human to apply

Add one rule to `test-discipline`: **where a live capture of the format exists in the tree, at
least one test must drive it.** A hand-built fixture encodes what the author believes the format
is, and the interesting defects are in the difference between that and what the format does.

The related rule this repo already learned from the other direction - "a dependency's error text
must be observed, not composed" (an invented fixture made a retry path dead code through two
fixes) - is the same finding for error strings. This generalises it to formats.

D25 forbids an agent amending the catalog, so this is filed rather than applied.

payload.name: requirements
payload.value: `test-discipline` states that where a live capture of a format exists in the tree, at least one test must drive it. A hand-built fixture alone is not sufficient evidence that a parser is right.

## Trigger

When the committed usage ledger ages far behind the unpromoted spool, I want a scheduled promotion and a gate that fails on staleness, so I can stop the never-used surface list from being wrong.

## Context

`docs/requirements/work-tracker.md` §3.0 reasons about which `br` surfaces are used from the
committed ledger `.basicly/ledger/tracker-usage.jsonl`. That file was last written 2026-07-30
(`dc094ad`) and holds **1,568 invocations**. The unpromoted spool
`.basicly/usage/tracker-usage.jsonl` holds **91,891** - the committed evidence is 58x
under-sampled.

The consequence is the exact failure §3.0 lines 167-171 warns about, recurring: "a never-used
entry is the only finding in this report that a measurement error can fabricate". **Fifteen
surfaces the committed ledger records as never used are in fact in use**: `where` (171), `init`
(28), `dep tree` (14), `dep cycles` (10), `stats` (9), `schema` (4), `dep` (5), `gate` (3),
`label list` (2), `version` (2), `delete` (1), `capabilities` (1), `robot-docs guide` (1),
`comments` (4), `label` (1).

Distinct real surfaces: **17 of 87 committed, 31 of 87 in the spool.** The read:write ratio the
doc cites as 3.4:1 is **24.3:1** in the spool, and the top surface is `show` at 50,714 calls
(55%), not `comments list`.

`basicly-vkh0.8` was supposed to have closed this class by stopping a worktree teardown
discarding recorded usage. It did - but the **promotion** step never ran again, so the
committed artifact silently aged into being wrong while the gate that would notice does not
exist.

Related and worth checking in the same unit: `show` at 55% of 91,891 calls is far above the
read amplification `basicly-tcmy.15` describes, so the spool may be recording a diagnostic
loop rather than real load. Attribute it before citing it.

## Proposed check

Promotion runs on a schedule the repo enforces rather than by hand, and a gate fails when the
committed ledger's newest entry is older than the spool's by more than a declared window. A
test asserts the gate fires on a stale committed ledger against a fresh spool.

payload.name: requirements
payload.value: Promotion of the usage spool into the committed ledger shall run on a schedule the repository enforces, not by hand. A gate shall fail when the committed ledger's newest entry is older than the spool's newest entry by more than a declared window.

payload.name: acceptance_criteria
payload.value:
- [ ] When the committed ledger's newest entry is older than the spool's by more than the declared window, the gate shall fail and name the staleness.
- [ ] A test shall assert the gate fires on a stale committed ledger compared against a fresh spool.
- [ ] Given a scheduled promotion runs, the committed ledger shall carry the spool's entries without a manual step.

## Trigger

When the working-set ceiling test resizes every historical lane from today's tree instead of its recorded occupancy, I want the ceiling derived from the measured `context_tokens` field where one exists, so I can stop the ceiling drifting upward whenever the repo grows.

## Context

DEFAULT_WORKING_SET_MAX is 256000 and the dispatch ledger advises 244286 from 50 samples labelled measured. The two instruments in this repo now disagree about the same constant and the ledger is the better measure by its own description: 'measured working set at the 0.9 quantile - the occupancy a finished lane really reported, not the scope-times-seed proxy this band was derived from twice before the field existed'.

The constant was raised 248000 -> 256000 in 53ed12c under basicly-wxr3 because tests/test_decompose.py demanded it. That test sizes every historical lane by re-reading its declared ## Scope from today's tree, so merely adding files pushed basicly-u2hl.14 from 246732 to 249216 and across the old ceiling. Its own docstring concedes 'it drifts as the scoped files grow' and names RunRecord.context_tokens as what should replace it.

So the ceiling is now derived from a proxy that ratchets upward with repo size while the field that measures the real quantity says it should come down. Every future file addition repeats this.

Acceptance: the ceiling test sizes lanes from the recorded occupancy field where one exists, falling back to the scope proxy only for records predating it; DEFAULT_WORKING_SET_MAX is re-derived on that basis; adding an unrelated file to the tree no longer moves it. Related: basicly-efw2 (one field serving two masters), basicly-z2wi, basicly-ipx2.

## MERGED FROM basicly-o486 (2026-08-13)

Same defect stated twice: the working-set ceiling is denominated in a scope-read proxy while
`RunRecord.context_tokens` now measures the real quantity. o486's contribution, carried here:

**The maximum was derived from its own estimator's output.** `config.py:455-466` records that
132000 was licensed by one lane completing at that declared size - so no field measured the
quantity the band is denominated in. o486 carried a 7-record table with a forecast:occupancy
ratio spread of **3.16x to 7.21x**.

o486 also recorded itself as blocked on `basicly-23ep`, which has been **closed** for over a
week - it was silently unblocked and nobody noticed, which is its own argument for the
dependency hygiene this audit found.

payload.name: requirements
payload.value: The ceiling test shall size a lane from its recorded occupancy field (`RunRecord.context_tokens`) where one exists, and shall fall back to the scope-read proxy only for records that predate it. `DEFAULT_WORKING_SET_MAX` shall be re-derived on that basis, so adding an unrelated file to the tree no longer moves it.

payload.name: acceptance_criteria
payload.value:
- [ ] Given a run record with `context_tokens` set, the ceiling test shall size that lane from `context_tokens`, not the scope-read proxy.
- [ ] Given a run record with no `context_tokens`, the test shall fall back to the scope-read proxy.
- [ ] When an unrelated file is added to the tree, the computed ceiling shall not change.
- [ ] `DEFAULT_WORKING_SET_MAX` shall be re-derived on the occupancy basis.

## Trigger

When `hooks-check` compares only the hooks already in the current spec list, missing anything build would add or remove, I want the check to compare the full rendered pre-commit config against the file on disk, so I can catch an added, removed or reordered hook the current comparison misses.

They survived only because that repo duplicates the gate in its own .scripts/git-hooks/pre-commit.py, which is luck and not something the next consumer has. The fix the reporter proposes is the right class - notice that a hook built before is no longer in the output - and there is a cheaper form already proved here: render_precommit_config over the current text diverges from the file on disk while hooks-check passes, so checking the render against the file catches adds, removes and reorders in one comparison. ## Trigger

When the `wsl` skill lists its technology but does not project into `.claude/skills/` on a WSL2 checkout, I want the detector's behaviour on this checkout diagnosed and fixed if broken, so I can stop WSL-specific instructions from being silently withheld on the platform they target.

## Context

`.basicly/core/skills/wsl/skill.yaml` declares `technologies: [wsl]`. On a WSL2 checkout
(Linux 6.6.87.2-microsoft-standard-WSL2) the skill is present in the catalog and absent from
`.claude/skills/`, so the detector did not fire.

Either the detector keys on something not present here, or WSL detection is broken. If it is
broken, every WSL-specific instruction the catalog carries is silently withheld on exactly
the platform it was written for.

Not yet diagnosed - the observation is the diff between `.basicly/core/skills/` and
`.claude/skills/`, which lists `wsl` alongside `tool-starship`, `tool-tmux`, `tool-wezterm`
and `tool-zsh` whose technologies genuinely are absent here.

## Proposed check

Run the detector directly on this checkout and report what it returns for `wsl`. If it is a
defect, a test asserts detection on a tree carrying the marker the detector should key on.

payload.name: requirements
payload.value: Running the detector directly on this checkout shall report what it returns for `wsl`. If detection is broken, a test shall assert detection succeeds on a tree carrying the marker the detector should key on.

payload.name: acceptance_criteria
payload.value:
- [ ] Given this WSL2 checkout, running the detector for `wsl` shall report a pass or fail result and the marker it checked.
- [ ] If the detector is broken, a test shall assert it detects `wsl` on a tree carrying the correct marker.
- [ ] If the detector is not broken, the record shall state which other condition withheld the `wsl` skill here.

## Trigger

When `basicly policy scaffold` still emits the built-in Definition-of-Ready headings while `basicly policy dor` judges a record against the configured section rules, I want the scaffold to read the same configuration, so I can stop the scaffold's own output failing the gate it exists to satisfy.

## The defect

basicly-vkh0.45 moved the per-work-type required sections into `[policy.type_sections]` in `basicly.toml`. It moved the **reader** that judges a record, not the **writer** that scaffolds one.

`policy.compose_body` and `policy.scaffold_body` hold no repository root, so they cannot reach the configuration. Their two callers — `decompose._child_body` and `cli._cmd_policy_scaffold` — were outside that record's scope fence, and the lane deliberately declined to add a `repo_root` parameter nothing passed.

The result is a split brain. A repository that declares `bug = ["## Repro Steps"]` gets a Definition-of-Ready that demands that heading, and a `basicly policy scaffold --type bug` that emits the built-in one instead. The scaffold's own output then fails the gate the scaffold exists to satisfy, and the failure message points the user back at the same command.

A second, smaller half: `policy._SECTION_HINTS` is keyed on the two built-in headings, so a configured heading scaffolds the generic `TODO: fill this in.` placeholder rather than a tailored hint.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. In `basicly.toml`, set `[policy.type_sections]` `bug = ["## Repro Steps", "## Impact"]`.
2. `uv run basicly policy scaffold --type bug` — read the headings it emits.
3. Create a record from exactly that scaffold output.
4. `uv run basicly policy dor <id>` on it.

Observed: step 2 emits the built-in headings. Step 4 reports NOT READY, missing the two configured ones, and advises running the command from step 2.
Expected: the scaffold emits the headings the configured rule requires, so its output passes Definition-of-Ready by construction.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/policy.py`
- `src/basicly/decompose.py`
- `src/basicly/cli.py`
- `tests/test_policy.py`

## Earlier acceptance text (the acceptance field is authoritative)

Given a repository that declares `[policy.type_sections]`, when `basicly policy scaffold --type <t>` runs, then it emits exactly the headings that work type's configured rule requires.
Given the scaffold's own output, when it is used as a record body unchanged, then `basicly policy dor` reports the section requirement satisfied, so the two halves cannot disagree.
Given a decomposed child body from `decompose._child_body`, then it is built from the same configured set.
Given a configured heading with no entry in the section hints, then the placeholder names the heading rather than printing a bare generic line.
Given no configuration, then the built-in set is scaffolded exactly as today.
Demonstrated by: uv run pytest tests/test_policy.py tests/test_decompose.py -k scaffold -q

payload.name: requirements
payload.value: `policy.scaffold_body` and `decompose._child_body` shall read `[policy.type_sections]` from the repository root, the same source `policy.dor` reads. A configured heading with no entry in `_SECTION_HINTS` shall scaffold a placeholder naming the heading, not a bare generic line.

payload.name: acceptance_criteria
payload.value:
- [ ] Given `[policy.type_sections]` declares headings for a work type, `basicly policy scaffold` shall emit exactly those headings for that type.
- [ ] Given the scaffold's own output used as a record body, `basicly policy dor` shall report the section requirement satisfied.
- [ ] Given a decomposed child body from `decompose._child_body`, it shall be built from the same configured set.
- [ ] Given a configured heading with no entry in the section hints, the placeholder shall name the heading rather than a bare generic line.
- [ ] Given no configuration, the built-in set shall scaffold exactly as today.

## Trigger

When a prefix remap on import rewrites only the id field and leaves the same prefix inside title, description, notes, close_reason and nested dependency edges, I want the migration runbook to name every touched field and the safe rewrite method, so I can stop an import from silently corrupting prose.

## Context

A consumer whose source prefix carries a hyphen must rewrite it before importing, and nothing tells them the prefix appears outside the id field. In the burndown-chart export it appeared in id, title, description, notes and close_reason, and dependency edges are nested rather than top level. Rewriting only record[id] yields a ledger that imports clean and whose prose points at ids that do not exist - nothing fails, which is what makes it dangerous. The reporter supplied a verified shape: match the prefix WITH its trailing hyphen, never the bare prefix, because the repo name is the prefix and a bare match corrupts prose; recurse through dicts and lists so nested edges are caught; enumerate the touched fields by scanning before rewriting rather than assuming; accept on 702 of 702 matching RECORD_ID_PATTERN and 702 unique. The import refusal now names the constraint (basicly-iehbmvu), so a consumer meets the one-way door in time; this is the other half - what to do once they have met it.

payload.name: requirements
payload.value: The migration runbook shall instruct matching the prefix with its trailing hyphen, never the bare prefix, across id, title, description, notes, close_reason and nested dependency edges. The runbook shall instruct scanning to enumerate touched fields before rewriting, rather than assuming a fixed field list.

payload.name: acceptance_criteria
payload.value:
- [ ] The migration runbook shall instruct matching the prefix WITH its trailing hyphen, never the bare prefix.
- [ ] The migration runbook shall instruct recursing through dicts and lists so nested dependency edges are rewritten.
- [ ] The migration runbook shall instruct scanning to enumerate touched fields before rewriting rather than assuming a fixed list.
- [ ] A command shall confirm every match of the record id pattern is rewritten and unique after migration, mirroring the reporter's verified count.

## Trigger

When a command uses `rg -r` as if it means recursive, I want a hook that refuses the command, so I can stop it from mangling output before it runs.

## Context

`rg -r` is `--replace`, not `--recursive`. It has already silently mangled a probe's output
in this repo, and it is recorded nowhere: a search for `rg -r` and `--replace` across
`.basicly/`, `docs/` and `.claude/` returns zero hits. Positive control: the same search
shape for `word.split` returns 3 files, so the probe discriminates.

`tool-ripgrep` does not carry it either, and that is the point - every footgun this repo has
actually captured was captured as an always-on fragment plus a hook, never as a tool-* card:

- zsh not word-splitting unquoted vars - `non-interactive-shell.fragment.yaml` plus
  `.basicly/core/hooks/unsplit-loop-guard.py`
- `shlex.split` mangling Windows paths - `python/skill.yaml` plus
  `.basicly/core/hooks/shell_tokens.py`

A `user`-invoked tool card cannot be the carrier: nothing routes to it, which is why
`catalog_lint.py:304-308` refuses to let it carry a description at all.

## Proposed check

A hook that refuses `rg -r` used as if it meant recursive, following `unsplit-loop-guard.py`,
with a test for the false positive: a genuine `--replace` use must pass.

payload.name: requirements
payload.value: The hook shall detect a `rg -r` invocation used with recursive intent and refuse it, naming the correct flag. A genuine `--replace` use shall still pass. The check shall be an always-on hook, following `unsplit-loop-guard.py`, not a `tool-*` skill card.

payload.name: acceptance_criteria
payload.value:
- [ ] When a shell command contains `rg -r` used without a replacement argument, the hook shall refuse it and name `--replace`.
- [ ] When a shell command contains a genuine `rg -r` use with a pattern and a replacement argument, the hook shall allow it.
- [ ] A test asserts both the refusal and the false-positive pass.
- [ ] `rg -r` and `--replace` stay absent from `.basicly/core/`, `docs/` and `.claude/` outside the new hook and its test.

## Trigger

When `src/basicly/repair_brief.py` and the `repair-in-place` skill both tell an agent how to repair in place and can drift apart, I want one source of truth between them, so I can trust the brief an implementer reads.

## Context

`src/basicly/repair_brief.py` (267 lines) composes the prompt the engine hands a repair

One source of truth. Either the brief is generated from the skill body or the skill is
reduced to what the brief cannot carry, with a test asserting the two cannot diverge.

- [ ] A test fails when the shared text is edited in only one of the two places.

## Trigger

When the Windows quality gate fails about one run in three on the same test while ubuntu and macos pass, I want the failing run's pytest and runner output kept as artefacts, so I can diagnose the cause instead of losing the logs to expiry.

## Measured
`gh run list --workflow=quality-gates.yml --limit 40`, read 2026-09-12:

- 39 completed runs
- 13 failures
- **33 percent**, one run in three

Every failure is the same job and the same step: `Quality gates on windows-latest`, in `Run full checks (ruff, format, pyright, bandit, pytest)`. In each of those runs the ubuntu and macos jobs passed. The failures span 2026-09-05 to 2026-09-12, so this is not a recent regression.

## The one instance still in the logs
Run 34716451926 on 4534b1e2:

```
assert outcome.result.returncode == 0, outcome.detail
AssertionError: runner exited 1
tests/test_integration_loop.py::test_a_supervisor_pass_runs_two_agent_processes_and_lands_both
```

A standin runner subprocess exited 1 under `D:/a/basicly/basicly/.venv/Scripts/python.exe`. The whole diff of that commit was a version string, a changelog fragment and the ledger, with zero files under `src/` or `tests/`, so the commit cannot be causal.

Logs for the older failures have expired, so I cannot say whether all thirteen are this test. That is the first thing to find out.

## Why it matters
A gate that fails a third of the time is not a gate. It trains everyone to re-run rather than read, and a real windows regression would arrive looking exactly like the noise. The repository ships to windows, linux and macos, and only one of the three is unreliable in CI.

## First step
Keep the failing artefacts. The step should upload the pytest output and the runner stdout and stderr on failure, so the next occurrence is diagnosable instead of expired. Then decide from three or four captured instances whether it is one test or several.

## Owner note
The owner said the windows gate "fails often" before this was measured. It does.

## Scope
- `.github/workflows/quality-gates.yml`
- `tests/test_integration_loop.py`

payload.name: requirements
payload.value: The Windows quality-gates job shall upload the pytest output and the runner stdout and stderr as artefacts on failure. After three or four captured failures, the record shall state whether they are one test or several. No change to `tests/test_integration_loop.py` behaviour is required until the captured evidence says what to fix.

payload.name: acceptance_criteria
payload.value:
- [ ] When the `Quality gates on windows-latest` job fails, the workflow shall upload the pytest output and the runner stdout and stderr as an artefact.
- [ ] The next three or four Windows CI failures are captured and read, not expired.
- [ ] The record states whether the captured failures are the same test (`test_a_supervisor_pass_runs_two_agent_processes_and_lands_both`) or a mix.
- [ ] The failure rate is re-measured with `gh run list --workflow=quality-gates.yml` after the artefact-capture change lands.

## Trigger

When a fresh install has no rank-1 floor declared, I want `catalog lint` to scaffold or treat the missing floor as advisory, so I can commit right after install without a hand edit.

## Context

Reported by a consumer canary and reproduced here: basicly catalog lint exits 1 immediately after a clean install with no rank-1 floor declared, and catalog-lint is a pre-commit hook, so the out-of-box state is a repo that fails its own gate and needs a hand edit before any commit. The refusal-to-guess design is right but the first-run experience is not. Two candidate fixes: scaffold the measured floor into basicly.toml at install time, or make the missing-floor case advisory on first run the way the unresolvable pin case was made advisory. A canary measured the identical 41/46 = 89.1% rate we do, which suggests the shipped catalog dominates and a scaffolded default would be stable.

payload.name: requirements
payload.value: `basicly install` shall write a measured rank-1 floor into `basicly.toml` at install time, or `catalog lint` shall treat a missing floor as advisory on first run. The scaffolded default shall come from the shipped catalog's measured rate, not an arbitrary number. A consumer shall not be blocked from committing over a number they cannot move.

payload.name: acceptance_criteria
payload.value:
- [ ] When `basicly install` runs with no `rank1_floor` declared, it writes a scaffolded floor or marks the check advisory.
- [ ] `basicly catalog lint` exits 0 right after a clean install with no hand edit to `basicly.toml`.
- [ ] The scaffolded floor value matches the measured rank-1 rate of the shipped catalog (41/46 = 89.1%).
- [ ] A consumer running the rank-1 gate is not blocked from its first commit by a number that is not theirs to move.

## Trigger

When `skills-check` tells a consumer to move an unmanaged skill into `.basicly/core/skills/`, a path that `install` overwrites wholesale, I want a durable overlay location for a consumer's own skill, so I can keep it across an upgrade.

## Context

skills-check flags an unmanaged skill and tells the consumer to move it into .basicly/core/skills/<slug>/skill.yaml, but .basicly/core is managed and install replaces it wholesale, so anything put there is destroyed on the next upgrade. An install or upgrade shall not delete a skill placed in the overlay location.

- [ ] The config paths schema in `src/basicly/config.py` accepts an `overlay_skills` key.
- [ ] `basicly install` does not delete a file under the overlay skills path.
- [ ] `skills-check`'s message for an unmanaged skill names the overlay path, not `.basicly/core/skills/`.
- [ ] A test places a skill in the overlay path, runs install, and asserts the skill still exists afterward.
